questions.concept: A conscious adult with complete foreign-body airway obstruction (unable to speak, cough or breathe) is treated with abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) until the object clears or the victim becomes unconscious, at which point CPR is started. Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper and are discouraged, and an emergency surgical airway is a last resort, not first-line.
questions.reference: AHA Guidelines for CPR & ECC 2020 — Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is choking on a foreign body but is still conscious. The correct sequence of manoeuvres is:
options: Alternating 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts
Blind finger sweeps to remove the object
Heimlich manoeuvre performed in the supine position
questions.concept: In a choking conscious infant, alternate 5 back blows (between the scapulae, head-down) with 5 chest thrusts, repeating until relief or unconsciousness. Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) are contraindicated in infants because the large, unprotected liver makes visceral injury likely. Blind finger sweeps are avoided; an object is removed only if it is directly visible.
questions.reference: AHA Guidelines for CPR & ECC 2020 — Infant Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: During neonatal resuscitation, the recommended chest compression-to-ventilation ratio is:
questions.concept: Neonatal resuscitation uses a 3:1 compression-to-ventilation ratio, delivering about 90 compressions and 30 breaths (120 events) per minute, because neonatal arrest is almost always asphyxial and effective ventilation is the priority. 30:2 and 15:2 are paediatric/adult ratios, and 5:1 is an obsolete ratio no longer used in any age group.
questions.reference: AHA/AAP Neonatal Resuscitation Program Guidelines 2020

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks gestation suffers cardiac arrest. Which modification to standard resuscitation is appropriate?
options: Manual left uterine displacement, and perimortem caesarean if no ROSC by ~4 minutes (aim to deliver by 5 minutes)
Place the patient fully prone during compressions
Withhold defibrillation because it is unsafe in pregnancy
Reduce compression depth in the third trimester
questions.concept: Maternal cardiac-arrest modifications include continuous manual left uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus, and preparing for perimortem caesarean delivery if there is no ROSC by about 4 minutes, aiming for delivery by 5 minutes, which improves both maternal and fetal outcomes. Compression depth is standard, the patient is not placed prone, and defibrillation is safe in pregnancy.
questions.reference: AHA Guidelines for CPR & ECC 2020 — Cardiac Arrest in Pregnancy

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Which of the following local anaesthetics has an ESTER linkage?
questions.concept: Local anaesthetics are classified by their intermediate linkage. Esters include procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, cocaine and benzocaine (a useful mnemonic is that esters have only one letter 'i' in the drug name before -caine). Amides include lignocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine and mepivacaine (they carry two 'i's). This matters clinically: esters are hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase and their PABA metabolite causes true allergy, whereas amides are metabolised in the liver and rarely cause allergy.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Amide local anaesthetics such as lignocaine and bupivacaine are primarily metabolised by:
questions.concept: Amide local anaesthetics undergo hepatic metabolism by cytochrome P450 microsomal enzymes and amidases, so their clearance is markedly reduced in severe hepatic disease, low hepatic blood flow (e.g. heart failure, beta-blockade) or the neonate, raising the risk of toxicity. This contrasts with ester agents, which are rapidly hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase. Only a negligible fraction is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so renal excretion of parent drug is not the main route.
questions.reference: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, 5th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Ester local anaesthetics are rapidly broken down in the plasma by:
questions.concept: Ester local anaesthetics are hydrolysed by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase, giving them a very short plasma half-life (procaine ~1 minute). A key by-product is para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), which accounts for the allergic potential of esters. Patients with atypical or deficient plasma cholinesterase (as also affects suxamethonium) clear ester agents slowly and are at higher risk of systemic toxicity. Amides, by contrast, are metabolised in the liver, not by plasma cholinesterase.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The property of a local anaesthetic that primarily determines its SPEED OF ONSET is its:
questions.concept: Onset depends chiefly on pKa, which sets the proportion of drug in the un-ionized (lipid-soluble) form at physiological pH. Agents with a pKa closer to 7.4 (e.g. lignocaine pKa ~7.7–7.9) have a larger un-ionized fraction, cross the nerve membrane faster and act quicker than those with a higher pKa (bupivacaine ~8.1). By convention lipid solubility governs potency and protein binding governs duration. Chloroprocaine is the classic exception: despite a high pKa it acts fast because it is used in high concentration.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The longer duration of action of bupivacaine compared with lignocaine is best explained by its greater:
questions.concept: Duration of action correlates most closely with protein binding. Bupivacaine is about 95% protein-bound versus roughly 65% for lignocaine; the drug bound at the sodium-channel receptor dissociates slowly, so the block lasts longer. A higher pKa would if anything slow onset, not prolong action, and greater water solubility or faster metabolism would shorten duration. Adding a vasoconstrictor further prolongs a block by slowing systemic absorption from the injection site.
questions.reference: Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed — Pharmacology of Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The POTENCY of a local anaesthetic correlates best with its:
questions.concept: Potency parallels lipid solubility: highly lipid-soluble agents (bupivacaine, tetracaine, etidocaine) penetrate the lipid nerve membrane readily and are effective at low concentrations, hence highly potent. In the standard framework pKa determines onset and protein binding determines duration, so those are not the primary correlates of potency. Molecular weight influences diffusion but is not the key determinant of intrinsic potency among clinical agents.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The maximum safe dose of PLAIN lignocaine (without adrenaline) for infiltration in an adult is approximately:
questions.concept: Plain lignocaine has a maximum dose of about 3 mg/kg (some texts quote up to 4.5 mg/kg), corresponding to roughly 200–300 mg in an average adult. Adding adrenaline slows absorption and raises the ceiling to about 7 mg/kg (up to ~500 mg). Exceeding these limits risks local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST). The 7 mg/kg figure specifically refers to the adrenaline-containing solution, not plain lignocaine.
questions.reference: Ajay Yadav, Short Textbook of Anaesthesia, 7th ed — Local Anaesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The generally accepted maximum safe dose of bupivacaine in an adult is approximately:
questions.concept: The maximum dose of bupivacaine is about 2 mg/kg (roughly 150 mg in an adult), and unlike lignocaine, adding adrenaline increases this ceiling only marginally because bupivacaine's absorption is less adrenaline-dependent. The therapeutic margin is narrow because bupivacaine is intensely cardiotoxic, so accidental overdose or intravascular injection can cause refractory cardiac arrest. This is why dosing discipline and aspiration before injection are emphasised.
questions.reference: Lee's Synopsis of Anaesthesia, 13th ed — Local Anaesthetic Agents

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Adrenaline is commonly added to a local anaesthetic solution mainly to:
options: Increase the pH and hasten onset
Lower the pKa of the drug
Provide additional analgesia by a central action
Cause local vasoconstriction, prolonging the block and reducing systemic absorption
questions.concept: Adrenaline produces local vasoconstriction, which slows systemic absorption of the local anaesthetic. This prolongs the duration of the block, lowers the peak plasma concentration (reducing systemic toxicity), permits use of a larger total dose and reduces surgical bleeding in the field. A sudden tachycardia after injection can also act as an early marker of accidental intravascular placement. It does not raise pH, alter pKa, or provide any central analgesic effect.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Local Anesthetics (Additives)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Adrenaline-containing local anaesthetic must be AVOIDED when performing a block of the:
options: Fingers, toes, penis and ear (end-artery territories)
questions.concept: Structures supplied by end arteries with little collateral flow—digits, penis, ear pinna and the tip of the nose—must not receive adrenaline-containing solutions, because intense vasoconstriction can cause ischaemia and gangrene. Well-vascularised regions such as the scalp, abdominal wall and limb tolerate adrenaline. Adrenaline is also avoided in intravenous regional anaesthesia. This is a classic and frequently tested safety rule in regional anaesthesia.
questions.reference: Ajay Yadav, Short Textbook of Anaesthesia, 7th ed — Local Anaesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Local anaesthetics produce conduction block mainly by:
options: Blocking voltage-gated sodium channels from the intracellular side, preferentially in the open/inactivated state
Blocking voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal
questions.concept: Local anaesthetics bind the alpha-subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel from its inner (cytoplasmic) aspect, preventing the sodium influx that generates and propagates the action potential. They act preferentially on channels in the open and inactivated states (state-dependent block). The drug must first cross the membrane in its un-ionized form and then act as the ionized cation inside the axon. They do not work through potassium channels, GABA receptors, or calcium channels as the primary mechanism.
questions.reference: Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed — Pharmacology of Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The phenomenon in which local anaesthetic block becomes more intense as the frequency of nerve firing increases is termed:
questions.concept: Local anaesthetics bind preferentially to sodium channels that are open or inactivated; the more frequently a nerve fires, the more often channels cycle into these states and the more drug gains access, deepening the block—this is use-dependent or phasic block. It underlies bupivacaine's cardiotoxicity, since the rapidly depolarising myocardium is especially vulnerable. Tachyphylaxis is a fall in effect with repeated dosing, wind-up is a spinal pain-facilitation phenomenon, and differential block refers to selective loss of fibre modalities.
questions.reference: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, 5th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: During the onset of spinal or epidural anaesthesia, which function is typically blocked FIRST?
questions.concept: The classic sequence of differential nerve block is: autonomic (small myelinated B fibres) first, then pain and temperature (Adelta and unmyelinated C fibres), then touch and pressure, and finally motor function (large Aalpha fibres); recovery occurs in the reverse order. Smaller and more heavily myelinated fibres are blocked at lower drug concentrations. Clinically this is why the sympathetic block level in spinal anaesthesia lies about two segments above the sensory level, and motor block is last to appear and first to recover.
questions.reference: Ajay Yadav, Short Textbook of Anaesthesia, 7th ed — Physiology of Nerve Block

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: In the management of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), the recommended initial bolus of 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is:
questions.concept: The ASRA protocol for LAST recommends a 20% lipid emulsion bolus of 1.5 mL/kg (lean body weight) over about 1 minute, followed by an infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min, with the bolus repeated for persistent collapse and a maximum of roughly 10–12 mL/kg. Lipid emulsion acts as a 'lipid sink' that sequesters lipophilic drug (especially bupivacaine). Alongside this: stop injecting, call for help, secure the airway, treat seizures with benzodiazepines, give small adrenaline doses (<1 mcg/kg) and avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel and beta-blockers.
questions.reference: ASRA Practice Advisory on Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (as cited in Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed)

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Bupivacaine is considered the most cardiotoxic of the common local anaesthetics primarily because it:
options: Is an ester hydrolysed to PABA
Binds cardiac sodium channels avidly and dissociates slowly ("fast-in, slow-out"), giving a low CC/CNS ratio
Is metabolised to o-toluidine, which oxidises haemoglobin
questions.concept: Bupivacaine enters cardiac sodium channels rapidly but dissociates very slowly during diastole ('fast-in, slow-out'), so it accumulates and provokes re-entrant ventricular arrhythmias and refractory cardiac arrest. Its cardiovascular collapse to CNS toxicity (CC/CNS) dose ratio is low, meaning cardiac collapse can occur with little warning after CNS signs. It is an amide (not an ester), is highly protein-bound, and does not form o-toluidine (that is prilocaine). The R-enantiomer is chiefly responsible, which is why levobupivacaine and ropivacaine are safer.
questions.reference: Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed — Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Which local anaesthetic is most classically associated with the development of methaemoglobinaemia?
questions.concept: Prilocaine is the amide most linked to methaemoglobinaemia because its metabolite o-toluidine oxidises haemoglobin iron from the ferrous (Fe2+) to the ferric (Fe3+) state. The effect is dose-related, typically after large doses (>600 mg). Benzocaine (an ester, often in topical sprays) is another important cause. Clinically the patient shows cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, chocolate-brown blood, and a characteristic saturation gap between pulse oximetry and arterial oxygen tension. This is why prilocaine is used cautiously, especially in neonates.
questions.reference: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, 5th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: The first-line treatment for symptomatic local-anaesthetic-induced methaemoglobinaemia is:
questions.concept: Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV is the treatment of choice. It is reduced by NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase to leucomethylene blue, which then reduces ferric methaemoglobin back to functional ferrous haemoglobin. An important caveat: in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency methylene blue is ineffective and may precipitate haemolysis, so alternatives such as ascorbic acid or exchange transfusion are used. Sodium nitrite actually induces methaemoglobin (used in cyanide poisoning), so it is contraindicated here.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: A patient given a benzocaine topical spray for awake fibreoptic intubation develops cyanosis, an SpO2 of 85% that does not improve with 100% oxygen, and chocolate-brown arterial blood. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Benzocaine topical spray is a well-known cause of acquired methaemoglobinaemia. The combination of cyanosis, a fixed low pulse-oximeter reading (SpO2 tends to plateau around 85% regardless of supplemental oxygen because metHb absorbs both oximeter wavelengths), oxygen-refractory desaturation and chocolate-brown blood is characteristic. Co-oximetry confirms an elevated methaemoglobin fraction. Management is to stop the agent, give oxygen and administer methylene blue. CO poisoning and PE do not give chocolate-brown blood, and anaphylaxis presents differently.
questions.reference: Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed — Adverse Effects of Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: True allergic reactions are more common with ester local anaesthetics because they are metabolised to:
questions.concept: Ester local anaesthetics are hydrolysed to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), a recognised allergen, so genuine hypersensitivity is more frequent with esters. True allergy to amides is rare; when it appears to occur it is often due to the preservative methylparaben, which is structurally similar to PABA. o-toluidine is the prilocaine metabolite causing methaemoglobinaemia, and monoethylglycinexylidide is a lignocaine metabolite—neither is the basis of ester allergy.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: In intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block), which agent is CONTRAINDICATED because of its cardiotoxicity?
questions.concept: Bupivacaine is contraindicated in intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block) because sudden release of the drug into the circulation on tourniquet deflation has caused fatal cardiac arrests. Preservative-free lignocaine (and prilocaine in some settings) is preferred. Safe practice includes reliable tourniquet inflation, keeping the cuff up for a minimum time (about 20–30 minutes) even if surgery finishes early, and cautious or cyclical deflation to limit the systemic bolus of drug.
questions.reference: Lee's Synopsis of Anaesthesia, 13th ed — Intravenous Regional Anaesthesia

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Which local anaesthetic has intrinsic vasoconstrictor activity (rather than causing vasodilatation)?
questions.concept: Cocaine is unique among local anaesthetics in producing vasoconstriction, which it achieves by blocking presynaptic reuptake of noradrenaline, potentiating sympathetic activity (also causing mydriasis). This makes it useful for topical anaesthesia of the vascular nasal mucosa in ENT surgery, but it carries risks of hypertension, tachyarrhythmias and myocardial ischaemia. Most other local anaesthetics cause vasodilatation, which is why adrenaline is co-administered; ropivacaine has only mild intrinsic vasoconstriction.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: EMLA cream is a eutectic mixture of which two agents?
questions.concept: EMLA (Eutectic Mixture of Local Anaesthetics) contains lignocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5%. Forming a eutectic mixture lowers the melting point so the actives exist as an oil at room temperature and can penetrate intact skin. It is applied under an occlusive dressing for about 45–60 minutes before venepuncture or minor skin procedures. Because it contains prilocaine, there is a risk of methaemoglobinaemia—particularly in neonates and infants—and it should not be used on mucous membranes or broken skin.
questions.reference: Ajay Yadav, Short Textbook of Anaesthesia, 7th ed — Local Anaesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Adding sodium bicarbonate to a local anaesthetic solution:
options: Prolongs the block by increasing protein binding
Hastens onset by increasing the un-ionized fraction of the drug
questions.concept: Alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate raises the solution's pH toward the drug's pKa, shifting the equilibrium toward the lipid-soluble, un-ionized base. More un-ionized drug crosses the nerve membrane, so onset is faster and injection is often less painful. This principle also explains why local anaesthetics work poorly in infected, acidic tissue where more drug stays ionized. Excess bicarbonate can cause the anaesthetic to precipitate, so only small amounts are added; it does not vasoconstrict.
questions.reference: Miller's Anesthesia, 9th ed — Local Anesthetic Additives

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: Compared with racemic bupivacaine, ropivacaine is best characterised as:
options: Having greater motor block at equipotent low doses
A pure S(-)-enantiomer that is less cardiotoxic and shows relatively more sensory than motor block
An ester agent metabolised by plasma cholinesterase
questions.concept: Ropivacaine is a pure S(-)-enantiomer (as is levobupivacaine), which reduces affinity for cardiac sodium channels and therefore lowers cardiotoxicity relative to racemic bupivacaine. It is slightly less potent, has mild intrinsic vasoconstrictor activity, and produces a useful sensory–motor differential (more sensory than motor block), making it popular for labour epidural analgesia. It is a long-acting amide (not an ester and not shorter than lignocaine) metabolised in the liver.
questions.reference: Stoelting's Pharmacology & Physiology in Anesthetic Practice, 5th ed — Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.stem: In an acidotic fetus, local anaesthetic given to the mother tends to ACCUMULATE in the fetal circulation mainly because of:
options: Reduced placental transfer of the drug
Rapid ester hydrolysis in fetal plasma
Ion trapping — the drug becomes ionized in acidic fetal plasma and cannot diffuse back across the placenta
questions.concept: Local anaesthetics are weak bases that cross the placenta in their un-ionized form. In an acidotic (distressed) fetus the lower fetal pH shifts more drug into the ionized state, which cannot readily diffuse back across the placenta, so it accumulates fetally—this is 'ion trapping' and predisposes to neonatal toxicity. Highly protein-bound agents such as bupivacaine cross less, while chloroprocaine is rapidly hydrolysed and is regarded as one of the safer agents in labour when speed of clearance matters.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Obstetric Anesthesia / Local Anesthetics

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The superficial (external) inguinal ring is a triangular deficiency in the aponeurosis of which muscle of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.concept: The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular gap in the external oblique aponeurosis, lying just above and lateral to the pubic tubercle; its margins (medial and lateral crura) are bridged by intercrural fibres. The deep inguinal ring, in contrast, lies in the fascia transversalis. Internal oblique and transversus form the roof and the conjoint tendon, not the ring itself.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Anterior Abdominal Wall & Inguinal Canal)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The deep (internal) inguinal ring, marking the entrance to the inguinal canal, is an opening in which layer of the abdominal wall?
questions.concept: The deep inguinal ring is an evagination of the fascia transversalis, situated about 1.25 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament and lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; it is the site through which an indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal. The superficial ring lies more medially in the external oblique aponeurosis, so the two rings do not overlie one another.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Inguinal Canal)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed throughout by the external oblique aponeurosis. In its lateral third, in front of the deep ring, it is additionally reinforced by which structure?
options: Fleshy fibres of the internal oblique
questions.concept: The anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis along the whole canal, reinforced laterally (in front of the deep ring) by the fleshy origin of the internal oblique. This puts a muscular reinforcement in front of the deep ring, while the conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially behind the superficial ring — so the two weak points (the rings) are each backed by a reinforcement on the opposite wall.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Inguinal Canal)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is strongest in its medial part, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Reason (R): The conjoint tendon reinforces the fascia transversalis in the medial part of the posterior wall. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is the fascia transversalis throughout, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis), formed from the internal oblique and transversus aponeuroses attaching to the pubic crest and pectineal line. This reinforcement lies exactly behind the superficial ring, protecting an otherwise weak point — so both statements are true and R correctly explains A. A direct hernia bulges through this wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Inguinal Canal)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis), which reinforces the medial part of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, is formed by the fusion of the aponeurotic fibres of which two muscles?
questions.concept: The conjoint tendon is formed by the lower aponeurotic fibres of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis, which arch over the spermatic cord and descend to attach to the pubic crest and the medial part of the pectineal line. It strengthens the posterior wall behind the superficial ring. The external oblique instead forms the anterior wall and the inguinal, lacunar and pectineal ligaments.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students, Chapter 4 — Abdomen (Anterior Abdominal Wall)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which of the following structures runs within the inguinal canal but is NOT a content of the spermatic cord (lying outside its coverings)?
questions.concept: The ilioinguinal nerve enters the canal by piercing the internal oblique and runs on the outer surface of the cord, leaving through the superficial ring; it is therefore in the canal but not a true content of the cord. True cord contents include the ductus deferens, testicular artery, artery to the vas, cremasteric artery, pampiniform plexus, genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, sympathetic fibres, lymphatics and the obliterated processus vaginalis.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Spermatic Cord)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A physician palpates the femoral artery pulsation at the mid-inguinal point. This point is defined as lying midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and which bony landmark?
questions.concept: The mid-inguinal point is midway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis and marks where the femoral artery enters the thigh. It must be distinguished from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament (midway between ASIS and pubic tubercle), which overlies the deep inguinal ring. Because the pubic tubercle lies lateral to the symphysis, these two surface points are close but not identical — a classic exam distinction.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Surface Anatomy)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During repair of a strangulated femoral hernia, the surgeon must carefully divide the sharp, crescentic medial boundary of the femoral ring. This structure is the:
questions.concept: The femoral ring is bounded anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, posteriorly by the pectineal ligament, laterally by the femoral vein (via a thin septum), and medially by the sharp crescentic lacunar ligament of Gimbernat. Strangulation occurs at this unyielding medial edge, which is the structure incised to relieve it — with care taken for an abnormal (aberrant) obturator artery that may cross the lacunar ligament.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Femoral Canal & Hernia)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: To distinguish a femoral from an inguinal hernia at the bedside, the clinician relates the neck of the sac to the pubic tubercle. The neck of a FEMORAL hernia characteristically lies:
options: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle
Above and lateral to the pubic tubercle
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
questions.concept: The neck of a femoral hernia emerges through the femoral ring, which lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, whereas an inguinal hernia exits through the superficial inguinal ring above and medial to the tubercle. This classic test uses the pubic tubercle as the reference point. Femoral hernias are commoner in women and have a high strangulation risk owing to the narrow, rigid femoral ring.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Hernias)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Below the arcuate line of Douglas, the aponeurotic posterior wall of the rectus sheath is absent. Here the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis is directly related to which structure?
options: Transversalis fascia (and, deep to it, peritoneum)
Posterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis
questions.concept: Below the arcuate line all three flat-muscle aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus, leaving no posterior aponeurotic sheath; the muscle then rests directly on the transversalis fascia and, deep to it, the extraperitoneal fat and peritoneum. Above the line the internal oblique aponeurosis splits, one lamina passing behind the rectus with the transversus aponeurosis. The inferior epigastric vessels enter the sheath at this line.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students, Chapter 4 — Abdomen (Rectus Sheath)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The arcuate line (linea semicircularis of Douglas), which marks the lower limit of the aponeurotic posterior rectus sheath, is typically located at approximately which level?
options: At the level of the umbilicus
At the level of the xiphisternum
At the level of the anterior superior iliac spine
Midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis
questions.concept: The arcuate line lies roughly midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis (a few centimetres below the umbilicus). Below it the rectus sheath has no posterior aponeurotic wall, and it is where the inferior epigastric vessels pass anterior to enter the sheath. The lateral edge of the rectus (linea semilunaris) is the recognised, though uncommon, site of a Spigelian hernia.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Rectus Sheath)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (of Winslow), which connects the greater and lesser sacs, is formed by the:
options: Free right border of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament)
questions.concept: The epiploic (omental) foramen is bounded anteriorly by the free right border of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament), which carries the portal triad — bile duct (right), hepatic artery proper (left) and portal vein (behind). Posteriorly lies the inferior vena cava, superiorly the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly the first part of the duodenum. It is the sole communication between the lesser sac and the greater sac.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Peritoneum)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which structure forms the POSTERIOR boundary of the epiploic foramen of Winslow?
questions.concept: The posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen is the inferior vena cava, covered by peritoneum. Anteriorly lies the hepatoduodenal ligament with the portal triad, superiorly the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly the first part of the duodenum with the horizontal course of the hepatic artery. Compressing the anterior boundary between finger and thumb (Pringle's manoeuvre) controls bleeding from the hepatic artery or portal vein.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Peritoneal Cavity)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which one of the following abdominal organs is PRIMARILY retroperitoneal?
questions.concept: The kidneys are primary retroperitoneal organs, lying behind the parietal peritoneum from the outset of development. The stomach, spleen and transverse colon are intraperitoneal, suspended by their mesenteries/ligaments. The mnemonic SAD PUCKER lists Suprarenals, Aorta/IVC, Duodenum (2nd–4th parts), Pancreas (except tail), Ureters, Colon (ascending/descending), Kidneys, Oesophagus (abdominal) and Rectum as retroperitoneal.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, Chapter 2 — Abdomen (Peritoneum)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The foregut is supplied by the coeliac trunk and the midgut by the superior mesenteric artery. The embryological foregut–midgut junction, marking this change in dominant arterial supply, lies at which point?
options: The junction of the first and second parts of the duodenum
The major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum
questions.concept: The foregut ends and the midgut begins at the level of the major duodenal papilla (opening of the bile duct) in the second part of the duodenum. Thus the coeliac trunk (via the gastroduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries) supplies proximal to this point, and the SMA (via the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery) supplies distal to it. This dual, anastomosing supply makes the duodenum relatively resistant to ischaemia.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students, Chapter 4 — Abdomen (Development & Blood Supply of the Gut)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: An elderly hypotensive patient develops ischaemic colitis. The most vulnerable 'watershed' zone lies at the splenic flexure, at the border between the territories of which two arteries?
options: Coeliac trunk and superior mesenteric artery
Superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery
Inferior mesenteric artery and internal iliac artery
Superior mesenteric artery and coeliac trunk
questions.concept: The splenic (left colic) flexure is the junction of midgut supply (SMA, via the middle colic artery) and hindgut supply (IMA, via the left colic artery). This anastomotic watershed — Griffith's point — has the least collateral flow and is the classic site of ischaemic colitis in low-flow states. A second watershed (Sudeck's point) lies at the rectosigmoid junction between the IMA/superior rectal and the internal iliac supply.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, Chapter 2 — Abdomen (Large Intestine Blood Supply)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis develops dilated tortuous veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae). This portosystemic anastomosis is between the para-umbilical veins and which systemic veins?
options: Superior and inferior epigastric (abdominal wall) veins
questions.concept: Caput medusae arises from anastomosis between the para-umbilical veins (which run to the left branch of the portal vein along the ligamentum teres) and the systemic superficial epigastric, superior epigastric and inferior epigastric veins of the anterior abdominal wall around the umbilicus. Other portosystemic sites are the oesophageal (left gastric–azygos), rectal (superior–middle/inferior rectal) and bare-area/retroperitoneal (of Retzius) anastomoses.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Portal Venous System)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The uncinate process of the pancreas has a key relationship to the superior mesenteric vessels. The uncinate process lies:
options: Anterior to the superior mesenteric vein and artery
Posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels
To the left of the abdominal aorta
Within the free border of the lesser omentum
questions.concept: The uncinate process is a hook-like leftward extension of the head of the pancreas that lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels — the SMV and SMA cross anterior to it — while it lies anterior to the abdominal aorta and IVC. Compression of the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly produces superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Pancreas)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament, extending from the hilum of the spleen to the posterior abdominal wall, contains which of the following structures?
options: Splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas
Short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels
questions.concept: The lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament runs from the spleen to the region of the left kidney/posterior wall and carries the splenic artery and vein together with the tail of the pancreas. The gastrosplenic ligament, in contrast, connects the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach and contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. Both ligaments bound the lesser sac at the splenic hilum.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students, Chapter 4 — Abdomen (Spleen)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: All of the following structures pass through the porta hepatis EXCEPT:
questions.concept: The porta hepatis transmits the portal vein, the hepatic artery proper and the hepatic (bile) duct, along with hepatic nerves and lymphatics. The hepatic veins do NOT pass through the porta hepatis; they leave the posterior (bare) surface of the liver and drain directly into the inferior vena cava in the groove for the IVC. This distinction matters in interpreting hepatic imaging and in Pringle's manoeuvre, which does not occlude the hepatic veins.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Liver)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In the majority of individuals, the vermiform appendix most commonly occupies which position relative to the caecum?
questions.concept: The retrocaecal/retrocolic position is the commonest position of the appendix (about 65–75% of cases), followed by the pelvic position (about 20–30%). A retrocaecal appendix may give atypical signs with a positive psoas sign, whereas a pelvic appendix may cause diarrhoea and irritate the bladder or rectum. The base of the appendix is constant, lying where the three taeniae coli converge on the caecum.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Caecum & Vermiform Appendix)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: McBurney's point, the surface marking of the base of the appendix, lies at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line joining the right anterior superior iliac spine to which landmark?
options: The tip of the 9th costal cartilage
questions.concept: McBurney's point lies at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the spino-umbilical line, drawn from the right ASIS to the umbilicus. Maximal tenderness here is a sign of acute appendicitis. It approximates the position of the base of the appendix, which arises from the posteromedial wall of the caecum at the convergence of the three taeniae coli.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Surface Anatomy)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The portal vein is typically formed, behind the neck of the pancreas, by the union of the superior mesenteric vein with which other vein?
questions.concept: The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas (about the level of L1–L2) by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein. The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein (or into the junction) before this confluence. The portal vein then ascends in the free border of the lesser omentum, behind the bile duct and hepatic artery, to reach the porta hepatis.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 2 — Abdomen & Pelvis (Portal Vein)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A ureteric calculus is most likely to impact at the site where the ureter is anatomically narrowest. This narrowest of the three normal ureteric constrictions is the:
options: Where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim over the common iliac bifurcation
Vesico-ureteric junction (entry into the bladder wall)
Where the ureter is crossed by the uterine artery or ductus deferens
questions.concept: The ureter has three normal constrictions: the pelvi-ureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and the vesico-ureteric junction as it passes obliquely through the bladder wall. The vesico-ureteric junction is the narrowest and the commonest site of calculus impaction. These constrictions correspond to the narrowings seen on an intravenous urogram.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy, Chapter 3 — Pelvis and Perineum (Ureter)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): A malignant tumour of the testis metastasises first to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. Reason (R): The testis develops on the posterior abdominal wall and its lymphatics drain along the testicular vessels to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at the level of L2. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is false and the reason is true, so the answer is D. The testis is a posterior abdominal wall organ that descends into the scrotum dragging its lymphatics along the testicular vessels; these drain to the para-aortic (lumbar) nodes near the origin of the testicular artery at L2. Hence testicular cancer spreads first to para-aortic — not inguinal — nodes. Only the scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 5 — The Abdomen (Testis & Lymphatic Drainage)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter and the pterygoids), along with mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini, are all derivatives of which pharyngeal arch?
questions.concept: The mesoderm of the first (mandibular) arch forms the muscles of mastication plus mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini, all supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal (V3), the nerve of the first arch. Second-arch muscles are the muscles of facial expression (VII); the third arch gives only stylopharyngeus (IX); the fourth arch gives cricothyroid and pharyngeal constrictors (X).
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (Pharyngeal/Branchial Apparatus)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The epidermis of the skin, together with hair, nails and the sebaceous and sweat glands, is derived from which germ layer?
questions.concept: The epidermis and its appendages (hair, nails, sebaceous and sweat glands, mammary glands) arise from surface (non-neural) ectoderm; the dermis beneath it is mesodermal (dermatome of somites over the trunk). Endoderm forms gut epithelium and its glands, while neural crest supplies melanocytes that migrate into the epidermis but does not form the keratinocyte layer itself.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Integumentary System / Third Week (Germ Layer Derivatives)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract and the parenchyma of the liver, pancreas and lungs are derived from which germ layer?
questions.concept: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the gut tube and the glandular/parenchymal cells of the liver, pancreas, thyroid, parathyroids, thymus and the respiratory epithelium of the lungs, as well as the lining of the bladder and urethra. The surrounding smooth muscle and connective tissue (stroma) of these organs are mesodermal (splanchnic/visceral mesoderm), and the extreme ends of the gut (mouth, anal canal) are ectodermal.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Digestive System / Germ Layer Derivatives

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which cranial nerve is the nerve of the third pharyngeal arch?
questions.concept: Each pharyngeal arch carries its own cranial nerve: arch 1 = trigeminal (V3), arch 2 = facial (VII), arch 3 = glossopharyngeal (IX), and arches 4 and 6 = branches of the vagus (superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves respectively). The glossopharyngeal nerve therefore supplies the single third-arch muscle, stylopharyngeus, and provides sensation to the posterior third of the tongue.
questions.reference: IB Singh Human Embryology — Pharyngeal Arches, Pouches and Clefts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Only one of the pharyngeal (branchial) clefts gives rise to a definitive adult structure. That first pharyngeal cleft forms which of the following?
questions.concept: The ectodermal first pharyngeal cleft (groove) persists as the external acoustic meatus, and its floor contributes to the outer layer of the tympanic membrane. Clefts 2, 3 and 4 are normally buried and obliterated as the cervical sinus; their persistence causes a branchial cyst or fistula. The auditory tube and tympanic cavity are endodermal first-POUCH derivatives, and the palatine tonsil arises from the second pouch, not from a cleft.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (Pharyngeal Clefts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Meckel's cartilage, the cartilage bar of the first pharyngeal arch, gives rise to which pair of middle-ear ossicles?
questions.concept: The dorsal end of Meckel's (first-arch) cartilage ossifies into the malleus and incus and also forms the sphenomandibular ligament and anterior ligament of the malleus; the mandible itself develops by intramembranous ossification lateral to this cartilage. The stapes, along with the styloid process, stylohyoid ligament and lesser cornu of the hyoid, is a derivative of Reichert's (second-arch) cartilage, which is why it is not a Meckel's derivative.
questions.reference: IB Singh Human Embryology — Pharyngeal Arch Cartilages / Development of the Ear

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During swallowing, a muscle that elevates the pharynx and larynx is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve and is the only muscle derived from the third pharyngeal arch. Which muscle is this?
questions.concept: Stylopharyngeus is the sole muscle of the third pharyngeal arch and is therefore supplied by that arch's nerve, the glossopharyngeal (IX). Stylohyoid is a second-arch muscle (facial nerve, VII); styloglossus is a tongue muscle derived from occipital myotomes and supplied by the hypoglossal (XII); palatopharyngeus is a fourth/sixth-arch derivative supplied by the vagus (X) via the pharyngeal plexus.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Head and Neck / Development of the Pharyngeal Arches

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The cricothyroid muscle, a derivative of the fourth pharyngeal arch, is supplied by which nerve?
questions.concept: The fourth arch gives rise to cricothyroid (and the pharyngeal constrictors and levator veli palatini), supplied by the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve of the vagus. All the remaining intrinsic laryngeal muscles are sixth-arch derivatives supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory (above the vocal folds), so it supplies no muscle.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (Fourth and Sixth Arch Derivatives)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The endoderm of the first pharyngeal pouch forms the tubotympanic recess, which develops into which of the following?
questions.concept: The first pharyngeal pouch expands into the tubotympanic recess, whose distal (dilated) part becomes the tympanic (middle-ear) cavity and mastoid antrum while its proximal (narrow) part becomes the auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube. The palatine tonsil comes from the second pouch; the inferior parathyroid and thymus come from the third pouch; the superior parathyroid and ultimobranchial body come from the fourth pouch.
questions.reference: IB Singh Human Embryology — Pharyngeal Pouches / Development of the Middle Ear

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The surface epithelium and the crypts of the palatine tonsil are derived from the endoderm of which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.concept: This question tests the second pharyngeal pouch, whose endoderm proliferates into buds that form the surface epithelium and lining of the tonsillar crypts of the palatine tonsil; the surrounding lymphoid tissue is later infiltrated by mesoderm-derived lymphocytes. The other listed structures belong to different pouches: middle ear = pouch 1, thymus = pouch 3, superior parathyroid = pouch 4, making palatine tonsil the correct second-pouch derivative.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (Pharyngeal Pouches)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus both develop from the endoderm of which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.concept: The dorsal wing of the third pouch forms the inferior parathyroid gland and the ventral wing forms the thymus. As the thymus migrates caudally into the thorax it drags the inferior parathyroid with it, so the inferior parathyroids end up BELOW the superior parathyroids, which arise from the fourth pouch and migrate less. This crossing-over of migration explains the paradoxical final positions of the parathyroid glands.
questions.reference: IB Singh Human Embryology — Pharyngeal Pouches (Parathyroid and Thymic Development)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The superior parathyroid glands and the ultimobranchial body develop from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.concept: The dorsal wing of the fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroid gland, while its ventral wing forms the ultimobranchial (postbranchial) body, which is incorporated into the thyroid and gives rise to the calcitonin-secreting parafollicular C cells. Because the superior parathyroids migrate only a short distance, they remain above the inferior parathyroids despite arising from a more caudal pouch than the third-pouch inferior glands.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (Fourth Pouch Derivatives)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland secrete calcitonin. Reason (R): The parafollicular C cells are derived from the ultimobranchial body of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. Choose the best option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are individually true: parafollicular C cells do secrete calcitonin, and they are indeed carried into the thyroid within the ultimobranchial body of the fourth pouch (the C cells themselves being neural-crest cells that colonise that body). However, the embryonic ORIGIN of the C cells does not explain WHY they secrete calcitonin, so the reason is not the correct explanation of the assertion, making B the right choice.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck / Thyroid Gland (Ultimobranchial Body)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 20-year-old presents with a smooth, painless, fluctuant swelling at the anterior border of the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It has been slowly enlarging and does not move on swallowing or tongue protrusion. Which lesion, arising from remnants of the cervical sinus, is most likely?
questions.concept: A branchial cyst results from failure of the cervical sinus (formed by the buried second, third and fourth clefts) to obliterate, producing a fluctuant swelling classically at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid; a persistent tract opening onto the skin is a branchial fistula. A thyroglossal cyst is midline and moves on tongue protrusion, a cystic hygroma is a soft transilluminant lymphatic malformation, and a dermoid lies in the midline floor of the mouth.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (Pharyngeal Cleft Anomalies)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 9-year-old child has a painless midline neck swelling near the level of the hyoid bone that moves upward when the tongue is protruded and when the child swallows. Which developmental anomaly does this describe?
questions.concept: A thyroglossal duct cyst arises from persistence of the thyroglossal duct, the tract along which the thyroid descended from the foramen cecum to the neck. Because the duct is attached superiorly to the foramen cecum of the tongue and passes in close relation to the hyoid, the cyst characteristically moves upward on protrusion of the tongue (and on swallowing) — a sign that distinguishes it from a laterally placed branchial cyst, a fixed lymph node, or a floor-of-mouth dermoid.
questions.reference: IB Singh Human Embryology — Development of the Thyroid Gland (Thyroglossal Duct)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The foramen cecum, located at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue, marks the point of origin of which structure?
questions.concept: The thyroid gland begins as a median endodermal thyroid diverticulum in the floor of the primitive pharynx at what becomes the foramen cecum, then descends in front of the hyoid and laryngeal cartilages to its adult position, remaining temporarily connected by the thyroglossal duct. The foramen cecum is the persistent adult remnant of this origin; failure of descent produces a lingual thyroid, and persistence of the duct produces a thyroglossal cyst.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck / Thyroid Gland

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A neonate presents with hypocalcemic tetany and seizures, recurrent viral and fungal infections due to absent T-cell immunity, and a conotruncal cardiac anomaly (interrupted aortic arch). These features result from maldevelopment of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 microdeletion) results from abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, giving thymic aplasia/hypoplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), parathyroid aplasia (hypocalcemia and tetany), and conotruncal cardiac defects such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot and interrupted aortic arch, with characteristic facies. It is often driven by defective neural-crest migration into the pharyngeal arches; the other listed conditions do not produce this pouch-derived triad.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Head and Neck (DiGeorge / Pharyngeal Pouch Anomalies)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The somites, which give rise to the vertebral column, the skeletal muscle of the trunk and limbs, and the dermis of the back, develop from which subdivision of the mesoderm?
questions.concept: Paraxial mesoderm segments into somites, each differentiating into a sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), a myotome (skeletal muscle) and a dermatome (dermis of the back). Intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system; lateral plate mesoderm splits into somatic and splanchnic layers forming the body-wall/limb connective tissue and the visceral serosa/gut wall. Neural crest is ectodermal, not a mesodermal subdivision, so paraxial mesoderm is the somite source.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Third to Eighth Week / Mesoderm (Paraxial and Somites)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The kidneys, ureters and gonads develop primarily from which subdivision of the mesoderm?
questions.concept: The urogenital system arises from intermediate mesoderm, which lies between the paraxial (somite) mesoderm and the lateral plate. It forms the nephrogenic cord and urogenital ridge, giving the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros (definitive kidney), the mesonephric and paramesonephric ducts, and the gonads. Paraxial mesoderm makes somites, lateral plate makes body-wall and visceral connective tissue, and the bladder/urethra lining is endodermal, so intermediate mesoderm is correct.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Urogenital System (Intermediate Mesoderm)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The adrenal (suprarenal) medulla is derived from neural crest cells. Reason (R): The adrenal cortex is also derived from neural crest cells. Choose the best option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: the adrenal medulla is populated by neural-crest-derived chromaffin cells that secrete catecholamines, essentially modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons. The reason is false: the adrenal cortex is NOT of neural-crest origin but arises from mesoderm (coelomic/mesothelial epithelium of the urogenital ridge). Because A is true and R is false, the correct choice is C. This dual origin is a classic embryology point tested in FMGE.
questions.reference: IB Singh Human Embryology — Neural Crest Derivatives / Development of Suprarenal Gland

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) results from a failure of neural crest cell migration into the wall of the distal bowel. Reason (R): Neural crest cells give rise to the enteric (myenteric and submucosal) ganglia. Choose the best option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are true and the reason directly explains the assertion. Vagal neural crest cells normally migrate craniocaudally to colonise the entire gut and form the parasympathetic myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) ganglia. If migration arrests before reaching the distal colon, that segment lacks ganglion cells (aganglionosis), stays tonically contracted and cannot relax, producing functional obstruction and proximal dilatation — Hirschsprung disease. Hence A is the correct option.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Digestive System / Neural Crest (Hirschsprung Disease)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The aorticopulmonary (spiral) septum, which divides the truncus arteriosus into the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk, is formed by cells derived from which source?
questions.concept: The aorticopulmonary septum is formed by cardiac neural crest cells that migrate from the occipital-cervical region into the truncal and bulbar (conotruncal) ridges; these ridges grow and spiral to separate the outflow tract into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Failure of this neural-crest-dependent septation causes conotruncal anomalies such as persistent truncus arteriosus, transposition of the great arteries and tetralogy of Fallot, which is why the same crest defect underlies DiGeorge syndrome.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Cardiovascular System (Outflow Tract Septation / Neural Crest)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The ductus arteriosus, which becomes the ligamentum arteriosum after birth, is a derivative of which embryonic aortic arch artery?
questions.concept: The distal part of the LEFT sixth aortic arch artery persists as the ductus arteriosus (later the ligamentum arteriosum), while the proximal parts of the sixth arches form the proximal pulmonary arteries; the right sixth arch loses its distal segment. For contrast: the left fourth arch forms the arch of the aorta, the right fourth forms the proximal right subclavian artery, and the third arch arteries form the common carotids and the proximal internal carotids.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Cardiovascular System (Aortic Arch Derivatives)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A newborn with a history of maternal polyhydramnios develops excessive frothy oral secretions and chokes and turns cyanotic with the first feed. A nasogastric tube cannot be advanced into the stomach and coils in the upper thorax on X-ray, yet gas is seen in the stomach. This anomaly of foregut division is best explained by which diagnosis?
questions.concept: The picture is the common (type C) esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula, arising from faulty division of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum. A blind upper esophageal pouch causes drooling, choking and an NG tube that coils in the thorax, while the distal fistula between trachea and lower esophagus lets air reach the stomach; maternal polyhydramnios reflects impaired fetal swallowing. Pyloric stenosis and duodenal atresia present with vomiting later, and a diaphragmatic hernia presents with respiratory distress and bowel in the chest.
questions.reference: Langman's Medical Embryology — Respiratory / Digestive System (Tracheoesophageal Septum and Fistula)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The dorsal (posterior) column–medial lemniscus pathway of the spinal cord is chiefly responsible for carrying which of the following sensory modalities?
options: Fine (discriminative) touch, vibration and conscious proprioception
Unconscious proprioception destined for the cerebellum
questions.concept: The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry fine discriminative touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and conscious joint-position sense. Fibers ascend ipsilaterally, synapse in the gracile/cuneate nuclei of the medulla, then cross as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. Pain and temperature instead travel in the lateral spinothalamic tract, and unconscious proprioception in the spinocerebellar tracts.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The lateral spinothalamic tract is the principal ascending pathway for which of the following sensations?
questions.concept: The lateral spinothalamic tract conveys pain and temperature. First-order fibers enter and travel a short distance in the dorsolateral tract of Lissauer and synapse in the dorsal horn; second-order fibers cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend contralaterally to the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus. Because the fibers cross close to their level of entry, a cord lesion causes contralateral pain/temperature loss beginning one to two segments below.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 55-year-old strict vegetarian with megaloblastic anaemia reports tingling in the feet, an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark, and stiff weak legs. Examination shows loss of vibration and joint-position sense, brisk knee jerks and extensor plantar responses. Which combination of spinal tracts is degenerating?
options: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Lateral spinothalamic and anterior corticospinal tracts
Spinocerebellar tracts and anterior horn cells
Dorsal columns and lateral spinothalamic tracts
questions.concept: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration, which simultaneously demyelinates the dorsal columns (sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, loss of vibration/position sense) and the lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic weakness, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar responses). The combination of a proprioceptive sensory ataxia with upper-motor-neuron signs — sometimes alongside absent ankle jerks from an associated peripheral neuropathy — is characteristic.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Diseases of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with untreated syphilis has a broad-based stamping gait, lightning-like shooting pains in the legs, and falls when he closes his eyes while washing his face. He has absent ankle jerks and small irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light. The primary site of spinal cord damage is:
options: The dorsal columns and dorsal (posterior) nerve roots
questions.concept: Tabes dorsalis is a form of tertiary neurosyphilis that degenerates the dorsal roots and dorsal columns, producing sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia, a positive Romberg sign, lightning pains, areflexia, and loss of vibration and joint-position sense. Argyll Robertson pupils — small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light — are the classic associated finding.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During repair of a thoracic aortic aneurysm a patient wakes with flaccid paraplegia and complete loss of pain and temperature sensation below the umbilicus, yet vibration and joint-position sense in the toes are entirely preserved. Which territory has been infarcted?
options: The anterior spinal artery territory, sparing the dorsal columns
The posterior spinal artery territory, sparing the corticospinal tracts
The entire cross-section of the cord at that level
A single dorsal root entry zone
questions.concept: Anterior spinal artery syndrome infarcts the anterior two-thirds of the cord: the corticospinal tracts (motor) and the spinothalamic tracts (pain/temperature) are lost bilaterally below the level, whereas the dorsal columns — supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries — are spared, so vibration and proprioception remain intact. It is a recognised complication of aortic cross-clamping and profound hypotension.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Vascular Diseases of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In the dorsal columns, the fasciculus gracilis (lying most medially) carries proprioceptive and fine-touch information from which region of the body?
options: The lower limb and lower trunk (below about the sixth thoracic segment)
The upper limb and upper trunk
questions.concept: The dorsal columns are somatotopically organised: the medially placed fasciculus gracilis carries fibers from the lower limb and lower trunk (below about T6), while the more lateral fasciculus cuneatus (present only above T6) carries fibers from the upper limb and upper trunk. A useful mnemonic is 'gracilis = ground/legs, and it lies medial'.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy — Spinal Cord: Ascending Pathways

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Second-order neurons of the pain and temperature pathway cross the midline within the spinal cord at which structure, and how far do they usually ascend before crossing?
options: The anterior (ventral) white commissure, ascending one to two segments before crossing
The posterior grey commissure, crossing within the same segment
The pyramidal decussation in the medulla
The internal arcuate fibers of the medulla
questions.concept: In the spinothalamic (anterolateral) system the second-order fibers cross in the anterior white commissure, typically ascending one to two segments above their level of entry before crossing. This delayed, oblique crossing explains why a cord hemisection produces contralateral pain/temperature loss beginning a segment or two below the lesion, and why a central (syrinx) lesion first interrupts these decussating fibers.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Approximately 85–90% of corticospinal (pyramidal) fibers cross the midline to form the lateral corticospinal tract at which anatomical site?
options: The pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla
The anterior white commissure of the spinal cord
The posterior limb of the internal capsule
The midbrain at the level of the red nucleus
questions.concept: Most corticospinal fibers decussate at the junction of the medulla and spinal cord (the pyramidal decussation) and descend as the crossed lateral corticospinal tract, which controls contralateral limb musculature. The uncrossed minority continues as the anterior corticospinal tract and crosses segmentally in the anterior white commissure to supply axial and proximal muscles.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Descending Tracts of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: An elderly man with cervical spondylosis falls forward, striking his forehead in a hyperextension injury. He now has marked weakness and a 'burning' sensory disturbance in both hands and forearms, but his legs are only mildly affected and he can still walk. Which pattern of cord injury best explains this?
options: Central cord syndrome, damaging the central grey and the medially placed cervical corticospinal fibers
questions.concept: Acute central cord syndrome, typical of a hyperextension injury in a spondylotic cervical spine, damages the central grey matter and the medially situated cervical (arm) fibers of the lateral corticospinal tract — arm fibers lie medial to leg fibers in the tract. The result is disproportionately greater weakness and sensory disturbance in the upper limbs than the lower limbs, often with a cape-like dissociated sensory loss.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has progressive painless weakness with wasting and fasciculations of the hands, together with spasticity, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses in the legs. Sensation is entirely normal and there are no sphincter or eye-movement problems. Which structures are affected?
options: The lateral corticospinal tracts together with the anterior horn cells, with sensory tracts spared
The dorsal columns and spinocerebellar tracts
The dorsal roots and posterior columns
questions.concept: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a motor neuron disease that combines upper-motor-neuron signs (lateral corticospinal tract degeneration → spasticity, hyperreflexia, extensor plantars) with lower-motor-neuron signs (anterior horn cell loss → wasting and fasciculations). Sensation is preserved because the ascending sensory tracts are not involved — a key clue that distinguishes it from myelopathies such as subacute combined degeneration.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis and Other Motor Neuron Diseases

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: An unimmunised child develops fever followed by rapidly progressive asymmetric flaccid weakness of one leg, with loss of tendon reflexes and later muscle wasting, but no sensory loss. The spinal structure selectively destroyed is:
questions.concept: Poliovirus has a selective tropism for the anterior horn (lower motor neuron) cells of the spinal cord, producing a pure lower-motor-neuron picture: asymmetric flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, areflexia and wasting, with completely preserved sensation because the sensory tracts and dorsal roots are spared. Involvement is typically patchy and asymmetric.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A teenager has progressive gait and limb ataxia, loss of vibration and joint-position sense, absent knee and ankle jerks but extensor plantar responses, along with pes cavus and scoliosis. This combination reflects degeneration of which set of spinal tracts?
options: Spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterior horn cells and lateral spinothalamic tracts
Dorsal roots and the anterior white commissure
questions.concept: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal-recessive GAA trinucleotide-repeat disorder that degenerates the spinocerebellar tracts (limb and gait ataxia), the dorsal columns (loss of vibration and position sense, sensory ataxia) and the corticospinal tracts (extensor plantar responses despite paradoxically absent tendon jerks). Pes cavus, scoliosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are characteristic associated features.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — The Hereditary Ataxias

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway, where does the first-order (primary) sensory neuron synapse onto the second-order neuron?
options: In the nucleus gracilis or nucleus cuneatus of the medulla
In the dorsal horn at the segmental level of entry
In the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus
questions.concept: Uniquely among the major sensory pathways, the first-order neuron of the dorsal column system ascends ipsilaterally the entire length of the cord before synapsing in the gracile or cuneate nucleus of the medulla. The second-order neuron then crosses as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus and terminates on the third-order neuron in the VPL of the thalamus, which projects to the primary sensory cortex.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy — Spinal Cord: Ascending Pathways

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient stands steadily with the eyes open but sways and nearly falls the moment the eyes are closed (a positive Romberg sign). This finding localises the lesion to which spinal pathway?
questions.concept: A positive Romberg sign indicates a sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia due to dorsal column dysfunction. With the eyes open, vision compensates for the lost joint-position sense; on closing the eyes that visual compensation is removed and the patient sways. A cerebellar ataxia, by contrast, is present even with the eyes open, so Romberg's test is negative in cerebellar disease.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A knife wound hemisects the left half of the spinal cord at the C6 level. Which of the following findings is expected below the lesion?
options: Loss of pain and temperature on the RIGHT side of the body, beginning a few segments below the lesion
Loss of pain and temperature on the LEFT side of the body
Loss of vibration and proprioception on the RIGHT side of the body
Flaccid paralysis of the right lower limb
questions.concept: In Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection) the spinothalamic fibers have already crossed, so pain and temperature are lost contralaterally (on the right), beginning one to two segments below the lesion. The dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts are still uncrossed at this level, so vibration/proprioception loss and spastic weakness are ipsilateral (on the left). Hence the expected finding is contralateral (right-sided) pain and temperature loss.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: To relieve intractable cancer pain in the right leg, a neurosurgeon divides the left anterolateral quadrant of the spinal cord (an anterolateral cordotomy). Which tract is being deliberately interrupted?
options: The lateral spinothalamic tract, carrying already-crossed pain and temperature fibers
questions.concept: Because pain and temperature fibers cross within the cord and then ascend in the contralateral lateral spinothalamic tract, cutting the left anterolateral quadrant abolishes pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the body below the lesion — the anatomical principle behind anterolateral cordotomy. Touch, vibration and proprioception are preserved because the dorsal columns are untouched.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord and Ascending Tracts

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A young adult with a known cervical syrinx, who already had a cape-like loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders, now develops wasting, weakness and areflexia of the small muscles of both hands. This new finding is due to the expanding cavity now involving:
options: The anterior horn cells at the affected cervical segments
The lateral spinothalamic fibers that have already crossed and ascended
questions.concept: A syrinx begins centrally and first interrupts the decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, producing dissociated 'cape' sensory loss (pain/temperature lost, touch/proprioception spared). As the cavity enlarges ventrolaterally it destroys the anterior horn cells, causing lower-motor-neuron wasting, weakness and areflexia of the hands; still later, lateral corticospinal involvement adds spastic weakness of the legs.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Spinal Cord (Clinical Notes)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The dorsal (posterior) spinocerebellar tract, which arises from the nucleus dorsalis of Clarke, conveys which type of information, and does it cross the midline?
options: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb, ascending uncrossed (ipsilateral) to the cerebellum
Conscious proprioception, crossing in the medulla
Pain and temperature, crossing in the spinal cord
Voluntary motor commands descending to the cerebellum
questions.concept: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates in the nucleus dorsalis of Clarke (roughly C8–L2/3) and carries unconscious proprioceptive information from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs of the lower limb and trunk. It remains uncrossed (ipsilateral) and enters the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, providing the input needed for coordination of posture and fine limb movement.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy — Spinal Cord: Ascending Pathways

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A discrete lesion damages only the lateral corticospinal tract on the right side of the spinal cord at the T8 level. On which side, and with what features, will the resulting motor deficit appear below the lesion?
