options: On the right (ipsilateral) side, with spastic weakness, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response
On the left (contralateral) side, with flaccid weakness and absent reflexes
On the right side, with flaccid paralysis and fasciculations
questions.concept: The corticospinal fibers have already decussated in the medulla, so within the spinal cord the lateral corticospinal tract carries fibers destined for the ipsilateral (same-side) muscles. A right-sided cord lesion therefore produces right-sided upper-motor-neuron signs below the level — spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response — not contralateral or flaccid weakness.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Descending Tracts of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which set of clinical signs indicates an upper motor neuron (corticospinal tract) lesion rather than a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: Spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor (upgoing) plantar response
Flaccidity, prominent fasciculations and marked early muscle wasting
Absent tendon reflexes with fully preserved power
Loss of pain and temperature with normal muscle power
questions.concept: Upper motor neuron (corticospinal) lesions produce spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, an extensor plantar (positive Babinski) response and only minimal (disuse) wasting. Lower motor neuron lesions instead cause flaccid weakness, hypotonia, hyporeflexia or areflexia, marked wasting and fasciculations. Correctly separating these two patterns is the first step in localising a lesion along the motor pathway.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy — The Descending Tracts of the Spinal Cord

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract is unusual in that its fibres cross the midline twice before reaching the cerebellum. Through which cerebellar peduncle does it finally enter the cerebellum?
questions.concept: The ventral (anterior) spinocerebellar tract arises from spinal border cells, crosses the midline in the cord, ascends, and then crosses back a second time within the cerebellum, entering through the superior cerebellar peduncle. The dorsal spinocerebellar tract from Clarke's column stays uncrossed and enters via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Both carry unconscious proprioception from the lower limb.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: For both the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway and the spinothalamic pathway, the third-order neuron that projects to the primary somatosensory cortex has its cell body located in which structure?
options: Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus
Substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn
questions.concept: For both the dorsal column–medial lemniscus and spinothalamic systems the third-order neuron lies in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus (the face is relayed by VPM). Its axon passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus. The nucleus gracilis houses second-order DCML cell bodies, and dorsal root ganglia contain the first-order neurons.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: On entering the spinal cord, first-order pain and temperature fibres ascend or descend one to two segments before synapsing in the dorsal horn. Within which structure do they travel during this short course?
questions.concept: Thinly myelinated and unmyelinated pain and temperature (and crude touch) fibres travel one to two segments up or down in the dorsolateral tract of Lissauer before synapsing on second-order neurons in the dorsal horn, chiefly the substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II). This is why the spinothalamic sensory level often lies a segment or two below the actual level of a cord lesion.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a slowly enlarging intramedullary spinal cord tumour in the thoracic region. He has lost pain and temperature sensation over the trunk and both lower limbs, yet sensation over the perineum and perianal 'saddle' area is strikingly preserved. This 'sacral sparing' is explained by which feature of the spinothalamic tract?
options: Sacral fibres are laminated most laterally and are spared by a centrally expanding lesion
Sacral fibres decussate only in the medulla
Sacral sensation is carried entirely in the dorsal columns
Sacral dermatomes have dual (bilateral) cord innervation
questions.concept: In the lateral spinothalamic tract fibres are somatotopically laminated, with sacral segments lying most laterally (superficially) and cervical segments most medially. A centrally arising intramedullary tumour or syrinx therefore destroys the medial cervical/thoracic fibres first while the laterally placed sacral fibres are spared, producing 'sacral sparing.' An extramedullary compressive lesion tends instead to involve sacral sensation early.
questions.reference: Vishram Singh, Textbook of Clinical Neuroanatomy, 3rd ed., Ch. 6 (Spinal Cord)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The fasciculus cuneatus is present in the dorsal columns only above the mid-thoracic (approximately T6) level. Which information does it convey?
options: Fine touch, vibration and conscious proprioception from the upper limb, upper trunk and neck
Pain and temperature from the lower limb
Conscious proprioception from the lower limb and lower trunk
Voluntary motor commands to the upper limb
questions.concept: The dorsal columns comprise a medial fasciculus gracilis and a lateral fasciculus cuneatus. The cuneatus is added at about the T6 level and carries discriminative touch, vibration and conscious proprioception from the upper limb, upper trunk and neck; below T6 only the gracilis (lower limb and lower trunk) is present. Cuneatus fibres synapse in the nucleus cuneatus of the medulla.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A comatose patient after a midbrain haemorrhage shows extension and internal rotation of all four limbs (decerebrate posturing). Loss of which descending influence, leaving vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal drive to the extensors unopposed, best explains this posture?
options: Rubrospinal tract facilitation of flexor tone
Lateral corticospinal tract control of the hands
questions.concept: Decerebrate rigidity (extension of all four limbs) follows a brainstem lesion below the level of the red nucleus. Removing the rubrospinal tract's facilitation of flexor muscle tone leaves the extensor drive of the lateral vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal tracts unopposed, so extensor tone dominates. A lesion above the red nucleus (e.g., internal capsule) spares rubrospinal flexor facilitation and instead produces decorticate posturing with arm flexion.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The largest neurons contributing axons to the corticospinal tract, the giant Betz cells, are found in which layer of the primary motor cortex?
questions.concept: Only about 30% of corticospinal fibres arise from the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4), with the rest from premotor and sensory areas. The giant Betz cells, the largest neurons of the primary motor cortex, lie in cortical layer V (the internal pyramidal layer) and contribute the fastest-conducting, largest-diameter corticospinal axons, though they form only a small fraction of the tract's total fibres.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient with a cervical syrinx develops a right-sided Horner's syndrome (partial ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis). Damage to which grey-matter structure, the origin of pre-ganglionic sympathetic fibres, accounts for this?
options: Intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) at C8–T2
questions.concept: Pre-ganglionic sympathetic neurons occupy the intermediolateral cell column (lateral horn) of spinal segments T1–L2, and those supplying the head and eye emerge from C8–T2 (the ciliospinal centre of Budge). A cervical syrinx expanding into this lateral horn interrupts the oculosympathetic outflow, producing an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome of partial ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Neuroanatomy, 8th ed., Ch. 4 (The Spinal Cord and the Ascending and Descending Tracts)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which of the following structures lies within the middle mediastinum?
questions.concept: The middle mediastinum contains the heart within its pericardium, the roots of the great vessels (ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, lower SVC and terminal arch of the azygos), the main bronchi and the phrenic nerves with pericardiacophrenic vessels. The thymus lies in the anterior (and superior) mediastinum, while the oesophagus and descending thoracic aorta are contents of the posterior mediastinum, so none of those three belongs to the middle division.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Mediastinum)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The narrowest of the normal oesophageal constrictions, situated about 15 cm from the incisor teeth and the commonest cervical site of foreign-body arrest, is produced by the:
options: Crossing of the arch of the aorta
Crossing of the left main bronchus
questions.concept: The oesophagus shows four constrictions measured from the incisors: cricopharyngeal at 15 cm (the narrowest, formed by cricopharyngeus / upper oesophageal sphincter), aortic arch at 22.5 cm, left main bronchus at 27.5 cm, and the diaphragmatic hiatus / cardia at ~40 cm. Because the cricopharyngeal segment is the tightest, ingested foreign bodies most often impact here in the neck; the lower three are relative narrowings due to adjacent structures rather than the tightest point.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Oesophagus)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has central chest pain; ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Occlusion of which coronary artery best explains this inferior-wall infarct?
questions.concept: In the common right-dominant heart, the right coronary artery gives the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) branch and supplies the diaphragmatic/inferior surface of the left ventricle, which is reflected in the inferior leads II, III and aVF. The RCA also usually supplies the SA and AV nodes, so inferior infarcts are often accompanied by bradyarrhythmias. The LAD supplies the anterior wall (V1–V4), the circumflex the lateral wall (I, aVL, V5–V6), and left main occlusion is typically catastrophic and widespread.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy — Thorax (Coronary Arteries)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In the majority of individuals, the artery supplying the sinuatrial (SA) node arises from the:
questions.concept: The sinuatrial nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in about 60% of hearts (near its origin, running to the node at the junction of SVC and right atrium) and from the left circumflex artery in the remaining ~40%. Because the pacemaker's blood supply most often comes from the RCA, proximal RCA disease can disturb impulse generation. The posterior interventricular artery supplies the posterior septum, not the SA node, and the LAD supplies the anterior septum and anterior LV.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Blood Supply of the Heart)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: In a right-dominant coronary circulation, the atrioventricular (AV) nodal branch that arises at the crux of the heart is a branch of the:
questions.concept: Coronary dominance is defined by which artery crosses the crux (the point where the posterior atrioventricular and interventricular grooves meet) to give the posterior descending artery and the AV nodal branch. In the right-dominant pattern (about 85–90% of people) the right coronary artery reaches the crux and supplies the AV node; hence inferior/RCA infarcts can cause AV block. In the ~10% left-dominant hearts the circumflex takes over this role.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students — Thorax (Cardiac Vessels and Dominance)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) artery principally supplies the:
options: Posterior third of the interventricular septum
Anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum and the cardiac apex
SA node and most of the right atrium
Entire left atrium and the coronary sinus wall
questions.concept: The left anterior descending artery runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, the anterior wall of the left ventricle, the adjacent right ventricular wall and the cardiac apex; it also gives septal perforators to the proximal bundle branches. The posterior third of the septum is supplied by the posterior interventricular artery (usually from the RCA), so LAD occlusion classically produces large anteroseptal infarcts.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Coronary Arteries)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The apex of the heart, where the apex beat is normally palpated, is formed by which chamber?
questions.concept: The apex of the heart is formed entirely by the left ventricle and points downward, forward and to the left, lying deep to the left fifth intercostal space just medial to the midclavicular line, where the apex beat is felt. The right ventricle forms most of the anterior/sternocostal surface and inferior border, the right atrium forms the right border, and the left atrium forms the base (posterior surface), not the apex.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (External Features of the Heart)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: On a frontal (PA) chest radiograph, the right border of the cardiac shadow is formed by the:
questions.concept: The right border of the heart is formed by the right atrium, which receives the SVC above and the IVC below. The inferior border is formed mainly by the right ventricle (with a small part of the left ventricle at the apex), and the left border by the left ventricle and the left auricle. The right atrium forming the right border is a standard landmark used when assessing cardiac silhouette and chamber enlargement on radiographs.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Borders and Surfaces of the Heart)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The coronary sinus, which drains most of the venous blood of the heart, opens into the:
questions.concept: The coronary sinus lies in the posterior part of the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and opens into the right atrium between the opening of the inferior vena cava and the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice; its mouth is guarded by the valve of the coronary sinus (Thebesian valve). It receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the oblique vein of the left atrium, and returns the bulk of cardiac venous blood to the right atrium.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students — Thorax (Cardiac Veins and Coronary Sinus)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The sounds of the mitral valve are best auscultated at which surface site, even though the valve itself lies deep to the left fourth costal cartilage?
options: Right second intercostal space at the sternal edge
Left second intercostal space at the sternal edge
Left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line (apex)
Lower left sternal border in the fourth–fifth intercostal space
questions.concept: Auscultation areas do not overlie the valves but lie downstream in the direction of blood flow, so the valve sounds are carried to where the blood is projected. The mitral valve is heard best at the apex (left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line), the tricuspid at the lower left sternal edge, the aortic in the right second intercostal space, and the pulmonary in the left second intercostal space. Thus the mitral area is at the apex despite the valve lying behind the left fourth costal cartilage.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy — Thorax (Surface Anatomy and Auscultation of Heart Valves)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which cardiac valve lies most superiorly and is auscultated in the left second intercostal space?
questions.concept: The pulmonary valve is the most superior and most anterior of the four valves, lying behind the medial end of the left third costal cartilage and the adjoining sternum; its sounds are heard in the left second intercostal space. In descending order of position the valves lie: pulmonary (highest), aortic (just below and to the right), then the mitral and tricuspid atrioventricular valves. The surface projections cluster along a line, so the listening areas are deliberately offset downstream.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Surface Marking of Heart Valves)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The three branches of the arch of the aorta, in order from right (proximal) to left (distal), are:
options: Left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian
Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian
Brachiocephalic trunk, left subclavian, left common carotid
Left subclavian, left common carotid, brachiocephalic trunk
questions.concept: The arch of the aorta gives three branches from its convex upper surface, in order from proximal to distal: the brachiocephalic trunk (which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries), the left common carotid artery, and the left subclavian artery. There is no right-sided single trunk equivalent to a left brachiocephalic artery because the right common carotid and right subclavian arise together from the brachiocephalic trunk.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Arch of the Aorta)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): An aneurysm of the arch of the aorta can produce hoarseness of the voice. Reason (R): The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks below the arch around the ligamentum arteriosum before ascending to the larynx. Choose the most appropriate option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve arises from the left vagus in the thorax, loops beneath the arch of the aorta immediately behind the ligamentum arteriosum, then ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove to supply the intrinsic laryngeal muscles. An aortic arch aneurysm can stretch or compress this nerve, causing left vocal-cord palsy and hoarseness (Ortner cardiovocal syndrome), so R correctly explains A. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve instead hooks under the right subclavian artery.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy — Thorax (Vagus and Recurrent Laryngeal Nerves)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The ligamentum arteriosum, the fibrous remnant of the ductus arteriosus, connects the:
options: Superior vena cava to the right atrium
Ascending aorta to the pulmonary trunk at the level of the valves
Left atrium to the descending thoracic aorta
Root of the left pulmonary artery (pulmonary trunk) to the arch of the aorta
questions.concept: The ligamentum arteriosum is the post-natal remnant of the ductus arteriosus; it connects the beginning of the left pulmonary artery (or the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk) to the inferior concave surface of the aortic arch, just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around it. Failure of the ductus to close produces a patent ductus arteriosus with a left-to-right shunt and a continuous machinery murmur.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Arch of Aorta and Ligamentum Arteriosum)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: After ascending on the right side of the vertebral column, the azygos vein arches forward over the root of the right lung to drain into the:
questions.concept: The azygos vein ascends in the posterior mediastinum on the right of the vertebral bodies, and at about the T4 level it arches forward over the root of the right lung (the arch of the azygos) to open into the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava, just before the SVC pierces the pericardium. It receives the right posterior intercostal veins, the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, and bronchial and oesophageal veins, and forms an important caval–caval collateral channel in IVC obstruction.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students — Thorax (Azygos System of Veins)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: An aspirated peanut in a supine adult is more likely to lodge in the right main bronchus because, compared with the left, the right main bronchus is:
options: Wider, shorter and more vertical (more in line with the trachea)
The first branch of the trachea, arising above the carina
Directly continuous with the lingular bronchus
questions.concept: The right main (principal) bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, running more directly in continuity with the trachea below the carina; consequently inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated material pass more readily into it and into the right lung. The left main bronchus is narrower, longer and more horizontal as it passes below the arch of the aorta. The carina is the internal ridge at the tracheal bifurcation, and both main bronchi arise there, not above it.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Trachea and Bronchi)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm, at the level of the T10 vertebra, transmits the oesophagus together with which nerves?
questions.concept: The oesophageal hiatus lies at the T10 level within the muscular sling of the right crus of the diaphragm and transmits the oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (derived mainly from the left and right vagi respectively after the oesophageal plexus) and the oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels. In contrast, the caval opening (T8) transmits the IVC and right phrenic branches, and the aortic hiatus (T12) transmits the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Diaphragm and its Openings)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The inferior vena cava pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of which vertebra?
questions.concept: The caval opening for the inferior vena cava lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 level and also transmits terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve; being in the tendon, its margins are attached to the vein, so descent of the diaphragm on inspiration widens it and aids venous return. The three main diaphragmatic apertures are remembered as T8 (caval), T10 (oesophageal) and T12 (aortic) — the mnemonic I ate (8) ten (10) eggs at twelve (12).
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Diaphragm)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The phrenic nerve, the sole motor supply to the diaphragm, arises from which spinal cord segments?
questions.concept: The phrenic nerve arises from the ventral rami of C3, C4 and C5 (chiefly C4), summarised as C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive. It provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm and carries sensory fibres from the fibrous pericardium, mediastinal parietal pleura and the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum. High cervical cord lesions above C3 therefore abolish diaphragmatic breathing, whereas lesions below C5 spare it.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Phrenic Nerve)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Irritation of the central diaphragmatic peritoneum (for example by a subphrenic abscess) is classically referred to the tip of the shoulder because the phrenic nerve shares its segmental origin with the supraclavicular nerves, namely:
questions.concept: The central part of the diaphragm receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve (C3–C5, predominantly C3–C4). The supraclavicular nerves supplying the skin over the shoulder tip also arise from C3–C4, so central diaphragmatic irritation is referred to the shoulder tip (as in Kehr sign with splenic rupture or subphrenic collections). The peripheral rim of the diaphragm is instead supplied by the lower intercostal nerves, so peripheral irritation is referred to the thoraco-abdominal wall.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy — Thorax (Phrenic Nerve and Referred Pain)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: During chest-drain insertion the instrument is passed immediately above the upper border of the lower rib of the space. This avoids the main intercostal neurovascular bundle, whose structures lie in the costal groove in which order from superior to inferior?
questions.concept: In the costal groove along the lower border of each upper rib the main intercostal neurovascular bundle is arranged from above downward as Vein, Artery, Nerve (mnemonic VAN). Because these lie tucked under the rib above the space, entry is made just above the upper border of the rib below the space (over the middle of the space), where only a smaller collateral bundle runs, minimising the risk of injuring the main vessels and nerve. The safe triangle for drains is bordered by pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and the fifth intercostal space.
questions.reference: Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions, Chapter 3 — The Thorax (Intercostal Spaces and Neurovascular Bundle)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The transverse pericardial sinus is a passage within the pericardial cavity that lies posterior to the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk and anterior to the:
options: Inferior vena cava and right ventricle
Superior vena cava and the left atrium
questions.concept: The transverse pericardial sinus is the space enclosed as the serous pericardium reflects around the arterial and venous groups of great vessels; it lies behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk (the arterial mesocardium) and in front of the superior vena cava and the atria (left atrium). A finger or ligature passed through this sinus can be used to clamp or ligate the aorta and pulmonary trunk together during cardiac surgery. The oblique pericardial sinus is a separate cul-de-sac behind the left atrium.
questions.reference: Gray's Anatomy for Students — Thorax (Pericardium and its Sinuses)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Assertion (A): A small but rapidly accumulating pericardial effusion may precipitate cardiac tamponade. Reason (R): The tough fibrous pericardium is relatively inextensible and cannot stretch acutely to accommodate the added volume. Choose the most appropriate option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The fibrous pericardium is a strong, inelastic sac, so fluid entering the pericardial cavity rapidly (as in trauma or aortic rupture) causes a steep rise in intrapericardial pressure that compresses the thin-walled atria and ventricles, impairing venous return and diastolic filling — cardiac tamponade, with Beck triad of hypotension, muffled heart sounds and raised jugular venous pressure. Slowly forming effusions allow the pericardium to stretch and can reach large volumes before compromise, so R correctly explains A.
questions.reference: Moore's Clinically Oriented Anatomy — Thorax (Pericardium and Cardiac Tamponade)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The thoracic duct, the largest lymphatic channel of the body, most commonly terminates by opening into the venous system at the junction of the:
options: Right subclavian and right internal jugular veins
Left brachiocephalic vein and the superior vena cava
Azygos vein and the superior vena cava
Left subclavian and left internal jugular veins
questions.concept: The thoracic duct begins at the cisterna chyli (about L1–L2), enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus (T12), ascends in the posterior mediastinum on the right, crosses to the left at about T5, and finally opens into the venous system at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins. It drains lymph from the whole body except the right head and neck, right upper limb and right hemithorax, which are drained by the right lymphatic duct.
questions.reference: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy Vol 1 — Thorax (Thoracic Duct)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which enzyme of the urea cycle catalyzes the reaction that directly yields urea?
questions.concept: Arginase catalyzes the fifth and final urea-cycle step, hydrolysing arginine into urea plus ornithine, and ornithine re-enters the mitochondrion to keep the cycle turning. CPS-I and ornithine transcarbamoylase form carbamoyl phosphate and citrulline, while argininosuccinate synthetase makes argininosuccinate; none of these liberate free urea, so arginase is the sole direct urea-generating enzyme.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — The Urea Cycle (Catabolism of Proteins & of Amino Acid Nitrogen)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A neonate develops lethargy, poor feeding and hyperammonemia; plasma citrulline is markedly elevated (>1000 µmol/L) while orotic acid is not raised. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely?
questions.concept: Argininosuccinate synthetase condenses citrulline with aspartate, so its deficiency (citrullinemia type I) blocks the cycle just after citrulline and plasma citrulline rises markedly, often above 1000 µmol/L, with hyperammonemia. OTC deficiency instead causes low citrulline with high orotic acid; CPS-I deficiency gives low citrulline and low orotate; arginase deficiency raises arginine — so grossly elevated citrulline is the decisive clue.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 19: Removal of Nitrogen from Amino Acids / Urea Cycle Disorders

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: An infant with hyperammonemia has abnormally brittle hair that fractures easily (trichorrhexis nodosa) and greatly elevated argininosuccinate in blood and urine. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.concept: Argininosuccinate lyase cleaves argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate; its deficiency (argininosuccinic aciduria) causes accumulation of argininosuccinate in blood and urine with hyperammonemia, and the characteristic brittle, easily fractured hair (trichorrhexis nodosa) attributed to arginine deficiency. OTC deficiency raises orotate, argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency raises citrulline, and arginase deficiency raises arginine — elevated argininosuccinate is diagnostic here.
questions.reference: Vasudevan — Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students — Urea Cycle and Metabolism of Ammonia

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the committed step of the urea cycle, is absolutely dependent on which allosteric activator?
questions.concept: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the rate-limiting mitochondrial entry enzyme of the urea cycle, is obligately dependent on the allosteric activator N-acetylglutamate, which is synthesized from glutamate and acetyl-CoA by N-acetylglutamate synthase and is itself stimulated by arginine. Aspartate enters later via argininosuccinate synthetase, fumarate is a downstream product, and GTP is unrelated — only N-acetylglutamate activates CPS-I.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — The Urea Cycle: Regulation and N-Acetylglutamate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 3-year-old child has progressive spastic diplegia, developmental regression and only episodic mild hyperammonemia, with elevated plasma arginine. Which urea-cycle enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.concept: Arginase deficiency (argininemia) is atypical among urea-cycle defects: rather than catastrophic neonatal hyperammonemia it usually presents later with progressive spastic diplegia or tetraplegia, developmental regression and seizures, raised plasma arginine, and only episodic mild hyperammonemia. CPS-I, OTC and citrullinemia typically manifest as severe neonatal encephalopathy, distinguishing them from this milder, spasticity-dominant presentation.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 19: Urea Cycle Disorders

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: How does sodium benzoate lower blood ammonia in a child with a urea-cycle disorder?
options: It converts ammonia directly into urea
It chelates ammonia directly in the blood
It conjugates with glycine to form hippurate, which is excreted in urine
questions.concept: Sodium benzoate opens a nitrogen-disposal route that bypasses the defective urea cycle: it conjugates with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is excreted renally, removing one nitrogen per glycine molecule. Sodium phenylacetate/phenylbutyrate similarly conjugate glutamine to phenylacetylglutamine. These agents do not synthesize urea, kill bacteria, or directly chelate ammonia — the mechanism is amino-acid conjugation followed by urinary excretion.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Metabolic Disorders of the Urea Cycle and Their Treatment

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: By which mechanism does oral lactulose reduce blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
options: It acts as a systemic antibiotic killing urease-producing bacteria
It acidifies the colonic lumen, trapping ammonia as non-absorbable ammonium for excretion
questions.concept: Lactulose, a non-absorbable disaccharide, is fermented by colonic bacteria to lactic and acetic acids that acidify the lumen; this shifts NH3 to non-absorbable ammonium (NH4+), which is trapped and excreted, while its cathartic effect and reduction of ammoniagenic flora further lower ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy. It is not an antibiotic, an antacid, or a stimulator of hepatic urea synthesis.
questions.reference: Vasudevan — Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students — Metabolism of Ammonia and Hepatic Coma

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which compound is the principal non-toxic transport form of ammonia in the blood?
questions.concept: Glutamine is the principal non-toxic transport form of ammonia in blood; glutamine synthetase incorporates free NH3 into glutamate to form glutamine (especially important in brain and muscle), which is carried to liver and kidney where glutaminase releases the ammonia. Alanine also shuttles nitrogen but chiefly via the glucose-alanine cycle, aspartate donates nitrogen within the urea cycle, and urea is the excretory end-product rather than a transport form.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Catabolism of Proteins & of Amino Acid Nitrogen (Ammonia Transport)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Glutamate dehydrogenase is the principal enzyme that liberates free ammonia from amino-acid nitrogen in the liver. Reason (R): Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes oxidative deamination of glutamate and can use either NAD+ or NADP+ as its coenzyme. Select the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Glutamate dehydrogenase is the major enzyme performing oxidative deamination: amino groups are first funnelled onto α-ketoglutarate to form glutamate by transamination, then glutamate dehydrogenase releases free ammonia and regenerates α-ketoglutarate, uniquely using either NAD+ or NADP+. It is inhibited by GTP/ATP and activated by ADP/GDP. Both statements are true and the reason correctly explains the mechanism by which ammonia is liberated, so the answer is A.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Catabolism of Proteins & of Amino Acid Nitrogen (Oxidative Deamination)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: In the glucose-alanine cycle, which amino acid carries amino-group nitrogen from skeletal muscle to the liver?
questions.concept: In the glucose-alanine cycle, muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine using amino groups derived from amino-acid catabolism; alanine travels to the liver, where it is transaminated back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis while its nitrogen enters the urea cycle. Glutamine is the other major nitrogen carrier but is not the muscle-specific glucogenic shuttle, and aspartate and glycine do not serve this transport role.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 19: The Glucose-Alanine Cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which pair of amino acids is exclusively (purely) ketogenic?
questions.concept: Leucine and lysine are the only two amino acids that are purely (exclusively) ketogenic — their carbon skeletons yield only acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate and cannot be used to make glucose. Isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and threonine are both glucogenic and ketogenic, whereas valine is purely glucogenic; therefore only the leucine-plus-lysine pairing is entirely ketogenic.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Catabolism of the Carbon Skeletons of Amino Acids

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following amino acids is both glucogenic and ketogenic?
questions.concept: Isoleucine is both glucogenic and ketogenic because its skeleton yields acetyl-CoA (ketogenic) and propionyl-CoA/succinyl-CoA (glucogenic). Leucine is purely ketogenic, whereas alanine and valine are purely glucogenic. The classic five amino acids that are both glucogenic and ketogenic are isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and threonine, so isoleucine is the correct dual-fate answer here.
questions.reference: Vasudevan — Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students — Glucogenic and Ketogenic Amino Acids

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is a nutritionally essential (indispensable) amino acid?
questions.concept: Methionine is a nutritionally essential (indispensable) amino acid that must be supplied in the diet because the human body cannot synthesize its carbon skeleton. The essentials are commonly memorized as PVT TIM HALL — phenylalanine, valine, threonine, tryptophan, isoleucine, methionine, histidine, arginine (semi-essential), leucine and lysine. Alanine, serine and glutamate are non-essential and synthesized endogenously, so methionine is the only essential option listed.
questions.reference: Satyanarayana — Biochemistry — Metabolism of Amino Acids (Essential and Non-essential Amino Acids)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: An infant with phenylketonuria is placed on a phenylalanine-restricted diet, yet develops seizures and progressive neurological deterioration despite normal blood phenylalanine. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.concept: Persisting neurological deterioration despite a phenylalanine-restricted diet and normal blood phenylalanine points to tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency, so-called malignant PKU, from defects in BH4 synthesis or dihydropteridine reductase. BH4 is the cofactor not only for phenylalanine hydroxylase but also for tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, so its lack cripples dopamine and serotonin synthesis; treatment must add BH4 plus L-DOPA and 5-HTP, not diet alone.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Phenylketonuria and Tetrahydrobiopterin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man notes that his urine turns black on standing and has bluish-black discoloration of the ear cartilage and sclerae with degenerative spinal arthritis. Deficiency of which enzyme is responsible?
questions.concept: Alkaptonuria is a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase (homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase) in the tyrosine degradation pathway, causing accumulation of homogentisic acid. Urine darkens on standing or alkalinization, and oxidized pigment deposits in cartilage and connective tissue (ochronosis), producing bluish-black ears and sclerae with a degenerative arthropathy of the spine. Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU, and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes tyrosinemia type I.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Catabolism of the Carbon Skeletons of Amino Acids (Alkaptonuria)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A neonate has poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy, and the urine smells like maple syrup; branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids are elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.concept: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which blocks oxidative decarboxylation of the keto acids of leucine, isoleucine and valine. These branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate, producing the sweet maple-syrup odour of urine and severe neonatal neurotoxicity; the complex uses thiamine (TPP), lipoate, FAD, NAD and CoA, and some cases are thiamine-responsive.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Maple Syrup Urine Disease

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A young adult with recurrent renal stones has hexagonal crystals in the urine and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test. Which defect best explains this?
options: Lysosomal accumulation of cystine within cells
Defective renal and intestinal transport of cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine
questions.concept: Cystinuria is an inherited defect of the renal tubular and intestinal transporter for the dibasic amino acids cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine (mnemonic COLA); poorly soluble cystine precipitates as characteristic hexagonal crystals and recurrent radio-opaque calculi, with a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test. It must be distinguished from cystinosis, a lysosomal cystine-storage disease causing renal Fanconi syndrome rather than stones, and from cystathionine β-synthase deficiency (homocystinuria).
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Disorders of Amino Acid Transport (Cystinuria)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step of catecholamine biosynthesis?
questions.concept: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyzes the rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis, converting tyrosine to L-DOPA using tetrahydrobiopterin; L-DOPA is then decarboxylated to dopamine, hydroxylated to noradrenaline by dopamine β-hydroxylase, and N-methylated to adrenaline by phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase. Because tyrosine hydroxylase controls flux into the whole pathway, it is the pace-setting enzyme, not the downstream steps.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Conversion of Amino Acids to Specialized Products (Catecholamines)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Serotonin and melatonin are synthesized from which amino acid?
questions.concept: Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine): tryptophan hydroxylase forms 5-hydroxytryptophan, which is decarboxylated to serotonin, and in the pineal gland serotonin is acetylated and methylated to melatonin. Tyrosine gives rise to catecholamines, histidine yields histamine, and glutamate yields GABA — only tryptophan produces both serotonin and melatonin.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Amino Acid-Derived Products (Serotonin and Melatonin)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient with Hartnup disease develops a pellagra-like photosensitive dermatitis. Reduced endogenous synthesis of which vitamin best explains this?
questions.concept: Tryptophan is converted via the kynurenine pathway to niacin/NAD, with roughly 60 mg tryptophan yielding about 1 mg niacin. In Hartnup disease the intestinal and renal transport of neutral amino acids including tryptophan is impaired, so less tryptophan is available for niacin synthesis and a pellagra-like dermatitis, diarrhoea and neurological signs appear. The deficient vitamin synthesizable from tryptophan is therefore niacin, not riboflavin, thiamine or folate.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Conversion of Amino Acids to Specialized Products (Tryptophan and Niacin)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Assertion (A): S-adenosylmethionine is the body's principal donor of methyl groups. Reason (R): S-adenosylmethionine is synthesized from methionine and ATP. Select the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), formed from methionine and ATP, is indeed the body's principal methyl donor in reactions such as synthesis of creatine, phosphatidylcholine, adrenaline and in DNA methylation, becoming S-adenosylhomocysteine after methyl transfer. However, the reason given describes only its formation, not why it donates methyl groups (which is the high-energy, reactive methyl-sulfonium bond); hence both statements are true but the reason does not explain the assertion, so the answer is B.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Conversion of Amino Acids to Specialized Products (S-Adenosylmethionine)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Remethylation of homocysteine to methionine by methionine synthase requires which pair of cofactors?
questions.concept: Remethylation of homocysteine to methionine is catalyzed by methionine synthase (homocysteine methyltransferase), which requires methylcobalamin (vitamin B12) as the enzyme cofactor and N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate as the methyl donor, linking folate and B12 metabolism. B12 deficiency traps folate as methyl-THF (the methyl-folate trap) and raises both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid; pyridoxal phosphate instead serves the alternative transsulfuration route, not remethylation.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Sulfur-Containing Amino Acids; Homocysteine, Folate and B12

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Glutathione is a tripeptide containing an atypical peptide linkage. Reason (R): In glutathione the glutamate residue is joined to cysteine through its γ-carboxyl group rather than its α-carboxyl group. Select the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Glutathione is the tripeptide γ-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine and the major intracellular antioxidant, reduced by glutathione reductase using NADPH from the HMP shunt. It contains an atypical peptide bond precisely because glutamate is joined to cysteine through its γ-carboxyl group rather than its α-carboxyl group, which protects it from ordinary peptidases. Both statements are true and the γ-linkage is exactly what makes the bond atypical, so the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Conversion of Amino Acids to Specialized Products (Glutathione)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which reaction is the major source of one-carbon units as N5,N10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate?
options: Conversion of serine to glycine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase
questions.concept: The largest source of one-carbon units is the conversion of serine to glycine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase, a pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent enzyme that transfers serine's β-carbon to tetrahydrofolate, generating N5,N10-methylene-THF. This folate-bound one-carbon pool feeds thymidylate, purine and methionine synthesis. β-oxidation of fatty acids, oxidative deamination of glutamate and decarboxylation of histidine do not supply the methylene-THF pool.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Folic Acid and One-Carbon Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Creatine is synthesized in the body from which three amino acids?
questions.concept: Creatine is synthesized from three amino acids: the kidney enzyme arginine-glycine amidinotransferase joins arginine and glycine to form guanidinoacetate (releasing ornithine), and the liver then methylates guanidinoacetate using S-adenosylmethionine derived from methionine to yield creatine. Creatine is phosphorylated to phosphocreatine in muscle and non-enzymatically cyclizes to creatinine, which is excreted. The correct trio is therefore glycine, arginine and methionine.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Conversion of Amino Acids to Specialized Products (Creatine and Creatinine)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes hepatic glucokinase from hexokinase?
options: Glucokinase has a low Km for glucose and is strongly inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase has a high Km for glucose and is not inhibited by physiological levels of glucose-6-phosphate
Glucokinase is present in all tissues, whereas hexokinase is confined to the liver
Glucokinase phosphorylates glucose only during hypoglycaemia
questions.concept: Glucokinase (hexokinase IV) has a high Km (~10 mmol/L), so it is only active after a carbohydrate meal, has a high Vmax, is induced by insulin, and is NOT inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate (it is regulated by GKRP). Hexokinase I-III are ubiquitous, have a low Km (~0.1 mmol/L) so are saturated at normal glucose, and are product-inhibited by G6P. Option A actually describes hexokinase; C reverses the distributions (hexokinase is ubiquitous); D is wrong because glucokinase acts postprandially when glucose is high, not in hypoglycaemia.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 8: Glycolysis (Hexokinase vs Glucokinase)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The single most potent allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) in the liver is:
questions.concept: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, produced by the kinase activity of PFK-2 in the fed/insulin state, is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1; it raises the enzyme's affinity for fructose-6-phosphate and overrides ATP-mediated inhibition. AMP also activates PFK-1. Citrate and ATP are inhibitors, signalling an energy-rich cell (high citrate = abundant biosynthetic precursors). Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is the PRODUCT of PFK-1 (it feed-forward activates pyruvate kinase, not PFK-1), so it is not the activator asked for.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 18: Glycolysis & the Oxidation of Pyruvate (Regulation of PFK-1)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: In glycolysis, ATP is generated by substrate-level phosphorylation at the reactions catalysed by:
questions.concept: Substrate-level phosphorylation means ATP is formed by direct transfer of a high-energy phosphate from a substrate to ADP. In glycolysis this occurs twice: phosphoglycerate kinase (1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 3-phosphoglycerate) and pyruvate kinase (phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate). Hexokinase and PFK-1 CONSUME ATP. GAPDH creates the high-energy 1,3-BPG and NADH but does not itself make ATP, and enolase only forms PEP; aldolase and triose phosphate isomerase are cleavage/isomerisation steps with no ATP change.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 18: Glycolysis & the Oxidation of Pyruvate

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The net ATP yield from the anaerobic conversion of one molecule of glucose to lactate is:
questions.concept: In anaerobic glycolysis, 2 ATP are invested (hexokinase and PFK-1) and 4 ATP are produced (two phosphoglycerate kinase and two pyruvate kinase reactions per glucose), giving a NET of 2 ATP. The NADH made at the GAPDH step is re-oxidised by lactate dehydrogenase (pyruvate to lactate) to regenerate NAD+, so it yields no additional ATP anaerobically. Complete aerobic oxidation yields roughly 30-32 ATP. Option A ignores the two net ATP; 6 and 8 overestimate the anaerobic yield.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 8: Glycolysis (Energy yield)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Arsenate (a pentavalent arsenic compound) reduces the net ATP yield of glycolysis without stopping the pathway because it:
options: Blocks lactate dehydrogenase and traps NADH
Chelates the Mg2+ ion required by pyruvate kinase
Substitutes for inorganic phosphate at the GAPDH step, forming an unstable 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate that hydrolyses spontaneously
questions.concept: Arsenate mimics inorganic phosphate at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step, forming 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate, which spontaneously hydrolyses to 3-phosphoglycerate without generating 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. This bypasses the phosphoglycerate kinase substrate-level phosphorylation (arsenolysis), so glycolysis continues and NADH is still made, but the net ATP is lost. Note that trivalent arsenite (not arsenate) is the species that inhibits lipoic-acid enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase; the other options describe unrelated toxic mechanisms.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 18: Glycolysis & the Oxidation of Pyruvate (Arsenate/Arsenite)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A blood sample for glucose estimation is collected in a grey-top tube containing sodium fluoride. Fluoride preserves the glucose value by inhibiting which glycolytic enzyme?
questions.concept: Sodium fluoride forms a magnesium-fluorophosphate complex that inhibits enolase (2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate), halting glycolysis in the collected sample so that red cells and leukocytes cannot continue consuming glucose in vitro — this prevents a falsely low reading. Fluoride is usually combined with potassium oxalate (the anticoagulant) in grey-top tubes. Hexokinase, pyruvate kinase and lactate dehydrogenase are not the specific targets of fluoride's glycolysis-preserving action.
questions.reference: Vasudevan's Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students, 9th ed. — Chapter: Major Metabolic Pathways of Glucose (Glycolysis)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Assertion (A): 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate shifts the erythrocyte oxygen dissociation curve to the right. Reason (R): 2,3-BPG binds to and stabilises the deoxygenated (T, taut) conformation of haemoglobin, lowering its affinity for oxygen. Select the correct option:
options: Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both the assertion and the reason are true, but the reason is NOT the correct explanation of the assertion
The assertion is true, but the reason is false
The assertion is false, but the reason is true
questions.concept: 2,3-BPG is produced in the erythrocyte Rapoport-Luebering shunt by bisphosphoglycerate mutase from 1,3-BPG. It binds in the central cavity between the beta-chains of deoxyhaemoglobin, stabilising the low-affinity T (taut) state; this lowers oxygen affinity and shifts the dissociation curve to the right, favouring oxygen unloading in tissues (it rises in chronic hypoxia, anaemia and at high altitude). Both statements are true and the reason correctly explains the assertion, so the answer is option A.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 18: Glycolysis (Rapoport-Luebering / 2,3-BPG) and Chapter 6: Proteins - Myoglobin & Haemoglobin

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child with chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia is found to have an autosomal recessive enzyme defect. Red cells show low ATP with markedly elevated 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. The deficient enzyme is:
questions.concept: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is the commonest glycolytic-enzyme defect causing hereditary (autosomal recessive) haemolytic anaemia. Mature red cells rely solely on glycolysis for ATP; a pyruvate kinase block lowers ATP, causing membrane cation-pump failure, dehydrated rigid cells and splenic haemolysis. Upstream intermediates accumulate, including 2,3-BPG, which right-shifts the oxygen curve and partly offsets the anaemia. G6PD deficiency instead causes episodic OXIDATIVE haemolysis with Heinz bodies (not a chronic low-ATP picture); hexokinase and PFK-1 deficiencies are far rarer.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 8: Glycolysis (Pyruvate kinase deficiency)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which set correctly lists all five coenzymes required by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex?
options: Biotin, thiamine pyrophosphate, NAD+, FAD, coenzyme A
Pyridoxal phosphate, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD+, coenzyme A
Thiamine pyrophosphate, biotin, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD+
Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, coenzyme A, FAD, NAD+
questions.concept: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex uses five coenzymes: thiamine pyrophosphate (E1, decarboxylation), lipoic acid (E2, acyl transfer), coenzyme A (accepts the acetyl group to form acetyl-CoA), FAD (E3, dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase) and NAD+ (final electron acceptor). A common mnemonic is 'Tender Loving Care For Nancy'. Biotin (used in carboxylations) and pyridoxal phosphate (used in transaminations) are NOT PDH cofactors, so options A, B and C are wrong. The same five cofactors serve the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 18: Oxidation of Pyruvate (Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Chronic arsenic (arsenite) poisoning impairs the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate. The molecular basis is that arsenite:
options: Competes with thiamine pyrophosphate at the E1 subunit
Prevents NAD+ from accepting electrons at E3
Binds the two adjacent thiol (-SH) groups of reduced lipoic acid, inactivating the complex
Cleaves coenzyme A into inactive fragments
questions.concept: Trivalent arsenicals (arsenite) bind covalently to the vicinal dithiol (two adjacent -SH) groups of reduced lipoic acid (dihydrolipoamide), inactivating both the pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes; pyruvate and lactate therefore accumulate. This is why dimercaprol (BAL), itself a dithiol, is the antidote — it competes with the tissue dithiols for the arsenic. Arsenite is not a TPP competitor, and neither NAD+ nor coenzyme A is its direct molecular target.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 9: TCA Cycle & Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (Arsenite/lipoic acid)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A neonate presents with severe congenital lactic acidosis and progressive neurological impairment. Blood shows elevated lactate and pyruvate with a normal lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. The most likely defect is:
questions.concept: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (often X-linked E1-alpha) blocks the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, so pyruvate builds up and is shunted to lactate, producing congenital lactic acidosis with neurological damage (the brain depends heavily on glucose oxidation). Because the block is BEFORE the electron-transport-dependent steps, both pyruvate and lactate rise and the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio stays normal (a high ratio suggests a respiratory-chain defect). Von Gierke disease also causes lactic acidosis but with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia; MCAD is a fatty-acid oxidation defect; OTC deficiency causes hyperammonaemia.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 18: Oxidation of Pyruvate (PDH deficiency, lactic acidosis)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Assay of which erythrocyte enzyme, tested for activation by added thiamine pyrophosphate in vitro, best confirms the underlying vitamin deficiency?
questions.concept: The triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia is Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, common in alcoholics. Erythrocyte transketolase — a TPP-dependent enzyme of the non-oxidative HMP pathway — has reduced activity in thiamine deficiency; adding TPP in vitro causes a large increase in activity (the 'TPP effect', typically greater than 15-25 percent), confirming the deficiency. G6PD is assayed for G6PD deficiency; glutathione reductase activation tests riboflavin (B2) status; pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin enzyme, not TPP-dependent.
questions.reference: Vasudevan's Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students, 9th ed. — Chapter: Vitamins (Thiamine) and HMP Shunt (Transketolase)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The only reaction of the citric acid cycle that directly produces a high-energy nucleoside triphosphate (GTP) by substrate-level phosphorylation is catalysed by:
questions.concept: Succinyl-CoA synthetase (succinate thiokinase) converts succinyl-CoA to succinate, using the energy of the thioester bond to phosphorylate GDP to GTP (in some tissues ADP to ATP). This is the sole substrate-level phosphorylation step of the TCA cycle. Citrate synthase forms citrate — the hydrolysis of its thioester merely drives the condensation, with no nucleotide made. Isocitrate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase are oxidations that generate NADH, not a nucleoside triphosphate.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 17: The Citric Acid Cycle

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Citrate synthase is the principal rate-limiting enzyme of the citric acid cycle. Reason (R): Isocitrate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by ADP and inhibited by ATP and NADH. Select the correct option:
options: Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both the assertion and the reason are true, but the reason is NOT the correct explanation of the assertion
The assertion is true, but the reason is false
The assertion is false, but the reason is true
questions.concept: The assertion is FALSE: isocitrate dehydrogenase — not citrate synthase — is generally taught as the principal rate-limiting and regulatory enzyme of the citric acid cycle. The reason is TRUE: isocitrate dehydrogenase is allosterically activated by ADP (and Ca2+) and inhibited by ATP and NADH, coupling cycle flux to the cellular energy charge. Citrate synthase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are additional control points, but the classic rate-limiting step is isocitrate dehydrogenase. A false assertion with a true reason is answer option D.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 17: The Citric Acid Cycle (Regulation)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Fluoroacetate (the rodenticide 'compound 1080') is lethal because it undergoes conversion in vivo to fluorocitrate, which inhibits the citric acid cycle enzyme:
questions.concept: Fluoroacetate is itself non-toxic until it is converted to fluoroacetyl-CoA and then condensed with oxaloacetate (by citrate synthase) to form fluorocitrate, a potent inhibitor of aconitase. This is the classic example of 'lethal synthesis' (Peters): the cycle stalls at the citrate-to-isocitrate isomerisation, citrate accumulates, and ATP production collapses. Fumarase, citrate synthase and succinate dehydrogenase are not the targets of fluorocitrate, which acts specifically on aconitase.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 9: Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle (Fluoroacetate / aconitase)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Pyruvate carboxylase is a key anaplerotic enzyme that replenishes oxaloacetate for the citric acid cycle. Reason (R): Pyruvate carboxylase requires biotin as its coenzyme. Select the correct option:
options: Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion
Both the assertion and the reason are true, but the reason is NOT the correct explanation of the assertion
The assertion is true, but the reason is false
The assertion is false, but the reason is true
questions.concept: Both statements are individually true. Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate and is the most important anaplerotic ('filling-up') reaction, replacing TCA intermediates withdrawn for biosynthesis; and it does require biotin (a CO2 carrier) plus allosteric activation by acetyl-CoA. However, the requirement for biotin is NOT the reason the enzyme is anaplerotic — its anaplerotic role stems from the fact that its product is oxaloacetate, a cycle intermediate. Two true statements where the reason does not explain the assertion is answer option B.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 17: The Citric Acid Cycle (Anaplerotic reactions)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: One complete turn of the citric acid cycle, oxidising one molecule of acetyl-CoA, directly yields:
questions.concept: Per acetyl-CoA, one turn of the citric acid cycle produces 3 NADH (isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase), 1 FADH2 (succinate dehydrogenase) and 1 GTP (succinyl-CoA synthetase), releasing 2 CO2. Through oxidative phosphorylation this corresponds to about 10 ATP (3 x 2.5 + 1 x 1.5 + 1). The other options misallocate the number of reduced coenzymes; only option C matches the correct 3 NADH : 1 FADH2 : 1 GTP stoichiometry.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 9: Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle (Energy yield)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Pyruvate carboxylase, the first committed enzyme of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate, requires which coenzyme and which allosteric activator, respectively?
questions.concept: Pyruvate carboxylase is a mitochondrial, biotin-dependent enzyme that carboxylates pyruvate to oxaloacetate (ATP-driven, with CO2 carried on biotin). It is allosterically ACTIVATED by acetyl-CoA: when acetyl-CoA is abundant it signals that pyruvate should be directed to oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis rather than through pyruvate dehydrogenase. TPP, lipoic acid and NADPH are cofactors of other enzymes, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate regulates glycolysis (PFK-1/PFK-2), not pyruvate carboxylase, so only option D is correct.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 19: Gluconeogenesis & the Control of Blood Glucose

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which enzyme, present in liver and kidney but absent in skeletal muscle, catalyses the final step — common to both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis — that releases free glucose into the blood?
questions.concept: Glucose-6-phosphatase, located on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane of liver, kidney and intestine, hydrolyses glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose, allowing these organs to export glucose to maintain blood levels. Skeletal muscle LACKS this enzyme, so muscle glycogen and glucose-6-phosphate cannot directly raise blood glucose. Its deficiency causes von Gierke disease (GSD type I) with fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis. Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase acts one step earlier and only in gluconeogenesis; phosphoglucomutase and glucokinase do not liberate free glucose.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 10: Gluconeogenesis (Glucose-6-phosphatase)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: In the Cori cycle, lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in exercising muscle is carried to the liver, where it is used mainly to:
options: Be completely oxidised to CO2 and water to power muscle contraction
Be reconverted to glucose by gluconeogenesis, which then returns to the muscle
Be converted to ketone bodies for use by the brain
Be excreted unchanged by the kidney
questions.concept: The Cori (lactic acid) cycle recycles carbon between muscle and liver: lactate released by exercising muscle travels in the blood to the liver, where lactate dehydrogenase regenerates pyruvate and gluconeogenesis remakes glucose. This glucose returns to the muscle. The process is energetically costly (about 6 ATP consumed in the liver versus 2 ATP gained in the muscle) but shifts the metabolic burden to the liver and prevents lactic acidosis. It is not net oxidation in the liver, ketogenesis, or renal excretion.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 19: Gluconeogenesis & the Control of Blood Glucose (Cori cycle)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A boy of Mediterranean descent develops acute haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies after eating fava beans. The enzyme he is deficient in normally supplies the erythrocyte with which protective molecule?
options: ATP for the membrane cation pumps
NADPH to keep glutathione in the reduced state against oxidative stress
questions.concept: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is the committed, rate-limiting enzyme of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and generates NADPH. In red cells NADPH keeps glutathione reduced (via glutathione reductase), the main defence against oxidant (H2O2) injury. In G6PD deficiency (X-linked; triggered by fava beans, oxidant drugs or infection) oxidised haemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, and splenic macrophages create 'bite' cells, causing haemolysis. Although the pathway also yields ribose-5-phosphate, in the mature erythrocyte the protective role is NADPH/glutathione, not nucleotide synthesis; ATP and 2,3-BPG come from glycolysis.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 12: Pentose Phosphate Pathway & NADPH (G6PD deficiency)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: An infant develops vomiting, hypoglycaemia, jaundice and hepatomegaly whenever fruit or sucrose is introduced into the diet, but remains well on breast milk alone. Deficiency of which enzyme, leading to accumulation of fructose-1-phosphate, is responsible?
questions.concept: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructokinase still forms fructose-1-phosphate, but aldolase B cannot cleave it, so fructose-1-phosphate accumulates: it sequesters inorganic phosphate and inhibits both glycogenolysis (phosphorylase) and gluconeogenesis, producing severe hypoglycaemia along with liver and kidney toxicity. Symptoms begin when fructose or sucrose is introduced (weaning, fruit), not on lactose-based breast milk. Fructokinase deficiency (essential fructosuria) is benign; galactokinase deficiency affects galactose (cataracts); glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is von Gierke disease.
questions.reference: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th ed. — Chapter 13: Metabolism of Monosaccharides (Hereditary Fructose Intolerance)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A healthy, asymptomatic child is incidentally found to have a urine sample that is positive on a copper-reduction (Benedict's) test but negative on a glucose-oxidase dipstick. The most likely benign explanation is deficiency of:
questions.concept: Essential fructosuria results from deficiency of fructokinase (ketohexokinase) and is a benign, asymptomatic condition: unmetabolised fructose spills into the urine, giving a POSITIVE reducing-sugar test (Benedict's, which detects any reducing sugar) but a NEGATIVE glucose-specific dipstick (glucose oxidase). No treatment is needed. Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) is symptomatic and dangerous; GALT deficiency causes classic galactosaemia; and G6PD deficiency causes haemolysis, not a reducing sugar in the urine — so the benign answer is fructokinase deficiency.
questions.reference: Vasudevan's Textbook of Biochemistry for Medical Students, 9th ed. — Chapter: Metabolism of Fructose and Galactose

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child has hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia and ketosis. Liver glycogen has abnormally short outer branches (a limit-dextrin-like structure), while blood lactate and uric acid are near normal. The deficient enzyme is:
questions.concept: Cori/Forbes disease (glycogen storage disease type III) is due to deficiency of the debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase): glycogen with short outer branches resembling limit dextrin accumulates. It is milder than von Gierke disease, and because gluconeogenesis is intact, blood lactate and uric acid are near normal. Myophosphorylase deficiency is McArdle disease (type V, exercise cramps, no rise in venous lactate on exercise); branching enzyme deficiency is Andersen disease (type IV, cirrhosis, amylopectin-like glycogen); acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency is Pompe disease (type II, lysosomal, cardiomegaly).
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st ed. — Chapter 20: Metabolism of Glycogen (Glycogen Storage Diseases)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Transport of long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane into the matrix for beta-oxidation depends on the carnitine shuttle. Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting step of this shuttle and is physiologically inhibited by malonyl-CoA?
questions.concept: CPT-I sits on the outer mitochondrial membrane and converts long-chain acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine; this is the rate-limiting and committed step of mitochondrial fatty acid entry, and it is inhibited by malonyl-CoA (the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis), coordinating synthesis and oxidation. CPT-II regenerates acyl-CoA on the matrix side (not rate-limiting), translocase merely exchanges acylcarnitine for free carnitine, and acyl-CoA synthetase activates the fatty acid in the cytosol before the shuttle even begins.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Oxidation of Fatty Acids: Ketogenesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with recurrent episodes of hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting or intercurrent illness, dilated cardiomyopathy, and skeletal muscle weakness. Plasma total and free carnitine levels are markedly reduced, and the defect localises to the OCTN2 plasma-membrane carnitine transporter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Primary carnitine deficiency results from a defect in the OCTN2 (SLC22A5) high-affinity carnitine transporter, causing renal carnitine wasting and low plasma/tissue carnitine, so long-chain fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria; the triad of hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and myopathy is classic and responds to carnitine supplementation. Von Gierke causes fasting hypoglycaemia but with hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis and normal carnitine; McArdle gives exercise intolerance with muscle cramps; MCAD lowers acylcarnitines with a specific C8 pattern but carnitine transport itself is intact.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Fatty Acid and Triacylglycerol Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A previously healthy 2-year-old develops vomiting, lethargy and non-ketotic (hypoketotic) hypoglycaemia after a prolonged fast with a viral illness. Investigations show dicarboxylic aciduria and elevated C8 (octanoyl) acylcarnitine on tandem mass spectrometry. A deficiency of which enzyme best explains this presentation?
questions.concept: MCAD deficiency is the commonest inherited fatty-acid oxidation defect; medium-chain (C6-C10) acyl-CoAs cannot be dehydrogenated, so fasting produces hypoketotic hypoglycaemia (impaired ketogenesis) with accumulation of medium-chain species that spill into microsomal omega-oxidation, giving dicarboxylic aciduria and a diagnostic C8-acylcarnitine peak. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes ketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis; myophosphorylase deficiency is a muscle glycogenosis; pyruvate carboxylase deficiency causes lactic acidosis, not this acylcarnitine profile.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — Inborn Errors of Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Each round of mitochondrial beta-oxidation of a saturated fatty acyl-CoA shortens the chain by two carbons. Which set of products is generated directly in a single round?
options: One FADH2, one NADH and one acetyl-CoA
One FADH2, one NADPH and one malonyl-CoA
One NADH, one GTP and one acetyl-CoA
questions.concept: The four steps of one beta-oxidation spiral are oxidation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase producing FADH2), hydration, a second oxidation (3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase producing NADH), and thiolytic cleavage releasing one acetyl-CoA while leaving an acyl-CoA shortened by two carbons. NADPH and malonyl-CoA belong to fatty acid synthesis, not oxidation; GTP is produced in the TCA cycle; and only the final round of an even-chain fatty acid yields two acetyl-CoA molecules, not every round.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Oxidation of Fatty Acids: Ketogenesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Ketone bodies are synthesised in hepatic mitochondria from acetyl-CoA. After thiolase and HMG-CoA synthase produce HMG-CoA, which enzyme cleaves HMG-CoA to yield acetoacetate plus acetyl-CoA, the committed step of ketogenesis?
questions.concept: In ketogenesis, HMG-CoA lyase splits mitochondrial HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA; acetoacetate is then reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate or decarboxylated to acetone. HMG-CoA reductase is the cytosolic/ER enzyme of cholesterol synthesis (converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate, not acetoacetate); HMG-CoA synthase forms HMG-CoA one step earlier; and thiophorase (SCOT) is an extrahepatic enzyme used for ketone utilisation, not synthesis. HMG-CoA lyase deficiency causes non-ketotic hypoglycaemia.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Fatty Acid and Triacylglycerol Metabolism (Ketone Bodies)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
