questions.stem: The liver synthesises ketone bodies for export to peripheral tissues but is itself unable to use them as a fuel. This inability is best explained by the hepatic absence of which enzyme?
questions.concept: To use ketone bodies, tissues must first re-activate acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA using thiophorase (SCOT), which transfers CoA from succinyl-CoA. The liver lacks thiophorase, so it cannot re-activate acetoacetate and therefore exports ketones rather than consuming them, ensuring fuel reaches the brain, heart and muscle during fasting. Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase and thiolase are present in the liver; HMG-CoA synthase is actually the ketogenic (synthetic) enzyme, so its presence, not absence, is what makes the liver ketogenic.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Oxidation of Fatty Acids: Ketogenesis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The committed, rate-limiting step of de novo fatty acid synthesis is the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA. Which statement about the enzyme catalysing this step is correct?
options: It is acetyl-CoA carboxylase, a biotin-dependent enzyme allosterically activated by citrate
It is fatty acid synthase, which is allosterically activated by malonyl-CoA
It is acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which is allosterically activated by palmitoyl-CoA
It is thiolase, a biotin-dependent condensing enzyme
questions.concept: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis; it uses biotin and bicarbonate to carboxylate acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, is allosterically activated by citrate (a signal of abundant fuel) and inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA (product feedback), and is inactivated by AMPK-mediated phosphorylation. Fatty acid synthase acts downstream and is not the regulatory bottleneck; palmitoyl-CoA inhibits rather than activates ACC; and thiolase is a beta-oxidation/ketogenesis enzyme, not biotin-dependent.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Fatty Acid and Triacylglycerol Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: In the well-fed state, active fatty acid synthesis prevents simultaneous futile beta-oxidation of the newly made fatty acids. This reciprocal control is achieved primarily because malonyl-CoA does what?
options: Inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, blocking fatty acyl entry into mitochondria
Activates acyl-CoA dehydrogenase to speed oxidation
questions.concept: Malonyl-CoA, the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase and the first committed intermediate of synthesis, allosterically inhibits CPT-I. This blocks entry of fatty acyl groups into mitochondria, so newly synthesised fatty acids are not immediately oxidised, giving tight reciprocal regulation of synthesis versus oxidation. It does not activate CPT-I (opposite effect); it does not feedback-inhibit acetyl-CoA carboxylase (that is done by palmitoyl-CoA); and it has no activating role on acyl-CoA dehydrogenase.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Biosynthesis of Fatty Acids

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Acetyl-CoA required for cytosolic fatty acid synthesis is generated inside mitochondria and cannot cross the inner membrane directly; it is exported as citrate. In the cytosol, citrate is cleaved back to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate by which enzyme?
questions.concept: The citrate (tricarboxylate) shuttle exports acetyl units: mitochondrial acetyl-CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to citrate, which leaves the mitochondrion and is split in the cytosol by ATP-citrate lyase into acetyl-CoA (for fatty acid synthesis) and oxaloacetate. Citrate synthase performs the mitochondrial condensation, not the cytosolic cleavage; aconitase isomerises citrate to isocitrate; and isocitrate dehydrogenase is a TCA oxidative-decarboxylation enzyme, none of which liberate cytosolic acetyl-CoA.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Fatty Acid and Triacylglycerol Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: De novo fatty acid synthesis consumes large amounts of NADPH as reducing power. In lipogenic tissues such as liver and adipose tissue, which pathway is the major source of this NADPH?
questions.concept: The oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase) is the principal NADPH generator for reductive biosynthesis such as fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis; the malic enzyme contributes additional NADPH via the citrate shuttle. Glycolysis produces NADH and ATP not NADPH; the TCA cycle produces NADH, FADH2 and GTP; oxidative phosphorylation consumes NADH/FADH2 to make ATP and does not generate NADPH.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — The Pentose Phosphate Pathway & Other Pathways of Hexose Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: The multienzyme fatty acid synthase complex adds two-carbon units repeatedly to build a fatty acid chain. Which fatty acid is the principal end product released by the mammalian fatty acid synthase?
questions.concept: Mammalian fatty acid synthase elongates a growing chain by successive addition of malonyl-CoA-derived two-carbon units and releases the saturated 16-carbon palmitate as its main product. Longer chains such as stearate are made by microsomal/ER elongation enzymes acting on palmitate; unsaturated fatty acids like oleate require desaturases; and arachidonate (a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid) is derived from the essential fatty acid linoleic acid, not synthesised de novo by fatty acid synthase.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Fatty Acid and Triacylglycerol Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Cholesterol biosynthesis proceeds in the cytosol and endoplasmic reticulum from acetyl-CoA. Which pairing correctly names the rate-limiting enzyme of this pathway and the principal transcription factor that upregulates it when cellular sterol is low?
questions.concept: HMG-CoA reductase converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate and is the rate-limiting, most heavily regulated step of cholesterol synthesis; when sterol levels fall, SREBP-2 is proteolytically released in the Golgi and travels to the nucleus to transcribe HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor. SREBP-1c preferentially drives lipogenic (fatty acid) genes; PPAR-alpha governs fatty acid oxidation; ChREBP responds to glucose for lipogenesis; and squalene epoxidase and mevalonate kinase are downstream, non-rate-limiting cholesterogenic enzymes.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Cholesterol Synthesis, Transport, & Excretion

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Humans lack the desaturases needed to introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9 of a fatty acid, so certain fatty acids must be obtained from the diet. Which pair are the true essential fatty acids in humans?
questions.concept: Linoleic (18:2, omega-6) and alpha-linolenic (18:3, omega-3) acids cannot be synthesised de novo because humans lack delta-12 and delta-15 desaturases; they are dietary essentials and precursors for arachidonic acid, EPA and DHA. Palmitic, stearic, oleic and palmitoleic acids are all synthesised endogenously (oleate and palmitoleate via the delta-9 desaturase). Arachidonic acid is only conditionally essential because it can be made from linoleate, so it is not counted with oleic acid as a primary essential pair.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Complex Lipid Metabolism (Essential Fatty Acids)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes are 20-carbon signalling lipids (eicosanoids). Which option correctly names their major fatty-acid precursor together with the enzyme irreversibly inhibited by aspirin?
questions.concept: Arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid, released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2) is the main eicosanoid precursor. The cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway makes prostaglandins and thromboxanes, while the lipoxygenase pathway makes leukotrienes. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates and inhibits COX (not lipoxygenase), reducing thromboxane A2 and giving its antiplatelet effect. Linoleic acid is the dietary precursor of arachidonate but not the direct eicosanoid substrate, and phospholipase A2 is inhibited by steroids, not aspirin.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Metabolism of Unsaturated Fatty Acids & Eicosanoids

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A neonate born at 29 weeks develops progressive respiratory distress with tachypnoea, grunting and a ground-glass chest radiograph within hours of birth, attributed to pulmonary surfactant deficiency. Which phospholipid is the principal surface-tension-lowering component of surfactant that is deficient?
questions.concept: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin) is the chief surfactant phospholipid secreted by type II pneumocytes; it lowers alveolar surface tension and prevents end-expiratory collapse, and its deficiency in prematurity causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease). Fetal lung maturity is judged by a lecithin-to-sphingomyelin (L:S) ratio above 2. Sphingomyelin stays roughly constant and is the ratio denominator; phosphatidylserine and cardiolipin (an inner-mitochondrial-membrane lipid) are not the key surfactant components.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — Diseases of Infancy and Childhood (Respiratory Distress Syndrome)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Plasma lipoproteins differ in density according to their protein-to-lipid ratio. Which lipoprotein class has the highest protein content (and thus highest density) and mediates reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues to the liver?
questions.concept: HDL has the highest protein-to-lipid ratio, hence the greatest density, and carries out reverse cholesterol transport, picking up peripheral cholesterol (via ABCA1 and LCAT esterification) and returning it to the liver. Density falls and particle size rises as lipid content increases: chylomicrons are the largest and least dense (mostly dietary triglyceride), VLDL carries endogenous triglyceride, and LDL is the main cholesterol carrier delivering cholesterol to tissues, all with lower protein fractions than HDL.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Cholesterol, Lipoprotein, and Steroid Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: ApoB-48 and ApoB-100 are produced from the same gene, differing because of tissue-specific mRNA editing. Which statement about these two apolipoproteins is correct?
options: ApoB-48 is found on VLDL and LDL, whereas ApoB-100 is found on chylomicrons
ApoB-48 is made in the intestine and coats chylomicrons, whereas ApoB-100 is made in the liver, coats VLDL/LDL and is the ligand for the LDL receptor
ApoB-48 is the ligand recognised by the hepatic LDL receptor
Both ApoB-48 and ApoB-100 are synthesised exclusively in the liver
questions.concept: Intestinal mRNA editing introduces a stop codon so enterocytes make the truncated ApoB-48 (about 48% of full length) that assembles chylomicrons, while the liver makes full-length ApoB-100 for VLDL, which becomes LDL and provides the ApoB-100 that the hepatic LDL receptor recognises for clearance. ApoB-48 lacks the LDL-receptor-binding domain, so it is not the receptor ligand; the class assignments in the other options are reversed or restricted to the wrong tissue.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Lipid Transport & Storage

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Lipoprotein lipase (LPL), anchored to capillary endothelium, hydrolyses the triglycerides carried in chylomicrons and VLDL so that free fatty acids can be taken up by tissues. Which apolipoprotein is the essential activator of lipoprotein lipase?
questions.concept: ApoC-II, transferred to chylomicrons and VLDL from HDL, is the obligatory cofactor that activates lipoprotein lipase; a deficiency of either LPL or ApoC-II causes fasting chylomicronaemia with severe hypertriglyceridaemia (type I pattern). ApoA-I instead activates LCAT on HDL; ApoB-100 is the LDL-receptor ligand and structural protein of VLDL/LDL; and ApoE mediates hepatic uptake of chylomicron and VLDL remnants via the LDL-receptor and LRP, not LPL activation.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Cholesterol, Lipoprotein, and Steroid Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has markedly elevated LDL cholesterol, tendon xanthomas over the Achilles tendons and knuckles, corneal arcus, and a strong family history of myocardial infarction before age 45 in an autosomal dominant pattern. Which underlying molecular defect best explains this disorder?
options: Defective or deficient LDL receptor (familial hypercholesterolaemia, type IIa)
questions.concept: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (Fredrickson type IIa) is caused by autosomal dominant loss-of-function mutations in the LDL receptor (or its ligand ApoB-100, or gain-of-function PCSK9), so LDL is not cleared and plasma LDL cholesterol is very high from birth, producing tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus and premature atherosclerotic coronary disease. LPL and ApoC-II deficiencies raise triglycerides (chylomicrons), not LDL; and an ABCA1 defect causes Tangier disease with very low HDL, the opposite lipid picture.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — Genetic Disorders (Familial Hypercholesterolemia)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child presents with chronic fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea, failure to thrive, spinocerebellar ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, and acanthocytes on the peripheral smear. Fasting lipids show very low total cholesterol and triglycerides, and apolipoprotein B is undetectable in plasma. Which molecular defect underlies this disorder?
options: Deficiency of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP)
Deficiency of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP)
questions.concept: Abetalipoproteinaemia results from loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP), which is required to load lipids onto ApoB during assembly of chylomicrons and VLDL; without it, no ApoB-containing lipoproteins are secreted, causing fat and fat-soluble-vitamin malabsorption. Vitamin E deficiency drives the neurological signs and retinitis pigmentosa, and acanthocytosis reflects abnormal red-cell membrane lipids. ApoA-I and LCAT defects lower HDL, and CETP deficiency raises HDL, none of which abolish ApoB or cause this malabsorptive picture.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Lipid Transport & Storage

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient has strikingly enlarged, yellow-orange tonsils, mild hepatosplenomegaly, a peripheral neuropathy, and near-absent plasma HDL cholesterol with low total cholesterol. The disorder arises from failure to transfer cellular free cholesterol and phospholipid onto lipid-poor ApoA-I. Which defect is responsible?
options: Defect in the ABCA1 transporter (Tangier disease)
questions.concept: Tangier disease is caused by mutations in the ABCA1 transporter, which normally effluxes cellular cholesterol and phospholipid onto nascent ApoA-I to form HDL; without it, lipid-poor ApoA-I is rapidly catabolised, HDL is nearly absent, and cholesteryl esters accumulate in reticuloendothelial cells, producing the classic orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly and neuropathy. LCAT deficiency causes corneal opacity and anaemia; ApoE2 homozygosity underlies type III dysbetalipoproteinaemia (remnant accumulation); CETP deficiency paradoxically raises HDL.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — Environmental and Nutritional Diseases / Lipoprotein Disorders

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is a plasma enzyme activated by apolipoprotein A-I. What is its principal role in HDL and reverse cholesterol transport?
options: It hydrolyses the triglycerides carried within HDL particles
It transfers cholesteryl esters from HDL to VLDL in exchange for triglyceride
It esterifies free cholesterol on the HDL surface, driving HDL maturation and cholesterol uptake
It catalyses hepatic synthesis of apolipoprotein A-I
questions.concept: LCAT, activated by ApoA-I on HDL, transfers a fatty acyl group from lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) to free cholesterol, forming hydrophobic cholesteryl esters that move into the HDL core; this converts discoidal nascent HDL into mature spherical HDL and maintains a gradient that keeps drawing free cholesterol out of peripheral cells. Triglyceride hydrolysis is done by lipases; the HDL-to-VLDL cholesteryl-ester/triglyceride swap is performed by CETP; and ApoA-I is synthesised by liver and intestine, not by LCAT.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — Cholesterol, Lipoprotein, and Steroid Metabolism

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent shows progressive loss of motor milestones, exaggerated startle response to sound, and a cherry-red spot at the macula, but notably NO hepatosplenomegaly. Accumulation of GM2 ganglioside is demonstrated. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible?
questions.concept: Tay-Sachs disease is a deficiency of hexosaminidase A, causing GM2 ganglioside accumulation predominantly in neurons; hence the neurodegeneration, hyperacusis-related exaggerated startle and cherry-red macula, with the distinguishing absence of hepatosplenomegaly (in contrast to Niemann-Pick, which has a cherry-red spot WITH hepatosplenomegaly). Beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease; sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick; and arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy (sulfatide accumulation).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — Genetic Disorders (Lysosomal Storage Diseases)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A young man reports episodic burning pain in the hands and feet, decreased sweating, and clusters of dark-red angiokeratomas over the lower trunk; he later develops proteinuria and left ventricular hypertrophy. The disorder is X-linked and involves accumulation of ceramide trihexoside (globotriaosylceramide). Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.concept: Fabry disease is an X-linked deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, causing accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (ceramide trihexoside) in vascular endothelium and other tissues; hallmarks are acroparaesthesias (burning pain), hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, and later renal failure and cardiac/cerebrovascular disease. Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency causes Hurler syndrome (a mucopolysaccharidosis); galactocerebrosidase deficiency causes Krabbe disease with globoid cells; and hexosaminidase A deficiency causes Tay-Sachs, which lacks these vascular skin lesions.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Glycosphingolipids / Robbins Lysosomal Storage Diseases

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Fibrates (for example fenofibrate) are the most effective agents for lowering markedly raised serum triglycerides. What is their principal mechanism of action?
options: Activation of PPAR-alpha, which increases lipoprotein lipase activity and hepatic fatty acid oxidation
Inhibition of intestinal cholesterol absorption via the NPC1L1 transporter
Binding of bile acids in the intestinal lumen to interrupt their enterohepatic recirculation
questions.concept: Fibrates are agonists of the nuclear receptor PPAR-alpha; activation induces lipoprotein lipase and reduces ApoC-III, enhancing triglyceride-rich lipoprotein clearance, and upregulates fatty acid oxidation, so they chiefly lower triglycerides and modestly raise HDL. HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is the mechanism of statins; NPC1L1 inhibition describes ezetimibe; and bile-acid binding describes resins such as cholestyramine, none of which is the fibrate mechanism.
questions.reference: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Pharmacology — Drugs Affecting the Cardiovascular System (Antihyperlipidemics)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A fasting lipid panel reports total cholesterol 200 mg/dL, HDL cholesterol 50 mg/dL and triglycerides 150 mg/dL. Using the Friedewald equation, what is the calculated LDL cholesterol?
questions.concept: The Friedewald equation estimates LDL cholesterol as LDL = Total cholesterol minus HDL minus (triglycerides divided by 5), where triglycerides/5 approximates VLDL cholesterol in mg/dL. Here LDL = 200 minus 50 minus (150/5) = 200 minus 50 minus 30 = 120 mg/dL. The formula requires a fasting sample and is invalid when triglycerides exceed about 400 mg/dL or when chylomicrons or type III dysbetalipoproteinaemia are present, because the fixed TG/5 VLDL estimate breaks down.
questions.reference: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — Cholesterol Synthesis, Transport, & Excretion (Clinical Laboratory)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is caused by which of the following organisms?
questions.concept: Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an obligate intracellular acid-fast bacillus and the first bacterium identified as a cause of human disease (Hansen, 1873). It cannot be grown on artificial media (propagated in the mouse foot-pad and nine-banded armadillo), has the longest generation time of any bacterium (~12-14 days), and is thermophile-averse, favouring cool superficial skin and peripheral nerves. Distractors: M. ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer, M. marinum causes fish-tank/swimming-pool granuloma, and M. tuberculosis causes tuberculosis.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Because M. leprae prefers cooler tissues, leprosy lesions characteristically SPARE which of the following relatively warm body areas?
questions.concept: M. leprae grows optimally at cooler temperatures (~27-30°C), so lesions favour cool, superficial, acral sites: ear lobes, dorsa of hands and feet, extensor limbs, face, and nerves where they run superficially over bone. Warm, well-perfused, covered or midline regions are characteristically spared — the axillae, groin, perineum, hairy scalp, and the warm midline of the back (sometimes called 'immune zones'). Recognising this temperature-dependent distribution helps separate leprosy from other hypopigmenting dermatoses.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna — Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: In tuberculoid (TT) leprosy on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum, the host immune response is BEST characterised as:
options: Strong Th1 cell-mediated response with well-formed epithelioid granulomas and a low (paucibacillary) load
Strong Th2 humoral response with foamy macrophages and a high bacillary load
Complete absence of cell-mediated immunity with abundant bacilli in skin
Predominant IgE-driven response with a heavy eosinophilic infiltrate
questions.concept: The Ridley-Jopling spectrum is governed by cell-mediated immunity. The tuberculoid (TT) pole shows a vigorous Th1 response (IFN-γ, IL-2) producing well-formed epithelioid-cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells and dense lymphocytes, few or no demonstrable bacilli (paucibacillary), and a positive lepromin test. The lepromatous (LL) pole is the mirror image — Th2 dominance, foamy (Virchow) macrophages stuffed with bacilli, and a negative lepromin test. Leprosy is not IgE/eosinophil driven, excluding option D.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Immunology of Leprosy / Ridley-Jopling Spectrum

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A skin biopsy in lepromatous leprosy (LL) would MOST characteristically show:
options: Well-formed epithelioid granulomas with only rare bacilli
Caseating necrosis surrounded by Langhans giant cells
A non-specific perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate only
Sheets of foamy macrophages (Virchow/lepra cells) laden with acid-fast bacilli, separated from the epidermis by a clear grenz zone
questions.concept: LL leprosy reflects failed cell-mediated immunity (Th2 skew): macrophages ingest but cannot kill M. leprae, becoming foamy 'Virchow/lepra cells' packed with bacilli in clumps (globi), giving a very high bacillary index. A clear subepidermal band of uninvolved dermis (the 'grenz zone') separates the infiltrate from a flattened, atrophic epidermis. Option A describes the tuberculoid pole; caseation (option B) is a feature of tuberculosis, not leprosy; option C is too non-specific for the classic LL picture.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Histopathology of Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which statement about the lepromin (Mitsuda) test is CORRECT?
options: It is a diagnostic test that is positive in all forms of leprosy
It is positive in tuberculoid (TT) leprosy and negative in lepromatous (LL) leprosy, reflecting cell-mediated immunity, and is used for classification/prognosis rather than diagnosis
It is positive in lepromatous and negative in tuberculoid leprosy
It becomes positive only during a type 2 (ENL) reaction
questions.concept: The lepromin test measures the host's cell-mediated immunity to M. leprae antigen, not the presence of infection, so it is NOT diagnostic — even healthy immunocompetent contacts can be positive. It is strongly positive at the tuberculoid (TT) pole (intact CMI, granuloma formation) and negative at the lepromatous (LL) pole (immunological anergy), grading progressively across BT-BB-BL. The late Mitsuda reaction (read at ~21-28 days) is used for classification and prognosis, making option B correct and A/C/D wrong.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna — Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, Lepromin Test

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: According to WHO, diagnosis of leprosy rests on at least one of three cardinal signs. Which of the following is NOT one of these cardinal signs?
options: A hypopigmented or reddish skin patch with definite loss of sensation
A thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensory/motor function
Demonstration of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear
questions.concept: WHO defines the diagnosis of leprosy by the presence of at least one of THREE cardinal signs: (1) a hypopigmented or reddish patch with definite sensory loss; (2) a thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of the muscles it supplies; and (3) presence of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear. The lepromin test measures host immunity, not infection, so it is used for classification and prognosis but is explicitly NOT a diagnostic cardinal sign — making option C the exception.
questions.reference: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A leprosy patient has a thickened ulnar nerve at the elbow, sensory loss over the little and medial half of the ring finger, and hyperextension at the MCP joints with flexion at the IP joints of the 4th and 5th fingers. This deformity is:
options: Ape-thumb deformity from median nerve palsy
Wrist drop from radial nerve palsy
Foot drop from common peroneal palsy
questions.concept: The ulnar nerve is the most commonly involved nerve trunk in leprosy; damage where it lies superficially at the elbow causes sensory loss over the little and medial ring finger and wasting/weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles (interossei, medial two lumbricals, hypothenar). Loss of the medial lumbricals produces the 'partial claw hand' — MCP hyperextension with IP flexion of the 4th and 5th fingers. A combined ulnar+median palsy extends clawing to all fingers ('complete claw'); radial palsy gives wrist drop; peroneal gives foot drop.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Nerve Involvement and Deformities in Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A leprosy patient develops inability to dorsiflex and evert the foot, a high-stepping gait, and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. The nerve MOST likely involved is the:
questions.concept: The common peroneal (lateral popliteal) nerve is frequently thickened in leprosy as it winds superficially around the neck of the fibula — a cool, exposed site. Its involvement weakens dorsiflexion and eversion, producing foot drop with a compensatory high-stepping gait and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and lateral leg. The posterior tibial nerve supplies the sole, so its damage instead causes plantar anaesthesia, clawing of toes, and trophic plantar ulcers. The sural nerve is purely sensory; the femoral nerve is not a leprosy predilection site.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Peripheral Nerve Involvement in Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which peripheral nerve, commonly thickened in leprosy, is a PURELY SENSORY nerve that can often be seen and rolled beneath the skin as it crosses the sternocleidomastoid?
questions.concept: Nerves commonly thickened in leprosy include the ulnar, median, common peroneal, posterior tibial, radial cutaneous, facial and greater auricular nerves. The greater auricular nerve is a purely sensory branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3) that runs superficially across the sternocleidomastoid — when enlarged it can be both seen and palpably rolled under the skin, a classic bedside sign. The facial nerve is motor (its zygomatic branch damage causes lagophthalmos); the ulnar and radial cutaneous are mixed/limb nerves and are not the answer here.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna — Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, Nerve Examination in Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A leprosy patient develops a painless, deep, punched-out ulcer over a metatarsal head on the sole. The PRIMARY underlying mechanism is:
options: Ischaemia due to a small-vessel vasculitis
Direct bacillary destruction of the skin
Loss of protective (pain) sensation leading to repeated unnoticed trauma
questions.concept: Trophic (neuropathic/plantar) ulcers in leprosy arise from anaesthesia — loss of protective pain and pressure sensation (posterior tibial nerve damage) means repeated trauma over weight-bearing points (metatarsal heads, heel) goes unnoticed, producing painless, deep, punched-out ulcers. They are a marker of established nerve damage and disability, not active infection or vasculitis. Management centres on protective/customised footwear, meticulous wound care, off-loading and preventing further trauma, not on antibacterial escalation alone.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Disability and Trophic Ulcers in Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: The WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) regimen classically used for adult PAUCIBACILLARY (PB) leprosy consists of:
options: Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) plus dapsone 100 mg daily, for 6 months
Rifampicin 600 mg once monthly plus dapsone 100 mg daily plus clofazimine, for 12 months
Dapsone 100 mg daily alone for 6 months
Rifampicin 600 mg daily plus dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months
questions.concept: The classic WHO adult PB MDT is rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) plus dapsone 100 mg daily, given for 6 months. Rifampicin is given monthly (not daily) to limit toxicity and cost while retaining potent bactericidal effect. IMPORTANT change-prone program fact: WHO's 2018 guideline recommends a UNIFORM three-drug regimen (adding clofazimine) for BOTH PB and MB, so many current NLEP programmes now use rifampicin+dapsone+clofazimine for PB too — verify against the current WHO/NLEP edition before quoting.
questions.reference: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018); NLEP guidelines

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: The standard WHO multidrug therapy (MDT) for adult MULTIBACILLARY (MB) leprosy is:
options: Rifampicin monthly plus dapsone daily for 6 months
Rifampicin daily plus dapsone daily plus clofazimine daily for 12 months
Dapsone plus clofazimine daily for 24 months
Rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + clofazimine 300 mg monthly (supervised) + clofazimine 50 mg daily + dapsone 100 mg daily, for 12 months
questions.concept: The WHO adult MB MDT is: rifampicin 600 mg once monthly (supervised) + clofazimine 300 mg once monthly (supervised), together with clofazimine 50 mg daily + dapsone 100 mg daily, given for 12 months. The monthly rifampicin and monthly clofazimine are the supervised 'pulse' doses. The older MB regimen ran for 24 months but was shortened to 12 months. Note duration/regimen details are periodically revised — verify against the current WHO/NLEP edition. Option A is the PB regimen; rifampicin is monthly, not daily (excluding B).
questions.reference: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018); NLEP guidelines

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient has a SINGLE skin lesion of leprosy with no peripheral nerve trunk involvement. Which single-dose regimen has been used by WHO for this presentation?
options: Rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine as a single combined dose
Rifampicin 600 mg + ofloxacin 400 mg + minocycline 100 mg (ROM) as a single dose
Dapsone 100 mg as a single dose
Rifampicin 600 mg as a single dose alone
questions.concept: For single-lesion paucibacillary leprosy (one patch, no nerve trunk involvement), WHO previously endorsed a single supervised dose of ROM: Rifampicin 600 mg + Ofloxacin 400 mg + Minocycline 100 mg. Change-prone caveat: current WHO (2018) guidance favours standard 6-month PB MDT even for single lesions in many programmes, so single-dose ROM is now of limited/declining use — verify against the current edition. Ofloxacin and minocycline (with clarithromycin) also serve as second-line agents for rifampicin resistance or intolerance.
questions.reference: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy (2018)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A borderline leprosy patient on MDT develops acute inflammation of existing skin lesions together with a NEW motor deficit from acute neuritis (a type 1 reversal reaction). The most appropriate first-line treatment is:
options: Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone) while continuing MDT
questions.concept: Type 1 (reversal) reactions are delayed cell-mediated (type IV) immunological upgrades occurring in borderline leprosy, causing acute inflammation of existing lesions and — critically — acute neuritis that can cause permanent nerve damage. Because deficits may become irreversible, first-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids (e.g., prednisolone, tapered over several weeks to months) to reduce nerve inflammation, WHILE antileprosy MDT is continued uninterrupted. Thalidomide (option A) is reserved for type 2/ENL reactions, not type 1; NSAIDs/clofazimine alone are inadequate for neuritis.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Lepra Reactions (Type 1 / Reversal Reaction)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Erythema nodosum leprosum (type 2 lepra reaction) is BEST characterised as:
options: An immune-complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity) reaction seen in lepromatous/borderline-lepromatous leprosy, with crops of tender erythematous nodules, fever and systemic features
A type IV cell-mediated reaction occurring only in tuberculoid leprosy
An IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction
Simple bacterial abscess formation from secondary infection
questions.concept: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL, type 2 reaction) is an immune-complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity) phenomenon occurring in high-bacillary-load forms (LL and BL), driven by antigen release and circulating immune complexes with a neutrophilic dermal infiltrate. It presents with recurrent crops of tender, erythematous subcutaneous nodules plus systemic features — fever, malaise, arthralgia, iridocyclitis, orchitis, lymphadenopathy and neuritis. Type 1 reactions, by contrast, are type IV cell-mediated events seen in borderline disease, distinguishing them from ENL.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Lepra Reactions (Type 2 / Erythema Nodosum Leprosum)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Thalidomide is highly effective for severe, recurrent erythema nodosum leprosum, but its use is ABSOLUTELY contraindicated in which situation?
options: Women of child-bearing potential / pregnancy, owing to severe teratogenicity
questions.concept: Thalidomide is very effective for severe, recurrent or steroid-dependent ENL (type 2 reaction), acting largely through TNF-α suppression. It is ABSOLUTELY contraindicated in pregnancy and in women of child-bearing potential without stringent contraception because it is a potent teratogen causing phocomelia and other limb-reduction defects (the historic thalidomide disaster). Other adverse effects include peripheral neuropathy, drowsiness and constipation. Safer alternatives for ENL include systemic corticosteroids and high-dose clofazimine, especially in women who may conceive.
questions.reference: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy — Management of ENL

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: The most important dose-related adverse effect of dapsone, especially in a G6PD-deficient patient, is:
options: Orange discoloration of urine and sweat
questions.concept: Dapsone characteristically produces dose-related oxidative haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, which are markedly worse in G6PD-deficient individuals — so G6PD status should be checked before starting where feasible. Other dapsone effects include dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (a DRESS-like reaction weeks after starting) and agranulocytosis. Reddish-black skin pigmentation (option A) is caused by clofazimine; orange discoloration of body fluids (option C) is caused by rifampicin; significant peripheral neuropathy (option D) is not a typical dapsone effect.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Antileprosy Drugs and Adverse Effects (Dapsone)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: About five weeks after starting MDT, a leprosy patient develops fever, a widespread morbilliform rash, facial oedema, generalised lymphadenopathy, hepatitis and marked eosinophilia. The MOST likely cause is:
questions.concept: Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (a DRESS-type reaction) typically appears 4-6 weeks after starting dapsone and presents with fever, a morbilliform or exfoliative rash, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis and eosinophilia (sometimes a mononucleosis-like picture). Management is IMMEDIATE dapsone withdrawal plus systemic corticosteroids; untreated it can be fatal. It is distinguished from lepra reactions, which involve inflammation of skin lesions/nerves rather than a diffuse drug-rash morphology, and from rifampicin's transient flu-like syndrome seen with intermittent dosing.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Dapsone Hypersensitivity (Dapsone Syndrome)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A well-known and largely reversible adverse effect of clofazimine used in MDT is:
options: Reddish-brown to bluish-black hyperpigmentation of the skin and lesions
questions.concept: Clofazimine characteristically causes a dose-dependent reddish-brown to bluish-black discoloration of the skin (most marked over lesions and sun-exposed areas), along with dryness/ichthyosis, and reddish discoloration of urine, sweat and conjunctivae; this pigmentation is cosmetically distressing but reversible over months to years after stopping and is a common cause of poor compliance. High doses can also cause GI/enteropathy effects. Haemolysis (option B) is a dapsone effect; nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are not typical MDT adverse effects.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna — Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, Antileprosy Drugs (Clofazimine)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: In the WHO disability grading for leprosy, GRADE 2 disability of the hand or foot refers to:
options: No anaesthesia and no visible deformity
Anaesthesia present but no visible deformity or damage
Visible deformity or damage of the hand/foot (e.g., ulcer, claw hand, foot drop, resorption)
questions.concept: WHO disability grading for hands and feet: Grade 0 = no anaesthesia and no visible deformity/damage; Grade 1 = loss of protective sensation (anaesthesia) present but NO visible deformity or damage; Grade 2 = VISIBLE deformity or damage — e.g., trophic ulcer, claw hand, foot drop, or resorption/shortening of digits. For the eye: Grade 1 = eye problems present but vision not severely affected; Grade 2 = severe visual impairment, lagophthalmos, or corneal changes. The Grade 2 disability rate is a key programme monitoring indicator.
questions.reference: WHO Guidelines for the Diagnosis, Treatment and Prevention of Leprosy — Disability Grading

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A child presents with a hypopigmented patch. Which single feature would MOST strongly favour leprosy over pityriasis alba or vitiligo?
options: Fine surface scaling within the patch
Definite loss of sensation within the patch
questions.concept: The key discriminator of a leprosy patch is DEFINITE loss of sensation (touch, temperature and/or pain) within it, often accompanied by dryness (loss of sweating), loss of hair, and sometimes a palpably thickened feeding nerve. Vitiligo is chalky-white DEPIGMENTATION with entirely intact sensation; pityriasis alba shows scaly HYPOpigmentation with intact sensation, typically on children's cheeks. Other sensation-intact mimics include pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation and naevus depigmentosus — none of which is anaesthetic.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna — Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, Differential Diagnosis of Hypopigmented Macules

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with a history of prolonged dapsone monotherapy develops multiple shiny, well-defined, dome-shaped cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules on apparently normal skin; smears show a very high bacillary load with spindle-shaped histiocytes. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Histoid leprosy is a distinct multibacillary variant, classically associated with dapsone monotherapy/resistance or irregular treatment, though it can arise de novo. It presents with characteristic shiny, firm, well-circumscribed, dome-shaped cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules and plaques on apparently NORMAL-looking skin. Histology shows interlacing spindle-shaped ('histoid') histiocytes packed with abundant acid-fast bacilli (very high bacillary index). It is not a reaction (unlike ENL or Lucio phenomenon) and is heavily bacillated, unlike the paucibacillary borderline tuberculoid form.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Histoid Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with untreated diffuse, non-nodular lepromatous (Lucio) leprosy develops painful, jagged/angulated, stellate purpuric skin lesions that necrose and ulcerate. This severe reaction is termed:
questions.concept: The Lucio phenomenon is a severe necrotizing reaction — essentially a cutaneous vasculitis/thrombotic vaso-occlusion with extensive endothelial invasion by bacilli — occurring in untreated diffuse, non-nodular lepromatous ('Lucio') leprosy, most classically reported from Mexico and Central America. It produces painful, sharply angulated/jagged, stellate purpuric plaques that undergo necrosis into irregular ulcers healing with atrophic scars; secondary sepsis can be fatal. It differs from ENL (crops of tender nodules) and from type 1 reactions (inflammation of existing lesions with neuritis).
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Lucio Leprosy and the Lucio Phenomenon

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A leprosy patient is unable to fully close one eye (lagophthalmos), placing the cornea at risk of exposure keratitis. This is MOST directly due to involvement of the:
options: Sensory branch of the trigeminal (V) nerve
Zygomatic/temporal branches of the facial (VII) nerve supplying orbicularis oculi
questions.concept: Lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eye) in leprosy results from paralysis of the orbicularis oculi due to involvement of the zygomatic and temporal branches of the facial (VII) nerve. The eye cannot be closed or blinked properly, leading to exposure keratitis, corneal ulceration and potentially blindness — hence eye protection, lubrication and lid-care are vital. Coexisting corneal anaesthesia from trigeminal (V) involvement compounds the risk. Lagophthalmos with visual threat constitutes a WHO grade-2 (eye) disability; the optic and oculomotor nerves are not the mechanism.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Ocular Complications and Facial Nerve Involvement in Leprosy

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the single most common clinical type of psoriasis, presenting as symmetrical, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent silvery scale over the elbows, knees, scalp and lumbosacral region?
questions.concept: Chronic plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris) accounts for roughly 80-90% of cases and is the classic presentation: symmetrical, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent silvery-white scale over extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp and lumbosacral area. Guttate, generalized pustular and erythrodermic forms are far less common and are distinguished by their morphology and acuity, making chronic plaque the single most common type.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, 6th ed. — Papulosquamous Disorders (Psoriasis)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with known psoriasis notices that new plaques have appeared exactly along the line of a recent surgical scar and along a linear scratch. This tendency of lesions to arise at sites of trauma is best termed:
questions.concept: The Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon is the development of lesions of an existing dermatosis at sites of trauma such as a scratch, scar or surgical wound, appearing along the line of injury; it is characteristically seen in psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo and viral warts. The Nikolsky sign (epidermal shearing) belongs to pemphigus, Darier sign (wheal on rubbing) to mastocytosis, and Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on scale removal) to psoriatic scale, so Koebner is the correct term for the response described.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Psoriasis (clinical signs; Koebner phenomenon)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Nail involvement is common in psoriasis. Which of the following nail changes is the most frequent and reflects disease of the proximal nail matrix?
options: Irregular pitting of the nail plate
questions.concept: Nail disease occurs in up to half of psoriatics and correlates with psoriatic arthritis. Irregular pitting of the nail plate is the most common finding and reflects psoriasis of the proximal nail matrix, where parakeratotic cells are shed leaving surface depressions. The 'oil-drop' sign, subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis arise from nail-bed disease, while dorsal pterygium is typical of lichen planus, longitudinal melanonychia of melanocytic activation, and Beau's lines of systemic illness.
questions.reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th ed. — Psoriasis (nail disease)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: On skin biopsy of a psoriatic plaque, collections of neutrophils are seen within the parakeratotic stratum corneum. This histological finding is known as:
questions.concept: The Munro microabscess is a collection of neutrophils within the parakeratotic stratum corneum and is a hallmark of psoriasis, together with the spongiform pustule of Kogoj (neutrophils in the upper spinous layer), regular acanthosis with elongated rete ridges, thinning of the suprapapillary plates and dilated dermal papillary capillaries. A Pautrier microabscess (intraepidermal atypical lymphocytes) points to mycosis fungoides, Civatte bodies indicate lichen planus, and the Max Joseph space is a lichen planus cleft, so Munro is correct.
questions.reference: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, 9th ed. — Psoriasis (histopathology)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which cytokine pathway is now regarded as the central driver of psoriasis and the principal target of modern biologic therapy?
questions.concept: The central immunopathogenic pathway of psoriasis is the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 axis: dendritic-cell-derived IL-23 sustains Th17 cells that secrete IL-17 and IL-22, driving keratinocyte hyperproliferation, with TNF-alpha amplifying the loop. This underlies biologics targeting IL-17 (secukinumab), IL-23 (guselkumab) and TNF. The IL-4/IL-13 (Th2) axis drives atopic dermatitis, IL-5 drives eosinophilic disease, and IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity underlies urticaria, not psoriasis.
questions.reference: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, 9th ed. — Psoriasis (pathogenesis; IL-23/IL-17 axis)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which of the following drugs is most classically associated with precipitating or aggravating psoriasis?
questions.concept: Several systemic drugs can precipitate or aggravate psoriasis; the classic offenders are lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials (chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and interferons, while abrupt systemic corticosteroid withdrawal can trigger pustular flares. Lithium is the most consistently implicated of the options given. Cetirizine, omeprazole and amoxicillin are not recognised as psoriasis-exacerbating drugs, making lithium the best answer.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Psoriasis (aggravating/precipitating drugs)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A man with long-standing plaque psoriasis is given oral prednisolone for back pain. As the steroid is tapered he develops high fever, malaise and waves of sterile pustules erupting on tender erythematous skin. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Von Zumbusch generalized pustular psoriasis is an acute, potentially life-threatening flare in which sheets of sterile pustules erupt on tender erythematous skin with high fever, leukocytosis and malaise; abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids is a classic trigger in a known psoriatic. AGEP is drug-induced and arises within days of a new drug (often an antibiotic), staphylococcal scalded skin shows toxin-mediated superficial peeling, and dermatitis herpetiformis is an intensely itchy vesicular eruption of coeliac disease.
questions.reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th ed. — Pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with erythrodermic psoriasis involving almost the entire body surface is admitted. Which of the following systemic complications is the chief reason this condition is a dermatological emergency?
questions.concept: Erythrodermic psoriasis involves more than 90% of the body surface with confluent erythema and scaling, disrupting the skin barrier and thermoregulation. Widespread cutaneous vasodilation causes heat and fluid loss with resulting hypothermia, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, protein loss and high-output cardiac failure, plus a risk of secondary sepsis. These systemic consequences, not glaucoma, diabetes insipidus or stroke, are what make erythroderma an emergency requiring admission.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, 6th ed. — Erythroderma and erythrodermic psoriasis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient presents with smooth, shiny, well-demarcated erythematous plaques bearing little or no scale in the axillae, groin and natal cleft, often mistaken for a fungal intertrigo. Which variant of psoriasis is this?
questions.concept: Inverse (flexural) psoriasis affects the body folds - axillae, groin, inframammary area and natal cleft - where moisture and friction leave the plaques smooth, shiny and well demarcated with little or no scale, so they are often mistaken for intertrigo or candidiasis. Nummular eczema produces coin-shaped exudative plaques on the limbs, guttate psoriasis shows scattered small drop-like papules, and erythroderma is generalised; the flexural, glazed, minimally scaly morphology defines inverse psoriasis.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Psoriasis (flexural/inverse psoriasis)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with psoriasis and rheumatoid-factor-negative arthritis affecting the distal interphalangeal joints, with a 'sausage' digit, has a destructive deformity on X-ray. Which radiographic finding is characteristic of psoriatic arthritis?
questions.concept: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative (RF-negative) spondyloarthropathy; distal interphalangeal involvement and dactylitis ('sausage digit') are characteristic, and progressive osteolysis produces the classic 'pencil-in-cup' deformity, seen in the destructive arthritis mutilans form. Symmetric marginal erosions with pannus typify rheumatoid arthritis, chondrocalcinosis suggests CPPD, and osteophytes with subchondral sclerosis indicate osteoarthritis, so pencil-in-cup is the psoriatic hallmark.
questions.reference: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, 9th ed. — Psoriatic arthritis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: During treatment of psoriasis a pale, blanched halo is noticed surrounding several resolving plaques (the Woronoff ring). This ring is best described as:
options: A pustular rim at the plaque margin
A pale, blanched ring of skin surrounding the plaque
Central clearing producing an annular lesion
questions.concept: The Woronoff ring is a pale, blanched halo of skin that appears around a psoriatic plaque, typically during resolution after phototherapy or topical treatment, and is attributed to local down-regulation of prostaglandins with cutaneous vasoconstriction. It is not a pustular margin, a scaly collarette, or central clearing; recognising this benign perilesional blanching prevents it being mistaken for spreading disease or a treatment reaction.
questions.reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th ed. — Psoriasis (clinical features; Woronoff ring)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which of the following topical antipsoriatic agents is a synthetic vitamin D3 analogue that inhibits keratinocyte proliferation and promotes differentiation?
questions.concept: Calcipotriol (calcipotriene) is a synthetic vitamin D3 analogue that binds the vitamin D receptor to inhibit keratinocyte proliferation and promote differentiation, and is a first-line topical agent for plaque psoriasis, often combined with a potent corticosteroid. Coal tar and dithranol (anthralin) are older keratolytic/antiproliferative agents, and tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor used mainly for facial and flexural disease, so calcipotriol is the vitamin D analogue.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Psoriasis (topical vitamin D analogues)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Regarding methotrexate used for severe psoriasis, which one of the following statements about its important adverse effects is correct?
options: Anaphylaxis occurs predictably with every dose
Cumulative dose-related hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis require liver monitoring
Gingival hyperplasia is its characteristic toxicity
It causes corneal verticillata requiring annual ophthalmology
questions.concept: Methotrexate, a dihydrofolate-reductase inhibitor, is used for severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis; its most important long-term concern is cumulative dose-related hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis, so liver function and fibrosis markers must be monitored, with folic acid supplementation. Acute pneumonitis and myelosuppression are other true risks, but per-dose anaphylaxis, gingival hyperplasia (ciclosporin/phenytoin) and corneal verticillata (amiodarone/chloroquine) are not features of methotrexate.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Systemic therapy of psoriasis (methotrexate)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) is widely used to grade disease. What does it primarily quantify?
options: The extent and severity of skin psoriasis (erythema, induration, scaling and area involved)
The severity of joint damage in psoriatic arthritis
The patient-reported itch and quality of life
questions.concept: The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) is the standard tool for grading disease burden in trials and practice; it scores the intensity of erythema, induration (thickness) and scaling in each of four body regions and weights them by the percentage area involved to yield a single score (0-72). It does not measure joint damage, isolated nail disease, or patient-reported itch and quality of life, which are captured by other instruments.
questions.reference: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, 9th ed. — Psoriasis severity assessment (PASI)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: The classic 'six Ps' description of the typical lesions of lichen planus refers to which set of features?
options: Pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules and plaques
questions.concept: The classic mnemonic for lichen planus is the six Ps: Pruritic, Purple (violaceous), Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped), Papules and Plaques, typically over the flexor wrists, forearms and ankles. The other option sets describe unrelated morphologies - pedunculated pustules, purpuric plaques or pigmented papillomatous papules - none of which fit lichen planus, so the pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar description is correct.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, 6th ed. — Lichen Planus

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about erosive oral lichen planus is correct?
options: It is always caused by Candida albicans infection
It reliably resolves within a few days without sequelae
It is entirely benign with no malignant potential whatsoever
It carries a small but definite risk of oral squamous cell carcinoma
questions.concept: Oral lichen planus most often shows an asymptomatic reticular (Wickham) network on the buccal mucosa, but the erosive/ulcerative form is painful and, importantly, carries a small but recognised risk of transformation to oral squamous cell carcinoma, so it warrants monitoring and biopsy of non-healing lesions. It is not caused by Candida, does not reliably resolve within days, and is not entirely without malignant potential, making the SCC-risk statement correct.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Oral lichen planus

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A middle-aged woman has patchy scalp hair loss with perifollicular erythema and follicular hyperkeratosis; affected areas show loss of the follicular openings (scarring). The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Lichen planopilaris is lichen planus of the hair follicle, producing perifollicular erythema and follicular hyperkeratosis that progress to patchy scarring (cicatricial) alopecia with loss of follicular ostia; frontal fibrosing alopecia is a clinical variant. Alopecia areata gives smooth non-scarring patches with exclamation-mark hairs, telogen effluvium is diffuse non-scarring shedding, and tinea capitis shows scaling with broken hairs and fungal positivity, so lichen planopilaris is the scarring cause described.
questions.reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th ed. — Lichen planopilaris and cicatricial alopecias

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which nail change is most characteristic of lichen planus?
questions.concept: Nail lichen planus classically causes longitudinal ridging and thinning and, most characteristically, a dorsal pterygium - a wing-like scarring adhesion of the proximal nail fold to the nail bed caused by focal matrix destruction, which can lead to permanent nail loss. The oil-drop sign and coarse pitting are features of psoriasis and splinter haemorrhages of trauma or endocarditis, so dorsal pterygium is the sign specific to lichen planus.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, 6th ed. — Lichen Planus (nail changes)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Lichen planus, especially its oral and erosive forms, is epidemiologically associated with chronic infection by which of the following viruses?
questions.concept: Lichen planus, particularly its oral and erosive forms, has a well-documented epidemiological association with chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and screening for HCV is often recommended in appropriate settings. Hepatitis A is a self-limiting enteric infection, hepatitis B is more strongly linked with polyarteritis nodosa and membranous nephropathy, and HIV has other cutaneous associations, so hepatitis C is the correct link with lichen planus.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Lichen planus (systemic associations; hepatitis C)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Which one of the following histopathological patterns is characteristic of lichen planus?
options: Subepidermal blister with neutrophilic papillary microabscesses
Acantholysis with a 'row of tombstones' basal layer
Band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermoepidermal junction with sawtooth rete ridges
questions.concept: The histology of lichen planus shows compact hyperkeratosis WITHOUT parakeratosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, irregular sawtooth acanthosis of the rete ridges, a dense band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate hugging the dermoepidermal junction, basal-cell vacuolar degeneration and apoptotic Civatte (colloid) bodies. Parakeratosis with Munro microabscesses defines psoriasis, subepidermal neutrophilic microabscesses suggest dermatitis herpetiformis, and a 'row of tombstones' acantholysis indicates pemphigus vulgaris.
questions.reference: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, 9th ed. — Lichen planus (histopathology)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A photodistributed lichenoid eruption that spares the mucosa develops in an elderly hypertensive patient and clears after a medication is stopped. Which of the following drugs is a recognised cause of a lichenoid drug eruption?
questions.concept: Lichenoid drug eruptions mimic idiopathic lichen planus but are often more eczematous or photodistributed and tend to spare the mucosa, resolving on drug withdrawal. Classic culprits include thiazide diuretics, antimalarials, gold, penicillamine, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs. Among the options a thiazide diuretic is the recognised trigger, whereas amlodipine, metformin and loratadine are not typical causes of lichenoid eruptions.
questions.reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th ed. — Lichenoid drug eruptions

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient has thick, hyperkeratotic, warty violaceous plaques on both shins that are intensely itchy and have persisted for years. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Hypertrophic lichen planus presents as thick, hyperkeratotic, verrucous violaceous plaques, most often on the shins and ankles, that are intensely pruritic and chronic; long-standing lesions carry a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma. Psoriasis of the shins shows silvery scale rather than violaceous hyperkeratosis, lichen sclerosus produces atrophic porcelain-white patches, and stasis dermatitis shows haemosiderin pigment and oedema, so hypertrophic lichen planus best fits the description.
questions.reference: IADVL Textbook of Dermatology — Lichen planus (hypertrophic variant)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Reactivation of which of the following viruses is most strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of pityriasis rosea?
questions.concept: Pityriasis rosea is a self-limiting papulosquamous eruption whose pathogenesis is most strongly linked to systemic reactivation of the human herpesviruses HHV-6 and HHV-7, supported by detection of viral DNA and occasional prodromal symptoms. It resolves spontaneously over 6-8 weeks and needs only reassurance and symptomatic care. HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, HPV causes warts, and parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum, so HHV-6/7 is the correct association.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, 6th ed. — Pityriasis rosea

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient has an orange-red scaling eruption with follicular keratotic papules, waxy orange palms and soles, and sharply outlined 'islands' of normal skin within the erythema. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is characterised by orange-red (salmon) scaly plaques, follicular keratotic papules giving a nutmeg-grater feel on the dorsa of the fingers, a waxy orange palmoplantar keratoderma and, most distinctively, sharply demarcated 'islands of sparing' (nappes claires) of normal skin within the erythema, often with cephalocaudal spread. Psoriasis, mycosis fungoides and erythrodermic atopic dermatitis lack these islands of sparing and the orange hue, making pityriasis rubra pilaris the diagnosis.
questions.reference: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology, 9th ed. — Pityriasis rubra pilaris

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: Erythema with greasy yellowish scales over the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds is characteristic of seborrhoeic dermatitis. Which organism is central to its pathogenesis?
questions.concept: Seborrhoeic dermatitis produces erythematous patches with greasy yellowish scales in sebum-rich areas - scalp (dandruff), eyebrows, nasolabial folds, ears and central chest - and is driven by an inflammatory response to Malassezia (Pityrosporum) yeasts, which is why antifungals such as ketoconazole are effective. It is characteristically severe and extensive in Parkinson's disease and HIV/AIDS. Trichophyton, Sarcoptes and Staphylococcus cause tinea, scabies and pyoderma respectively, not seborrhoeic dermatitis.
questions.reference: Neena Khanna, Illustrated Synopsis of Dermatology & STD, 6th ed. — Seborrhoeic dermatitis

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.stem: A patient with long-standing patches and plaques develops erythroderma, generalised lymphadenopathy and circulating atypical CD4+ lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Sézary syndrome is the leukaemic, erythrodermic variant of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, defined by the triad of erythroderma, generalised lymphadenopathy and circulating atypical CD4+ T cells with cerebriform (Sézary) nuclei, often evolving from long-standing mycosis fungoides patches and plaques. Erythrodermic psoriasis, DRESS and pemphigus foliaceus can also cause widespread skin disease but lack the circulating cerebriform lymphocytes, so Sézary syndrome fits the described picture.
questions.reference: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology, 9th ed. — Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Tardieu spots, frequently listed among the signs of asphyxial death, are best described as:
options: Areas of postmortem hypostasis in the dependent parts of the body
Antemortem bruises produced by the margins of a ligature
Pinpoint (petechial) subpleural and subpericardial haemorrhages caused by an acute rise in venous pressure and anoxic capillary damage
Fungal colonies developing on the skin during decomposition
questions.concept: Tardieu spots are pinpoint petechial haemorrhages classically found beneath the visceral pleura and epicardium (and other serous membranes) in asphyxia. They arise from an acute rise in intracapillary venous pressure together with anoxic damage to capillary endothelium during the convulsive stage. They are a general, supportive sign of asphyxia rather than a specific one, and may also be seen in some sudden natural deaths and within areas of hypostasis; hence they suggest but never prove asphyxia. They are neither hypostasis, ligature bruises, nor a decomposition artefact.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Mechanical Asphyxia

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: During a dinner party an elderly denture-wearing man who had been drinking suddenly clutches his throat and collapses dead. Autopsy shows a large bolus of meat impacted in the laryngopharynx and a structurally normal heart. This is an example of:
questions.concept: Café coronary is sudden collapse and death due to impaction of a large bolus of food in the laryngopharynx during eating, so named because it is easily mistaken for a myocardial infarction. Death results from acute obstruction of the airway and, importantly, from reflex vagal cardiac inhibition triggered by stimulation of the larynx. Predisposing factors include intoxication, old age, dentures and neurological swallowing disorders. The manner is accidental and the heart is typically normal, which distinguishes it from a true coronary event.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Asphyxial Deaths (Choking)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: 'Cutis anserina' (goose skin) observed on a body recovered from water is produced by:
options: Rigor mortis limited to the muscles of the face
Contraction of the erector pilae (arrector pili) muscles of the skin
Antemortem scald burns from hot water
Gas formation in the subcutaneous tissues during putrefaction
questions.concept: Cutis anserina (goose skin/gooseflesh) is a puckered skin appearance with erection of the hair follicles caused by contraction or rigidity of the arrector pili (erector pilae) muscles, provoked by cold water and by postmortem rigor. It is a sign of immersion — i.e. that the body was in cold water — and can develop whether the person entered the water alive or was already dead. It is therefore not proof of antemortem drowning, and is unrelated to burns or to putrefactive gas formation.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Death from Drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Which of the following combinations best represents the classical general (non-specific) signs of asphyxia?
options: Pallor of the skin, contracted pupils and early rigor mortis
Cherry-red postmortem lividity with skin blistering
Rectangular contact burns with reddened margins
Cyanosis, visceral congestion, petechial haemorrhages and fluidity of the blood
questions.concept: The classical general signs of asphyxia are cyanosis, congestion of the internal organs, petechial (Tardieu) haemorrhages, and dark fluid blood (the blood remaining fluid because of increased fibrinolytic activity and high carbon dioxide). These are supportive but non-specific and may be seen in other modes of death. Cherry-red lividity points to carbon monoxide poisoning rather than asphyxia, while pallor with contracted pupils and rectangular contact burns are not features of the asphyxial picture.
questions.reference: The Synopsis of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology (K.S. Narayan Reddy) — Asphyxia

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The finding of 'washerwoman's hands' (bleached, sodden, wrinkled palms and soles) in a body taken from water indicates:
options: A definite antemortem struggle within the water
Conclusive proof that drowning was the cause of death
Only that the body was immersed in water for some hours (a sign of immersion, not of drowning)
That death was due to electrocution while in water
questions.concept: 'Washerwoman's hands and feet' refers to bleaching and sodden, corrugated wrinkling of the thick keratin of the palms and soles due to imbibition of water. It develops after some hours of immersion and merely indicates that the body lay in water for a period. It is a sign of IMMERSION and occurs whether the person drowned or was already dead when they entered the water; therefore it is not proof of antemortem drowning, of a struggle, or of electrocution.
questions.reference: Parikh's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In the majority of cases of ordinary (non-judicial) hanging, the principal immediate mechanism of death is:
options: Cerebral anoxia due to compression/occlusion of the carotid and vertebral arteries and jugular veins
Air embolism entering torn neck veins
Reflex vagal cardiac inhibition in every case
questions.concept: In ordinary hanging very little weight is needed to compress the neck structures — roughly 2 kg occludes the jugular veins, about 5 kg the carotids and 15 kg the trachea. The commonest mechanism of death is therefore cerebral anoxia/ischaemia from occlusion of the carotid and vertebral arteries and jugular veins, causing rapid loss of consciousness. Airway occlusion (asphyxia proper) and, less often, reflex vagal cardiac arrest contribute, while cervical fracture-dislocation is essentially confined to judicial hanging with a long drop.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Hanging

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In judicial hanging employing a calculated long drop with a submental (under-chin) knot, death is chiefly caused by:
options: Fracture-dislocation of the upper cervical vertebrae ('hangman's fracture' of the axis) with transection of the upper cord and medulla
Slow simple asphyxia developing over several minutes
Aspiration of gastric contents into the lungs
Exsanguinating haemorrhage from rupture of both carotid arteries
questions.concept: In judicial hanging the drop length is calculated from body weight and a submental knot is used, so that at the end of the fall the neck is suddenly hyperextended and distracted. This produces a fracture-dislocation of the axis — classically bilateral fractures through the pars interarticularis/pedicles of C2 (the 'hangman's fracture') with dislocation of C2 on C3 — and transection or crushing of the upper spinal cord and medulla, giving near-instantaneous death. Ordinary suicidal hanging, lacking a drop, rarely fractures the spine.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Hanging

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about hanging is TRUE?
options: The body must be completely suspended with the feet clear of the ground for death to occur
Contact of the feet with the floor automatically excludes a diagnosis of hanging
Hanging is impossible in the sitting or kneeling posture
Death can occur in partial hanging, because only a few kilograms of force are needed to compress the neck vessels
questions.concept: Hanging is classed as complete (body fully suspended, feet off the ground) or partial (part of the body — feet, knees or buttocks — resting on a surface). Because only a few kilograms of weight are needed to occlude the jugular veins and carotid arteries, partial hanging in the sitting, kneeling or even lying position is entirely possible and is common in suicides. Therefore contact of the feet with the ground does not exclude hanging, and full suspension is not required for a fatal outcome.
questions.reference: The Synopsis of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology (K.S. Narayan Reddy) — Hanging

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: At autopsy a ligature groove on the neck shows congestion of its margins, ecchymosis and extravasation of blood into the underlying subcutaneous tissue and muscle. This vital reaction indicates that the mark is:
options: A postmortem mark produced to simulate suicidal hanging
Nothing more than postmortem lividity in the neck
questions.concept: The distinction between antemortem and postmortem ligature marks rests on vital reaction. An antemortem mark shows congestion of the margins, ecchymosis and extravasation of blood into the subcutaneous tissue and muscle beneath the groove, and sometimes tears of the carotid intima — all evidence of a living circulation reacting to injury. A postmortem mark (as when a body is suspended after death to fake suicide) lacks vital reaction, has a soft pale base and shows no extravasation. The described features therefore denote an antemortem mark.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Hanging

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Compared with the mark of hanging, the ligature mark of ligature strangulation is typically:
options: Oblique, incomplete and situated high on the neck above the thyroid cartilage
Horizontal (transverse), continuous and completely encircling the neck, and low at or below the thyroid cartilage
V-shaped with its apex behind the ear
questions.concept: In ligature strangulation the constricting force is applied horizontally by an assailant, so the mark is transverse, usually continuous and completely encircling the neck, and lies low — at or below the level of the thyroid cartilage. In hanging, by contrast, the mark is oblique, incomplete (interrupted at the site of the knot) and high up above the thyroid, directed toward the point of suspension. Direction, completeness and level thus reliably separate strangulation from hanging.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Strangulation

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In forensic terminology, 'mugging' as a mode of violent asphyxia refers to:
options: Compression of the neck with a ligature that is twisted tight by means of a stick or rod
Manual strangulation using the thumbs and fingers
Strangulation by holding the victim's neck in the bend of the elbow (an arm-lock chokehold)
Occlusion of the nose and mouth with a pillow
questions.concept: Mugging is a form of strangulation in which the victim's neck is compressed within the bend/angle of the elbow (an arm-lock or chokehold), usually from behind. It is distinct from garroting (a ligature suddenly thrown around the neck from behind and tightened, classically for robbery or execution), from bansdola (compression of the neck or chest between two bamboo sticks or rods), and from throttling (manual strangulation with the hands and thumbs). Each of these leaves characteristically different neck marks.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Strangulation

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Smothering, as a form of mechanical asphyxia, is defined as:
options: Mechanical occlusion of the external air passages — the nose and mouth — so that breathing is prevented
Obstruction of the internal airway by an impacted food bolus
Compression of the chest that prevents respiratory movements
Closure of the glottis by sustained laryngeal spasm
questions.concept: Smothering is asphyxia produced by mechanical occlusion of the external respiratory orifices — the nose and mouth — for example by a hand, pillow, plastic bag or adhesive tape. It is most often homicidal (in infants, the elderly or the intoxicated) and, with plastic bags, may be suicidal or accidental.
