It is distinct from choking (internal airway obstruction by a foreign body or bolus), from traumatic asphyxia (chest compression) and from laryngospasm closing the glottis.
questions.reference: The Synopsis of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology (K.S. Narayan Reddy) — Smothering

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: During a robbery a cloth is forced into and tied across the victim's mouth; the victim is later found dead with the sodden cloth still in place. The asphyxial mechanism is best termed:
questions.concept: Gagging is obstruction of the mouth (and frequently the nose) by a cloth or similar material pushed into or tied across the mouth, usually to stop the victim calling for help during a crime. Death results from blockage of the air passages, often accelerated as the gag becomes soaked with saliva and mucus and swells, and by aspiration. It is typically accidental in the course of a felony. Choking is internal foreign-body obstruction, café coronary is bolus impaction during eating, and overlaying is accidental infant smothering.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Gagging

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In fresh-water drowning, absorption of the hypotonic aspirated water from the alveoli into the circulation classically produces:
options: Haemodilution, hypervolaemia, haemolysis with hyperkalaemia, and ventricular fibrillation
No appreciable change in circulating blood volume
Marked pulmonary oedema from fluid drawn osmotically into the alveoli
questions.concept: Fresh water is hypotonic relative to blood, so water aspirated into the alveoli is rapidly absorbed across the alveolar-capillary membrane into the circulation, causing haemodilution and hypervolaemia within a couple of minutes. Dilution plus haemolysis of red cells releases potassium, and the resulting hyperkalaemia together with anoxia precipitates ventricular fibrillation, so death may be very rapid. This contrasts with salt-water drowning, where hypertonic water draws plasma into the alveoli producing haemoconcentration and pulmonary oedema.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Relative to fresh-water drowning, salt-water (sea-water) drowning characteristically produces:
options: Haemoconcentration, hypovolaemia, hypernatraemia and marked pulmonary oedema
Immediate ventricular fibrillation as the usual mode of death
A fall in the serum sodium and chloride concentrations
questions.concept: Sea water is hypertonic (about 3% salt). Water aspirated into the alveoli therefore draws plasma osmotically OUT of the pulmonary capillaries into the alveolar spaces, producing intense pulmonary oedema together with haemoconcentration, hypovolaemia and hypernatraemia. Death tends to be somewhat slower than in fresh-water drowning, resulting from hypoxia and pulmonary oedema over several minutes rather than the rapid ventricular fibrillation of fresh-water drowning. This osmotic contrast is the basis of the Gettler chloride test.
questions.reference: Parikh's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Gettler's test, described for the diagnosis of antemortem drowning, is based on demonstrating a difference between the left and right sides of the heart in the concentration of:
questions.concept: The Gettler test compares the chloride (sodium chloride) concentration of blood drawn from the left and right ventricles. In fresh-water drowning the diluted blood returning to the left heart gives a LOWER left-sided chloride than the right; in salt-water drowning the left-sided chloride is HIGHER. A difference of about 25 mg/100 ml or more was regarded as significant. In practice the test is unreliable because of postmortem diffusion and resuscitation effects and is now largely of historical/academic value, but it remains a classic examination fact.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Paltauf's haemorrhages, seen in some cases of drowning, are:
options: Petechiae confined to the palpebral conjunctivae
Haemorrhages into the cavity of the middle ear
Small nodular haemorrhages scattered through the brain substance
Pale, bluish-red subpleural haemorrhages, larger than Tardieu spots, on the surface of the lungs
questions.concept: Paltauf's haemorrhages are subpleural haemorrhages of drowning — pale, bluish-red, and larger and more diffuse than Tardieu petechiae — found chiefly on the anterior and interlobar surfaces of the lungs. They result from rupture of alveolar walls and capillaries together with dilution of the blood by inhaled water. With voluminous water-logged lungs (emphysema aquosum) and fine froth in the airway they support antemortem drowning. Middle-ear haemorrhage is a separate drowning sign and is not Paltauf's spots.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Drowning

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The diatom (acid-digestion) test for antemortem drowning depends chiefly on which property of diatoms, and how is a positive result in the marrow of a closed long bone interpreted?
options: Their calcium-carbonate shells dissolve in acid, so any diatoms recovered must be postmortem contaminants
Their silica frustules resist strong-acid digestion; diatoms in the marrow of a closed bone imply they were carried there by the circulation during active (antemortem) drowning
Diatoms are proteinaceous and are destroyed by acid digestion, so their ABSENCE proves drowning
Diatoms enter closed bones equally by passive diffusion after death, so the test cannot indicate antemortem drowning
questions.concept: Diatoms are microscopic algae whose cell wall (frustule) is made of silica and resists the strong nitric/sulphuric acid digestion used to destroy the surrounding soft tissue in the test. For diatoms to reach the marrow of a 'closed' bone such as the femur they must have been inhaled with water and distributed by a beating heart — so their presence there indicates antemortem drowning. Reliable interpretation requires matching the diatom species and counts with those of the drowning medium and rigorous laboratory controls, since contamination and mere presence in the lungs are far less conclusive.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Drowning (Diatom Test)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A labourer is pinned across the chest under a collapsed wall for several minutes and dies. The face, neck and upper chest are deeply blue-purple with florid petechiae and marked subconjunctival haemorrhage, sharply demarcated at the level of compression. This 'masque ecchymotique' is characteristic of:
questions.concept: Traumatic (crush or compression) asphyxia occurs when the chest, or chest and upper abdomen, is forcibly compressed — crowd crushes, vehicle or wall collapse, cave-ins — preventing respiratory movement. The abrupt rise in intrathoracic and cranial venous pressure drives blood backward into the valveless veins of the head and neck, producing intense congestion, cyanosis, countless petechiae over the face, neck and upper chest, and subconjunctival haemorrhage — the 'ecchymotic mask' (masque ecchymotique of Morestin), sharply bordered at the compression line. Death is from inability to breathe, not from vascular occlusion.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Traumatic Asphyxia

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A heavily intoxicated man is found dead having slumped head-downward, doubled up in the narrow gap between a bed and the wall; there is no injury or natural disease to account for death. The most probable mechanism is:
questions.concept: Postural (positional) asphyxia is death resulting from a body position that mechanically impairs respiration. Typically an incapacitated person — through alcohol, drugs, restraint or a seizure — becomes trapped head-down or with the neck and chest sharply flexed so that diaphragmatic and chest-wall movement, or the airway itself, is obstructed, and the person cannot extricate themselves. It is diagnosed largely by exclusion together with a position known to compromise breathing, is usually accidental, and is important in deaths during restraint or in custody.
questions.reference: The Synopsis of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology (K.S. Narayan Reddy) — Traumatic and Postural Asphyxia

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A previously healthy 2-month-old infant who had been co-sleeping with an intoxicated adult is found dead in the bed with no injuries and no natural disease. The classic accidental asphyxial mechanism to be considered is:
options: Traumatic asphyxia from a crowd crush
questions.concept: Overlaying (overlying) is accidental mechanical asphyxia of an infant when a co-sleeping adult — often intoxicated or in deep sleep — rolls over and covers the baby's nose and mouth or compresses its chest, preventing breathing. It is characteristically accidental. It must be carefully distinguished from Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) and from deliberate smothering; the sleeping arrangement, the position in which the infant is found and the absence of any other cause guide interpretation, although definite proof is often difficult.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Smothering and Overlaying

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A young man is found dead alone in a locked room, partially suspended by a ligature that has soft padding beneath it, cross-dressed, surrounded by mirrors and pornographic material, with a self-release mechanism within reach that had failed. The most appropriate conclusion regarding the manner of death is:
options: Accidental death due to autoerotic (sexual) asphyxia
questions.concept: Autoerotic (sexual) asphyxia is self-induced partial asphyxia, usually by neck compression with a ligature, undertaken to heighten sexual pleasure through cerebral hypoxia; death occurs accidentally when the self-rescue mechanism fails. Characteristic scene findings include a solitary victim in a locked room, protective padding under the ligature, a binding or escape device within reach, erotic paraphernalia, mirrors, cross-dressing or bondage, usually no suicide note, and evidence of repeated previous activity. The manner of death is accidental, not suicide or homicide.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Sexual (Autoerotic) Asphyxia

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: 'Burking', named after the notorious 19th-century body-snatching murderers, is a homicidal method of asphyxia that combines:
options: Ligature strangulation followed by drowning of the victim
Manual throttling followed by hanging of the body
Smothering (closing the nose and mouth) together with traumatic asphyxia produced by sitting or kneeling on the chest
Gagging combined with administration of a chemical sedative
questions.concept: Burking is the method used by Burke and Hare in Edinburgh in the 1820s, who killed people to sell their bodies for dissection. The assailant sits or kneels on the victim's chest — producing traumatic/compression asphyxia by fixing the chest — while simultaneously closing the mouth and nose with the hands (smothering). The combination causes rapid death with very few external marks: no ligature mark and minimal neck injury. This is medicolegally important because the true cause of death can easily be overlooked.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, 26th ed. — Smothering (Burking)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In a case of ligature strangulation, which single finding most strongly favours a HOMICIDAL rather than a suicidal manner of death?
options: Multiple defence injuries on the hands and forearms with signs of a struggle and disturbed surroundings
A neatly tied single-loop knot at the front of the neck
A hesitantly written note found beside the body
A ligature short enough to have been applied by the deceased themselves
questions.concept: Ligature strangulation is nearly always homicidal, because a person usually loses consciousness before a self-applied ligature can be tightened enough to be fatal; self-strangulation is possible only rarely, using a special self-locking knot or tourniquet that stays tight after consciousness is lost. Features favouring homicide include defence wounds on the hands and forearms, evidence of a struggle, disturbed clothing and surroundings, a knot tied at the back out of the victim's reach, and multiple or crossing marks. A self-applicable ligature or a note does not by itself establish suicide.
questions.reference: The Synopsis of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology (K.S. Narayan Reddy) — Strangulation (Medicolegal Aspects)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A man dives into very cold water and dies almost instantly, before any water can be aspirated; autopsy shows none of the usual signs of drowning. This 'immersion syndrome' (hydrocution) is best explained by:
options: Massive pulmonary oedema caused by hypertonic water
Sustained laryngospasm trapping air within the lungs
Sudden reflex cardiac arrest (vagal inhibition) triggered by cold water striking the skin, pharynx or larynx
questions.concept: Immersion syndrome ('hydrocution') is sudden death within seconds of entering water — usually cold water — from reflex vagal cardiac arrest (bradycardia proceeding to asystole) provoked by cold water striking the skin, or stimulating the pharynx and larynx, sometimes potentiated by alcohol or by a very full or empty stomach. Because no water is aspirated, the classic signs of drowning are absent. It is distinct from 'dry drowning' (laryngospasm) and from ordinary wet drowning.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 34th ed. — Drowning (Immersion Syndrome)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In so-called 'dry drowning', which accounts for a minority of drowning deaths, the lungs at autopsy contain little or no water because death resulted from:
options: Immediate absorption of all the aspirated water into the bloodstream
Persistent laryngeal spasm that seals the airway when water contacts the larynx, causing asphyxia with minimal aspiration
Reflex vagal cardiac arrest from cold-water shock
Postmortem drainage of water out of the lungs before autopsy
questions.concept: 'Dry drowning' accounts for roughly 10-15% of drowning deaths. Contact of water with the sensitive laryngeal mucosa provokes intense, sustained laryngospasm that closes the glottis and prevents entry of both water and air, so death is from asphyxia with dry, non-oedematous lungs and little aspirated water. It is distinct from immersion syndrome, in which death is due to reflex vagal cardiac arrest, and from typical 'wet' drowning in which the lungs are voluminous and water-logged (emphysema aquosum).
questions.reference: Parikh's Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Drowning (Dry Drowning)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Molecular (cellular) death, as distinct from somatic death, is best defined as which of the following?
options: The irreversible stoppage of the functions of the brain, heart and lungs together
The death of individual cells and tissues, occurring a few hours after somatic death
The point at which the electroencephalogram first becomes isoelectric
The instant at which the heart stops but respiration briefly continues
questions.concept: Somatic death is the irreversible cessation of the three interdependent systems — nervous, circulatory and respiratory. Molecular or cellular death follows it: individual cells and tissues survive briefly and die gradually, roughly 3-4 hours after somatic death, as their oxygen supply ceases. This residual cellular life is what allows tissues such as cornea and skin to be harvested for a short while after death. Option A actually defines somatic death, not molecular death.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Thanatology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: According to Bichat's classification, the three modes of death are coma, syncope and asphyxia. Syncope as a mode of death results from primary failure of which system?
questions.concept: In Bichat's classical grouping, the mode of death names which of the three vital systems fails first. Coma is death from primary failure of the brain (nervous system), syncope is death from sudden and complete failure of the heart's action (circulation), and asphyxia is death from primary failure of respiration and oxygenation. Syncope may follow massive haemorrhage, a cardiac arrhythmia or vagal inhibition. The kidney is not one of Bichat's three modes.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Death and its Causes

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A ventilated patient in an intensive care unit is being assessed for brainstem death. Which one of the following findings is COMPATIBLE with the diagnosis and does NOT exclude it?
options: A brisk pupillary reaction to light
Spontaneous respiratory effort during the apnoea test
An intact corneal reflex on both sides
Preserved spinal reflexes such as a deep tendon jerk
questions.concept: Brainstem death requires demonstrable, irreversible loss of all brainstem functions: fixed non-reacting pupils and absent corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, gag and cough reflexes, with no respiratory drive on a formal apnoea test. Spinal-cord-mediated reflexes (deep tendon jerks, limb withdrawal, the Lazarus sign) may persist because the cord is still perfused, and their presence does NOT exclude brainstem death. A reacting pupil, an intact corneal reflex, or spontaneous respiration would each refute the diagnosis.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Death and Brainstem Death

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the postmortem body-temperature (algor mortis) curve?
options: It is sigmoid, with an initial plateau during which cooling is minimal before the rapid phase
It is perfectly linear, the body losing exactly one degree Celsius every hour until it reaches ambient temperature
The core temperature always rises steadily for the first six hours before it begins to fall
Cooling is fastest at the very end, as the body nears the surrounding temperature
questions.concept: Although Newton's law of cooling (rate proportional to the body-environment gradient) is often invoked, in practice the cooling curve is sigmoid. There is an initial plateau or lag period (about half an hour to three hours) when the surface cools but core temperature falls little, because metabolism and internal equilibration continue; then a steep near-linear middle phase; then the rate slows again as the body approaches ambient temperature. Cooling is therefore slowest, not fastest, at the end.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Death and its Signs

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: As a simple rule of thumb in a temperate climate, at approximately what rate does a body lose heat during the early hours after death?
options: About 1.5 degrees Fahrenheit (roughly 0.8 degree Celsius) per hour
questions.concept: A widely quoted approximation is that in temperate conditions the body cools by roughly 1.5 degrees Fahrenheit (about 0.8 degree Celsius) per hour during the first several hours, cooling more slowly thereafter. This gives the classical rough estimate that hours since death is approximately (98.4 minus the rectal temperature in Fahrenheit) divided by 1.5. Because the rate depends heavily on body build, clothing and environment, temperature-based estimates of time since death are only approximate.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Thanatology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Four bodies are discovered at the same postmortem interval. Which one would be expected to have cooled the MOST rapidly?
options: An obese adult wrapped in a thick blanket in a warm room
A muscular adult, fully clothed, in a room at body temperature
An emaciated infant lying unclothed on a cold stone floor
A heavily built adult who died of a septic fever in a warm ward
questions.concept: The rate of cooling rises with the ratio of body surface area to mass and with the temperature gradient to the surroundings. A thin infant has a very high surface-area-to-mass ratio, little insulating fat, no clothing, and lies on a cold conducting surface, so it cools fastest. Obesity, clothing or blankets, a warm environment, and a febrile state (a raised temperature at the moment of death) all slow apparent cooling. Hence the emaciated unclothed infant on cold stone cools most quickly.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Cooling of the Body

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The muscular stiffening of rigor mortis is produced by which underlying biochemical change?
options: Depletion of ATP, so that actin and myosin remain locked together as inextensible actomyosin
Excess ATP that drives continuous active muscle contraction after death
Coagulation of muscle proteins by lactic-acid-induced heat
Bacterial gas production that mechanically splints the muscles
questions.concept: During life ATP keeps the actin and myosin filaments dissociated, allowing muscle to relax. After death glycogen is consumed and ATP can no longer be regenerated; once ATP falls below roughly 85 percent of normal, actin and myosin bind irreversibly into rigid actomyosin, and the muscle becomes stiff and slightly shortened. Rigor passes off only when autolytic and putrefactive enzymes break down the actomyosin. It is thus an ATP-depletion phenomenon, not active contraction or bacterial gas.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Rigor Mortis

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: According to Nysten's rule for the sequence of rigor mortis in the voluntary muscles, in which muscles does rigor typically first become apparent?
options: The large muscles of the lower limbs
The muscles of the eyelids, face and lower jaw
The muscles of the trunk and abdominal wall
The small muscles of the fingers and toes
questions.concept: Nysten's rule states that rigor mortis appears first in involuntary muscle (the heart) and then, in the voluntary muscles, follows a cranio-caudal (descending) sequence: eyelids, face and lower jaw, then neck, thorax and upper limbs, then trunk, and finally the lower limbs. It disappears in the same order in which it appeared. This ordered onset and passing-off is what underlies its use in estimating the time since death.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Rigor Mortis

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Which single feature most reliably distinguishes cadaveric spasm from ordinary rigor mortis?
options: It typically involves every voluntary muscle of the body at once
It can be easily broken by the examiner and will then re-form
It is always preceded by a period of primary muscular flaccidity
It appears instantaneously at the moment of death, without any primary flaccidity
questions.concept: Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor or cataleptic rigidity) sets in at the very instant of death with no preceding primary flaccidity, whereas ordinary rigor is preceded by 1-2 hours of flaccidity and takes hours to develop. Cadaveric spasm usually affects only one group of muscles that were in strong contraction at death (commonly the hand), is linked with intense emotion or exertion, cannot be reproduced and once broken cannot re-form, and its exact cause is unknown. Ordinary rigor affects all muscles and, if broken early, re-forms.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Cadaveric Spasm

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body recovered from a house fire is heavily charred and lies in a flexed 'pugilistic (boxer's) attitude'. What is the correct interpretation of this posture?
options: Heat-induced coagulation and shortening of muscles, with flexors overpowering the extensors
Cadaveric spasm proving the victim was fighting the flames while conscious
Ordinary rigor mortis that developed after the fire was extinguished
Deliberate positioning of the body by an assailant before ignition
questions.concept: Exposure to intense heat (above roughly 65 degrees Celsius) coagulates and denatures muscle proteins, producing heat stiffening. Because the bulkier flexor muscles shorten more than the extensors, the limbs assume the flexed 'pugilistic' or boxer's attitude. Crucially, this posture develops whether the person was alive or already dead when burnt, so it has NO value in deciding whether the victim was alive in the fire. It is not cadaveric spasm and not ordinary rigor mortis.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Injuries from Heat and Thanatology

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body left in a freezing environment becomes rigid within a short time. This 'cold stiffening', which disappears on rewarming, is due to what?
options: Very rapid depletion of ATP producing true rigor within minutes
Coagulation of the muscle proteins by the extreme cold
Freezing of the tissue fluids and solidification of the subcutaneous fat
Instantaneous cadaveric spasm triggered by the cold
questions.concept: Cold stiffening is a physical, not biochemical, phenomenon: at freezing temperatures the body fluids freeze and the subcutaneous and other fat solidifies, making the body rigid, and on moving such a body the joints may crackle. When the body is rewarmed this stiffness disappears, and true rigor mortis then develops in the normal way. It must not be mistaken for genuine rigor, and it is distinct from heat stiffening, which is caused by coagulation of muscle proteins.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Rigor Mortis and Cold Stiffening

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In which of the following circumstances would rigor mortis be expected to appear UNUSUALLY early and also pass off quickly?
options: Death from massive haemorrhage in a person kept in a cold room
Death from strychnine poisoning after prolonged convulsions
Death of a healthy, well-rested young adult in a cool environment
Death of a well-nourished person immersed in cold water
questions.concept: The onset and duration of rigor depend largely on how much ATP and glycogen remain in the muscle at death and on the temperature. When muscles are exhausted before death — as after strychnine or tetanus convulsions, violent exertion, high fever or an exhausting illness — ATP is already depleted, so rigor develops rapidly and also passes off quickly. Cold environments and a rested, well-nourished state delay its onset and prolong it. Hence strychnine convulsions produce early, short-lasting rigor.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Rigor Mortis

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Postmortem lividity (hypostasis) is said to become 'fixed' — no longer shifting when the position of the body is changed — after approximately how long?
options: Within the first 30 minutes after death
Only after 48 hours, coinciding with putrefaction
questions.concept: Lividity begins as dull-red patches within about half an hour to one hour of death, coalesces, and is usually well developed by about 4 hours; up to that time it shifts if the body is turned. By roughly 6 to 8 hours it becomes 'fixed' owing to haemoconcentration, transudation and damage to the vessel walls, so that it no longer moves with a change of posture and no longer blanches fully on pressure. Fixation of lividity is therefore a useful, if approximate, marker of time since death and of original body position.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Postmortem Lividity

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A dark brown (chocolate-coloured) postmortem lividity is most characteristic of poisoning by which of the following?
options: Carbon monoxide from a faulty room heater
Hydrogen sulphide gas in a sewer
Nitrites, potassium chlorate or aniline compounds
questions.concept: The colour of postmortem staining can hint at the cause of death. Methaemoglobin-forming poisons — nitrites, nitrates, potassium chlorate, aniline, nitrobenzene and acetanilide — turn the blood, and hence the lividity, dark brown (chocolate). Carbon monoxide and cyanide give a cherry-red or bright pink hue, hydrogen sulphide and early putrefaction give a greenish discolouration, and simple asphyxia gives deep bluish-purple lividity. Recognising the brown tint points toward a methaemoglobinaemia-producing agent.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Postmortem Lividity

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: At autopsy an incision is made into a purple discolouration of the skin. Which finding indicates postmortem lividity rather than a bruise (contusion)?
options: Blood lies free within the vessels and washes away, leaving the tissues uninfiltrated
Blood is clotted, infiltrates the subcutaneous tissues, and cannot be washed off
There is swelling and elevation of the overlying skin
The colour changes progressively through green and yellow over several days
questions.concept: Lividity is intravascular: on incision the blood remains inside the vessels and can be wiped or washed away, the cut surface is clean, the tissues are not infiltrated and there is no swelling. A bruise is extravascular: blood has escaped into and coagulated within the tissues, so on incision it infiltrates the subcutaneous tissue, cannot be washed off, is often swollen or elevated, and its colour evolves over days if the person survived. These features reliably separate hypostasis from a true contusion.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Postmortem Lividity and Bruises

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The small dark petechial haemorrhages known as 'Tardieu spots', seen in the dependent parts of a body, are caused by what?
options: Antemortem trauma indicating a struggle before death
Bacterial colonisation of the skin during early putrefaction
Fat embolism lodging in the dermal capillaries
Rupture of distended capillaries in areas of intense postmortem hypostasis
questions.concept: Tardieu spots are pin-point (about 0.1-0.5 mm) petechial haemorrhages that appear in the most dependent, deeply congested parts of a body, particularly where hypostasis is intense and where death was associated with asphyxia. They result from the raised intravascular pressure of pooled, settling blood rupturing small distended capillaries and venules. They are a postmortem phenomenon and should not be misread as evidence of antemortem injury or of disease.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Postmortem Lividity

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Within an area of well-developed livor mortis, the skin over pressure points such as the shoulder blades and buttocks remains pale. Why?
options: These areas have no blood vessels in the dermis
Bacterial decomposition bleaches these regions first
Compression of the capillaries prevents blood from settling in them
Livor selectively spares areas with thicker skin
questions.concept: Livor mortis develops as gravity draws blood into the dependent capillaries and small vessels. Wherever the body presses firmly against a supporting surface, or where tight clothing or a ligature compresses the skin, the underlying capillaries are squeezed shut and blood cannot pool there, so those areas stay pale — 'contact pallor' or contact flattening. The pattern of these pale pressure marks helps indicate the position of the body after death and the presence of constricting objects.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Postmortem Lividity

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: The earliest external sign of putrefaction is a greenish discolouration of the skin appearing first over which region of the body?
options: The right iliac fossa, over the caecum
questions.concept: The first external sign of putrefaction is a greenish discolouration of the skin over the right iliac fossa, appearing in temperate climates in about 12-18 hours (sooner in the tropics). The caecum lies superficially there, is loaded with bacteria and fluid, and its contents are thin; hydrogen sulphide generated by the bacteria combines with haemoglobin to form greenish sulphaemoglobin, which stains the overlying skin. From there the discolouration spreads over the abdomen and then the rest of the body.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Putrefaction

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: During putrefaction a branching, reddish-brown to greenish network becomes visible over the shoulders, chest and thighs, following the line of the superficial veins. This 'marbling' is produced by what?
options: Dilatation of lymphatic channels filled with chyle
Deposition of bile pigment along the venous walls
Antemortem thrombosis of the superficial veins
Haemolysed blood reacting with hydrogen sulphide along the superficial veins
questions.concept: Marbling appears roughly 36-48 hours into putrefaction. Blood haemolyses within the superficial veins, and the released haemoglobin reacts with hydrogen sulphide produced by bacteria to form reddish-brown and then greenish sulphaemoglobin and iron sulphide, which stain the vessel walls and the adjacent skin. This outlines the branching pattern of the subcutaneous veins, giving the marbled or arborescent appearance, most obvious over the shoulders, chest, abdomen, groin and limbs.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Putrefaction

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Casper's dictum states that, other conditions being equal, the putrefaction of a body exposed to air for one week corresponds to that of a body immersed in water, or buried in earth, for what respective periods?
options: Two weeks in water and eight weeks in earth
Eight weeks in water and two weeks in earth
Four weeks in water and eight weeks in earth
One week in water and one week in earth
questions.concept: Casper's dictum expresses the relative rates of putrefaction in the three common environments as a ratio of air : water : earth = 1 : 2 : 8. In other words a body decomposes in air about twice as fast as in water and about eight times as fast as when buried in earth; thus one week of decomposition in air corresponds roughly to two weeks in water and eight weeks in the ground, assuming comparable temperature and other conditions. Burial, especially in deep, dry, cool soil, greatly retards decomposition.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Putrefaction

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body recovered after several weeks from a damp, waterlogged grave shows a greyish-white, greasy, wax-like material replacing the subcutaneous fat. Formation of this change (adipocere) requires which conditions?
options: A hot, dry environment with free circulation of air
Moisture together with a warm environment, hydrolysing and hydrogenating the body fat
The complete absence of any bacteria
questions.concept: Adipocere (saponification) is a modification of putrefaction in which body fat is converted into a greyish-white, greasy, wax-like substance of fatty acids and their salts. It needs moisture (from the body itself or a damp or watery surrounding) and warmth, and is promoted by anaerobic bacteria such as Clostridium welchii, whose lipases hydrolyse fat to fatty acids that are then hydrogenated. It develops in bodies immersed in water or lying in wet graves; earliest changes take about three weeks and full formation several months. A hot dry environment favours mummification instead.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Adipocere

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body recovered from a hot, dry desert is shrivelled and dry, with brown, leathery skin, the features still recognisable and no offensive smell. This form of preservation (mummification) develops under which conditions?
options: Immersion in cold running water for several weeks
Burial in a damp, poorly drained clay soil
Storage in a cold, humid mortuary environment
A hot, dry atmosphere with free circulation of air, causing rapid dehydration
questions.concept: Mummification is the dehydration and desiccation of the tissues that occurs when a body lies in a hot, dry environment with good air circulation, as in deserts or dry vaults. Rapid loss of water dries and shrinks the tissues before bacteria can multiply, so putrefaction is arrested; the skin becomes brown, dry and leathery, the body shrivels, yet the features and even injuries may remain recognisable. Moisture favours adipocere instead, and mere cold only delays decomposition without producing mummification.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Mummification

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: In forensic entomology, the minimum time since death of a decomposing body is estimated chiefly from which observation?
options: Identifying the species and the developmental stage (instar) of the oldest maggots present
Counting the total number of adult flies hovering around the body
Measuring the ambient humidity at the scene at the moment of discovery
Weighing the body and comparing it with the expected antemortem weight
questions.concept: Blowflies and flesh flies are attracted to a body within minutes to hours and lay eggs in the natural orifices and wounds. The eggs hatch into first-instar larvae (maggots), which grow through successive instars, pupate, and emerge as adults on a known, temperature-dependent timetable. By identifying the fly species and the developmental stage of the oldest and largest larvae or pupae, and correcting for temperature, an entomologist estimates the minimum postmortem interval. The mere number of adult flies, or the ambient humidity alone, cannot date the death.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Estimation of Time Since Death

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: Which biochemical change in the vitreous humour of the eye is used to help estimate the time since death?
options: A progressive fall in the potassium concentration
A progressive rise in the potassium concentration
A steady rise in the glucose concentration
A rapid rise in the sodium concentration
questions.concept: After death potassium leaks out of the retinal and other ocular cells into the vitreous humour, so its concentration rises steadily and fairly predictably with the postmortem interval, usefully up to about 100 hours. Because the vitreous is anatomically isolated and resists putrefaction, it gives more reliable postmortem chemistry than blood. In contrast, vitreous sodium and chloride tend to fall and glucose falls after death; it is the RISE in potassium that is applied to estimate the time since death.
questions.reference: Modi's A Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology — Estimation of Time Since Death

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body is found with the eyes open. A yellowish to brownish-black horizontal band is seen across the exposed sclera on either side of the cornea. This 'tache noire' is due to what?
options: Deposition of bile pigment in scleral jaundice
Desiccation (drying) of the exposed area of sclera after death
A malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva
questions.concept: When the eyelids remain open after death, the strip of sclera exposed on either side of the cornea dries out. As it desiccates it first appears yellowish and then forms a brownish-black band called the tache noire de la sclerotique. It is purely a postmortem drying artefact and is neither haemorrhage, jaundice nor tumour. The exposed cornea similarly loses its lustre and becomes cloudy and opaque as it dries, which is another early ocular postmortem change.
questions.reference: Nandy, Principles of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Changes in the Eye after Death

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: At autopsy the stomach is found full of recently eaten, easily recognisable and largely undigested food. In relation to the last meal, this finding most reliably suggests that death occurred approximately when?
options: About 12 hours after the last meal
About 24 hours after the last meal
Several days after the last meal
Within roughly 1 to 2 hours of the last meal
questions.concept: The stomach normally begins to empty soon after eating and is largely empty within a few hours (a light meal in about 2 hours, a full meal in about 4-6 hours). A stomach full of recently ingested, recognisable and undigested food therefore indicates death within roughly one to two hours of the last meal, and the nature of the food may itself help identify the meal. Because gastric emptying is affected by illness, emotion, drugs and the type of meal, this estimate of time since the last meal is only a rough guide and must be corroborated.
questions.reference: Reddy's The Essentials of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology — Estimation of Time Since Death

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Mycobacterium tuberculosis retains carbol fuchsin despite decolourization with acid-alcohol during Ziehl-Neelsen staining. This acid-fast property is chiefly attributable to which component of its cell wall?
questions.concept: Acid-fastness results from the thick, waxy mycolic acid layer of the mycobacterial cell wall, which resists decolourization by acid-alcohol so bacilli retain carbol fuchsin and appear red against a methylene-blue counterstain. Peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid are Gram-positive wall features; LPS/endotoxin is Gram-negative. This lipid-rich wall also underlies slow growth and disinfectant resistance.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Tuberculosis (microbiology); Ananthanarayan & Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Mycobacterium

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A sputum sample is sent for mycobacterial culture. Compared with solid Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium, the automated liquid MGIT (Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube) system chiefly offers which advantage?
options: It detects rifampicin resistance directly without drug-susceptibility testing
It yields a positive result faster, typically within 1-2 weeks
It is more specific because contamination never occurs
It does not require a biosafety level 3 laboratory
questions.concept: Liquid MGIT culture detects growth (via fluorescence from oxygen consumption) in roughly 1-2 weeks versus 2-8 weeks for solid LJ medium, and is more sensitive, so WHO/NTEP prefer liquid culture where feasible. However, liquid systems have higher contamination rates, still require BSL-3 containment, and culture alone does not identify drug resistance — that needs phenotypic DST or molecular tests. LJ remains cheaper and useful for colony morphology.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Laboratory diagnosis; WHO liquid culture policy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Sputum smear microscopy is far less sensitive than culture for diagnosing pulmonary tuberculosis. Approximately what minimum bacillary load per millilitre of sputum is generally required for a smear to be reliably positive?
questions.concept: Smear microscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen or fluorescent) needs roughly 5,000-10,000 acid-fast bacilli per mL of sputum to be consistently positive, which is why smear-negative but culture-positive or CBNAAT-positive disease is common. Culture can detect as few as 10-100 viable bacilli/mL, and CBNAAT around 130 bacilli/mL, making both far more sensitive. This threshold explains the value of molecular testing in paucibacillary and HIV-associated TB.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Tuberculosis (diagnosis); API Textbook of Medicine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with 4 weeks of cough submits sputum for CBNAAT (GeneXpert MTB/RIF). Besides confirming the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, this single assay simultaneously detects resistance to which drug?
questions.concept: GeneXpert MTB/RIF (CBNAAT) is a cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test that detects M. tuberculosis DNA and rpoB gene mutations conferring rifampicin resistance, giving results in about 2 hours. It does NOT detect isoniazid, ethambutol or pyrazinamide resistance — those need line probe assay or phenotypic DST. Rifampicin resistance serves as a surrogate marker for likely MDR-TB and triggers further DST under NTEP's Universal DST policy.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Molecular diagnostics; WHO Xpert MTB/RIF policy

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Under NTEP, the first-line Line Probe Assay (LPA) is used on smear-positive specimens or cultures. It rapidly detects resistance to which combination of drugs?
questions.concept: First-line LPA (GenoType MTBDRplus) detects rifampicin resistance (rpoB) and isoniazid resistance (katG for high-level, inhA for low-level) within 1-2 days. Second-line LPA (MTBDRsl) detects fluoroquinolone and second-line injectable resistance. LPA thus adds isoniazid resistance information that CBNAAT (rifampicin only) cannot provide, helping distinguish isoniazid mono/poly-resistant TB from MDR-TB and guide regimen selection.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Line Probe Assay; WHO LPA policy update

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) is performed with 5 TU of PPD injected intradermally. Which statement about its correct interpretation is TRUE?
options: Erythema diameter is measured at 24 hours
Induration is measured transversely at 48-72 hours
A positive test confirms active tuberculosis disease
Prior BCG vaccination never affects the result
questions.concept: The Mantoux test is read at 48-72 hours by measuring the transverse diameter of INDURATION (not erythema). It indicates infection/immune sensitisation, not active disease, and may be positive from prior BCG or non-tuberculous mycobacteria (false positive) or falsely negative in HIV, miliary TB, malnutrition or immunosuppression. Cutoffs vary by risk group (>=5 mm in HIV/close contacts, >=10 mm in others in India). Verify programme cutoffs against current NTEP guidance.
questions.reference: NTEP guidelines; Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Tuberculosis (TST)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Choose the correct option. Assertion (A): Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) are preferred over the tuberculin skin test for detecting TB infection in BCG-vaccinated individuals. Reason (R): IGRAs use the antigens ESAT-6 and CFP-10, which are absent from the BCG vaccine strain and from most non-tuberculous mycobacteria.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: IGRAs (QuantiFERON-TB Gold, T-SPOT.TB) measure interferon-gamma release from T-cells stimulated by M. tuberculosis-specific antigens ESAT-6 and CFP-10, encoded in the RD1 region deleted from BCG and absent from most NTM. Hence IGRAs are not confounded by prior BCG vaccination, unlike the TST, so R correctly explains A. Like the TST, however, IGRA cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Tuberculosis (IGRA); CDC/WHO IGRA guidance

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A paediatric chest radiograph shows a peripheral subpleural parenchymal focus in the right lower zone together with enlarged ipsilateral hilar lymph nodes. This combination is best described as:
options: A cavitary lesion of the right upper lobe (post-primary TB)
questions.concept: Primary TB typically produces a peripheral parenchymal Ghon focus (often mid/lower zones) plus draining hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy — together the Ghon (primary) complex; when calcified it becomes the Ranke complex. Post-primary (reactivation) TB classically favours the apical/posterior segments of upper lobes with cavitation. Miliary TB shows diffuse millet-seed nodules. Recognising primary versus post-primary patterns aids age-appropriate diagnosis in children.
questions.reference: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine — Tuberculosis; Harrison's 21st ed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Under the NTEP daily fixed-dose combination regimen for a new case of drug-sensitive pulmonary TB, the continuation phase consists of which drugs and duration?
questions.concept: In the NTEP daily regimen, new drug-sensitive pulmonary TB is treated with a 2-month intensive phase of HRZE followed by a 4-month continuation phase of HRE — ethambutol is retained through the continuation phase (unlike older thrice-weekly regimens that used only HR). Pyrazinamide is stopped after the intensive phase; total duration is 6 months. Regimen composition and durations are change-prone; verify against current NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Treatment of drug-sensitive TB

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 60-kg adult with newly diagnosed drug-sensitive pulmonary TB is started on the NTEP daily FDC regimen. In the intensive phase, how many adult four-drug FDC tablets (HRZE) should he receive each day?
questions.concept: NTEP daily FDC dosing is weight-band based: 25-39 kg = 2 tablets, 40-54 kg = 3, 55-69 kg = 4, and >=70 kg = 5 tablets daily. A 60-kg patient falls in the 55-69 kg band and receives 4 adult HRZE tablets daily in the intensive phase (and 4 HRE tablets in the continuation phase). Weight-band tablet counts are change-prone; verify against current NTEP guidelines and re-band the patient if weight changes.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Weight-band dosing

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Under NTEP outcome definitions, a bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patient who completes treatment and is documented smear- or culture-negative at the end of treatment (and on at least one earlier occasion) is classified as:
questions.concept: 'Cured' applies to a bacteriologically confirmed patient who is smear/culture-negative at the end of treatment AND on at least one previous occasion. 'Treatment completed' is one who finished treatment without evidence of failure but WITHOUT the documented end-of-treatment negative result (test not done/unavailable). 'Failure' is sputum positive at month 5 or later. 'Lost to follow-up' is treatment interrupted for >=1 consecutive month. Verify exact wording against current NTEP.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Treatment outcome definitions

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 30-year-old malnourished man on antitubercular therapy develops numbness and burning in both feet. Which drug is responsible, and which agent prevents this adverse effect?
questions.concept: Isoniazid causes dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy by interfering with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) metabolism and increasing its excretion; risk is higher in malnutrition, alcoholism, diabetes, pregnancy, HIV and renal failure. Prophylactic pyridoxine (10 mg/day, more for treatment) prevents and treats it. Ethambutol causes optic neuritis, rifampicin causes orange secretions/hepatotoxicity, and pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia — none is the cause here.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Antituberculous drugs; KD Tripathi Pharmacology

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Choose the correct option. Assertion (A): Orange-red discolouration of urine in a patient on rifampicin indicates hepatotoxicity and mandates immediately stopping the drug. Reason (R): Rifampicin can cause drug-induced hepatitis.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: Orange-red discolouration of urine, sweat, tears and other secretions is a harmless, expected effect of rifampicin (it may permanently stain soft contact lenses) and is NOT a sign of hepatotoxicity, so the drug should be continued with reassurance — the Assertion is false. The Reason is true: rifampicin genuinely can cause drug-induced hepatitis, which is detected by symptoms and rising transaminases/bilirubin, not by urine colour.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Pharmacology — Antitubercular drugs; Harrison's 21st ed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Choose the correct option. Assertion (A): Pyrazinamide can precipitate arthralgia and acute gout in patients on antitubercular therapy. Reason (R): Pyrazinamide is a bactericidal drug that is most active against intracellular bacilli in an acidic environment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are individually true, but the Reason does not explain the Assertion. Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia because its metabolite pyrazinoic acid inhibits renal tubular secretion of uric acid, precipitating arthralgia/gout — this is unrelated to its separate, true property of being bactericidal against intracellular bacilli in acidic (phagolysosomal) conditions. Hence the answer is 'both true, R not the correct explanation'.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Pharmacology — Pyrazinamide; Harrison's 21st ed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: Streptomycin, an aminoglycoside occasionally used in TB treatment, most characteristically causes which pair of adverse effects?
options: Optic neuritis and red-green colour blindness
questions.concept: Streptomycin damages the vestibulocochlear (eighth cranial) nerve causing vestibular disturbance and hearing loss, and is nephrotoxic — classic aminoglycoside toxicities that are largely dose- and age-related and often partly irreversible. It is contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal ototoxicity). Optic neuritis is ethambutol, neuropathy is isoniazid, and hyperuricemia is pyrazinamide — matching those toxicities to the wrong drug is a common exam trap.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Pharmacology — Streptomycin; Harrison's 21st ed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: WHO (2022) and NTEP now recommend a 6-month oral regimen for eligible rifampicin-resistant/MDR-TB known by the acronym BPaLM. Which four drugs does BPaLM comprise?
questions.concept: BPaLM = Bedaquiline + Pretomanid + Linezolid + Moxifloxacin, a WHO-recommended (2022) all-oral 6-month regimen for RR/MDR-TB, replacing longer injectable-containing regimens for eligible patients; where fluoroquinolone resistance is confirmed the 'M' is dropped (BPaL). Key toxicities include linezolid myelosuppression/neuropathy and bedaquiline/moxifloxacin QT prolongation. DR-TB regimens change frequently — verify eligibility and composition against current NTEP/WHO guidance.
questions.reference: WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Drug-Resistant TB Treatment 2022; NTEP DR-TB guidelines

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: According to the revised WHO 2021 definitions, extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is MDR/RR-TB with additional resistance to:
options: Any fluoroquinolone AND at least one of bedaquiline or linezolid
questions.concept: In the WHO 2021 revision, pre-XDR-TB = MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone; XDR-TB = MDR/RR-TB plus resistance to any fluoroquinolone AND to at least one additional Group A drug (bedaquiline or linezolid). The older definition (fluoroquinolone plus a second-line injectable) is now outdated because injectables were deprioritised. These definitions are change-prone; verify against current WHO/NTEP guidance.
questions.reference: WHO 2021 revised definitions of pre-XDR and XDR-TB; NTEP DR-TB guidelines

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A newly diagnosed HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 40 cells/µL) is found to have pulmonary TB. Regarding sequencing of therapy, the recommended approach is:
options: Start antitubercular treatment first, then initiate ART as early as within 2 weeks
Start ART first and defer antitubercular treatment until viral suppression
Start both simultaneously on day 1 in every patient regardless of CD4
Withhold ART entirely until antitubercular treatment is completed
questions.concept: In TB-HIV coinfection, antitubercular treatment is started first and ART is added early: with CD4 <50 cells/µL, ART should begin within 2 weeks of starting ATT; with higher CD4, within 2-8 weeks. Early ART reduces mortality but risks paradoxical immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), especially at very low CD4. ART is indicated in ALL TB-HIV patients regardless of CD4; never defer it until ATT completion. Note rifampicin-antiretroviral drug interactions.
questions.reference: NACO/NTEP TB-HIV guidelines; WHO HIV-associated TB guidelines; Harrison's 21st ed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A household contact is offered TB preventive treatment (TPT) after active TB is excluded. The '3HP' regimen used in expanded NTEP TPT refers to:
options: 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (12 doses)
3 months of daily pyrazinamide plus rifampicin
questions.concept: 3HP is a short-course TB preventive regimen of once-weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine for 3 months (12 doses); rifapentine's long half-life permits weekly dosing, improving completion versus 6 months of daily isoniazid (6H). NTEP has expanded shorter TPT options (3HP, 3HR, 1HP) alongside 6H. Active TB must always be excluded before starting TPT. TPT options are change-prone; verify eligibility and dosing against current NTEP guidance.
questions.reference: NTEP Guidelines for Programmatic Management of TB Preventive Treatment in India; WHO TPT guidelines

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A 25-year-old with weeks of fever, weight loss and dyspnoea has a chest radiograph showing innumerable uniform 1-3 mm nodules evenly distributed throughout both lung fields; fundoscopy may reveal choroidal tubercles. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Miliary TB results from haematogenous dissemination of bacilli, producing myriad uniform millet-sized (1-3 mm) nodules diffusely across both lungs; choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy are highly suggestive. It is often smear-negative (paucibacillary), so diagnosis relies on imaging, biopsy/culture and clinical context, and it can be complicated by TB meningitis. Cavitary upper-lobe disease and lobar pneumonia produce quite different radiographic patterns.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Miliary TB; API Textbook of Medicine

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with drug-sensitive pulmonary TB. Which antitubercular drug is contraindicated in pregnancy owing to fetal ototoxicity?
questions.concept: Streptomycin (and other aminoglycosides) crosses the placenta and can cause irreversible fetal eighth-nerve damage (congenital deafness), so it is contraindicated in pregnancy. The standard first-line oral drugs — isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol — are considered safe, and TB should be treated promptly in pregnancy. Pyridoxine is co-administered with isoniazid. Untreated TB poses greater risk to mother and fetus than the first-line drugs.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — TB in pregnancy; NTEP guidelines

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A new smear-positive pulmonary TB patient is on the NTEP 6-month daily regimen. Under standard monitoring, the FIRST scheduled follow-up sputum smear examination is performed at:
options: The end of the intensive phase (end of 2nd month)
The end of the 4th month only
Only at the end of treatment (6th month)
questions.concept: Follow-up sputum smears assess response: the first is done at the end of the intensive phase (end of month 2). If positive at that point, further evaluation and drug-susceptibility testing are undertaken (routine IP extension has been dropped in favour of assessing for resistance). Subsequent smears are done in the continuation phase and at the end of treatment (month 6); positivity at month 5 or later defines treatment failure. Monitoring schedules are change-prone; verify against current NTEP guidelines.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Treatment monitoring

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: A patient on HRZE develops nausea and jaundice; serum ALT is 6 times the upper limit of normal. The most appropriate immediate step is to:
options: Continue all drugs and add a hepatoprotective agent
Stop only ethambutol and continue HRZ
Halve the dose of all four drugs
Stop all hepatotoxic antitubercular drugs and monitor liver function
questions.concept: Antitubercular drug-induced hepatitis warrants stopping the hepatotoxic drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide) when ALT is >=3x ULN with symptoms/jaundice or >=5x ULN without symptoms. Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic. Once transaminases and bilirubin normalise and symptoms resolve, drugs are reintroduced sequentially (rechallenge) under monitoring; a non-hepatotoxic bridging regimen may be used if treatment cannot be interrupted. Continuing or merely reducing doses risks fulminant hepatic failure.
questions.reference: ATS/IDSA hepatotoxicity statement; NTEP guidelines; Harrison's 21st ed

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In the DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course) strategy, the phrase 'directly observed treatment' specifically means that:
options: A physician must personally prescribe every dose in a hospital
The patient records each self-administered dose in a diary
A trained treatment supporter watches the patient swallow each dose
Sputum is directly examined before each dose is given
questions.concept: The 'directly observed' component of DOTS means a trained treatment supporter or health worker actually watches the patient swallow each dose to ensure adherence and completion, reducing treatment failure, relapse and acquired drug resistance. DOTS has five pillars: political/administrative commitment, diagnosis by quality-assured bacteriology, standardized supervised treatment with patient support, uninterrupted drug supply, and standardized recording/reporting with outcome monitoring.
questions.reference: WHO DOTS/Stop TB strategy; NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.stem: In India's National TB Elimination Programme, 'Ni-kshay' primarily refers to:
options: The web-based portal for TB case notification and patient management
A new fixed-dose combination antitubercular tablet
A surgical procedure for drug-resistant TB
questions.concept: Ni-kshay is the national web- and app-based information system of NTEP used to notify, register and longitudinally manage TB patients — including private-sector notification, drug logistics and monitoring outcomes. The linked Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana provides direct-benefit nutritional support to notified patients. It is a surveillance/case-management platform, not a drug, diagnostic cartridge or procedure. Programme features evolve; verify current Ni-kshay functions against NTEP.
questions.reference: NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines for TB Control in India 2023 — Ni-kshay and surveillance

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The acid-fast property of Mycobacterium tuberculosis — its ability to resist decolourisation by acid-alcohol after staining with carbol fuchsin — is attributed primarily to which component of its cell wall?
options: A thick outer capsule of hyaluronic acid
Long-chain mycolic acids in a waxy, high-lipid cell wall
questions.concept: Acid-fastness is due to the exceptionally high lipid content of the mycobacterial cell wall, dominated by long-chain (C60-C90) mycolic acids covalently linked to the arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan skeleton; this waxy coat traps carbol fuchsin and resists 20% sulphuric-acid-alcohol decolourisation. Hyaluronic-acid capsules belong to streptococci, teichoic acid to Gram-positive cocci, and LPS/endotoxin to Gram-negative outer membranes — none confer acid-fastness.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Mycobacterium tuberculosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Mycobacterium tuberculosis shows a marked predilection for the apices of the lungs and grows preferentially in the upper part of a Lowenstein-Jensen slant. This behaviour is best explained by the fact that the organism is:
questions.concept: M. tuberculosis is a strict (obligate) aerobe, so it thrives where oxygen tension is highest — the well-ventilated lung apices and the exposed upper surface of a culture slant. This aerobic requirement, coupled with a slow generation time (~15-20 hours), underlies the classic upper-lobe cavitary disease. It is not a facultative anaerobe or microaerophile, and although added CO2 modestly aids primary isolation it is not an obligate capnophile like some fastidious organisms.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Mycobacteria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: On smears from virulent strains of M. tuberculosis the bacilli line up in parallel, rope-like 'serpentine cords'. The surface glycolipid responsible for this cord formation and correlated with virulence is:
questions.concept: Cord factor is trehalose 6,6'-dimycolate (TDM), a glycolipid of the cell surface that causes virulent tubercle bacilli to grow as intertwined serpentine cords; it is toxic to mammalian cells, inhibits leukocyte migration, and contributes to granuloma formation. LAM modulates the host immune response and phosphatidylinositol mannosides anchor LAM, but neither produces cords; Wax D acts as an adjuvant (Freund's), not the cording factor.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Virulence factors)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A slow-growing acid-fast isolate is being biochemically identified. Which combination of results most strongly supports Mycobacterium tuberculosis rather than a non-tuberculous mycobacterium?
options: Niacin negative, nitrate negative, heat-stable catalase
Niacin negative, urease negative, arylsulfatase positive
Niacin positive, nitrate positive, arylsulfatase positive at 3 days
Niacin positive, nitrate reduction positive, catalase heat-labile (negative at 68°C)
questions.concept: M. tuberculosis characteristically accumulates niacin (positive niacin test), reduces nitrate to nitrite (nitrate positive), and possesses a weak catalase that is heat-labile — destroyed after heating to 68°C at pH 7, so it is 68°C-catalase negative. Most NTM are niacin negative and many have a heat-stable catalase; rapid arylsulfatase positivity at 3 days points instead to rapid growers such as M. fortuitum, making the other combinations wrong.
questions.reference: Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology — Mycobacteria (Biochemical identification)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In the classical Ziehl-Neelsen technique for demonstrating acid-fast bacilli, the primary stain applied with the aid of heat is:
questions.concept: In Ziehl-Neelsen staining the primary stain is carbol fuchsin (basic fuchsin in phenol), driven into the waxy cell wall by heating until vapours rise; the smear is then decolourised with acid-alcohol (e.g., 20% H2SO4) and counterstained with methylene blue, so acid-fast bacilli appear red against a blue background. Malachite green is used in Lowenstein-Jensen medium and spore staining, and crystal violet is the primary dye of the Gram stain — not of ZN.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Laboratory diagnosis of tuberculosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A laboratory wants an acid-fast staining method that avoids the fire/heating step of conventional Ziehl-Neelsen. Which modification achieves this by using a more concentrated carbol fuchsin plus a wetting agent, requiring no heat?
questions.concept: The Kinyoun method is the 'cold' acid-fast stain: it raises the concentration of basic fuchsin and phenol and adds a wetting agent (e.g., tergitol) so the dye penetrates the waxy wall without heating. Auramine-rhodamine is a fluorochrome method needing a fluorescence microscope, Fite-Faraco is a weak-acid modification for M. leprae/Nocardia, and Albert's stain demonstrates metachromatic granules of Corynebacterium diphtheriae — none is simply a heat-free ZN.
questions.reference: Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology — Acid-fast staining methods

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A high-volume TB laboratory switches from Ziehl-Neelsen to auramine-rhodamine fluorescence microscopy for sputum smears. The principal advantage that improves case detection is that fluorescence microscopy:
options: Distinguishes live from dead bacilli reliably
Allows scanning at lower magnification so smears are read faster with higher sensitivity
questions.concept: Auramine-rhodamine binds mycolic acids and makes bacilli glow bright yellow-green against a dark background; because bright objects are seen at lower magnification, a larger field is scanned per view, so slides are examined faster and more sensitively than by ZN (bacilli are easier to spot at low loads). It cannot judge viability, does not detect rifampicin resistance (a molecular function of Xpert/LPA), and it still requires acid-alcohol decolourisation.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Laboratory diagnosis of mycobacteria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Branching, filamentous Gram-positive organisms from a lung abscess are decolourised by routine 20% sulphuric-acid Ziehl-Neelsen but retain the stain when a weaker (1%) acid is used. This 'modified acid-fast' (partial acid-fastness) is most characteristic of:
questions.concept: Nocardia is only partially (weakly) acid-fast: its lower mycolic-acid content means it is decolourised by the strong acid of standard ZN but retains carbol fuchsin when a modified stain with weak (1%) sulphuric acid is used. M. tuberculosis is fully acid-fast even with strong acid. Actinomyces and Streptomyces are branching filaments too but are not acid-fast at all, so weak-acid retention specifically flags Nocardia.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Nocardia (modified acid-fast stain)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: On Lowenstein-Jensen medium, colonies of Mycobacterium tuberculosis are classically described as:
options: Smooth, moist, mucoid and grey within 24-48 hours
Dry, rough, wrinkled and buff-coloured after several weeks
Flat, spreading with a 'medusa head' edge in 1-2 days
questions.concept: M. tuberculosis grows slowly (2-8 weeks) on egg-based Lowenstein-Jensen medium, forming characteristic 'rough, tough and buff' colonies — dry, wrinkled/raised, adherent and pale buff (cream) in colour. Rapid 24-48 hour growth of moist grey or medusa-head colonies describes ordinary fast-growing bacteria (e.g., Bacillus), and small non-pigmented colonies in 3-5 days would suggest a rapidly growing mycobacterium, not classic M. tuberculosis.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Culture of tubercle bacilli

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A clinician needs the fastest culture-based confirmation of M. tuberculosis with drug-susceptibility testing. Compared with solid Lowenstein-Jensen medium, an automated liquid system such as the MGIT (Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube) offers which key advantage?
options: Detects mycobacterial growth in about 1-2 weeks rather than several weeks
Eliminates the need for prior sputum decontamination
Identifies the species without any supplementary testing
Removes the requirement for biosafety containment
questions.concept: Liquid culture systems (MGIT, BACTEC) detect metabolic growth via an oxygen-quenched fluorescent sensor within roughly 1-2 weeks — substantially faster than the 3-8 weeks needed for visible colonies on solid LJ — and support rapid liquid drug-susceptibility testing. They still require Petroff/NALC-NaOH decontamination of sputum, still need identification tests (e.g., MPT64 antigen or probes) to name the species, and being live-culture systems still demand full biosafety containment.
questions.reference: Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology — Liquid culture systems for mycobacteria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Before inoculating sputum onto Lowenstein-Jensen medium, Petroff's method is used. The chemical basis of this pre-treatment is that:
options: Oxalic acid selectively concentrates Pseudomonas-contaminated specimens
4% NaOH liquefies the specimen and kills faster-growing contaminants while tubercle bacilli survive
Chlorhexidine sterilises the sample completely before culture
5% oxalic acid decolourises the smear for staining
questions.concept: Petroff's method uses 4% sodium hydroxide to digest (liquefy) mucoid sputum and decontaminate it: the relatively resistant, lipid-rich tubercle bacilli survive brief alkali exposure while the more delicate commensal/contaminating flora are killed, allowing selective isolation on culture. The specimen is then neutralised and concentrated by centrifugation. Oxalic acid is reserved for Pseudomonas-contaminated samples, and complete sterilisation would kill the mycobacteria too, so those options are wrong.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Concentration and decontamination of specimens

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Lowenstein-Jensen medium contains coagulated egg, glycerol, asparagine, mineral salts and malachite green. The specific role of malachite green in this medium is to:
options: Provide the sole carbon source for mycobacterial growth
Neutralise toxic fatty acids in the specimen
Act as a pH indicator that turns yellow on acid production
Inhibit growth of contaminating bacteria (selective agent) and impart colour
questions.concept: Malachite green is the selective (inhibitory) ingredient of Lowenstein-Jensen medium: it suppresses growth of contaminating commensal bacteria while permitting slow-growing mycobacteria to develop, and it also gives the medium its green colour against which buff colonies stand out. Glycerol/asparagine supply carbon and nitrogen (not malachite green), and although some formulations add serum/charcoal or albumin to neutralise toxic fatty acids, that is not malachite green's function, and it is not a pH indicator.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Lowenstein-Jensen medium

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A reference laboratory processes a culture isolate on a line probe assay (e.g., GenoType MTBDRplus). Compared with the initial rapid cartridge NAAT, the distinctive capability of this reverse-hybridisation strip assay is that it:
options: Grows the organism to confirm viability
Simultaneously detects mutations conferring both rifampicin AND isoniazid resistance
Detects only rifampicin resistance via the rpoB gene
Provides a phenotypic minimum inhibitory concentration
questions.concept: Line probe assays amplify mycobacterial DNA and hybridise it to immobilised wild-type and mutant probes on a strip; the first-line MTBDRplus detects rpoB mutations (rifampicin) together with katG and inhA mutations (isoniazid), so it reports both drugs at once, unlike a single-drug rifampicin cartridge test. It is a molecular, not culture, method (no viability/MIC output), and detecting only rpoB understates its dual first-line coverage; second-line LPA (MTBDRsl) extends to fluoroquinolone/aminoglycoside loci.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Molecular detection of drug resistance (line probe assay)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Isoniazid is a prodrug that must be activated inside the mycobacterium before it can block mycolic acid synthesis. High-level isoniazid resistance most commonly results from mutation of which gene, whose product normally activates the drug?
questions.concept: Isoniazid must be activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase encoded by katG; loss-of-function katG mutations prevent activation and cause high-level INH resistance, while mutations in inhA (the enoyl-ACP reductase target/promoter) give low-level resistance with ethionamide cross-resistance. rpoB mutations underlie rifampicin resistance, embB confers ethambutol resistance, and pncA mutations cause pyrazinamide resistance — none activate isoniazid.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Mechanisms of antimycobacterial drug resistance

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Rapid molecular assays for rifampicin resistance in M. tuberculosis target a short hot-spot region of a single gene, because most resistance mutations cluster there. This gene encodes the drug's target, the:
questions.concept: Rifampicin binds the beta subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; about 95% of resistant strains carry mutations within the 81-bp rifampicin-resistance-determining region (RRDR) of rpoB, which is why cartridge NAAT and line probe assays interrogate that hot-spot. gyrA mutations cause fluoroquinolone resistance, rpsL underlies streptomycin resistance, and embB confers ethambutol resistance — so those are the wrong targets for a rifampicin assay.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Rifampicin resistance (rpoB)

questions.subject: Microbiology
