questions.stem: In the laboratory classification of drug resistance, an isolate is defined as multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) when it is resistant to at least:
questions.concept: MDR-TB is defined by in-vitro resistance to at least the two most powerful first-line agents — isoniazid AND rifampicin — regardless of resistance to other drugs. Resistance to rifampicin alone is termed rifampicin-resistant (RR) TB and is often used as a surrogate marker, and isoniazid mono-resistance is not MDR; 'any two first-line drugs' is too loose because the definition specifically requires INH plus RIF. Extensively drug-resistant TB adds fluoroquinolone plus further second-line resistance.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Drug resistance in tuberculosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The Mantoux tuberculin test, in which purified protein derivative (PPD/RT23) is injected intradermally and read at 48-72 hours, is an in-vivo demonstration of:
questions.concept: The tuberculin (Mantoux) reaction is the prototype of delayed-type (type IV), cell-mediated hypersensitivity: previously sensitised T cells recognise PPD antigens and recruit macrophages, producing an indurated response that peaks at 48-72 hours (hence the delayed reading and measurement of induration, not erythema). It is not antibody-dependent, so type I (IgE/immediate), type II (cytotoxic) and type III (immune-complex) mechanisms do not explain it.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Tuberculin test

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A child with confirmed miliary tuberculosis has a completely negative Mantoux test. Which explanation best accounts for this false-negative tuberculin reaction?
options: Anergy from overwhelming/disseminated infection depressing cell-mediated immunity
Prior BCG vaccination boosting the response
Recent recovery from a mild bacterial pharyngitis
Use of a fresh, potent PPD RT23 preparation
questions.concept: Overwhelming disease such as miliary or advanced TB can suppress cell-mediated immunity, producing anergy and a falsely negative tuberculin test despite active infection; other causes of false negatives include HIV/immunosuppression, corticosteroids, measles or other viral illness, sarcoidosis, malnutrition, and testing within the early window before hypersensitivity develops. BCG vaccination and a potent fresh antigen would tend to enhance, not abolish, the reaction, and an ordinary bacterial pharyngitis does not typically cause anergy.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Tuberculin test (false-negative reactions)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) remain positive-specific for TB infection even in BCG-vaccinated individuals. Reason (R): IGRAs use the antigens ESAT-6 and CFP-10, encoded in the RD1 region that is deleted from the BCG strain and absent from most non-tuberculous mycobacteria.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: IGRAs measure interferon-gamma released by sensitised T cells stimulated with M. tuberculosis-specific peptides ESAT-6 and CFP-10 (and TB7.7). These are encoded within the RD1 (region of difference 1) genomic segment, which was lost during attenuation of BCG (M. bovis BCG) and is absent from most NTM; therefore prior BCG vaccination does not cause false positives, making the reason the correct explanation of the assertion. A few NTM (e.g., M. kansasii, M. marinum) retain RD1, but the principle holds for BCG.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Interferon-gamma release assays

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In Runyon's classification of non-tuberculous mycobacteria, an organism that produces yellow-orange pigment ONLY after exposure to light belongs to which group, exemplified by which species?
options: Group III non-photochromogens — Mycobacterium avium complex
Group IV rapid growers — Mycobacterium fortuitum
questions.concept: Runyon Group I photochromogens produce pigment only after light exposure and are slow growers; the classic examples are M. kansasii (pulmonary disease) and M. marinum (swimming-pool/fish-tank granuloma). Group II scotochromogens (M. scrofulaceum, M. gordonae) make pigment in both light and dark; Group III non-photochromogens (M. avium complex, M. ulcerans) make little/no pigment; and Group IV are rapid growers — so only Group I fits light-dependent pigmentation.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Non-tuberculous (atypical) mycobacteria: Runyon classification

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Several patients develop injection-site and post-surgical wound abscesses; cultures yield acid-fast bacilli that form visible colonies on subculture within 3-7 days. These features point to which category of mycobacteria?
options: Rapidly growing mycobacteria (Runyon Group IV) such as M. fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. abscessus
questions.concept: Runyon Group IV rapid growers (M. fortuitum, M. chelonae, M. abscessus) produce visible colonies within 7 days and are notorious for iatrogenic skin and soft-tissue infections — injection abscesses, post-surgical wound and catheter-related infections, and contaminated-instrument outbreaks. M. tuberculosis and scotochromogens are slow growers (weeks), and M. leprae cannot be cultured on artificial media at all, so the rapid subculture growth with wound abscesses specifically indicates the rapid growers.
questions.reference: Bailey & Scott's Diagnostic Microbiology — Rapidly growing mycobacteria

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with advanced AIDS and a CD4 count below 50 cells/µL develops disseminated infection with fever, weight loss and diarrhoea; blood cultures grow a slow-growing, non-photochromogenic acid-fast organism. The most likely causative mycobacterium is:
questions.concept: Mycobacterium avium complex (M. avium plus M. intracellulare) is the classic cause of disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease in advanced AIDS (CD4 < 50), presenting with fever, wasting, diarrhoea and mycobacteraemia; it is a slow-growing, non-photochromogenic (Runyon Group III) organism recoverable from blood. M. marinum causes localised skin granulomas, M. scrofulaceum causes cervical lymphadenitis in children, and M. ulcerans causes Buruli ulcer — not disseminated AIDS disease.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Mycobacterium avium complex

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Mycobacterium leprae cannot be grown on any artificial (cell-free) culture medium. Which experimental system is used to propagate it and yields large numbers of bacilli for study?
questions.concept: M. leprae is non-cultivable in vitro; it is propagated in vivo, classically in the mouse footpad (Shepard's model, small yields) and especially in the nine-banded armadillo, whose low core body temperature favours growth and produces enormous bacillary loads for antigen and drug studies. Chick embryo yolk sac is used for rickettsiae/chlamydiae, buffered charcoal-yeast extract for Legionella, and Middlebrook 7H11 grows cultivable mycobacteria — none supports M. leprae.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Mycobacterium leprae (cultivation)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In a slit-skin smear from a leprosy patient stained by the Fite-Faraco method, the index that expresses the PERCENTAGE of uniformly (solid) stained bacilli and thereby reflects the proportion of viable organisms is the:
questions.concept: The Morphological Index (MI) is the percentage of uniformly, solidly stained bacilli out of the total counted; solid-staining forms are considered viable, so a falling MI on treatment indicates response and reduced infectivity. The Bacterial Index (BI) grades total bacillary density (live plus dead/fragmented) on Ridley's 0-6+ logarithmic scale. The lepromin test is a prognostic (not diagnostic) tool assessing cell-mediated immunity, and Ridley-Jopling is a clinico-pathological classification, not a smear count.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Laboratory diagnosis of leprosy (bacterial and morphological index)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A stool sample from a child with acute icteric hepatitis is examined virologically. The agent responsible for hepatitis A is best classified as which type of virus?
options: An enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus of the family Hepadnaviridae
An enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae
A non-enveloped, single-stranded (positive-sense) RNA virus of the family Picornaviridae
A non-enveloped, double-stranded RNA virus of the family Reoviridae
questions.concept: HAV is a small (27 nm) non-enveloped icosahedral virus with a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome, classified in family Picornaviridae, genus Hepatovirus; its lack of an envelope makes it stable to acid, ether and heat, which favours feco-oral spread. Hepadnaviridae (dsDNA) is HBV, Flaviviridae (enveloped ssRNA) is HCV, and Reoviridae (dsRNA) is unrelated to the hepatitis viruses.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis Viruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with 5 days of fever, anorexia, dark urine and jaundice after a picnic. Serology shows IgM anti-HAV positive and IgG anti-HAV negative. Which conclusion is correct?
options: This indicates acute, recent hepatitis A infection
This indicates past infection with lifelong immunity
This indicates successful hepatitis A vaccination
This indicates chronic hepatitis A carriage
questions.concept: IgM anti-HAV appears at the onset of symptoms and persists for about 3-6 months, so its presence signifies acute or recent HAV infection; IgG anti-HAV rises later and denotes past infection or vaccination with lifelong immunity. Because IgG is still negative here, this is an early acute infection rather than recovery or vaccination. HAV has no chronic carrier state, which excludes option D.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis A Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the hepatitis A vaccine in routine use?
options: It is a live attenuated oral vaccine similar to the oral polio vaccine
It is a formalin-inactivated (killed) whole-virus vaccine given intramuscularly
It is a recombinant surface-antigen (subunit) vaccine produced in yeast
It is a toxoid prepared by formaldehyde treatment of a bacterial exotoxin
questions.concept: The widely used hepatitis A vaccine is a formalin-inactivated whole-virus preparation grown in cell culture and given intramuscularly, inducing durable protective anti-HAV. The recombinant yeast-derived surface-antigen vaccine describes hepatitis B, and toxoids are bacterial products (diphtheria/tetanus). A live attenuated HAV vaccine exists only in limited settings and is not the standard product being referenced.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Hepatitis Viruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Hepatitis B virus is unique among the human hepatitis viruses in its genome and replication strategy. It is correctly classified as:
options: An enveloped, partially double-stranded (circular) DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae)
questions.concept: HBV belongs to family Hepadnaviridae; its 42 nm enveloped Dane particle carries a small partially double-stranded, circular DNA genome and a virus-encoded polymerase with reverse-transcriptase activity, making it the only DNA virus among the hepatitis agents. Picornaviridae (HAV) and Flaviviridae (HCV) are RNA viruses, and the remaining options misassign HBV to unrelated virus families.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis B Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: On electron microscopy of serum from a hepatitis B patient, three particles are seen: 22 nm spheres, 22 nm filaments/tubules, and larger 42 nm double-shelled particles. The 42 nm double-shelled particle represents:
options: The complete, infectious HBV virion (Dane particle)
Free hepatitis B core antigen released from lysed hepatocytes
Delta (hepatitis D) virions coated with HBsAg
questions.concept: The 42 nm double-shelled Dane particle is the complete, infectious HBV virion, comprising an outer HBsAg envelope enclosing the nucleocapsid (HBcAg), the partially dsDNA genome and DNA polymerase. The far more numerous 22 nm spheres and filaments are surplus, non-infectious HBsAg produced in excess. Free HBcAg is not found in serum, and delta virions require separate HDV RNA, which excludes those options.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis B Virus (Morphology)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Although hepatitis B virus carries a DNA genome, its replication requires the enzyme reverse transcriptase. Reason (R): HBV copies its genome directly by semiconservative DNA-to-DNA replication without any RNA intermediate. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: HBV, despite being a DNA virus, transcribes a full-length pregenomic RNA that is then reverse-transcribed back into DNA by the reverse-transcriptase activity of its polymerase. The reason is false because replication is NOT a direct DNA-to-DNA process; it obligately passes through a pregenomic RNA intermediate. Hence A is true and R is false, giving option C.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Hepatitis B Virus (Replication)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In the serological diagnosis of hepatitis B, all of the following markers can be detected free in the patient's serum EXCEPT:
questions.concept: HBcAg (core antigen) is not found free in serum because it remains sequestered within the hepatocyte nucleus and within the core of assembled Dane particles; only the corresponding anti-HBc antibody is measured serologically. In contrast, HBsAg, the secreted HBeAg, and circulating HBV-DNA are all readily detectable in serum and form the backbone of HBV serology and viral-load testing.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis B Antigens

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An asymptomatic 40-year-old blood donor has HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, and total anti-HBc (predominantly IgG) positive; HBeAg and IgM anti-HBc are negative. The most accurate interpretation is:
options: Acute hepatitis B in the window period
Immunity due to past, resolved natural HBV infection
questions.concept: The combination of anti-HBs positivity WITH anti-HBc (IgG) positivity indicates recovery from, and immunity after, a past natural HBV infection — the immune system has encountered the whole virus, hence the anti-HBc. Vaccine-induced immunity produces anti-HBs alone with anti-HBc negative, which excludes option A. Absence of HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc rules out chronic carriage and acute or window-period infection.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Interpretation of HBV Markers

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient is HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative but anti-HBc (total) positive; sensitive PCR detects low-level HBV-DNA in serum and liver. This picture is best termed:
options: False-positive anti-HBc with no true infection
Acute hepatitis B in the window period
questions.concept: Occult HBV infection is defined by detectable HBV-DNA in serum or liver in a person who is HBsAg negative, most often anti-HBc positive (with or without anti-HBs). Persistent covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) sustains low-level replication, posing risks of reactivation on immunosuppression and of transmission via transfusion or transplant. Detectable DNA excludes a mere false-positive or a truly sterilising resolved infection, and the chronic setting excludes an acute window period.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Occult Hepatitis B

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with long-standing HBsAg positivity has persistently raised ALT and a high serum HBV-DNA, yet HBeAg is negative and anti-HBe is positive. The best explanation for active disease despite a negative HBeAg is:
options: Precore / basal-core-promoter mutant (HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B)
Inactive carrier state with no significant liver disease
Recent successful seroconversion to a fully resolved infection
Acute co-infection with hepatitis A virus
questions.concept: A precore (classically the G1896A stop-codon) or basal-core-promoter mutation abolishes or reduces HBeAg production, so the patient is HBeAg negative and anti-HBe positive yet continues active viral replication with high HBV-DNA and ongoing hepatitis — HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B. The high DNA and raised ALT exclude an inactive carrier (low DNA, normal ALT) or a resolved infection, and HAV co-infection would not sustain HBV replication.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis B (Mutants)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B is started on tenofovir. Which single laboratory test is the most appropriate for monitoring the virological response to antiviral therapy?
options: Serial qualitative HBsAg detection by ELISA
Serial quantitative HBV-DNA by real-time PCR (viral load)
questions.concept: Quantitative HBV-DNA measured by real-time PCR (viral load) directly reflects the level of viral replication and is the standard marker for monitoring the response to nucleos(t)ide analogues such as tenofovir — a falling DNA level signals success. HBsAg stays positive for long periods, total anti-HBc reflects past exposure rather than replication, and IgM anti-HBc marks acute infection or flares rather than a quantitative treatment response.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Laboratory Diagnosis of Viral Hepatitis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): During the window period of acute hepatitis B, IgM anti-HBc may be the only detectable serological marker of infection. Reason (R): The window period is the interval after anti-HBs has appeared but before HBsAg has disappeared from serum. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: in the window period HBsAg has already cleared while anti-HBs has not yet risen, so IgM anti-HBc is often the sole marker of recent infection. The reason is false because it reverses the sequence — the window is the gap AFTER HBsAg disappears and BEFORE anti-HBs appears, not the other way round. Therefore A is true and R is false, giving option C.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Window Period in Hepatitis B

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In highly endemic regions of Asia, what is the predominant route by which the pool of chronic hepatitis B infection is maintained?
options: Perinatal (mother-to-child) transmission around the time of birth
Respiratory droplet spread between household contacts
questions.concept: In high-prevalence areas such as much of Asia, HBV is chiefly propagated by perinatal (vertical) transmission from HBsAg/HBeAg-positive mothers to their newborns, mostly at the time of delivery through blood and secretion contact rather than transplacentally. Because neonatal infection carries about a 90% chronicity risk, this route perpetuates the chronic reservoir. HBV is blood-borne and sexually transmitted, not feco-oral (that is HAV/HEV) or droplet-spread.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Epidemiology of Hepatitis B

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Adults who acquire acute hepatitis B infection progress to chronic infection in about 90% of cases. Reason (R): The risk of progression to chronic HBV infection is inversely related to the age at which the infection is acquired. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is false: immunocompetent adults clear HBV in the great majority of cases, with only about 5% becoming chronic; it is neonates and infants who become chronic in roughly 90%. The reason is true — chronicity risk is inversely related to age at infection because the immature, tolerised neonatal immune system fails to clear the virus. Thus A is false while R is true, giving option D.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Natural History of Hepatitis B

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A baby is born to a mother who is HBsAg positive. To most effectively prevent perinatal hepatitis B transmission, the newborn should receive:
options: Hepatitis B vaccine alone, starting at 6 weeks with the routine schedule
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) PLUS hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) alone, with no vaccine
A course of oral tenofovir given to the neonate for 6 months
questions.concept: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers should receive both passive immunisation with hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth (at separate sites), followed by completion of the vaccine series — combined active-passive prophylaxis prevents about 90-95% of perinatal transmission. Vaccine alone or delayed dosing is less effective, HBIG alone gives only transient protection, and neonatal antivirals are not standard prophylaxis.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Prophylaxis of Hepatitis B

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A nurse sustains a deep needlestick injury from a hollow-bore needle used on a source patient who is co-infected with HBV (HBeAg positive), HCV and HIV. Per single percutaneous exposure, transmission risk is HIGHEST for which of these viruses?
options: The transmission risk is identical for all three
questions.concept: Per-exposure transmission risk after a percutaneous injury is highest for HBV, reaching roughly 30% when the source is HBeAg positive, compared with about 3% for HCV and about 0.3% for HIV — a useful 30/3/0.3 rule of thumb reflecting the very high circulating titres of HBV. This is why post-exposure HBV prophylaxis (vaccine and/or HBIG) is emphasised; the risks are clearly not equal across the three viruses.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Occupational Exposure to Blood-borne Viruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Hepatitis C virus is correctly classified as:
options: A non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus of family Picornaviridae
An enveloped, partially double-stranded DNA virus of family Hepadnaviridae
An enveloped, single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus of family Flaviviridae
A non-enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus of family Hepeviridae
questions.concept: HCV is an enveloped virus with a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome, placed in family Flaviviridae (genus Hepacivirus); its error-prone RNA polymerase generates extensive genetic diversity (six major genotypes and quasispecies), which underlies its high chronicity and the absence of a vaccine. Picornaviridae is HAV, Hepadnaviridae is HBV, and Hepeviridae is HEV, which excludes the other options.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis C Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A blood donor screens positive for anti-HCV antibody by ELISA. Which test should be performed next to confirm current, active HCV infection (viraemia)?
options: Repeat the anti-HCV ELISA on a fresh sample
Measure IgM anti-HCV to prove recent infection
Test for HCV core antigen by a rapid card test only
Detect and quantify HCV-RNA by PCR (nucleic acid testing)
questions.concept: A positive anti-HCV ELISA indicates exposure but cannot distinguish current infection from a resolved past one, and false positives occur; active viraemia is confirmed by detecting HCV-RNA using PCR / nucleic-acid testing, which also provides viral load and guides therapy. Simply repeating the antibody test does not prove viraemia, there is no reliable IgM anti-HCV assay for staging, and RNA quantitation — not a card test alone — is the confirmatory standard.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Laboratory Diagnosis of Hepatitis C

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Regarding the natural history of, and prophylaxis against, hepatitis C, which statement is correct?
options: Fewer than 10% of infections become chronic, and an effective vaccine is available
The majority (around 80%) of infections become chronic, and no effective vaccine is available
Chronicity is rare, but lifelong protective immunity follows a single infection
It is transmitted mainly by the feco-oral route and causes water-borne epidemics
questions.concept: HCV has the highest chronicity among the hepatitis viruses: roughly 80% (commonly quoted as 55-85%) of acute infections persist as chronic infection, a major cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Because of marked genomic variability (quasispecies) no effective vaccine exists, and prior infection does not confer solid protective immunity. HCV is blood-borne/parenteral, not feco-oral, which excludes options A, C and D.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis C (Clinical Features)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Hepatitis D (delta) virus is described as a 'defective' virus because it:
options: Lacks any nucleic acid and consists only of protein
Cannot replicate its genome without a co-infecting retrovirus
Requires HBsAg from hepatitis B virus to form its envelope and become infectious
Can infect only cells that have been transformed by a DNA tumour virus
questions.concept: HDV is a defective, sub-viral agent with a small circular single-stranded RNA genome and the delta antigen, but it lacks genes for its own envelope; it therefore needs the helper hepatitis B virus to supply HBsAg as its coat, so HDV infection occurs only in HBsAg-positive individuals. It does contain RNA (excluding a prion-like protein-only option) and depends specifically on HBV, not on a retrovirus or a DNA tumour virus.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis D (Delta) Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A previously healthy adult develops acute hepatitis. Serology shows IgM anti-HBc positive, HBsAg positive AND IgM anti-HDV positive. This pattern is most consistent with:
options: HDV superinfection of a long-standing chronic HBV carrier
Isolated acute hepatitis D in a person never exposed to HBV
Chronic hepatitis B with an unrelated false-positive delta result
questions.concept: The simultaneous presence of IgM anti-HBc (marking ACUTE HBV) together with IgM anti-HDV indicates that HBV and HDV were acquired at the same time — acute co-infection, which is usually self-limited with a low rate of chronicity. Superinfection instead occurs in an established chronic carrier, where anti-HBc would be IgG (not IgM); HDV cannot infect without HBsAg, which excludes isolated delta infection, and the IgM anti-HBc excludes a purely chronic picture.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Hepatitis D Co-infection vs Superinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which set of features correctly characterises hepatitis E virus?
options: Non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus (Hepeviridae), transmitted by the feco-oral / water-borne route
Enveloped double-stranded DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae), transmitted parenterally
Enveloped single-stranded RNA virus (Flaviviridae), transmitted sexually
Defective RNA virus requiring HBsAg, transmitted vertically
questions.concept: HEV is a small non-enveloped virus with a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome, classified in family Hepeviridae; like HAV it spreads by the feco-oral route, characteristically through faecally contaminated water causing large epidemics, and is diagnosed by IgM anti-HEV. Genotypes 1 and 2 are human/water-borne while genotypes 3 and 4 are zoonotic (pigs). The other options describe HBV, HCV and HDV respectively.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Hepatitis E Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Among the five human hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D and E), which one has a DNA genome, the rest being RNA viruses?
questions.concept: Hepatitis B virus is the only DNA virus among the hepatitis agents, carrying a partially double-stranded circular DNA genome (Hepadnaviridae); hepatitis A (Picornaviridae), C (Flaviviridae), D (the delta agent) and E (Hepeviridae) are all RNA viruses. A quick memory aid is that only 'B' breaks the RNA pattern, which also explains why HBV alone is the target of nucleos(t)ide analogues that act on reverse transcription.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Comparative Features of Hepatitis Viruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is an enveloped RNA virus that establishes lifelong infection. To which family and genus does it belong?
options: Family Herpesviridae, an enveloped double-stranded DNA virus
Family Orthomyxoviridae, a segmented RNA virus
questions.concept: HIV is a retrovirus of the genus Lentivirus (subfamily Orthoretrovirinae), named for its 'slow' course; it carries reverse transcriptase and integrates a DNA provirus into the host genome. Herpesviridae are dsDNA viruses (HHV-8, EBV, CMV cause HIV-related disease but are not HIV); Orthomyxoviridae is influenza (segmented RNA); Flaviviridae/Hepacivirus is hepatitis C — none is a retrovirus.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Human Immunodeficiency Virus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the genome packaged within a mature HIV virion?
options: A single molecule of negative-sense single-stranded RNA
Double-stranded DNA transcribed directly by host RNA polymerase
Two identical copies of positive-sense single-stranded RNA (a diploid genome)
Eight separate segments of single-stranded RNA
questions.concept: HIV is unique in being effectively 'diploid', packaging two identical copies of positive-sense (+) single-stranded RNA of about 9.7 kb each. Despite being positive-sense, the RNA is not translated directly on entry; reverse transcriptase first copies it into double-stranded DNA (provirus) that integrates into host DNA. A single negative-sense molecule describes rhabdo/paramyxoviruses, dsDNA is not the virion form, and eight RNA segments describe influenza A.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — Retroviruses (HIV)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The HIV gag gene encodes a p55 polyprotein that is later cleaved to yield which group of viral components?
options: The core structural proteins — matrix (p17), capsid (p24) and nucleocapsid (p7)
The envelope glycoproteins gp120 and gp41
The enzymes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease
The regulatory proteins Tat and Rev
questions.concept: gag encodes the internal structural proteins: p17 matrix lining the envelope, p24 capsid forming the conical core, and p7/p9 nucleocapsid binding the RNA. p24 is the antigen detected earliest in serum and by fourth-generation combo assays. The envelope glycoproteins gp120/gp41 arise from env, the enzymes reverse transcriptase/integrase/protease from pol, and Tat and Rev are regulatory (non-structural) gene products — none is a gag product.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — HIV: morphology and genome

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The three virally encoded enzymes essential to HIV replication are products of the pol gene. Which of the following enzymes is NOT encoded by HIV?
questions.concept: pol encodes reverse transcriptase (transcribes RNA to DNA, with RNase-H activity), integrase (inserts proviral DNA into the host chromosome) and a protease (cleaves gag and gag-pol polyproteins during maturation) — the classic antiretroviral drug targets alongside entry/fusion. Neuraminidase is an influenza surface enzyme (the oseltamivir target) and has no role in HIV, which uses gp120/gp41 rather than a neuraminidase for its life cycle.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — HIV genome and enzymes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The HIV env gene product gp160 is cleaved into two glycoproteins. Which pairing of glycoprotein to function is correct?
options: gp120 mediates attachment to the CD4 receptor; gp41 mediates fusion of viral and cell membranes
gp120 mediates membrane fusion; gp41 binds the CD4 receptor
gp120 is the transmembrane anchor; gp41 is reverse transcriptase
Both gp120 and gp41 are internal capsid proteins
questions.concept: env's precursor gp160 is cleaved into surface gp120 (SU), which binds CD4 and then a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), and transmembrane gp41 (TM), which drives fusion of the viral envelope with the host membrane; gp41 is the target of the fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide. Reversing their roles is wrong, gp41 is not an enzyme, and neither is an internal capsid protein — that internal core role belongs to p24 from gag.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — HIV envelope glycoproteins

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Regarding HIV-2 compared with HIV-1, which statement is correct?
options: HIV-2 causes the global pandemic and spreads faster than HIV-1
HIV-2 is largely confined to West Africa, is less transmissible, and progresses to AIDS more slowly
HIV-2 is fully susceptible to all non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs)
HIV-2 shares more than 90% genome homology with HIV-1
questions.concept: HIV-2 is endemic in West Africa, is less transmissible, carries lower viral loads and has a longer latent period with slower progression to AIDS; genetically it is closer to SIV (only about 40-50% homology with HIV-1). Importantly, HIV-2 is intrinsically resistant to NNRTIs and to enfuvirtide, so option C is false. HIV-1 group M, not HIV-2, drives the worldwide pandemic, making option A wrong.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — HIV-1 and HIV-2

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): HIV shows extremely high genetic variability, which is a major obstacle to vaccine development. Reason (R): HIV reverse transcriptase is error-prone and lacks 3'-to-5' exonuclease proofreading activity. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: HIV reverse transcriptase has no 3'-to-5' exonuclease proofreading, so it introduces roughly one error per genome per replication cycle; combined with rapid viral turnover and recombination between the two RNA copies, this generates enormous quasispecies diversity that drives immune escape, drug resistance and vaccine failure. Thus both statements are true and R is precisely the mechanism explaining A, making option A correct.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — HIV variability and reverse transcriptase

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: After HIV enters a CD4 cell, which molecular event is directly catalysed by reverse transcriptase and forms the target of nucleoside analogues such as zidovudine?
options: Cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein into mature enzymes
Insertion of proviral DNA into the host chromosome
Synthesis of double-stranded DNA from the viral single-stranded RNA template
Budding of assembled virions through the plasma membrane
questions.concept: Reverse transcriptase is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that copies the (+)ssRNA genome into complementary DNA and then double-stranded DNA, while its RNase-H activity degrades the original RNA template; this step is inhibited by NRTIs such as zidovudine and by NNRTIs. Polyprotein cleavage is the job of protease, chromosomal insertion is performed by integrase, and budding is a late assembly event — none of these is catalysed by reverse transcriptase.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — HIV replication cycle

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Enfuvirtide, an antiretroviral peptide, blocks HIV at which step of its replication cycle?
options: Fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane by binding gp41
Integration of proviral DNA into the host genome
Proteolytic maturation of the assembled virion
questions.concept: Enfuvirtide (T-20) is a fusion inhibitor that binds the HR1 region of gp41, preventing the conformational change that fuses the viral envelope with the cell membrane after gp120 engages CD4 and its co-receptor; entry is therefore blocked. Maraviroc, a distinct entry inhibitor, instead blocks the CCR5 co-receptor. Reverse transcription is blocked by NRTIs/NNRTIs, integration by integrase inhibitors, and maturation by protease inhibitors — not by enfuvirtide.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — antiretroviral drug targets

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Protease inhibitors (e.g., ritonavir, lopinavir) exert their antiviral effect by producing which outcome?
options: Preventing viral RNA from being reverse-transcribed into DNA
Blocking gp120 binding to the CCR5 co-receptor
Stopping proviral DNA from integrating into host DNA
Preventing cleavage of gag-pol polyproteins, yielding immature non-infectious virions
questions.concept: HIV protease is an aspartyl protease that cleaves the gag and gag-pol polyproteins into functional structural proteins and enzymes during and just after budding; inhibiting it produces immature, non-infectious virions. It acts at a late maturation step, distinct from reverse transcription (blocked by NRTIs/NNRTIs), co-receptor entry (blocked by maraviroc) and integration (blocked by integrase inhibitors) described in the other options.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — HIV protease and protease inhibitors

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A fourth-generation HIV screening immunoassay ('combo' assay) is superior to earlier antibody-only tests mainly because it additionally detects which marker, allowing earlier diagnosis?
options: The p24 core antigen, in addition to HIV-1/2 antibodies
questions.concept: Fourth-generation combo assays detect both HIV-1/2 antibodies and the p24 capsid antigen. Because p24 antigen appears roughly 2-3 weeks after infection — before antibodies become detectable — the combo assay shortens the window period compared with first- to third-generation antibody-only tests. It does not measure CD4 counts (an immune marker by flow cytometry) or proviral DNA (a separate NAT/PCR technique), and detecting a single antibody such as gp41 alone offers no such advantage.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — HIV laboratory diagnosis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A man exposed to HIV 10 days ago is anxious and requests testing. A standard antibody-based rapid test is negative. Which explanation and next step is most appropriate?
options: He is definitely uninfected; no further testing is required
Antibody tests are never useful in HIV and should be abandoned
He can be reassured that antibodies reliably appear within 24 hours of exposure
He may be in the 'window period' before antibodies are detectable; a p24 antigen/nucleic acid (NAT) test or repeat testing after the window is advised
questions.concept: The window period is the interval between infection and the appearance of detectable markers; antibodies can take 3-12 weeks, so an early antibody test may be falsely negative while the person is already viraemic and highly infectious. p24 antigen (detectable from about 2-3 weeks) or HIV RNA/NAT (from about 1-2 weeks) identifies infection sooner, and antibody testing should be repeated after the window. Declaring him uninfected or claiming 24-hour seroconversion is incorrect.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — window period and HIV testing

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In the conventional serial HIV testing algorithm, a repeatedly reactive ELISA is traditionally confirmed by Western blot. A Western blot is interpreted as POSITIVE when antibodies are detected against which of the following?
options: Any single band anywhere on the strip
At least two bands including an envelope glycoprotein (e.g., gp160/gp120/gp41), per standard criteria
questions.concept: Western blot separates HIV proteins (env gp160/gp120/gp41, gag p24/p55, pol p31/p51/p66) so specific antibodies can be identified. A result is called positive only when defined criteria are met — typically reactivity to at least two bands including at least one envelope glycoprotein (for example gp41 plus gp120/160). A single band is 'indeterminate', p24 alone is insufficient, and reactivity to host proteins is non-specific. Nucleic acid testing is now often used as an alternative confirmatory/supplemental assay.
questions.reference: Jawetz, Melnick & Adelberg's Medical Microbiology — confirmatory Western blot

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Under the NACO (India) HIV testing framework, the strategy used to DIAGNOSE HIV infection in an asymptomatic individual (e.g., at a voluntary counselling and testing centre) requires:
options: A single reactive rapid/ELISA test, after which the person is declared HIV positive
Three sequential tests using different antigens or principles, all of which must be reactive
Two tests used only for transfusion/blood-bank screening
A CD4 count below 200 cells/µL as the sole diagnostic criterion
questions.concept: NACO adapts the WHO strategies. Strategy I (one test) is for blood/organ safety and surveillance, where a single reactive result suffices for that purpose. Strategy II (up to two tests) covers surveillance and diagnosis of symptomatic patients. Strategy III (three tests using different antigen preparations or principles, all reactive) diagnoses asymptomatic individuals so that false positives are minimised. A single reactive test never confirms diagnosis, and a CD4 count stages disease rather than diagnosing infection.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — NACO/WHO HIV testing strategies

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient stable on antiretroviral therapy needs monitoring of treatment response. Which laboratory test is the most appropriate PRIMARY marker of the virological response to ART?
options: Plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load by quantitative PCR
questions.concept: Plasma HIV-1 RNA (viral load) measured by quantitative RT-PCR directly quantifies circulating virus and is the key marker of virological response — the goal of ART is an undetectable viral load, and a rising load signals treatment failure, resistance or poor adherence. CD4 count tracks immune recovery rather than viral suppression. Serological tests (combo assay, Western blot) merely confirm infection and remain positive during treatment, so they cannot monitor response; the tuberculin test screens for TB, not HIV.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — HIV: monitoring viral load

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Independent of clinical symptoms, an HIV-infected adult is classified as having AIDS (severe immunosuppression) when the CD4+ T-lymphocyte count falls below which threshold?
questions.concept: A CD4 count below 200 cells/µL is itself AIDS-defining (CDC category 3), reflecting the level at which opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia become common; the normal CD4 count is about 500-1500/µL. A count below 500 indicates only moderate immunosuppression, not AIDS; below 50 marks very advanced disease with risk of CMV and disseminated MAC but is not the defining cut-off; 750 lies within/near the normal range.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — HIV/AIDS: CD4 staging

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: At which CD4 count should primary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia be started, and with which drug of choice?
questions.concept: Primary Pneumocystis (PCP) prophylaxis is indicated once the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/µL (or with oral candidiasis or another AIDS-defining illness), and the drug of choice is co-trimoxazole, which conveniently also protects against toxoplasmosis. Azithromycin is used for MAC prophylaxis (CD4 < 50), fluconazole for cryptococcal disease, and isoniazid for TB preventive therapy — each addresses a different pathogen and threshold.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An HIV patient with a CD4 count of 80 cells/µL presents with fever, headache and focal seizures. Contrast CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia; Toxoplasma IgG is positive. The most likely organism is:
questions.concept: In advanced HIV (CD4 < 100), multiple ring-enhancing lesions with a predilection for the basal ganglia and grey-white junction, in a Toxoplasma-IgG-seropositive patient, are classic for cerebral toxoplasmosis due to reactivation; empirical pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is standard. Cryptococcus causes meningitis rather than ring lesions, JC virus causes PML with non-enhancing white-matter demyelination, and MAC causes disseminated febrile illness — not focal brain lesions. Primary CNS lymphoma is the main radiological mimic.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An AIDS patient (CD4 60/µL) has two weeks of headache, fever and neck stiffness. CSF microscopy with India ink shows round budding yeast surrounded by a wide clear halo. The most useful CONFIRMATORY rapid test on CSF/serum is:
options: Cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) latex agglutination / lateral-flow assay
questions.concept: The wide clear halo on India ink represents the polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans, the commonest cause of fungal meningitis in advanced HIV. Detection of the capsular polysaccharide by the cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) latex agglutination or lateral-flow assay on CSF/serum is highly sensitive and specific and is the confirmatory test of choice. Acid-fast staining targets mycobacteria, the Mantoux test screens for TB, and KOH-visible septate hyphae suggest moulds such as Aspergillus — none identifies Cryptococcus.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — Cryptococcus neoformans

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with very advanced AIDS (CD4 30/µL) complains of floaters and progressive painless visual loss. Fundoscopy reveals perivascular yellow-white retinal infiltrates with haemorrhages ('pizza-pie' appearance). The most likely cause is:
questions.concept: CMV retinitis is the classic sight-threatening opportunistic infection at CD4 < 50, producing the characteristic 'pizza-pie' (or 'cheese-and-ketchup') fundus of yellow-white necrotising retinitis with perivascular haemorrhages and exudates; it is treated with ganciclovir/valganciclovir. Toxoplasma chorioretinitis usually shows a focal lesion beside an old scar, herpes zoster ophthalmicus involves the trigeminal dermatome with pain and vesicles, and Candida endophthalmitis produces fluffy vitreous 'string-of-pearls' lesions in candidaemia — not the pizza-pie pattern.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — CMV retinitis in AIDS

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: An AIDS patient with a CD4 count of 25/µL has persistent fever, night sweats, weight loss, anaemia and hepatosplenomegaly. Blood cultures on special media grow an acid-fast organism, and there are no pulmonary cavities. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Disseminated MAC (M. avium-intracellulare) is a late opportunistic infection appearing at CD4 < 50, presenting with high fever, night sweats, weight loss, anaemia, hepatosplenomegaly and positive mycobacterial blood cultures WITHOUT the cavitary pulmonary disease typical of M. tuberculosis. Azithromycin is used for prophylaxis when CD4 < 50. PCP is a pneumonia, toxoplasmosis is focal CNS disease, and candidiasis causes mucosal/oesophageal lesions — none matches a disseminated febrile mycobacteraemia.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) — a demyelinating disease of advanced AIDS with progressive focal deficits and non-enhancing white-matter lesions on MRI — is caused by reactivation of which virus?
questions.concept: PML results from reactivation of the JC polyomavirus, which infects and destroys oligodendrocytes, causing progressive multifocal demyelination with focal neurological deficits and characteristically non-enhancing white-matter lesions without mass effect; there is no specific antiviral, and immune reconstitution with ART is the mainstay of management. HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, EBV is linked to primary CNS lymphoma and oral hairy leukoplakia, and CMV causes retinitis/colitis — not PML.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — JC virus and PML

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Kaposi sarcoma, the most common HIV-associated malignancy, is caused by co-infection with which virus?
questions.concept: Kaposi sarcoma is an angioproliferative, AIDS-defining tumour driven by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8, also called KSHV). Other HIV-related cancers have distinct viral causes: EBV underlies primary CNS lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma, HPV drives cervical and anal carcinoma, and HBV/HCV cause hepatocellular carcinoma — but none of these causes Kaposi sarcoma, which is specifically HHV-8-related.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology — HHV-8 and Kaposi sarcoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: In the context of global blindness, cataract is best described as which of the following?
options: The leading cause of irreversible childhood blindness
A cause of blindness for which no surgical remedy currently exists
The commonest cause of treatable (reversible) blindness worldwide
A refractive error correctable with spectacles alone
questions.concept: Cataract is the leading cause of blindness worldwide and, because sight is restored by surgery, it is the commonest cause of treatable or reversible blindness (C). It is not irreversible (A), it has an excellent surgical remedy (B), and it is a media opacity rather than a refractive error correctable by spectacles (D). Recognising cataract as reversible is the rationale behind large-scale cataract-surgery blindness-control programmes.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Regarding the crystalline lens capsule, which statement is correct?
options: It is thickest at the posterior pole and thinnest at the equator
It is the thickest basement membrane in the body and is thinnest at the central posterior pole
It is composed mainly of type I collagen secreted by the iris
It is a vascular membrane supplied by the long posterior ciliary arteries
questions.concept: The lens capsule is a true basement membrane (predominantly type IV collagen) secreted by the lens epithelium and is the thickest basement membrane in the human body; it is thickest in the pre-equatorial zones and thinnest at the central posterior pole, which explains why the posterior capsule is so fragile during surgery (B). It is not iris-derived type I collagen (C) and is avascular (D); option A reverses the true thickness pattern.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Anatomy and Physiology (The Crystalline Lens)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The lens depends on the aqueous humour to meet its metabolic needs. Reason (R): The lens is avascular and devoid of any blood or nerve supply. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The lens is avascular and has no nerve supply; it therefore depends entirely on the aqueous humour (and, posteriorly, on the vitreous) for glucose, oxygen and metabolic exchange, and it discharges waste into the aqueous. Because this avascularity is precisely the reason the lens must rely on the aqueous, both statements are true and the reason correctly explains the assertion (A).
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Anatomy and Physiology (The Crystalline Lens)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The crystalline lens meets the bulk of its energy (ATP) requirement through which metabolic pathway?
options: Aerobic oxidative phosphorylation in the lens nucleus
The pentose phosphate (HMP) shunt as the principal ATP source
questions.concept: The lens is metabolically active yet relatively hypoxic, so roughly 80-85% of its glucose is metabolised by anaerobic glycolysis to generate ATP (B). Aerobic oxidative phosphorylation (A) is limited and confined mainly to the epithelium; the HMP/pentose-phosphate shunt (D) chiefly supplies NADPH for the antioxidant glutathione system rather than bulk ATP; and fatty-acid beta-oxidation (C) is not an operative lens pathway.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Anatomy and Physiology (Biochemistry of the Lens)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Eighteen months after uncomplicated extracapsular cataract surgery with a posterior chamber IOL, a patient reports gradual painless dimming of vision; slit-lamp shows a wrinkled, pearl-studded membrane behind the IOL. The definitive treatment is:
questions.concept: A wrinkled, pearly, opacified posterior capsule months to years after extracapsular/phaco surgery is posterior capsular opacification (after-cataract) caused by proliferation of residual lens epithelial cells (Elschnig pearls and Soemmering ring). The definitive, quick, non-incisional treatment is Nd:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy, which clears the visual axis (C). IOL exchange (A), steroids (B) and anti-VEGF (D) do not clear a fibrosed opaque capsule.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (After-cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly man who has worn reading glasses for years is now able to read newsprint without them, although his distance vision has become blurred; the lens nucleus is brunescent. This 'second sight' phenomenon is due to:
options: A hypermetropic shift from cortical spoke opacities
Index myopia from an increasing refractive index of the sclerosed nucleus
Accommodative spasm of the ciliary muscle
Astigmatism induced by a subluxated lens
questions.concept: Progressive nuclear sclerosis raises the refractive index of the lens nucleus, producing an acquired index myopia; this myopic shift lets a previously presbyopic or hypermetropic patient read again without glasses, the classic 'second sight', while distance vision blurs (B). It is not a hypermetropic shift (A), not ciliary accommodative spasm (C), and not astigmatism from lens subluxation (D).
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye — The Crystalline Lens (Senile cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient complains of seeing several overlapping images of a single object with one eye; the extra images persist when the fellow eye is covered. The most likely explanation is:
options: Monocular polyopia due to irregular refraction by an early lens opacity
Binocular diplopia from a sixth cranial nerve palsy
Homonymous hemianopia from an occipital lobe lesion
questions.concept: Multiple or overlapping images arising from a single eye that persist when the other eye is occluded constitute monocular diplopia/polyopia, caused by irregular refraction across zones of differing refractive index within an early cataract (A). Binocular diplopia (B) disappears on covering one eye; retinal detachment (C) and homonymous hemianopia (D) cause field or visual loss, not overlapping duplicate images.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Symptoms of cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Wedge-shaped (cuneiform) opacities radiating like spokes from the periphery toward the centre, with intervening water clefts and vacuoles, are characteristic of which morphological type of senile cataract?
questions.concept: Cortical senile cataract begins as wedge-shaped (cuneiform) opacities and spokes extending from the periphery toward the centre, with water clefts and vacuoles forming between hydrated lens fibres (C). Nuclear cataract (A) is a central, brunescent opacity; posterior subcapsular cataract (B) is a plaque lying just in front of the posterior capsule; and anterior polar cataract (D) is a small central capsular opacity.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Morphological classification of cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Regarding the iris-shadow (shadow) test performed with an obliquely thrown torchlight to help stage a senile cataract, which statement is correct?
options: A well-formed iris shadow indicates a mature cataract
Absence of an iris shadow is typical of an incipient cataract
The test primarily assesses the depth of the posterior capsule
A crescentic iris shadow on the lens indicates an immature cataract, whereas it is absent in a mature cataract
questions.concept: In the oblique torch (shadow) test, an immature cataract still has clear cortex between the pupillary margin and the opacity, so a crescentic iris shadow falls on the greyish lens; in a mature cataract the opacity reaches the anterior capsule and no shadow is cast (D). Thus a present shadow means immature (not mature, A), absence is typical of mature (not incipient, B), and the test does not gauge posterior capsule depth (C).
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye — The Crystalline Lens (Stages and examination of senile cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): In a Morgagnian cataract the liquefied cortex allows the dense nucleus to sink inferiorly within the capsular bag. Reason (R): The lens capsule is the thickest basement membrane in the body. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: A Morgagnian cataract is a hypermature cataract in which the cortex liquefies to milky fluid and the heavy nucleus sinks to the bottom of the capsular bag, so the assertion is true; the lens capsule is indeed the thickest basement membrane in the body, so the reason is also true. However, capsular thickness has nothing to do with why the nucleus sinks, so the reason does not explain the assertion (B).
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Hypermature cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant with failure to thrive, hepatomegaly and bilateral central 'oil-droplet' lens opacities is investigated. The most likely underlying enzyme deficiency is:
questions.concept: An oil-droplet cataract in an infant with hepatomegaly and failure to thrive points to classic galactosaemia caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), leading to galactitol accumulation and osmotic lens changes that are reversible if a galactose-free diet is started early (C). Alpha-galactosidase A (A) causes Fabry disease, BCKAD (B) maple syrup urine disease, and phenylalanine hydroxylase (D) phenylketonuria; none produce the classic oil-droplet cataract.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Congenital and developmental cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A neonate born to a mother who had a febrile rash with lymphadenopathy in the first trimester has bilateral pearly-white nuclear cataracts, a continuous machinery murmur and fails the newborn hearing screen. The most likely aetiology of the cataract is:
questions.concept: First-trimester maternal rubella causes congenital rubella syndrome, whose classic triad is cataract (a pearly-white nuclear opacity), sensorineural deafness and cardiac defects such as a patent ductus arteriosus (machinery murmur), often with a salt-and-pepper retinopathy (A). Toxoplasmosis (B) typically causes chorioretinitis, Lowe syndrome (C) adds glaucoma and renal disease, and birth trauma (D) would be unilateral and acquired.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye — The Crystalline Lens (Congenital cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A neonate is found to have a dense unilateral congenital cataract that obscures the fundus. Which management principle is most appropriate?
options: Defer surgery until 2 years of age to allow the eye to grow
Manage conservatively with atropine and spectacles indefinitely
Surgery is unnecessary because congenital cataracts rarely affect vision
Operate early (ideally within about the first 6 weeks), then provide optical correction and vigorous amblyopia therapy
questions.concept: A dense unilateral congenital cataract deprives the developing visual cortex of form vision and rapidly causes irreversible stimulus-deprivation amblyopia, so during this critical period the lens should be removed early (about the first 6 weeks), followed by prompt aphakic optical correction (contact lens or IOL) and aggressive amblyopia therapy (D). Deferring (A), conservative atropine/spectacles (B) or withholding surgery (C) all risk permanent amblyopia.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Management of congenital cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Two weeks after being struck in the eye by a cricket ball, a young man has a stellate, feathery posterior subcapsular opacity, and a ring of iris pigment is imprinted on the anterior lens capsule. This pigment ring is termed:
questions.concept: Blunt ocular trauma classically produces a rosette-shaped (stellate, feathery) subcapsular cataract, and imprinting of the pupillary-margin iris pigment onto the anterior lens capsule produces a circular pigment ring called the Vossius ring (D). The Kayser-Fleischer ring (A) is corneal copper in Wilson disease, the Fleischer ring (B) encircles a keratoconus cone, and the Soemmering ring (C) is residual equatorial lens matter after capsule rupture.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Traumatic cataract)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Before cataract surgery the surgeon calculates intraocular lens power. The two principal biometric measurements required for standard IOL power formulae are:
options: Axial length of the globe and corneal curvature (keratometry)
Intraocular pressure and central corneal thickness
Anterior chamber cell grade and pupil diameter
Colour vision score and contrast sensitivity
questions.concept: Standard IOL power formulae (such as SRK and its successors) require the eye's axial length, measured by A-scan ultrasound biometry or optical biometry (e.g. the IOLMaster), together with the corneal power obtained by keratometry (A). Intraocular pressure and pachymetry (B), anterior chamber cell grade and pupil size (C), and colour or contrast testing (D) are not inputs to IOL power calculation; axial length error is the largest source of refractive surprise.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Biometry and IOL power calculation)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of phacoemulsification cataract surgery?
options: A 10-12 mm limbal incision with removal of the lens within its intact capsule
Delivery of the whole nucleus intact through a scleral tunnel without ultrasound
Ultrasonic fragmentation and aspiration of the nucleus through a small (~2-3 mm) incision after a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis
Routine removal of the entire posterior capsule as part of the procedure
questions.concept: Phacoemulsification uses an ultrasonic probe to fragment and aspirate the nucleus through a small (~2-3 mm) self-sealing incision after fashioning a continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis, leaving the posterior capsule intact to support a foldable IOL (C). A large incision with intact-capsule removal describes ICCE (A), intact nuclear delivery through a scleral tunnel describes manual SICS/ECCE (B), and the posterior capsule is deliberately preserved, not removed (D).
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Cataract surgery: phacoemulsification)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: During phacoemulsification there is sudden deepening of the anterior chamber, a pupillary snap and loss of followability of the nuclear fragments. This most commonly signals which intraoperative complication, the commonest of cataract surgery?
questions.concept: Posterior capsule rupture is the commonest intraoperative complication of cataract surgery; sudden anterior chamber deepening, a pupillary snap and loss of nuclear followability are classic signs, and it predisposes to vitreous loss, dropped nucleus, and later cystoid macular oedema or endophthalmitis (B). Expulsive haemorrhage (A) is rare and dramatic, while Descemet detachment (C) and zonular dialysis (D) are less common and present differently.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Complications of cataract surgery)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly woman with an immature senile cataract presents with sudden ocular pain, coloured haloes and a red eye. The lens appears swollen, the anterior chamber is shallow and the intraocular pressure is markedly raised. The type of cataract responsible is:
options: Intumescent (swollen) cataract precipitating phacomorphic angle-closure glaucoma
questions.concept: An immature senile cataract that imbibes water becomes intumescent (swollen), increasing lens thickness, shallowing the anterior chamber and pushing the iris forward; this can precipitate acute secondary angle-closure, i.e. phacomorphic glaucoma, with pain, haloes and a high IOP (D). A Morgagnian (hypermature) cataract (A) tends to cause phacolytic open-angle glaucoma, whereas nuclear (B) and posterior polar (C) cataracts do not swell the lens in this way.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Glaucoma (Lens-induced glaucomas)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly patient with a long-standing hypermature cataract develops a painful red eye with very high IOP; the anterior chamber shows numerous cells and iridescent particles, and gonioscopy reveals an open angle. The mechanism of this secondary glaucoma is:
options: Leaked high-molecular-weight lens proteins engulfed by macrophages that obstruct the open trabecular meshwork (phacolytic glaucoma)
Pupillary block from a swollen lens closing the angle
Neovascularisation of the angle from chronic ocular ischaemia
questions.concept: In phacolytic glaucoma a hypermature (often Morgagnian) cataract leaks high-molecular-weight soluble lens proteins through an intact but permeable capsule; these proteins and the macrophages that engulf them obstruct an open trabecular meshwork, raising IOP acutely (A). It is not a pupillary-block angle-closure (B), not neovascular (C) and not steroid-induced (D); definitive treatment is prompt cataract extraction after controlling the pressure.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Glaucoma (Lens-induced glaucomas)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The secondary angle-closure glaucoma produced when an intumescent, swollen cataractous lens pushes the iris-lens diaphragm forward is best termed:
questions.concept: Phacomorphic glaucoma is a secondary angle-closure glaucoma that occurs when an intumescent, swollen cataractous lens increases in thickness and pushes the iris-lens diaphragm forward, mechanically closing the drainage angle (B). Phacolytic glaucoma (A) is an open-angle glaucoma from leaked lens proteins, phacoantigenic reaction (C) is a lens-induced uveitis, and pigmentary glaucoma (D) is unrelated to cataract.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Glaucoma (Lens-induced glaucomas)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Phacoanaphylactic (lens-induced) uveitis is a granulomatous inflammation that follows rupture of the lens capsule from trauma or surgery. Reason (R): It is an IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity reaction to lens proteins. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: Phacoanaphylactic (phacoantigenic, lens-induced) uveitis is a granulomatous, zonal inflammatory response to lens proteins exposed after capsule rupture from trauma or surgery, so the assertion is true. However it is not an IgE-mediated type I reaction; it is an autoimmune (predominantly type III immune-complex and type IV) granulomatous response to previously sequestered lens antigen, so the reason is false (C). Treatment is removal of the residual lens matter.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Uvea and Lens (Lens-induced uveitis)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A male infant presents with bilateral congenital cataracts and congenital glaucoma, together with hypotonia, developmental delay and features of renal (Fanconi-type) tubular dysfunction. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Lowe (oculocerebrorenal) syndrome is an X-linked disorder of the OCRL gene affecting male infants, characterised by the combination of congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma and neurological involvement (hypotonia, intellectual disability), plus proximal renal (Fanconi-type) tubular dysfunction (D). Congenital rubella (A) lacks this renal tubulopathy, galactosaemia (B) gives an oil-droplet cataract without glaucoma, and myotonic dystrophy (C) presents in adulthood.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Congenital cataract: systemic associations)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with frontal balding, temporalis wasting, difficulty releasing his grip after a handshake and percussion myotonia is found on slit-lamp to have fine, multicoloured iridescent crystalline lens opacities ('Christmas-tree' cataract). The underlying disorder is:
questions.concept: Myotonic dystrophy (autosomal dominant, a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the DMPK gene) features frontal balding, temporalis and facial wasting, grip and percussion myotonia, and characteristically fine polychromatic iridescent lens crystals ('Christmas-tree' cataract) that evolve into a posterior subcapsular cataract (A). Wilson disease (B) gives a sunflower cataract, Marfan (C) causes lens subluxation, and NF2 (D) is associated with posterior subcapsular cataract but not myotonia.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye — The Crystalline Lens (Cataract in systemic disease)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: In the SRK (Sanders-Retzlaff-Kraff) regression formula for intraocular lens power, P = A - 2.5L - 0.9K, the terms 'L' and 'K' respectively denote:
options: Limbal white-to-white distance and anterior chamber depth
Axial length of the eye and average keratometry (corneal power)
Refractive index of the lens and pupil size
questions.concept: In the SRK formula P = A - 2.5L - 0.9K, P is the emmetropic IOL power, A is the lens-specific A-constant, L is the axial length of the eye in millimetres, and K is the average keratometry (corneal dioptric power) (C). The other options misidentify L and K; because the coefficient of L is large, small axial-length measurement errors produce the biggest postoperative refractive surprises.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Biometry and IOL power calculation)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Three days after uneventful cataract surgery a patient returns with severe ocular pain, marked reduction of vision, lid oedema, circumcorneal congestion and a hypopyon. The most appropriate immediate step, and the commonest causative organism, are:
options: Observation with topical lubricants; organism usually Pseudomonas
Increase topical steroids only; organism usually fungal
Nd:YAG capsulotomy; organism usually Propionibacterium acnes
Vitreous tap with intravitreal antibiotics (e.g. vancomycin plus ceftazidime); commonest organism coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (Staph. epidermidis)
questions.concept: Acute postoperative endophthalmitis presents within days of surgery with severe pain, marked visual loss, lid oedema, circumcorneal congestion and a hypopyon; it is a sight-threatening emergency managed by immediate vitreous tap/aspirate plus intravitreal antibiotics such as vancomycin with ceftazidime, and the commonest causative organisms are coagulase-negative staphylococci (Staph. epidermidis) (D). Observation (A), steroids alone (B) or capsulotomy (C) would be dangerous.
questions.reference: A.K. Khurana — Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Diseases of the Lens (Postoperative endophthalmitis)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Aqueous humour, which maintains intraocular pressure, is actively secreted by which ocular structure?
options: Non-pigmented epithelium of the ciliary processes
questions.concept: Aqueous humour is secreted mainly by the non-pigmented (inner) epithelium of the ciliary processes (pars plicata) through active transport (Na-K ATPase and carbonic anhydrase), supplemented by ultrafiltration and diffusion. The trabecular meshwork is the site of drainage, not production; the corneal endothelium regulates corneal deturgescence; and the lens epithelium plays no role in aqueous formation.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Chapter on Glaucoma (Aqueous humour dynamics)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The accepted statistical normal range of intraocular pressure in the adult population, and the pattern of its diurnal variation, is best described as:
options: 10-21 mmHg, with a diurnal peak typically in the early morning hours
10-21 mmHg, identical at every hour of the day
questions.concept: The mean IOP is about 16 mmHg and the normal range is taken as 10-21 mmHg (mean plus or minus two standard deviations). IOP shows a diurnal rhythm, usually varying 3-5 mmHg in normal eyes and more in glaucoma, and characteristically peaks in the early morning. A fluctuation greater than 5-8 mmHg is suspicious, and persistent readings above 21 mmHg warrant evaluation.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Glaucoma (Intraocular pressure)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: In the normal human eye, the majority of aqueous humour drains from the anterior chamber via which pathway?
options: Trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm
Active pumping by the retinal pigment epithelium
questions.concept: The conventional (trabecular) pathway accounts for roughly 80-90% of aqueous outflow: aqueous passes through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm's canal, then via collector channels and aqueous veins to the episcleral veins. The uveoscleral (unconventional) route drains the remaining 10-20%, is relatively pressure-independent, and is the pathway enhanced by prostaglandin analogues; the cornea and RPE play no drainage role.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Glaucoma (Aqueous outflow)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought with persistent watering, marked intolerance to light and squeezing of the eyelids; both corneas appear enlarged and hazy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: The classic triad of primary congenital glaucoma is epiphora, photophobia and blepharospasm. Because an infant's sclera is distensible, raised IOP enlarges the globe (buphthalmos) and cornea (diameter over 12 mm), causing corneal haze and horizontal breaks in Descemet's membrane (Haab's striae). Nasolacrimal duct obstruction gives watering and discharge with a normal cornea; ophthalmia neonatorum gives purulent discharge; retinoblastoma presents with leukocoria.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Congenital and developmental glaucomas

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Goldmann applanation tonometry, the clinical gold standard for measuring intraocular pressure, is based on which physical principle?
options: Imbert-Fick law (pressure equals force divided by the area of applanation)
questions.concept: Goldmann applanation tonometry flattens a fixed corneal area of 3.06 mm diameter. By the Imbert-Fick principle, the pressure inside a dry, thin-walled sphere equals the applied force divided by the applanated area. The 3.06 mm diameter is chosen so that corneal rigidity and the tear-film surface tension cancel out, and the force in grams multiplied by ten gives IOP in mmHg.
