Readings are influenced by central corneal thickness.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Tonometry

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Latanoprost, a prostaglandin analogue commonly used as first-line therapy in primary open-angle glaucoma, lowers intraocular pressure mainly by:
options: Decreasing aqueous production by the ciliary body
Increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour
Constricting the pupil to open the trabecular meshwork
questions.concept: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost) act on FP receptors and remodel the ciliary muscle extracellular matrix through matrix metalloproteinases, thereby enhancing the pressure-independent uveoscleral outflow. They are potent, once-daily first-line agents. Characteristic side effects include conjunctival hyperaemia, increased iris and periocular pigmentation, eyelash lengthening (hypertrichosis) and cystoid macular oedema in predisposed eyes.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Medical management of glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient is found to have a thin central corneal thickness of 480 microns. Compared with the true intraocular pressure, Goldmann applanation tonometry in this eye will most likely:
options: Be completely unaffected by corneal thickness
questions.concept: Goldmann tonometry is calibrated for an average central corneal thickness of about 520-545 microns. A thin cornea offers less resistance to applanation, so the measured pressure reads lower than the true IOP (underestimation) — an important reason why thin-cornea ocular hypertensives progress and are under-treated. A thick cornea causes overestimation. This is why pachymetry is part of every glaucoma work-up, especially after LASIK.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Tonometry and central corneal thickness

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: On gonioscopy using the Shaffer grading system, which grade denotes an angle that is closed (no angle structures visible) and carries the highest risk of angle closure?
questions.concept: The Shaffer system grades the angle by the angular width between the iris and trabecular meshwork: Grade 4 (35-45 degrees, wide open), Grade 3 (20-35 degrees, open), Grade 2 (about 20 degrees, closure possible), Grade 1 (about 10 degrees, closure probable) and Grade 0 (0 degrees, closed, with iris touching the meshwork). Grade 0 therefore represents a closed angle at greatest risk, whereas Grade 4 is the widest and safest.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Gonioscopy and angle grading

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 68-year-old with open-angle glaucoma shows, on slit-lamp examination, greyish-white flaky dandruff-like deposits on the anterior lens capsule in a target pattern and along the pupillary margin. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Pseudoexfoliation syndrome deposits fibrillar grey-white basement-membrane-like material on the anterior lens capsule (a central disc plus a peripheral band separated by a clear zone), the pupil margin, zonules and trabecular meshwork; meshwork obstruction raises IOP. It is the commonest identifiable cause of secondary open-angle glaucoma, is often asymmetric, is associated with weak zonules (cataract-surgery risk) and produces higher, more resistant IOP spikes than POAG.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Secondary open-angle glaucomas

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A young myopic man has raised IOP; gonioscopy shows dense homogeneous pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork and slit-lamp shows a vertical spindle-shaped pigment deposit on the corneal endothelium. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: In pigment dispersion syndrome a concave, posteriorly bowed iris rubs against the lens zonules, liberating pigment that deposits on the corneal endothelium as a vertical Krukenberg spindle and heavily pigments the trabecular meshwork, producing pigmentary glaucoma. It classically affects young myopic males, and exercise or pupil dilation can trigger IOP spikes. Mid-peripheral iris transillumination defects are characteristic, distinguishing it from the flaky deposits of pseudoexfoliation.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Pigmentary glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Topical timolol should be avoided in a patient with bronchial asthma. Reason (R): Timolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker that can precipitate bronchospasm and bradycardia through systemic absorption. Select the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Timolol, a non-selective beta-blocker, lowers IOP by reducing aqueous secretion from the ciliary epithelium. Systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal mucosa can cause bronchospasm (beta-2 blockade), bradycardia and heart block (beta-1 blockade); hence it is contraindicated in asthma or COPD, sinus bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block and decompensated heart failure. Punctal occlusion reduces systemic effects, so the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Antiglaucoma drugs (beta-blockers)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Oral acetazolamide lowers intraocular pressure primarily by which mechanism?
options: Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase to reduce aqueous humour secretion
questions.concept: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (oral acetazolamide and topical dorzolamide or brinzolamide) block carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary epithelium, reducing bicarbonate formation and thereby aqueous production, which lowers IOP. Acetazolamide is a sulphonamide; systemic effects include paraesthesiae, metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, renal stones and malaise, and it should be avoided in sulpha allergy and sickle-cell disease. It is useful for acute IOP control in angle closure.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A diabetic with proliferative retinopathy now has a painful red eye, IOP of 44 mmHg, new vessels on the iris (rubeosis) and a fibrovascular membrane crossing the angle on gonioscopy. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Neovascular glaucoma follows retinal ischaemia (proliferative diabetic retinopathy, central retinal vein occlusion, ocular ischaemic syndrome), which drives VEGF release and rubeosis iridis. A fibrovascular membrane grows over the angle, first causing a secondary open-angle picture and then contracting to produce synechial angle closure with a high, painful IOP. Management targets the underlying ischaemia with pan-retinal photocoagulation and anti-VEGF agents, along with IOP control and drainage surgery.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Neovascular glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Which visual field defect is most characteristic of early to moderate glaucomatous optic nerve damage?
options: Arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma with a nasal step
questions.concept: Glaucoma damages the arcuate retinal nerve-fibre bundles, so field defects arc around fixation from the blind spot along the nerve-fibre distribution: paracentral scotomas, arcuate (Bjerrum) scotomas and a nasal step (Roenne's) from asymmetric involvement across the horizontal raphe. Central vision is spared until late, ending as tunnel vision and then a temporal island. Bitemporal, homonymous and central defects instead indicate chiasmal, retrochiasmal or macular disease.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Perimetry in glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Chronic use of topical corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure mainly by:
options: Increasing aqueous production by the ciliary body
Increasing resistance to aqueous outflow at the trabecular meshwork
questions.concept: Corticosteroids raise IOP by increasing trabecular outflow resistance: they cause accumulation of glycosaminoglycans and extracellular matrix, reduce phagocytosis of debris and induce myocilin (TIGR) in meshwork cells, producing an open-angle picture. About one-third of people are steroid responders, more so in POAG patients and relatives, high myopes and diabetics. It can follow topical, periocular, inhaled or systemic steroids, and IOP usually falls after the steroid is stopped.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Steroid-induced glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly patient with a long-standing, now swollen (intumescent) mature cataract presents with acute pain and IOP of 46 mmHg; the anterior chamber is shallow only in that eye and gonioscopy shows a closed angle. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Phacomorphic glaucoma is a secondary angle-closure glaucoma: an intumescent mature or hypermature lens pushes the iris-lens diaphragm forward, shallowing the anterior chamber and closing the angle with a sudden rise in IOP. A unilaterally shallow chamber in an eye with an advanced cataract is the key clue. Treatment is to control IOP medically and then remove the lens. It contrasts with phacolytic glaucoma (open-angle, from leaked lens protein) and lens-particle glaucoma (retained cortex after surgery or trauma).
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Lens-induced glaucomas

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Pilocarpine lowers IOP in primary angle-closure. Reason (R): As a muscarinic agonist it contracts the ciliary muscle and sphincter pupillae, pulling the peripheral iris away from the angle and increasing trabecular outflow. Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.concept: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting muscarinic (cholinergic) agonist. It contracts the sphincter pupillae to produce miosis and contracts the ciliary muscle; ciliary contraction pulls on the scleral spur to open the trabecular meshwork and increase outflow, while miosis pulls the peripheral iris out of a crowded angle, breaking appositional closure in angle-closure. The two effects are causally linked, so the reason correctly explains the assertion. Side effects include brow ache and induced myopia.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Miotics in glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: What is the definitive treatment to relieve and prevent recurrence of primary angle closure caused by pupillary block?
questions.concept: In pupillary-block angle closure, aqueous is trapped behind the iris and bows it forward to close the angle. A laser peripheral iridotomy (usually Nd:YAG) creates an alternative channel that equalises pressure between the posterior and anterior chambers and flattens the iris, relieving and preventing the block; the fellow at-risk eye is treated prophylactically. Trabeculectomy is filtering surgery for uncontrolled glaucoma, trabeculoplasty is for open-angle disease, and cyclophotocoagulation reduces production in refractory eyes.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Management of primary angle-closure glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An elderly patient with a hypermature (Morgagnian) cataract develops acute pain and IOP of 40 mmHg; the anterior chamber shows heavy flare with floating white particles, yet gonioscopy reveals an open angle. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: In phacolytic glaucoma, high-molecular-weight lens proteins leak through the intact but permeable capsule of a hypermature cataract; protein-laden macrophages and the free proteins clog an open trabecular meshwork, raising IOP as an open-angle secondary glaucoma. The clue is dense anterior-chamber flare with a hypermature lens and an open angle. Treatment is IOP control followed by cataract extraction. Phacomorphic glaucoma is angle closure from a swollen lens, uveitis lacks the hypermature lens, and neovascular glaucoma shows angle vessels.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Phacolytic (lens-protein) glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Which class of drug is contraindicated (should be avoided) in an eye at risk of, or with, primary angle closure because it can precipitate an acute attack?
questions.concept: Mydriatics and anticholinergics (atropine, homatropine, tropicamide, and systemic anticholinergics, some antihistamines and tricyclics) dilate the pupil to a mid-dilated position that maximises iris-lens contact and peripheral iris crowding, precipitating pupillary-block angle closure in a narrow angle; adrenergic mydriatics carry a similar risk. In contrast, pilocarpine (a miotic), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, beta-blockers and hyperosmotics are therapeutic in angle closure because they lower IOP.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Drugs contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Regarding hyperosmotic agents used to rapidly lower intraocular pressure, which statement is correct?
options: Intravenous mannitol is freely metabolised to glucose and is therefore safe in cardiac failure
Oral glycerol should be avoided in diabetics because it is metabolised and can cause hyperglycaemia
Hyperosmotic agents act by increasing trabecular outflow of aqueous
Isosorbide is contraindicated in diabetics, so glycerol is preferred in them
questions.concept: Hyperosmotic agents (intravenous mannitol, oral glycerol, oral isosorbide) raise plasma osmolality and draw water from the vitreous to lower IOP acutely, for example in acute angle closure. Glycerol is metabolised (caloric) and can cause hyperglycaemia or ketoacidosis, so it is avoided in diabetics; isosorbide, which is not metabolised, is preferred in them. Mannitol is not metabolised and expands the intravascular volume, so it is used cautiously in cardiac and renal failure.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Hyperosmotic agents

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Mitomycin-C or 5-fluorouracil is applied during trabeculectomy in high-risk eyes. Reason (R): These antimetabolites inhibit fibroblast proliferation and so reduce scarring of the filtering bleb, improving surgical success. Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Trabeculectomy creates a guarded fistula that drains aqueous into a subconjunctival bleb; failure is usually due to fibroblast-driven scarring at the sclera and conjunctiva. Antifibrotic antimetabolites, mitomycin-C (an alkylating agent) and 5-fluorouracil, inhibit fibroblast proliferation and reduce bleb fibrosis, improving IOP control, especially in high-risk eyes (young, dark-skinned, previous failed surgery, neovascular). Risks include thin avascular blebs, hypotony, leaks and blebitis, so the reason explains the assertion.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Filtration surgery and antimetabolites

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old has glaucomatous optic disc cupping and arcuate field loss, but repeated readings show IOP of 14-16 mmHg with open angles and a normal central corneal thickness; the disc shows a splinter haemorrhage at its margin. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Primary open-angle glaucoma with high IOP
questions.concept: Normal-tension glaucoma shows characteristic glaucomatous disc and field damage despite IOP consistently at or below 21 mmHg with open angles, implicating vascular dysregulation, reduced ocular perfusion and a susceptible lamina cribrosa. Disc (Drance or splinter) haemorrhages, focal notching and deeper defects closer to fixation are typical. It is a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out spurious low readings from a thin cornea, prior steroid use, intermittent spikes and compressive neurological lesions). Treatment still aims to lower IOP by about 30%, unlike ocular hypertension, which has a raised IOP but a normal disc and field.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Normal-tension glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A man sustained blunt trauma to one eye from a cricket ball several years ago; that eye now has raised IOP, and gonioscopy shows an abnormally deep, widened ciliary-body band with a torn iris root over part of the angle. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Blunt ocular trauma can tear the face of the ciliary body between the longitudinal and circular muscle fibres (angle recession), seen on gonioscopy as a segment of abnormally widened and deepened ciliary-body band with a torn iris root. Associated scarring of the trabecular meshwork reduces outflow, and glaucoma may develop months to years later as an open-angle disease, so long-term IOP follow-up after blunt trauma is essential. Involvement of more than 180-270 degrees of the angle increases the risk; the mechanism is distinct from neovascular, phacolytic and pseudoexfoliative glaucomas.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Post-traumatic (angle-recession) glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The preferred initial (definitive) treatment of primary congenital glaucoma is:
questions.concept: Primary congenital glaucoma results from maldevelopment of the angle (trabeculodysgenesis) that obstructs outflow. The definitive treatment is angle surgery: goniotomy when the cornea is clear enough to visualise the angle, or trabeculotomy when the cornea is hazy; both incise the abnormal trabecular tissue to restore drainage. Trabeculectomy with a tube or a combined trabeculotomy-trabeculectomy is used when these fail. Medications are only a temporising adjunct; laser iridotomy addresses pupillary block (not the mechanism here) and enucleation is not indicated.
questions.reference: Khurana's Comprehensive Ophthalmology, 7th ed. — Management of congenital glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) and argon laser trabeculoplasty (ALT) lower IOP by acting on which structure, and in which type of glaucoma are they mainly used?
options: They create a hole in the peripheral iris and are used in angle-closure glaucoma
They treat the trabecular meshwork to improve outflow and are used in open-angle glaucoma
They ablate the ciliary body to reduce aqueous production and are used only in refractory glaucoma
They surgically cut the trabecular meshwork and are used in congenital glaucoma
questions.concept: Laser trabeculoplasty applies laser energy to the trabecular meshwork to enhance conventional (trabecular) aqueous outflow, lowering IOP in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. SLT uses low-energy, pigment-selective Q-switched Nd:YAG (repeatable, with minimal tissue damage), whereas ALT uses thermal argon burns; either can be first-line or adjunctive. In contrast, iridotomy makes an iris hole for angle closure, cyclophotocoagulation ablates the ciliary body in refractory cases, and goniotomy is a surgical angle incision for congenital glaucoma.
questions.reference: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye, 22nd ed. — Laser therapy in glaucoma

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: In an emmetropic eye at complete physiological rest (accommodation fully relaxed), where do parallel rays of light coming from infinity come to a focus?
options: In front of the retina, in the vitreous
On the retinal pigment epithelium behind the choroid
questions.concept: Emmetropia is the ideal state in which the axial length and total refractive power are balanced, so parallel rays from infinity focus precisely on the retina without any accommodative effort; the far point lies at infinity. A focus in front of the retina defines myopia and a focus behind it defines hypermetropia, while the RPE lies deep to the neurosensory retina and is never the image plane.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Optics and Refraction (Errors of Refraction)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Which structure contributes the greatest amount of static refractive (dioptric) power to the resting human eye?
questions.concept: The cornea (mainly its air–tear interface) is the principal refracting surface, providing about 43–44 D of the eye's total ~58–60 D. The crystalline lens adds only ~15–20 D at rest but is the sole variable element that changes power during accommodation. Aqueous and vitreous humour have refractive indices close to their surroundings and contribute negligible refracting power.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Physiological Optics

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A myopic eye in which the total dioptric power of the refracting media is normal but the anteroposterior axial length is longer than normal is best classified as:
questions.concept: Axial myopia is due to an increased anteroposterior length with normal refracting power; roughly each 1 mm of extra axial length adds about 3 D of myopia, and most simple and pathological myopia is axial. Curvatural myopia results from steeper corneal/lens curvature, index myopia from a rise in refractive index (e.g. nuclear sclerosis or hyperglycaemia), and positional myopia from anterior displacement of the lens.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Myopia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The far point (punctum remotum) of an uncorrected myopic eye lies:
options: Behind the eye, as a virtual point
At the anterior focal point of the cornea
At a finite distance in front of the eye
questions.concept: In myopia the far point is a real point situated a finite distance in front of the eye; the greater the myopia the nearer this point (a −2 D myope's far point is 0.5 m, a −4 D myope's is 0.25 m). In an emmetrope the far point is at infinity, whereas in a hypermetrope it is virtual and lies behind the eye. Knowing the far point lets one calculate the concave lens power needed for correction.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Refractive Errors

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A young man with well-corrected daytime distance vision complains that objects appear blurred and he tends to under-estimate distances only while driving at night. The most likely explanation is:
options: Night (twilight) myopia from pupil dilation and dark-focus of accommodation
Accommodative spasm that is relieved in the dark
questions.concept: In dim light the pupil dilates, increasing spherical aberration, and accommodation drifts to an intermediate resting dark-focus of about 1–1.5 D; together with the Purkinje shift this produces a relative myopia at night that a small extra concave (minus) correction can relieve. Early cataract and against-the-rule astigmatism blur vision by day too, and accommodative spasm is worsened, not relieved, in the dark.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Myopia (Night Myopia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Which type of myopia is physiological in nature, usually appears around puberty, rarely exceeds −6 D, gives good corrected acuity, and is not associated with degenerative fundus changes?
questions.concept: Simple myopia is a physiological (correlation-type) variation with onset near puberty, magnitude usually below −5 to −6 D, normal corrected acuity and no degenerative fundus changes. Pathological myopia is progressive and high (often beyond −6 to −8 D) with staphyloma, lacquer cracks and chorioretinal degeneration; congenital myopia is present from birth and often high, while index myopia arises from lens sclerosis in later life.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Types of Myopia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient with −14 D pathological myopia has a raised, circular, pigmented macular lesion representing organised subretinal haemorrhage arising from choroidal neovascularisation. This lesion is known as:
questions.concept: In degenerative myopia, lacquer cracks (breaks in Bruch's membrane) predispose to choroidal neovascularisation; organised subretinal bleeding leaves a raised pigmented macular scar called the Foster-Fuchs spot, causing central vision loss. Elschnig spots and Siegrist streaks are signs of hypertensive choroidopathy, and Gunn's dots are normal light reflections around the disc, not degenerative lesions.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Complications of Myopia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: The full amount of hypermetropia that becomes evident only after complete paralysis of accommodation by cycloplegia is termed:
questions.concept: Total hypermetropia equals latent plus manifest hypermetropia. The latent component is masked by resting ciliary muscle tone and is revealed only under full cycloplegia (e.g. atropine), so total hypermetropia can be measured only after cycloplegic refraction. Manifest hypermetropia is itself divided into facultative (overcome by accommodation) and absolute (not overcome by accommodation) parts.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Hypermetropia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 3-year-old with +5 D hypermetropia develops a convergent squint that disappears completely when full hypermetropic spectacles are worn. The underlying mechanism and definitive management are:
options: Excess accommodation drives convergence; full convex (plus) spectacle correction
questions.concept: Uncorrected hypermetropia forces sustained accommodation, and the linked accommodative convergence produces an accommodative esotropia. Full cycloplegic plus correction relaxes accommodation and straightens the eyes; a high AC/A ratio may need bifocals. If left uncorrected it risks amblyopia. A sixth-nerve palsy and Duane syndrome give incomitant deviations that are not abolished by plus lenses.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Complications of Hypermetropia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A myopic patient has a far point 1 metre in front of the eye and a near point at 20 cm. What is his amplitude of accommodation?
questions.concept: Amplitude of accommodation equals the dioptric difference between the far point and the near point = (1 / 0.20 m) − (1 / 1.0 m) = 5 D − 1 D = 4 D. It represents the maximum increase in dioptric power the crystalline lens can generate. This amplitude falls steadily with age as the lens hardens, which is the physiological basis of presbyopia.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Accommodation

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): In presbyopia the near point of the eye recedes with advancing age. Reason (R): The crystalline lens progressively hardens and loses elasticity, reducing its ability to increase curvature during accommodation. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Presbyopia is the age-related decline of accommodation caused chiefly by lens sclerosis and loss of capsular elasticity, with some contribution from ciliary muscle change; because the lens can no longer steepen enough, the near point moves further away, so both the assertion and the reason are true and the reason correctly explains it. Convex (plus) reading additions restore comfortable near vision.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Presbyopia)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old emmetrope needs reading glasses. Which near addition (add) is most appropriate for comfortable reading at about 33 cm?
questions.concept: The presbyopic add increases with age: roughly +1.00 D at 40–45, +1.50 D at 45–50, +2.00 D at 50–55, +2.50 D at 55–60 and up to +3.00 D beyond 60. A 50-year-old therefore typically needs about +2.00 D for a 33 cm working distance. Too strong an add (e.g. +3.50 or +4.00) forces an uncomfortably short working distance, while +0.50 D is inadequate. The add is prescribed over any distance correction.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Presbyopia (Prescribing the Add)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: In with-the-rule astigmatism, the meridian with the greatest refractive power and the appropriate correcting lens are:
options: Horizontal meridian, steepest; concave cylinder at axis 90°
Vertical meridian, steepest; concave cylinder at axis 90°
Oblique meridian, steepest; corrected with a spherical lens only
Vertical meridian, steepest; concave (minus) cylinder at axis 180°
questions.concept: In with-the-rule astigmatism (common in the young) the vertical meridian is steeper and more powerful, so it is corrected by a minus cylinder with its axis at 180° (equivalently a plus cylinder at 90°). Against-the-rule astigmatism, common in the elderly, has the horizontal meridian steeper and is corrected with a minus cylinder at 90°. Astigmatism cannot be corrected by a spherical lens alone.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Astigmatism)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient has irregular astigmatism with an uneven anterior corneal surface after a healed corneal ulcer. Which correction gives the best visual result?
questions.concept: In irregular astigmatism the principal meridians are not regular or mutually perpendicular, so a cylindrical spectacle lens cannot neutralise the error. A rigid gas-permeable contact lens masks the surface irregularity by forming a smooth new refracting surface with the tear film beneath it, restoring good acuity. Cylindrical spectacle lenses correct only regular astigmatism, and bifocals address presbyopia, not corneal irregularity.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Astigmatism (Irregular Astigmatism)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A teenager with atopy and habitual eye-rubbing has progressive myopic astigmatism, an oil-droplet red reflex, Vogt's striae and a Fleischer ring at the base of a corneal cone. To halt disease progression the intervention of choice is:
questions.concept: These are classic features of keratoconus — progressive non-inflammatory corneal ectasia with irregular myopic astigmatism, Fleischer ring, Vogt striae, oil-droplet reflex and Munson sign. Corneal collagen cross-linking stiffens the stroma with riboflavin and UV-A to arrest progression; rigid contact lenses restore vision, and keratoplasty is reserved for advanced scarring. LASIK is strictly contraindicated because ablation accelerates ectasia.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Diseases of the Cornea (Keratoconus)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A spectacle prescription reads −3.00 DS / −1.50 DC × 90. What is its spherical equivalent?
questions.concept: Spherical equivalent = sphere + (cylinder / 2) = −3.00 + (−1.50 / 2) = −3.00 + (−0.75) = −3.75 D. It corresponds to the dioptric position of the circle of least confusion and is used when only a spherical lens is available, for example when fitting a spherical soft trial contact lens or reporting a single-value refraction.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Astigmatism (Spherical Equivalent)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient wears a +5.00 D spherical spectacle lens that is decentred 4 mm from the visual axis. What is the induced prismatic power?
questions.concept: By Prentice's rule the prismatic effect (in prism dioptres) equals the decentration in centimetres multiplied by the lens power in dioptres = 0.4 cm × 5 D = 2 prism dioptres. Deliberate decentration can incorporate prism, but unwanted decentration induces prism and asthenopia. One prism dioptre deviates a ray of light 1 cm at a distance of 1 metre.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Prisms (Prentice's Rule)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: During subjective refraction, the Jackson cross cylinder is used mainly to:
options: Refine the power and axis of the cylindrical (astigmatic) correction
Detect the presence of colour blindness
Determine the near addition for presbyopia
questions.concept: The Jackson cross cylinder is a lens combining equal plus and minus cylinders whose axes are 90° apart, with the handle bisecting them. By flipping it and comparing images the examiner first refines the cylinder axis and then its power, fine-tuning the astigmatic correction. It has no role in measuring accommodation, testing colour vision or determining a presbyopic add.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Subjective Refraction (Cross Cylinder)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: On the duochrome (red-green) test a patient reports that the black letters on the RED half are clearer and blacker than those on the green half. This indicates the eye is:
options: Under-minused / relatively myopic — add minus power
Amblyopic — no refractive change is possible
questions.concept: The duochrome test exploits the eye's chromatic aberration: longer red wavelengths focus behind and shorter green wavelengths in front of the retina. If the red side is clearer the overall focus lies anterior to the retina (the myopic/under-minused side), so minus power should be added; if green is clearer, add plus (mnemonic RAM-GAP). The endpoint is reached when both halves appear equally clear.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Subjective Refraction (Duochrome Test)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A patient's unaided visual acuity is 6/36 but improves to 6/9 when tested through a pinhole. This most strongly suggests:
questions.concept: A pinhole admits only central paraxial rays and eliminates the blur circle produced by ametropia, so vision that improves with a pinhole indicates a refractive error correctable by glasses. Little or no improvement points instead to a media opacity such as dense cataract, or to organic macular or optic-nerve disease. The pinhole thus helps separate refractive from non-refractive causes of reduced acuity.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Clinical Methods (Pinhole Test)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: During plane-mirror streak retinoscopy performed at 1 metre, the retinal reflex moves in the SAME direction as the streak (a "with" movement). Before applying the working-distance correction, this indicates the eye is:
options: Myopic greater than 1 D — neutralise with minus lenses
Exactly 1 D myopic, at the point of reversal
Irregularly astigmatic and cannot be neutralised
Hypermetropic, emmetropic, or myopic less than 1 D — neutralise with plus lenses
questions.concept: A "with" movement means the far point lies behind the retinoscope peephole, so the eye is hypermetropic, emmetropic, or myopic by less than the working-distance dioptre, and plus lenses are added to neutralise it. An "against" movement (myopia greater than the working distance) needs minus lenses. At neutralisation the far point lies at the peephole; the working-distance value (1 D at 1 m) is then subtracted to give the true error.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Retinoscopy

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: For accurate refraction of a 3-year-old child with a suspected accommodative convergent squint and high hypermetropia, the cycloplegic agent of choice is:
questions.concept: Young children and darkly pigmented irides have strong ciliary tone, and accommodative esotropia demands complete relaxation of accommodation, so atropine 1% — the most powerful cycloplegic — is preferred for full cycloplegic refraction despite its slow onset and long duration (with counselling about systemic toxicity). Tropicamide is a weak, short-acting cycloplegic used mainly for mydriasis; phenylephrine and brimonidine have no cycloplegic action.
questions.reference: Khurana, Theory and Practice of Optics and Refraction — Refraction in Children (Cycloplegics)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A soft contact lens wearer who habitually sleeps in her lenses presents with a painful red eye, photophobia, and a corneal stromal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect. The most sight-threatening diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Overnight lens wear causes corneal hypoxia and epithelial breakdown, greatly increasing the risk of microbial keratitis (notably Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba), the most serious, potentially blinding complication that demands urgent corneal scraping, culture and intensive fortified antibiotics. Giant papillary conjunctivitis, dry eye and superficial neovascularisation cause discomfort and blur but are not immediately vision-threatening emergencies.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Contact Lenses (Complications)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old with stable −13 D myopia and a thin central cornea of 480 µm wishes to be spectacle-independent. LASIK is inadvisable here because of insufficient residual stromal bed. The most appropriate option is:
options: Higher-ablation LASIK to fully correct the −13 D
Bilateral clear lens extraction as the first-choice procedure
questions.concept: High myopia combined with a thin cornea exceeds the safe ablation limit for LASIK or PRK, risking iatrogenic ectasia and too little residual stroma, so a phakic intraocular lens (implantable collamer lens, ICL) is preferred because it corrects large errors without removing corneal tissue and is reversible. Radial keratotomy is obsolete and unstable, and clear lens extraction in a young high myope carries a significant retinal detachment risk and abolishes accommodation.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Refractive Surgery (Phakic IOL / ICL)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.stem: An adult with +1.00 D hypermetropia in the right eye and +6.00 D in the left develops troublesome asthenopia and a difference in the size of the two retinal images when wearing spectacles. The optical correction that best minimises this aniseikonia is:
options: A balancing prism in the spectacles
questions.concept: This is anisometropia (a 5 D interocular difference) causing aniseikonia, because a spectacle lens sits well in front of the eye and magnifies or minifies the retinal image (about 1–2% per dioptre) and creates differential prism on eccentric gaze. Contact lenses lie at the corneal plane, producing far less image-size disparity and prismatic difference, and so best relieve the aniseikonia and asthenopia. Large uncorrected childhood anisometropia is a major cause of amblyopia.
questions.reference: Khurana, Comprehensive Ophthalmology — Errors of Refraction (Anisometropia and Aniseikonia)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Which single organism is the commonest cause of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis across all age groups?
questions.concept: Staphylococcus aureus is by far the most frequent organism in acute haematogenous osteomyelitis at all ages because of its adhesins that bind bone matrix and its ability to survive intracellularly. Streptococcus pyogenes causes a minority of cases; Pseudomonas is linked to IV drug use and puncture wounds; Salmonella is characteristic of sickle-cell disease. Knowing S. aureus predominates guides empirical anti-staphylococcal antibiotic choice before cultures return.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Bone and Joint Infections (Acute Osteomyelitis)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 7-year-old known to have sickle-cell disease develops fever with pain and swelling of the forearm and is diagnosed with osteomyelitis. Which organism is characteristically associated with osteomyelitis in this setting?
questions.concept: Salmonella osteomyelitis is classically over-represented in sickle-cell disease, attributed to micro-infarction of gut and bone that seeds Salmonella and to functional hyposplenism impairing clearance of encapsulated organisms. Although Staphylococcus aureus is still numerically common even in sickle-cell patients, Salmonella is the association exams test. E. coli and Group B Strep suit neonates, and gonococcus causes septic arthritis in sexually active adults, not this presentation.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Acute Haematogenous Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Assertion (A): In neonatal osteomyelitis, spread of infection into the adjacent joint (secondary septic arthritis) is rare. Reason (R): In neonates and infants, some metaphyseal blood vessels cross the physis (growth plate) to reach the epiphysis. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is false: in neonates and infants joint spread is actually common, not rare. The reason is true — before about 18 months some metaphyseal vessels perforate the physis into the epiphysis, so infection readily reaches the joint, causing secondary septic arthritis and growth-plate damage. In older children the physis acts as a barrier, confining infection to the metaphysis. Because a false assertion pairs with a true reason, the answer is 'A false, R true'.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Osteomyelitis in Infants

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 26-year-old intravenous drug user presents with pain, swelling and warmth of the sternoclavicular joint with adjacent bone involvement. Besides Staphylococcus aureus, which organism is classically associated with bone and joint infection at unusual sites in this population?
questions.concept: Intravenous drug users classically develop infection at unusual axial sites (sternoclavicular, sacroiliac, vertebral) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the organism characteristically over-represented in this group along with S. aureus. Salmonella suggests sickle-cell disease, Group B Streptococcus suits neonates, and coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) characterise prosthetic/implant infection via biofilm. Recognising the IVDU-Pseudomonas link influences empirical anti-pseudomonal cover and imaging of axial joints.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th ed — Osteomyelitis (special settings)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children characteristically begins in the metaphysis of long bones. Which feature best explains this predilection?
options: The metaphysis has the richest anastomotic arterial supply, promoting rapid bacterial clearance
Sluggish blood flow in the hairpin loops of non-anastomosing metaphyseal capillaries favours bacterial lodgement
The growth plate is the most vascular part of the bone and acts as the primary nidus
Metaphyseal bone is covered by unusually thick periosteum that traps organisms
questions.concept: In the child's metaphysis, nutrient-artery branches form hairpin loops that empty into wide, non-anastomosing venous sinusoids where blood flow is sluggish and phagocytic activity is relatively low; this stasis lets circulating bacteria settle and multiply. It is a low-flow, poorly-defended zone, not a rich anastomotic bed (so A is wrong). The physis is relatively avascular and acts as a barrier rather than a nidus (C wrong), and periosteal thickness does not explain metaphyseal seeding (D wrong).
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Pathology of Acute Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: In chronic osteomyelitis, a fragment of dead, avascular bone that has separated from surrounding living bone is termed:
questions.concept: A sequestrum is a piece of necrotic, avascular bone that has separated from viable bone; because it is dead and lacks blood supply, antibiotics cannot penetrate it and it perpetuates infection until surgically removed (sequestrectomy). By contrast, an involucrum is the new living bone laid down by periosteum around it, a cloaca is the opening through the involucrum through which pus escapes, and a Brodie's abscess is a walled-off subacute focus. Radiologically a sequestrum appears denser than the surrounding osteopenic living bone.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Chronic Osteomyelitis (terminology)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The layer of new, living bone laid down by the stripped and elevated periosteum, which comes to surround infected or dead bone in chronic osteomyelitis, is called:
questions.concept: The involucrum is the sheath of new living bone formed by the periosteum, which is lifted off by subperiosteal pus; it envelops the infected/dead bone and can eventually reconstitute the shaft. It is perforated by openings called cloacae through which pus and sequestra discharge to a skin sinus. The involucrum is living and vascular, opposite to the dead sequestrum it surrounds; distinguishing the two is central to planning saucerisation and sequestrectomy in chronic osteomyelitis.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Chronic Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: In chronic osteomyelitis, the openings in the involucrum through which pus and small pieces of dead bone are discharged are known as:
questions.concept: Cloacae are the holes in the involucrum through which pus, granulation tissue and small sequestra escape, ultimately reaching the skin via a sinus tract. A sequestrum is the dead bone itself; a Brodie's abscess is a localised subacute abscess with a sclerotic rim; a ring sequestrum is the specific circumferential dead bone seen around a pin track or amputation stump. Understanding that cloacae are conduits, not dead bone, clarifies why simply draining pus without removing the sequestrum fails to cure the infection.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Chronic Osteomyelitis (terminology)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy has several months of intermittent, dull pain near the upper end of the tibia with little systemic upset. Radiograph shows a well-defined round lucency surrounded by a rim of reactive sclerosis in the metaphysis. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: A Brodie's abscess is a localised subacute osteomyelitis, typically in the proximal tibial metaphysis of a child or adolescent, presenting with chronic low-grade pain and minimal systemic signs; the classic X-ray is a round lucency with a sclerotic margin. Osteoid osteoma also has a lucent nidus with sclerosis but causes night pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs. Ewing's sarcoma shows an aggressive permeative lesion with lamellated periosteal reaction and systemic upset; a giant cell tumour is epiphyseal/subarticular in a skeletally mature patient.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Subacute Osteomyelitis (Brodie's abscess)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A child has clinical features strongly suggestive of acute osteomyelitis, but the plain radiograph of the limb is normal. Which imaging investigation is the most sensitive for detecting early disease?
questions.concept: MRI is the most sensitive imaging test in early osteomyelitis: marrow oedema (low T1, high T2/STIR signal) appears within days, well before plain-film changes, and it also delineates subperiosteal or soft-tissue abscesses to guide drainage. Plain radiographs lag by 10-14 days, so repeating them early is low-yield; ultrasound can show subperiosteal collections but is less sensitive for marrow; CT is best for cortical detail and sequestra but is poor for early marrow oedema and adds radiation.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Investigations in Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Assertion (A): A normal plain radiograph in the first few days does not exclude acute osteomyelitis. Reason (R): Bony radiographic changes such as osteopenia and periosteal reaction lag behind the disease, appearing only after about 10-14 days. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Detectable bone loss on plain film requires roughly 30-50% demineralisation, which takes about 10-14 days; hence early films are often normal, and the earliest visible change is deep soft-tissue swelling, not bone destruction. Because bony signs lag, a normal early radiograph cannot rule out osteomyelitis and MRI or bone scan should be used when clinical suspicion is high. The lag directly justifies the assertion, so option A is correct.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Imaging in Acute Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A three-phase Technetium-99m MDP bone scan is performed for suspected osteomyelitis. Which statement best describes its role?
options: It is highly specific and reliably separates infection from fracture or tumour
It becomes positive only after two weeks, later than the plain radiograph
It is the investigation of choice for demonstrating a sequestrum
It becomes positive early (within 24-72 hours) and is sensitive, but is relatively non-specific
questions.concept: A radionuclide (Tc-99m MDP) bone scan turns positive within 24-72 hours, well before plain films, and is sensitive, so it is useful when MRI is unavailable or when multifocal disease is suspected; however increased uptake also occurs with fracture, tumour, surgery and arthropathy, making it non-specific. It is thus not confirmatory (A wrong), it is earlier than X-ray not later (B wrong), and CT — not scintigraphy — best shows a sequestrum's dense cortical detail (C wrong). MRI generally supersedes it for anatomical localisation.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th ed — Imaging of Musculoskeletal Infection

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: What is the most definitive method to establish the causative organism in acute haematogenous osteomyelitis?
options: Culture of a bone aspirate or biopsy, together with blood cultures
questions.concept: Definitive identification of the organism — essential for targeted, prolonged antibiotic therapy — comes from culture of material aspirated or biopsied from the infected bone/subperiosteal collection, ideally with paired blood cultures (positive in roughly 50-60% of acute cases). CRP and total leucocyte count are sensitive markers of inflammation and useful for monitoring response but do not name the organism. MRI localises and characterises infection but is not microbiological. Whenever feasible, samples should be taken before starting antibiotics.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Diagnosis of Acute Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 9-year-old with acute haematogenous osteomyelitis is started on appropriate intravenous antibiotics. Which management principle is correct?
options: Antibiotics are given for three days and stopped once the child is afebrile
Surgical drainage is contraindicated in all cases of osteomyelitis
Antibiotics are continued for about 4-6 weeks; surgical drainage is indicated if there is an abscess or no clinical improvement within about 48 hours
Oral antibiotics alone are adequate from the outset regardless of severity
questions.concept: Acute osteomyelitis needs a prolonged course — typically initial IV antibiotics followed by oral therapy for a total of about 4-6 weeks — because dead/poorly-vascularised bone clears organisms slowly, and premature cessation invites chronic osteomyelitis. Surgery is indicated when there is a drainable abscess (subperiosteal/soft-tissue) or when there is no clinical response within roughly 48 hours of adequate antibiotics. Thus three days is far too short (A), surgery is sometimes essential (B), and severe cases require initial IV therapy, not oral alone (D).
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Treatment of Acute Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has had a chronically discharging sinus over the tibia from long-standing osteomyelitis for 30 years. The sinus margin has recently become raised, everted and ulcerated with a foul discharge. The most likely complication is:
questions.concept: A Marjolin's ulcer is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronically inflamed tissue such as a long-standing osteomyelitis sinus, burn scar or ulcer; the tell-tale signs are raised everted margins, increasing size and foul discharge after years of a stable sinus, warranting biopsy. It is typically slow-growing but can metastasise. Amyloidosis is a systemic sequela of chronic suppuration, not a change at the sinus margin; basal cell carcinoma does not arise this way; and chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis is a distinct non-suppurative paediatric condition.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Complications of Chronic Osteomyelitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The Cierny-Mader classification is used to stage which condition, and on what basis?
options: Chronic osteomyelitis, based on the anatomic type of bone involvement combined with the physiologic (host) status
Acute septic arthritis, based on the synovial fluid cell count
Spinal tuberculosis, based on the number of vertebrae involved
Prosthetic joint infection, based only on the time since surgery
questions.concept: The Cierny-Mader system stages adult chronic osteomyelitis by combining an anatomic type (I medullary, II superficial, III localised, IV diffuse) with a physiologic host class (A normal, B compromised locally/systemically, C treatment worse than disease). This links extent of bone disease with host healing capacity to guide surgery and prognosis. It is not a septic-arthritis, spinal-TB or purely time-based prosthetic-infection scheme, which is why the other options are wrong; recognising host class B explains why comorbidities (diabetes, smoking, vascular disease) worsen outcomes.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th ed — Chronic Osteomyelitis (Cierny-Mader staging)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Which is the most commonly affected joint in acute septic (pyogenic) arthritis in adults?
questions.concept: In adults the knee is the most commonly involved joint in acute septic arthritis, being large, superficial and frequently exposed to trauma and haematogenous seeding; it presents with a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender joint held in slight flexion with global restriction of movement. In infants and young children the hip is the classic site. The shoulder, ankle and wrist are affected less often. Rapid diagnosis matters because pus digests articular cartilage within days, threatening permanent joint destruction.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Acute Septic Arthritis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 23-year-old sexually active woman presents with migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrist, and scattered pustular skin lesions, along with an acutely inflamed knee. The most likely cause of her arthritis is:
questions.concept: In a young, sexually active adult the triad of migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustular/vesicopustular skin lesions is the classic disseminated gonococcal infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae; it may evolve into frank purulent monoarthritis and responds to ceftriaxone. Staphylococcus aureus typically causes single-joint pyogenic arthritis without the dermatitis-tenosynovitis picture. Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic and symmetrical, and reactive arthritis follows urethritis/dysentery with a seronegative, culture-negative aseptic joint. Recognising gonococcus prompts genital cultures and partner treatment.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Gonococcal Arthritis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Kocher's criteria help differentiate septic arthritis of the hip from transient synovitis in a child. Which option correctly lists these four predictors?
options: Age under 2 years, groin pain, limp, and a positive hip ultrasound
Fever, raised CRP, positive blood culture, and a joint effusion
Night pain, weight loss, raised ESR, and a positive Mantoux test
Inability to bear weight, temperature above 38.5°C, ESR above 40 mm/hr, and WBC above 12,000/mm3
questions.concept: Kocher's four independent predictors of septic arthritis of the hip are: non-weight-bearing on the affected side, temperature above 38.5°C, ESR above 40 mm/hr, and serum white cell count above 12,000/mm3; the probability of septic arthritis rises steeply as more criteria are met (from a few percent with one to over 90% with all four). The other option sets mix in ultrasound, blood culture or TB features that are not part of Kocher's original prediction rule, which is why they are incorrect for this classic decision aid.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th ed — Septic Arthritis in Children (Kocher criteria)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 4-year-old has confirmed acute septic arthritis of the knee with frank pus obtained on aspiration. What is the most appropriate management principle?
options: Urgent surgical drainage/washout of the joint plus intravenous antibiotics, because pus rapidly destroys articular cartilage
A trial of oral antibiotics for one week before considering any drainage
Immobilisation and NSAIDs alone, reserving antibiotics for failure
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection to reduce inflammation
questions.concept: Frank pus in a joint is a surgical emergency: proteolytic and lysosomal enzymes from leucocytes and bacteria digest articular cartilage within days, so treatment is urgent drainage (arthrotomy, arthroscopic washout or repeated aspiration) combined with prompt intravenous antibiotics. Delaying with oral antibiotics alone (B), relying on NSAIDs/immobilisation without antibiotics (C), or injecting steroids (D) all allow irreversible cartilage loss, growth-plate damage and later degenerative arthritis. Early decompression preserves the joint and reduces sequelae.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Treatment of Acute Septic Arthritis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A patient with tuberculosis of the lower lumbar spine develops a soft, fluctuant, non-tender swelling in the groin/femoral triangle. This cold abscess has most likely tracked along which structure?
questions.concept: A tuberculous cold abscess from the lumbar spine typically dissects along the psoas (iliopsoas) muscle sheath and may present as a fluctuant swelling in the groin/femoral triangle, or point below the inguinal ligament; hence the term psoas abscess. It is 'cold' because it lacks the acute inflammatory signs of a pyogenic abscess. Tracking does not follow the adductor longus or sartorius, and although the abscess appears near the femoral vessels it descends within the psoas sheath, not the arterial sheath. A psoas abscess may cause a positive psoas (hip-flexion) sign.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — Spinal Tuberculosis (cold abscess)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Destruction and anterior collapse of adjacent vertebral bodies in Pott's disease of the spine typically produces which characteristic deformity?
questions.concept: Because tuberculosis preferentially destroys the anterior parts of the vertebral bodies, they wedge and collapse forward, producing a gibbus — a localised, sharp, angular kyphosis (a knuckle-shaped prominence) rather than a smooth rounded curve. This is the classic deformity of spinal TB and can be palpated as a prominent spinous process. Scoliosis is a lateral curve, lordosis is a reversed sagittal curve, and flat-back is loss of normal lordosis; none reflects the anterior vertebral-body collapse of Pott's disease.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Tuberculosis of the Spine (deformity)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Assertion (A): In tuberculous spondylitis the intervertebral disc space is relatively preserved until late in the disease. Reason (R): Mycobacterium tuberculosis lacks the proteolytic (disc-digesting) enzymes produced by pyogenic bacteria. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are true and R explains A. Unlike pyogenic organisms, M. tuberculosis does not elaborate proteolytic enzymes that rapidly destroy the disc, so in spinal TB the disc space is relatively spared while adjacent vertebral bodies are eroded (paradiscal lesion) and the infection spreads under the anterior longitudinal ligament to affect multiple contiguous levels. In pyogenic spondylodiscitis the disc is destroyed early with rapid narrowing. This disc-preservation-versus-early-destruction contrast is a key radiological discriminator, making option A correct.
questions.reference: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma, 10th ed — TB versus Pyogenic Spondylodiscitis

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A patient with Pott's disease has vertebral involvement but no neurological deficit and a clinically stable spine. Which statement about management is correct?
options: Radical surgical debridement is required in every case before anti-tubercular drugs are started
Anti-tubercular therapy is unnecessary provided a spinal brace is applied
Immediate spinal fusion is indicated for all patients who have a cold abscess
Anti-tubercular chemotherapy is the mainstay; surgery is reserved for progressive or non-responding neurological deficit, gross instability/deformity, or a large abscess
questions.concept: The mainstay of spinal TB treatment is prolonged multidrug anti-tubercular chemotherapy (typically 4-drug intensive phase then continuation, often 12-18 months), and most patients without neurological deficit heal on drugs plus supportive measures. Surgery (decompression, debridement, stabilisation) is reserved for specific indications: neurological deficit that is progressive or fails to respond to ATT, gross instability or severe/progressive kyphotic deformity, and a large or non-resolving abscess. Hence ATT is not optional (B), and neither routine pre-treatment debridement (A) nor fusion for every abscess (C) is warranted.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics, 6th ed — Treatment of Spinal Tuberculosis (indications for surgery)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A patient develops an indolent, low-grade infection of a total hip replacement several months after surgery. Which organism is most characteristically responsible, owing to its ability to form biofilm on the implant?
questions.concept: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, chiefly Staphylococcus epidermidis, are the organisms most characteristically responsible for delayed, low-grade prosthetic joint infection because they produce a glycocalyx biofilm on the implant surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defences, causing an indolent course with subtle pain and loosening rather than florid sepsis. Staphylococcus aureus tends to cause more acute, aggressive infection; E. coli and Streptococcus pyogenes are less typical implant biofilm formers. Eradication usually requires implant removal or exchange plus prolonged antibiotics, since biofilm cannot be cleared by drugs alone.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics, 14th ed — Prosthetic (Periprosthetic) Joint Infection

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common benign bone tumour?
questions.concept: Osteochondroma is the commonest benign bone tumour, arising from the metaphysis of long bones (typically around the knee) as a bony projection capped by cartilage that points away from the adjacent joint. Malignant change to chondrosarcoma is rare (~1%), suggested by a cartilage cap thicker than 2 cm or renewed growth after skeletal maturity. Osteoid osteoma, enchondroma and giant cell tumour are all less common.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Bone Tumours (Benign Tumours)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 19-year-old man complains of well-localised bone pain that is worst at night and is dramatically relieved by aspirin or other NSAIDs. Radiograph shows a small (<1 cm) radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense reactive sclerosis in the femoral cortex. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Osteoid osteoma classically causes night pain relieved by NSAIDs because the nidus produces prostaglandins; the nidus is a small (<1 cm) radiolucent focus with surrounding reactive sclerosis, best localised on CT. Osteoblastoma is larger (>2 cm), favours the spine and has less night-pain/NSAID response. Brodie's abscess is subacute osteomyelitis, and a stress fracture shows a periosteal reaction along a stress line rather than a discrete nidus.
questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Bone Tumours

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The combination of multiple enchondromas with soft-tissue haemangiomas is known as:
questions.concept: Maffucci syndrome is multiple enchondromatosis plus soft-tissue haemangiomas, whereas Ollier disease is multiple enchondromatosis without haemangiomas; both carry an increased risk of malignant transformation to chondrosarcoma, higher in Maffucci. McCune-Albright is polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with café-au-lait spots and endocrinopathy, and Gardner syndrome combines colonic polyposis with osteomas and desmoid tumours.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Bone Tumours (Cartilaginous Tumours)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 16-year-old presents with knee pain. Radiograph shows a well-defined lytic lesion confined to the epiphysis of the proximal tibia with fine internal calcification, and the growth plate is still open. Biopsy shows chondroid cells with 'chicken-wire' calcification. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Chondroblastoma is a rare benign tumour arising in the epiphysis/apophysis of a skeletally immature patient (open physis), showing 'chicken-wire' calcification and S-100 positivity. Giant cell tumour is also epiphyseal but occurs after physeal closure in the mature skeleton. Chondromyxoid fibroma is metaphyseal, and osteosarcoma is an aggressive metaphyseal lesion with bone destruction and periosteal reaction, not a well-defined epiphyseal lesion.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics — Benign Bone Tumours

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Osteosarcoma most commonly arises at which anatomical location?
questions.concept: Osteosarcoma most commonly arises in the metaphysis of long bones around the knee (distal femur > proximal tibia), followed by the proximal humerus, typically in adolescents. Radiological hallmarks are sunburst/sunray spiculation and Codman's triangle from aggressive periosteal reaction. The diaphysis is the classic site of Ewing sarcoma, the epiphysis suggests chondroblastoma or giant cell tumour, and vertebral bodies are common sites for metastases and myeloma.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Malignant Bone Tumours (Osteosarcoma)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The characteristic cytogenetic translocation of Ewing sarcoma is:
questions.concept: Ewing sarcoma is defined by t(11;22)(q24;q12) producing the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion; it is a small round blue cell tumour that is CD99 (MIC2) positive with PAS-positive intracytoplasmic glycogen, arising in the diaphysis with an onion-skin (laminated) periosteal reaction. t(9;22) is the Philadelphia chromosome of CML/ALL, t(X;18) is seen in synovial sarcoma, and t(2;13) occurs in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — Bones and Joints (cross-referenced with Apley's)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has back pain, anaemia and a markedly raised ESR. Skull radiograph shows multiple well-defined 'punched-out' lytic lesions without a sclerotic rim, and urine contains Bence-Jones protein. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Multiple myeloma is a plasma-cell malignancy causing punched-out lytic lesions without a sclerotic rim, Bence-Jones (light-chain) proteinuria, an M-band, rouleaux formation, hypercalcaemia and renal failure; lesions are typically 'cold' on a technetium bone scan because there is no osteoblastic reaction. Prostatic metastases are characteristically osteoblastic, and hyperparathyroidism produces brown tumours and a salt-and-pepper skull rather than discrete punched-out lesions.
questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Bone Tumours (Myeloma)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The most common malignant tumour of bone overall is:
questions.concept: Metastatic carcinoma is by far the commonest malignant tumour of bone; the primaries are recalled by 'BLT-KP' — Breast, Lung, Thyroid, Kidney and Prostate — and they favour the axial (red-marrow) skeleton. Osteosarcoma is the commonest primary malignant bone tumour if myeloma is excluded. Most metastases are osteolytic, while prostate carcinoma is characteristically osteoblastic.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Metastatic Bone Tumours

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Which primary malignancy most characteristically produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases?
questions.concept: Prostate carcinoma classically causes osteoblastic (sclerotic) metastases, associated with a raised alkaline phosphatase and PSA, whereas breast cancer produces mixed lesions. Renal cell and thyroid carcinomas typically give expansile, vascular, osteolytic 'blow-out' metastases (which can be pulsatile), and lung carcinoma metastases are usually lytic. Recognising blastic versus lytic patterns helps direct the search for the primary tumour.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics — Metastatic Disease of Bone

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has distal femoral pain. Radiograph shows an eccentric, expansile 'soap-bubble' lytic lesion at the epiphysis extending up to the subchondral bone, with no surrounding sclerotic rim, and the growth plate is fused. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Giant cell tumour (osteoclastoma) is benign but locally aggressive, occurring in the mature skeleton (after physeal closure, typically 20-40 years) at the epi-metaphyseal region extending to subchondral bone; it shows an eccentric lytic 'soap-bubble' appearance without a sclerotic margin. It has a high local recurrence after curettage and rarely gives benign lung metastases. Campanacci grading describes its radiological aggressiveness; ABC shows fluid-fluid levels and osteosarcoma shows aggressive bone destruction.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Giant Cell Tumour

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Fluid-fluid levels on MRI within an expansile, eccentric metaphyseal lytic lesion in an adolescent are most characteristic of:
questions.concept: An aneurysmal bone cyst contains blood-filled spaces that produce fluid-fluid levels on MRI/CT due to sedimentation; it is an eccentric, expansile 'blown-out' metaphyseal lesion in patients under 20 and may be secondary to other lesions such as GCT, chondroblastoma or osteosarcoma. A simple bone cyst is centrally located, an enchondroma shows chondroid calcification, and osteoid osteoma has a sclerotic nidus. Because telangiectatic osteosarcoma can also show fluid-fluid levels, biopsy is still needed.
questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Cystic Lesions of Bone

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy sustains a pathological fracture through a well-defined central lytic lesion in the proximal humeral metaphysis. A small bony fragment is seen lying within the lesion (the 'fallen fragment sign'). The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: A unicameral (simple) bone cyst is a fluid-filled cavity that is centrally located in the proximal humeral or femoral metaphysis in children and often presents as a pathological fracture; the 'fallen fragment/leaf sign' — a cortical fragment sinking to the dependent part of the fluid-filled cyst — is pathognomonic. An aneurysmal bone cyst is eccentric with fluid-fluid levels, and treatment of a simple cyst is by aspiration and steroid injection or curettage with bone grafting.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Simple Bone Cyst

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A young girl has precocious puberty, café-au-lait macules with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders, and a ground-glass lytic lesion of the proximal femur producing a 'shepherd's crook' deformity. This constellation is best described as:
questions.concept: McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders and endocrinopathy (classically precocious puberty), caused by a post-zygotic GNAS1 mutation. Fibrous dysplasia gives a ground-glass appearance and a 'shepherd's crook' (coxa vara) deformity of the proximal femur. Neurofibromatosis type 1 has smooth 'coast of California' café-au-lait spots with neurofibromas, distinguishing it from this presentation.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics — Fibrous Dysplasia

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: An asymptomatic, well-defined eccentric metaphyseal lucent lesion with a sclerotic scalloped margin, found incidentally in a child and usually regressing spontaneously, is:
questions.concept: Non-ossifying fibroma (fibroxanthoma), when small and cortex-based, is called a fibrous cortical defect; it is a very common, asymptomatic, incidental eccentric metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic scalloped border in children and adolescents, and it typically ossifies and regresses spontaneously. It is a 'leave-me-alone/do-not-touch' lesion needing no treatment unless it is large and threatens pathological fracture. Chondrosarcoma and osteosarcoma are aggressive, and Brodie's abscess is subacute osteomyelitis.
questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Fibrous Lesions of Bone

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Which statement about chondrosarcoma is correct?
options: It typically affects children under 10 years of age
It is largely radio- and chemo-resistant and is treated by wide surgical excision
It arises most often in the small bones of the hand
Codman's triangle and sunburst spiculation are its radiological hallmarks
questions.concept: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilage-forming tumour of older adults (40-60 years) affecting axial and flat bones such as the pelvis, proximal femur, ribs and shoulder girdle; it is relatively radio- and chemo-resistant, so wide en-bloc surgical excision is the mainstay of treatment. It is not a childhood tumour, enchondromas of the small hand bones rarely turn malignant, and sunburst/Codman's triangle are features of osteosarcoma rather than chondrosarcoma.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Chondrosarcoma

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Which of the following is a fundamental principle of bone-tumour biopsy?
options: Excisional biopsy is preferred for all suspected malignant tumours
Biopsy should always precede clinical and radiological assessment
The biopsy tract should be placed transversely, away from the definitive resection plane
The biopsy tract must be placed so that it can be excised en-bloc with the definitive resection
questions.concept: Biopsy is the last step, performed after clinical evaluation and imaging and ideally at the definitive treating centre; the tract must be longitudinal and positioned so it can be removed en-bloc with the tumour at definitive surgery, because a poorly placed or transverse tract seeds tumour and can convert a limb-salvage case into an amputation. For suspected malignancy, incisional or core-needle biopsy is preferred over excisional biopsy. Enneking's surgical staging uses grade, site/compartment and metastasis.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics — Principles of Tumour Biopsy and Enneking Staging

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: The deformities of congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV) are remembered by the mnemonic 'CAVE'. Which of the following is NOT a component of CTEV?
questions.concept: The four components of clubfoot (CTEV) are given by CAVE: Cavus of the midfoot, Adductus of the forefoot, Varus of the hindfoot and Equinus of the ankle. The hindfoot in CTEV is in VARUS, not valgus, so hindfoot valgus is not a component. In the Ponseti sequence the cavus is corrected first and the hindfoot varus and equinus are corrected last, equinus often requiring a tendo-Achilles tenotomy.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: In the Ponseti method for idiopathic clubfoot, after serial weekly manipulation and casting the residual ankle equinus is most often corrected by:
questions.concept: In the Ponseti technique, serial manipulation and casting correct the cavus, then adductus, then varus; a tight tendo-Achilles causing residual equinus is corrected by a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy in roughly 80-90% of cases, after which a foot-abduction (Denis Browne) brace is worn to prevent relapse. Extensive posteromedial soft-tissue release is now largely avoided because it causes stiffness, while triple arthrodesis and tendon transfers are reserved for older or relapsed feet.
