questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Clubfoot (Ponseti Method)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Idiopathic CTEV generally responds better to Ponseti casting than syndromic clubfoot. Reason (R): Syndromic clubfoot, as in arthrogryposis and myelomeningocele, is rigid, more resistant to correction and has a higher relapse rate. Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Idiopathic clubfoot is supple and responds well to Ponseti casting, whereas syndromic or teratologic clubfoot associated with arthrogryposis, spina bifida/myelomeningocele or diastrophic dysplasia is rigid, resistant to correction and relapses more often, frequently requiring surgery. Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the rigidity/resistance described in the reason is precisely why syndromic feet respond less well, so R correctly explains A.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics — Congenital Clubfoot (Idiopathic vs Syndromic)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: During newborn hip screening, the examiner adducts the flexed hip and applies a posteriorly directed force, feeling the femoral head slip out of the acetabulum. This provocative manoeuvre is the:
questions.concept: The Barlow test is the provocative (dislocating) test: the flexed hip is adducted and pushed posteriorly, and a dislocatable head is felt to slip out of the acetabulum. The Ortolani test is the reduction test, in which abduction with an anterior lift relocates an already-dislocated hip with a palpable clunk. The Galeazzi sign detects unequal knee heights from femoral shortening/dislocation, and the Thomas test assesses a fixed flexion deformity of the hip.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (Clinical Tests)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: For diagnosing developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in an infant younger than 6 months, the investigation of choice is:
questions.concept: Before about 4-6 months the femoral head is largely cartilaginous and its ossific nucleus has not appeared, so plain radiographs are unreliable; ultrasonography (Graf's method, using alpha and beta angles) is the imaging modality of choice and allows dynamic assessment. After roughly 6 months, once the ossific nucleus appears, plain radiographs become useful using Hilgenreiner's and Perkin's lines, Shenton's line and the acetabular index. CT/MRI are reserved for complex or post-reduction assessment.
questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (Imaging)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a painless limp. Examination shows a positive Trendelenburg sign, limb shortening and an extra thigh skin crease, and neglected unilateral DDH is diagnosed. The most appropriate management is:
options: Open reduction with femoral and/or pelvic osteotomy
Closed reduction with a hip spica cast alone
questions.concept: A Pavlik harness is effective only in early infancy (younger than about 6 months); in a walking child with neglected/established DDH, closed reduction usually fails, so open reduction combined with femoral shortening-derotation and/or a pelvic osteotomy (Salter or Pemberton) is required to achieve and maintain a concentric, stable hip. A positive Trendelenburg sign reflects abductor (gluteus medius) insufficiency because the dislocated head loses its normal fulcrum. Simple observation would leave the hip dysplastic and painful.
questions.reference: Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (Late Presentation)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Achondroplasia, the commonest form of short-limb (rhizomelic) dwarfism, is caused by a mutation in which gene?
questions.concept: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant condition (most cases arising from new mutations, with a paternal age effect) caused by a gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3 that impairs endochondral ossification, producing rhizomelic (proximal) limb shortening, a trident hand, frontal bossing, spinal canal stenosis, but a normal trunk and normal intelligence. COL1A1 mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta, FBN1 causes Marfan syndrome, and GNAS1 is implicated in fibrous dysplasia/McCune-Albright syndrome.
questions.reference: Maheshwari's Essential Orthopaedics — Skeletal Dysplasias (Achondroplasia)

questions.subject: Orthopedics
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Osteogenesis imperfecta classically presents with recurrent fractures and blue sclerae. Reason (R): It results from a qualitative or quantitative defect in type I collagen. Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Osteogenesis imperfecta ('brittle bone disease') arises from defective type I collagen (COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations), producing fragile bones with recurrent low-trauma fractures, blue sclerae (thin sclera revealing the underlying choroid), dentinogenesis imperfecta, conductive hearing loss, ligamentous laxity and wormian bones in the skull. Both the assertion and the reason are true, and the type I collagen defect directly explains both the fragility and the blue sclerae, so R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.reference: Apley's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures — Osteogenesis Imperfecta

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A pleural fluid aspirate has a specific gravity of 1.025, a high protein content (fluid/serum protein ratio greater than 0.5) and abundant inflammatory cells. This fluid is best classified as:
questions.concept: An exudate is a protein-rich, cell-rich extravascular fluid with specific gravity above 1.020 (and a high LDH); it results from increased vascular permeability during inflammation. A transudate is a protein-poor ultrafiltrate (specific gravity below 1.012) produced by hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance, as in heart failure or hypoalbuminaemia, with few cells. Lymph and chyle differ in origin; chyle is milky and triglyceride-rich from lymphatic disruption. The high protein and cellularity here define an exudate.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The initial, transient, low-affinity interaction (rolling) of neutrophils along activated venular endothelium in acute inflammation is mediated chiefly by which class of molecules?
options: Selectins binding sialylated oligosaccharides such as sialyl-Lewis X
questions.concept: Rolling is mediated by selectins: E-selectin on endothelium (induced by TNF and IL-1), P-selectin from Weibel-Palade bodies (redistributed by histamine and thrombin) and leukocyte L-selectin, which bind sialyl-Lewis X-containing glycoproteins. Firm adhesion is a later step mediated by leukocyte integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) whose affinity is upregulated by chemokines, binding endothelial ICAM-1 and VCAM-1. Transmigration (diapedesis) uses PECAM-1 (CD31). Cadherins hold cells together at junctions and are not recruitment molecules.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The four classic cardinal signs of acute inflammation are rubor, tumor, calor and dolor. The fifth sign, added later by Virchow, is:
questions.concept: Celsus described four cardinal signs: rubor (redness, from vasodilation and increased blood flow), tumor (swelling, from exudate and oedema), calor (heat, from increased blood flow) and dolor (pain). Virchow added functio laesa, loss of function of the inflamed part. Redness and heat are driven by vasodilator mediators such as histamine, prostaglandins and nitric oxide; pain is produced by bradykinin and prostaglandin E2 sensitizing nerve endings, plus mechanical pressure from the exudate.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed. — Chapter 6: Inflammation and Healing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Accumulation of thin, protein-poor, cell-poor fluid such as that within a burn blister or a mild viral pleural effusion is characteristic of which morphologic pattern of acute inflammation?
questions.concept: Serous inflammation is an outpouring of watery, low-protein fluid derived from plasma or from serosal mesothelial cell secretion, as seen in a skin blister or mild body-cavity effusion. Fibrinous inflammation occurs with greater vascular permeability, allowing large fibrinogen molecules to escape and polymerize into fibrin, typically on serosal surfaces such as the pericardium. Suppurative inflammation produces pus (neutrophils and liquefactive necrosis), and pseudomembranous inflammation forms a necroinflammatory membrane.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Phagocytosis of a bacterium is greatly enhanced when the microbe is coated by opsonins. Which of the following acts as a major opsonin?
questions.concept: The principal opsonins are C3b (and its cleavage product iC3b) from complement, the Fc portion of IgG antibody, and plasma lectins such as mannose-binding lectin; they coat microbes and bind leukocyte receptors (complement receptors CR1/CR3 and Fc-gamma receptors) to promote engulfment. C5a is a potent chemoattractant and anaphylatoxin, not an opsonin. Histamine mediates early vasodilation and increased permeability. Leukotriene B4 is a strong neutrophil chemoattractant and activator but does not opsonize.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A neonate has delayed separation of the umbilical cord (beyond 30 days), recurrent bacterial skin and mucosal infections without formation of pus, and a markedly elevated peripheral neutrophil count. The most likely underlying defect is:
options: Deficiency of the beta-2 integrin subunit (CD18) impairing firm leukocyte adhesion
Deficiency of NADPH oxidase impairing the respiratory burst
questions.concept: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 arises from mutation of the beta-2 integrin subunit CD18 (shared by LFA-1 and Mac-1), so neutrophils cannot firmly adhere to ICAM-1 or transmigrate. The result is recurrent infections with no pus despite blood neutrophilia, and delayed umbilical cord separation. NADPH oxidase deficiency is chronic granulomatous disease (a killing defect). Defective phagolysosome fusion is Chediak-Higashi. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is usually mild. LAD type 2 instead affects the selectin ligand sialyl-Lewis X.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Among complement fragments generated during activation, which one is BOTH a potent anaphylatoxin AND the most powerful complement-derived neutrophil chemoattractant?
questions.concept: C5a is the most potent complement-derived chemoattractant and a strong anaphylatoxin: it triggers mast-cell histamine release, increases vascular permeability, and activates neutrophil adhesion and the oxidative burst. C3a and C4a are anaphylatoxins but are weaker and are not chemotactic. C3b and iC3b are opsonins. C5b-9 assembles into the membrane attack complex, a lytic transmembrane pore. C1q initiates the classical pathway by binding antigen-antibody complexes.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Within minutes of a bee sting, the affected skin becomes red, swollen and warm. The mediator responsible for this immediate, transient increase in venular permeability, released chiefly from mast cells, is:
questions.concept: Histamine is stored preformed in mast cell granules (and in basophils and platelets) and is released on degranulation triggered by IgE cross-linking, C3a/C5a or physical stimuli. It mediates the immediate transient phase of increased permeability by causing endothelial cell contraction in postcapillary venules, along with arteriolar vasodilation. Bradykinin produces pain and permeability but via the slower kinin cascade. The cysteinyl leukotrienes C4/D4/E4 cause a more sustained permeability increase. IL-1 is a cytokine mediating endothelial activation and the systemic acute-phase response, not immediate permeability.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed. — Chapter 6: Inflammation and Healing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease develops bronchospasm after taking aspirin, because cyclooxygenase inhibition shunts arachidonic acid toward the lipoxygenase pathway. Which drug directly inhibits the 5-lipoxygenase ENZYME (rather than the leukotriene receptor)?
questions.concept: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase, blocking synthesis of all leukotrienes (LTB4 and the cysteinyl leukotrienes C4/D4/E4). Montelukast and zafirlukast antagonize the cysteinyl-leukotriene receptor CysLT1 rather than the enzyme. Aspirin and celecoxib inhibit cyclooxygenase: aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2, whereas celecoxib is COX-2 selective. In aspirin sensitivity, COX blockade diverts arachidonate into the lipoxygenase pathway, increasing bronchoconstrictor leukotrienes and precipitating bronchospasm.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics develops profuse diarrhoea; colonoscopy shows adherent yellow-white plaques composed of fibrin, mucus, necrotic epithelium and neutrophils overlying an ulcerated mucosa. This pattern of inflammation is termed:
questions.concept: Pseudomembranous inflammation is a superficial necroinflammatory membrane of fibrin, sloughed necrotic epithelium, mucus and inflammatory cells overlying an ulcerated surface. The classic cause is Clostridioides difficile colitis (toxins A and B) after antibiotic use, and Corynebacterium diphtheriae in the pharynx. Serous inflammation is thin effusion; granulomatous inflammation is a chronic pattern with epithelioid macrophages; fibrinoid necrosis is a bright eosinophilic vessel-wall change in vasculitis and malignant hypertension, not a mucosal membrane.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A localized, walled-off collection of pus within a tissue, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, is best described as:
questions.concept: An abscess is a focal collection of purulent exudate (neutrophils, liquefied necrotic cells and oedema fluid) walled off within a tissue, typically produced by pyogenic organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. The centre undergoes liquefactive necrosis and may be surrounded by preserved neutrophils, granulation tissue and fibrosis forming a pyogenic membrane. An ulcer is a local excavation of an epithelial surface from sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue. A serous effusion is thin fluid, and a granuloma is an organized collection of epithelioid macrophages characteristic of chronic inflammation.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed. — Chapter 6: Inflammation and Healing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which growth factor is the principal driver of angiogenesis (formation of new capillaries) during the development of granulation tissue in wound healing?
questions.concept: VEGF (particularly VEGF-A) is the key promoter of angiogenesis: it stimulates endothelial proliferation and migration and increases vascular permeability, and is upregulated by hypoxia through HIF-1-alpha. TGF-beta is the dominant fibrogenic cytokine, stimulating fibroblast synthesis of collagen and fibronectin while suppressing matrix degradation, thereby driving scar formation, and it is also anti-inflammatory. PDGF recruits and activates fibroblasts and smooth muscle and contributes to angiogenesis but is not the principal endothelial mitogen. EGF stimulates epithelial and fibroblast proliferation.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: By the end of the remodeling phase (about 3 months), approximately what proportion of the original unwounded tensile strength does a sutured skin wound typically recover?
questions.concept: Wound tensile strength is only about 10% of normal at 1 week, when the wound is held largely by sutures; it then rises rapidly over the next 4 weeks and slows, reaching a plateau of roughly 70 to 80% of unwounded skin by about 3 months, and it essentially never regains full 100% strength. This recovery reflects not only collagen accumulation but remodeling: replacement of the initial type III collagen by stronger cross-linked type I collagen, mediated by matrix metalloproteinases and lysyl oxidase cross-linking.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A dark-skinned patient develops a raised, firm scar at the site of an ear piercing that extends well beyond the original wound margins and recurs after excision. This lesion is best described as:
questions.concept: A keloid is exuberant scar tissue with excess collagen (predominantly type III, later type I) that grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound, does not regress, and tends to recur after excision; it is more frequent in darker-skinned individuals with a genetic predisposition. A hypertrophic scar is also raised but remains confined within the wound margins and may regress with time. Contracture is exaggerated wound shrinkage driven by myofibroblasts, limiting movement across joints or after burns. Wound dehiscence is mechanical rupture of a wound.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed. — Chapter 6: Inflammation and Healing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Alternatively activated (M2) macrophages, induced by interleukins 4 and 13, differ from classically activated (M1) macrophages chiefly in that M2 macrophages predominantly:
options: Produce nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species to kill microbes
Promote tissue repair, angiogenesis and fibrosis with anti-inflammatory IL-10 and TGF-beta
Are activated by interferon-gamma and microbial lipopolysaccharide
Secrete IL-12 to drive Th1 differentiation
questions.concept: M1 (classically activated) macrophages are induced by interferon-gamma from Th1 and NK cells and by microbial products such as LPS acting through Toll-like receptors; they secrete IL-1, IL-12 and TNF, generate reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide, and are microbicidal and pro-inflammatory. M2 (alternatively activated) macrophages are induced by IL-4 and IL-13 from Th2 cells; they secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta, dampen inflammation, and promote tissue repair, angiogenesis and fibrosis. The M1-to-M2 shift helps terminate inflammation and begin healing.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Histologically, granulation tissue is characterized by which combination of components?
options: Epithelioid macrophages and multinucleate giant cells
Central caseous necrosis rimmed by lymphocytes
Proliferating fibroblasts and new thin-walled capillaries (neovascularization)
Sheets of neutrophils within liquefied tissue
questions.concept: Granulation tissue, the hallmark of tissue repair, consists of proliferating fibroblasts laying down loose connective tissue together with new leaky capillaries formed by angiogenesis, plus scattered macrophages and other inflammatory cells, giving a soft, pink, granular appearance. It must not be confused with a granuloma, which is an aggregate of epithelioid macrophages with or without giant cells seen in granulomatous inflammation, nor with caseating tuberculous granulomas or suppurative (pus-filled) inflammation. Over time granulation tissue matures into a fibrous collagenous scar.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed. — Chapter 6: Inflammation and Healing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A peripheral blood differential showing a marked absolute eosinophilia is MOST classically associated with which of the following?
options: Helminthic parasitic infestation and type-I hypersensitivity or allergy
questions.concept: Eosinophilia is characteristic of helminthic parasitic infections and of IgE-mediated allergic and atopic disorders such as asthma, hay fever and drug reactions, driven largely by IL-5. Acute pyogenic bacterial infection typically causes neutrophilic leukocytosis with a left shift toward immature band forms. Most acute viral infections produce lymphocytosis. Typhoid fever (Salmonella), some other viral infections and overwhelming sepsis characteristically cause leukopenia or neutropenia. Recognizing these leukocyte response patterns aids differential diagnosis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child with partial oculocutaneous albinism, recurrent pyogenic infections, mild bleeding tendency and peripheral neuropathy has neutrophils containing giant cytoplasmic granules on a blood smear. The underlying defect is in:
options: The lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST), impairing phagolysosome fusion
questions.concept: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal-recessive defect in the LYST (lysosomal trafficking regulator) gene, causing defective fusion of lysosomes and granules with phagosomes. This produces giant abnormal granules in leukocytes and other cells, impaired bacterial killing with recurrent pyogenic infections, partial albinism from a melanosome defect, a bleeding tendency from a platelet dense-granule defect, and neurological abnormalities. NADPH oxidase deficiency is chronic granulomatous disease and CD18 deficiency is LAD-1; neither produces giant granules or albinism, and C3 deficiency causes pyogenic infection without these features.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A boy has recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus, Serratia, Burkholderia) and forms granulomas; a dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow-cytometry test is abnormal. The defective process is:
options: Generation of the respiratory (oxidative) burst by NADPH oxidase
questions.concept: Chronic granulomatous disease results from mutations in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex (most often X-linked gp91phox, encoded by CYBB), so phagocytes cannot generate superoxide and hydrogen peroxide for oxygen-dependent killing. Patients suffer recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms, which destroy their own hydrogen peroxide and thereby deny the phagocyte a borrowed microbial substrate, and they form granulomas. Diagnosis rests on an abnormal dihydrorhodamine-123 oxidation test or nitroblue tetrazolium test. Selectin, LYST and antibody defects are unrelated to the oxidative burst.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Regarding eicosanoids derived from arachidonic acid, which pairing of mediator with its predominant vascular and platelet action is CORRECT?
options: Thromboxane A2 causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation
Prostacyclin (PGI2) causes vasoconstriction and promotes platelet aggregation
Thromboxane A2 causes vasoconstriction and promotes platelet aggregation
Leukotriene B4 is a potent vasodilator
questions.concept: Thromboxane A2, produced by platelets via cyclooxygenase and thromboxane synthase, causes vasoconstriction and promotes platelet aggregation. Prostacyclin (PGI2), produced by endothelium, has the opposite effect, causing vasodilation and inhibiting platelet aggregation; the TXA2/PGI2 balance regulates haemostasis and vascular tone. Prostaglandins E2, D2 and I2 are vasodilators that also potentiate oedema, pain and fever. Leukotriene B4 is a potent chemoattractant and neutrophil activator rather than a vasodilator, while the cysteinyl leukotrienes C4/D4/E4 cause vasoconstriction, bronchospasm and increased permeability.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Following injury, which of the following cell types is PERMANENT (terminally differentiated and non-dividing) and therefore heals predominantly by scar rather than by regeneration?
questions.concept: Cells are classified by proliferative capacity. Labile cells divide continuously and regenerate readily (surface epithelia of gut and skin, and bone marrow). Stable or quiescent cells rest in G0 but divide when stimulated (hepatocytes, renal tubular epithelium, endothelium and fibroblasts) and regenerate after injury. Permanent cells are terminally differentiated and non-dividing (neurons, cardiac myocytes and skeletal muscle); consequently a myocardial infarct heals by fibrous scar rather than muscle regeneration. Skeletal muscle shows only limited regeneration via satellite cells.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: During scar maturation the initially deposited type III collagen is progressively replaced by type I collagen. The enzymes primarily responsible for degrading old collagen during this remodeling are:
questions.concept: Extracellular matrix remodeling depends on matrix metalloproteinases (collagenases, gelatinases and stromelysins), zinc-dependent enzymes secreted by fibroblasts, macrophages and neutrophils, whose activity is restrained by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). They degrade type III collagen so it can be replaced by cross-linked type I collagen, increasing tensile strength. Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent enzyme that cross-links collagen; prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases require vitamin C to hydroxylate procollagen; myeloperoxidase is a microbicidal enzyme of neutrophils, not a collagenase.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: During the systemic acute-phase response driven mainly by interleukin-6, plasma levels of most acute-phase proteins rise. Which plasma protein instead DECREASES (a negative acute-phase reactant)?
questions.concept: Positive acute-phase reactants, whose hepatic synthesis rises under IL-6 (with IL-1 and TNF), include C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A, fibrinogen, hepcidin, haptoglobin, ferritin and complement components. Elevated fibrinogen makes red cells form rouleaux, raising the erythrocyte sedimentation rate; hepcidin sequesters iron and causes the anaemia of chronic disease. Albumin and transferrin are negative acute-phase reactants, whose hepatic synthesis falls during inflammation, contributing to the hypoalbuminaemia seen in chronic illness.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The pathway by which bacterial lipopolysaccharide produces fever culminates in which final mediator acting on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centre?
options: Interleukin-1 acting directly on skeletal muscle
questions.concept: Exogenous pyrogens such as LPS stimulate leukocytes to release endogenous pyrogens (IL-1, IL-6 and TNF), which act on the hypothalamus, especially the preoptic area and organum vasculosum, to induce cyclooxygenase and raise prostaglandin E2. PGE2 resets the hypothalamic thermostat to a higher set-point, producing fever. Antipyretics such as aspirin and other NSAIDs reduce fever precisely by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and thus PGE2 synthesis. Bradykinin and histamine mediate vascular permeability and pain rather than the febrile set-point.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Chapter 3: Inflammation and Repair

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which pairing of a multinucleate giant cell type with its characteristic setting is CORRECT?
options: Langhans giant cell has nuclei scattered randomly throughout the cytoplasm
Aschoff giant cell is characteristically seen in foreign-body reactions
Foreign-body giant cell has nuclei arranged in a peripheral horseshoe
Touton giant cell has a ring of nuclei surrounding central foamy lipid-rich cytoplasm and is seen in xanthomas
questions.concept: Touton giant cells have a wreath or ring of nuclei encircling central lipid-laden foamy cytoplasm, typical of xanthomas, fat necrosis and xanthogranulomas. Langhans giant cells have nuclei arranged peripherally in a horseshoe or ring pattern, classic of tuberculosis and other granulomas. Foreign-body giant cells have nuclei scattered haphazardly and engulf foreign material. Aschoff giant cells (derived from Anitschkow cells) are found in the Aschoff bodies of rheumatic carditis, not in foreign-body reactions, making option D the only correct pairing.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed. — Chapter 6: Inflammation and Healing

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with new-onset seizures. MRI shows a well-defined, calcified mass in the left frontal cortex. Biopsy reveals sheets of uniform cells with round nuclei surrounded by clear perinuclear halos ('fried-egg' appearance) and a delicate branching ('chicken-wire') capillary network. Which molecular finding in this tumour predicts the best response to chemotherapy?
questions.concept: Oligodendroglioma classically shows 'fried-egg' cells (perinuclear halo, a formalin-fixation artefact), delicate 'chicken-wire' vasculature, and dystrophic calcification, often frontal with seizures. Combined 1p/19q codeletion (with IDH mutation) defines the tumour and predicts favourable chemosensitivity (PCV/temozolomide) and prognosis. EGFR amplification typifies primary glioblastoma; 22q deletion is seen in meningioma/schwannoma; and it is retention/gain of MGMT methylation, not its loss, that favours temozolomide response.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Gliomas: Oligodendroglioma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old child presents with headache, vomiting and ataxia due to obstructive hydrocephalus. A tumour is found filling the fourth ventricle. Histology shows tumour cells arranged around blood vessels with nucleus-free zones of fibrillary processes radiating toward the vessel wall. What is the characteristic histologic structure described?
questions.concept: Ependymomas in children arise most often in the fourth ventricle, causing obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus, and characteristically form perivascular pseudorosettes — tumour cells radiating GFAP-positive processes toward a central vessel, creating an anuclear perivascular zone; true ependymal rosettes/canals are less common. Homer-Wright rosettes (neuroblastic, around neuropil) occur in medulloblastoma/neuroblastoma; Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (true central lumen) in retinoblastoma; Verocay bodies in schwannoma.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Ependymoma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl has a several-month history of clumsiness and morning headaches. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule. Histology shows a biphasic pattern of loose and compact areas with bipolar 'hair-like' cells and brightly eosinophilic, corkscrew-shaped condensations. These eosinophilic structures are known as:
questions.concept: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common glioma of childhood, typically a cystic cerebellar mass with a mural nodule and an indolent WHO grade 1 course. Its hallmark is Rosenthal fibres — thick, eosinophilic, corkscrew-like condensations of GFAP — alongside eosinophilic granular bodies and a biphasic loose/compact architecture; BRAF fusion (KIAA1549-BRAF) is common. Psammoma bodies occur in meningioma, Negri bodies in rabies-infected neurons, and Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Pilocytic astrocytoma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy develops truncal ataxia and signs of raised intracranial pressure. Imaging shows a midline cerebellar (vermian) mass. Histology reveals sheets of small round blue cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, some arranged around a central tangle of neuropil. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Medulloblastoma is a highly malignant WHO grade 4 embryonal tumour of the cerebellar vermis in young children, composed of small round blue cells (high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio) forming Homer-Wright (neuroblastic) rosettes around central neuropil. It disseminates through CSF as 'drop metastases' down the neuraxis. Ependymoma forms perivascular pseudorosettes; pilocytic astrocytoma is cystic with Rosenthal fibres and benign; hemangioblastoma is a vascular tumour of adults with foamy stromal cells.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Embryonal/Medulloblastoma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with advanced untreated HIV (CD4 count 40/µL) presents with confusion and focal deficits. MRI shows a periventricular enhancing lesion. CSF and tumour tissue are positive for Epstein-Barr virus, and biopsy shows sheets of atypical lymphoid cells cuffing blood vessels. The most likely diagnosis and cell of origin are:
options: Primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
questions.concept: Primary CNS lymphoma is the most common CNS neoplasm in immunocompromised (especially AIDS) patients and is almost always an EBV-driven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It is typically periventricular/deep and multifocal and shows angiocentric growth — malignant cells cuffing vessels. It is aggressive but steroid-responsive (a 'ghost tumour' that can transiently vanish on steroids). T-lymphoblastic and Hodgkin lymphomas rarely involve the CNS primarily, and sporadic Burkitt is not the classic EBV-associated CNS lymphoma.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Primary CNS lymphoma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and infertility. Serum prolactin is markedly elevated and MRI shows a pituitary microadenoma. This is the most common type of hyperfunctioning pituitary adenoma. From which cell type does it arise?
questions.concept: Prolactinoma (lactotroph adenoma) is the most common functioning pituitary adenoma. Prolactin excess causes amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido and infertility in women, allowing early detection as microadenomas; men present later with mass effects. Dopamine agonists (cabergoline/bromocriptine) shrink them. Corticotroph adenomas cause Cushing disease, somatotroph adenomas cause acromegaly/gigantism, and gonadotroph adenomas are usually clinically silent, presenting via mass effect.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Endocrine System (Pituitary adenomas)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man reports difficulty seeing objects to either side and repeated collisions with door frames. Perimetry confirms a bitemporal hemianopia, and MRI shows a sellar/suprasellar mass. Compression of which structure produces this visual field defect?
options: Meyer loop in the temporal lobe
questions.concept: A pituitary macroadenoma expanding out of the sella compresses the overlying optic chiasm, where fibres from the nasal halves of both retinas (carrying the temporal visual fields) decussate; interrupting them produces bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract lesions cause a contralateral homonymous hemianopia; Meyer loop (temporal) damage gives a 'pie-in-the-sky' superior quadrantanopia; and occipital cortex lesions cause homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Endocrine System (Pituitary mass effects)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma suddenly develops a severe ('thunderclap') headache, ophthalmoplegia, acute visual loss and hypotension, and is found to have acute cortisol deficiency. Which process best explains this emergency?
options: Ischaemic infarction of the postpartum pituitary (Sheehan syndrome)
Craniopharyngioma cyst rupture spilling motor-oil fluid
Acute haemorrhage/infarction into the pituitary adenoma (pituitary apoplexy)
questions.concept: Pituitary apoplexy is sudden haemorrhage or infarction into a (usually pre-existing) pituitary adenoma, causing thunderclap headache, ophthalmoplegia (cavernous sinus cranial nerves), acute visual loss and life-threatening secondary adrenal insufficiency that requires urgent glucocorticoids. Sheehan syndrome is postpartum ischaemic pituitary necrosis with a gradual course; lymphocytic hypophysitis is autoimmune and subacute; and craniopharyngioma fluid is characteristic but does not cause this acute apoplectic syndrome.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Endocrine System (Pituitary apoplexy/hypopituitarism)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy has growth failure and a bitemporal field defect. CT shows a partly cystic, calcified suprasellar mass. At surgery the cyst contains dark, viscous 'machinery-oil' fluid, and histology shows stratified squamous epithelium with peripheral palisading and nodules of 'wet' keratin. This tumour arises from remnants of:
questions.concept: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma is a childhood suprasellar tumour derived from Rathke pouch (oral ectoderm) remnants (CTNNB1/Wnt pathway). It is classically cystic and calcified, contains cholesterol-rich brownish 'motor-oil' fluid, and shows adamantinomatous epithelium with peripheral palisading, stellate reticulum and nodules of 'wet' keratin. Notochord remnants give chordoma, arachnoid cap cells give meningioma, and neural crest gives schwannoma/melanoma — none produce this classic picture.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Craniopharyngioma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A well-circumscribed, encapsulated tumour is resected from a peripheral nerve. Histology shows two patterns: compact cellular areas with spindle cells whose nuclei align in parallel rows around anuclear zones, and looser, myxoid, hypocellular areas. The tumour is strongly and diffusely S100-positive. What are the palisaded nuclear rows called?
questions.concept: Schwannoma is an encapsulated, uniformly S100-positive nerve sheath tumour with two zones: Antoni A (compact, cellular) containing Verocay bodies — two parallel rows of palisaded nuclei separated by anuclear cytoplasmic zones — and Antoni B (loose, myxoid, hypocellular). It grows eccentrically, displacing rather than engulfing the parent nerve. Call-Exner bodies occur in granulosa cell tumours, Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes, and Russell bodies are immunoglobulin-stuffed plasma cells.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Peripheral Nerves (Schwannoma; Antoni A/B, Verocay bodies)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Two peripheral nerve sheath tumours are compared. Tumour X is encapsulated, grows eccentrically and can be shelled off the nerve. Tumour Y is unencapsulated, infiltrates and expands the nerve so that axons run through it, and in its plexiform form is essentially pathognomonic of a phakomatosis. Which statement is correct?
options: Tumour X is a neurofibroma associated with neurofibromatosis type 2
Tumour Y is a neurofibroma, and its plexiform form is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1
Tumour Y is a schwannoma and is uniformly S100-positive throughout
Tumour X undergoes malignant transformation far more often than tumour Y
questions.concept: Schwannoma (tumour X) is encapsulated, arises eccentrically and can be separated from the nerve, sparing axons. Neurofibroma (tumour Y) is unencapsulated and intermixes with the nerve so axons traverse it; the plexiform variant is essentially pathognomonic of NF1 and carries a real risk of transformation to malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST). Neurofibroma is a mixed cell population (only partly S100-positive), unlike the uniformly S100-positive schwannoma, and NF2 is linked to schwannomas/meningiomas, not neurofibromas.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — Peripheral Nerves (Neurofibroma vs Schwannoma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presents with cerebellar signs and is found to have a raised haematocrit. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule; histology shows abundant thin-walled capillaries and interspersed vacuolated, lipid-laden stromal cells. He also has retinal angiomas and renal cysts. What best explains his elevated haematocrit?
options: Occult gastrointestinal bleeding causing a reactive change
Ectopic erythropoietin production by the tumour stromal cells
questions.concept: Cerebellar hemangioblastoma, part of von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL tumour suppressor, chromosome 3p), is a highly vascular tumour of thin-walled vessels and lipid-rich stromal cells (the neoplastic element). The stromal cells can secrete erythropoietin, producing secondary polycythaemia (raised haematocrit). VHL also features retinal/CNS hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and renal/pancreatic cysts. Compression hypoxia, GI bleeding and ectopic ACTH do not explain this classic EPO-driven erythrocytosis.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Hemangioblastoma; VHL)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 62-year-old smoker presents with headache and seizures. MRI shows multiple well-circumscribed enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction surrounded by extensive oedema. Regarding intracranial tumours in adults, which statement is correct?
options: Metastases are the most common intracranial tumours overall
Glioblastoma is the most common intracranial tumour overall
Meningioma is the most common intracranial tumour overall
Primary CNS lymphoma is the most common intracranial tumour overall
questions.concept: Metastatic tumours account for roughly half of all intracranial tumours and are the most common CNS neoplasm overall in adults. They are typically multiple, sharply demarcated and lodge at the grey-white junction, where the abrupt change in vessel calibre traps tumour emboli, and they provoke prominent surrounding vasogenic oedema. Glioblastoma and meningioma are the most common primary malignant and primary benign tumours respectively, but metastases outnumber all primary tumours combined.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Metastatic tumours)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which primary malignancy is the single most common source of brain metastases in adults?
questions.concept: Lung carcinoma is the most common source of brain metastases overall, followed by breast carcinoma, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and gastrointestinal (colorectal) cancers. Melanoma has the highest per-tumour propensity to spread to the brain and characteristically bleeds. Prostate, ovarian and oesophageal cancers rarely metastasise to the brain — prostate favours bone (osteoblastic deposits). Knowing the common primaries guides the workup of a patient with multiple grey-white junction lesions.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Metastatic tumours)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Psammoma bodies are the defining histologic hallmark of glioblastoma. Reason (R): Glioblastoma (IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4) is characterised by pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (glomeruloid) endothelial proliferation. Select the single best option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is false: psammoma bodies (concentric laminated calcifications) are hallmarks of meningioma (also papillary thyroid carcinoma and serous ovarian tumours), not glioblastoma. The reason is true: the WHO grade 4 defining features of glioblastoma are pseudopalisading necrosis (tumour cells crowding around serpentine necrosis) plus microvascular/glomeruloid endothelial proliferation. Because A is false while R is true, option D is correct — glioblastoma's true hallmarks are necrosis and vascular proliferation, not calcified psammoma bodies.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Glioblastoma; Meningioma)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which histologic hallmark is correctly paired with its tumour?
questions.concept: Homer-Wright (neuroblastic) rosettes — cells encircling a central fibrillary neuropil core without a true lumen — are characteristic of medulloblastoma and neuroblastoma, so option D is correctly paired. Verocay bodies belong to schwannoma (ependymoma instead shows perivascular pseudorosettes); Rosenthal fibres belong to pilocytic astrocytoma (oligodendroglioma shows fried-egg cells and calcification); and psammoma bodies (laminated calcifications) are seen in meningioma, not glioblastoma.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Tumour histologic hallmarks)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In grading a diffuse astrocytic glioma, which combination of histologic features indicates the highest-grade (WHO grade 4) lesion?
options: Microvascular (glomeruloid) proliferation and/or necrosis with high mitotic activity and marked pleomorphism
Mild hypercellularity with nuclear atypia only
Nuclear atypia plus a single mitotic figure but no necrosis
Uniform cells with perinuclear halos and stippled calcification
questions.concept: Diffuse astrocytoma grading rests on progressively acquired features: grade 2 shows nuclear atypia only; grade 3 (anaplastic) adds brisk mitoses and greater cellularity/pleomorphism; grade 4 (glioblastoma) adds microvascular (glomeruloid) proliferation and/or necrosis. Thus the grade 4 combination is necrosis/vascular proliferation with high mitoses and marked pleomorphism (option A). Option D (perinuclear halos, calcification) instead describes oligodendroglioma, while the atypia-only and single-mitosis options describe lower grades.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Astrocytoma grading)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 4-year-old child with a history of infantile spasms has hypopigmented 'ash-leaf' macules and facial angiofibromas. Brain imaging shows cortical tubers and subependymal nodules, one of which has enlarged near the foramen of Monro. Which lesion and gene are most relevant?
options: Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma; TSC1/TSC2 mutation
questions.concept: Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/hamartin or TSC2/tuberin mutation, causing mTOR overactivation) presents with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum), shagreen patches, cardiac rhabdomyomas and renal angiomyolipomas. A subependymal nodule near the foramen of Monro can grow into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Optic glioma/NF1, hemangioblastoma/VHL and bilateral vestibular schwannomas/NF2 are the other phakomatoses.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Familial tumour syndromes: Tuberous sclerosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: An infant has a unilateral facial port-wine (capillary malformation) stain in the ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal distribution, seizures and glaucoma. A skull radiograph shows 'tram-track' gyriform cortical calcification. What is the underlying intracranial lesion?
options: A ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis
An arteriovenous fistula of a dural venous sinus
A cavernous haemangioma of the brainstem
questions.concept: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis, somatic GNAQ mutation) features a facial port-wine stain (usually V1), an ipsilateral leptomeningeal capillary-venous angiomatosis, seizures, intellectual disability and glaucoma. Chronic cortical ischaemia beneath the angioma produces the classic 'tram-track' gyriform calcification on imaging. Berry aneurysms, dural arteriovenous fistulas and brainstem cavernomas are distinct vascular lesions not linked to the facial naevus and cortical calcification of this syndrome.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Sturge-Weber syndrome)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): 'Red neurons' are the earliest reliable morphologic marker of irreversible acute hypoxic-ischaemic neuronal injury. Reason (R): They develop about 12 to 24 hours after the insult, showing cell-body shrinkage with intense cytoplasmic eosinophilia and nuclear pyknosis. Select the single best option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Red neurons (acute neuronal injury) are the earliest histologic evidence of irreversible hypoxic-ischaemic damage, and it is precisely their appearance at 12-24 hours — with cell-body shrinkage, cytoplasmic hypereosinophilia and nuclear pyknosis/karyorrhexis — that makes them that early marker, so option A is correct. Selectively vulnerable sites include hippocampal CA1 (Sommer sector), Purkinje cells and cortical layers 3, 5 and 6.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Cellular reactions: neuronal injury)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with a brain tumour develops swelling due to breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, allowing protein-rich plasma fluid to leak preferentially into the white matter extracellular space. This type of cerebral oedema is best classified as:
questions.concept: Vasogenic oedema results from blood-brain barrier disruption (tumours, abscess, trauma, inflammation), letting protein-rich plasma extravasate into the extracellular space, chiefly of the white matter; corticosteroids help by restoring the barrier. Cytotoxic oedema is intracellular swelling from failure of the ATP-dependent Na/K pump (e.g., hypoxia-ischaemia). Interstitial oedema is transependymal CSF seepage in hydrocephalus, and osmotic oedema follows plasma hypo-osmolality — each mechanistically distinct from vasogenic oedema.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Cerebral oedema)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with a rapidly expanding temporal lobe haematoma develops a fixed, dilated pupil on the same side and contralateral hemiparesis. Progressive brainstem compression later produces midline pontine (Duret) haemorrhages. Which herniation syndrome is responsible?
options: Tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum
questions.concept: Uncal (medial temporal, transtentorial) herniation pushes the uncus over the tentorial edge, compressing the ipsilateral CN III (fixed dilated pupil, 'down-and-out' eye), the cerebral peduncle (contralateral hemiparesis, or ipsilateral via a Kernohan notch) and eventually the brainstem, tearing perforating vessels to cause midline Duret haemorrhages. Subfalcine herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery, tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla (respiratory/cardiac arrest), and transcalvarial herniation is through a skull defect.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Herniation syndromes)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has a triad of gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and progressive cognitive decline. CT shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy, and lumbar puncture reveals a normal opening pressure. This condition is:
questions.concept: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is a communicating hydrocephalus (impaired CSF resorption at the arachnoid granulations) with the classic triad 'wet, wobbly and wacky' — urinary incontinence, a magnetic gait apraxia and dementia — plus ventriculomegaly with a normal LP pressure; some patients improve with CSF shunting. Non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus follows aqueductal stenosis; hydrocephalus ex vacuo is passive ventricular enlargement from parenchymal loss; and idiopathic intracranial hypertension has raised pressure with papilloedema.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Hydrocephalus)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system?
options: They are derived from neuroectoderm, like astrocytes and neurons
They form the myelin sheaths of central axons
They line the ventricular system and produce cerebrospinal fluid
They are the phagocytic cells of the CNS and are of bone-marrow (monocyte/mesodermal) origin
questions.concept: Microglia are the resident macrophages/phagocytes of the CNS and, unlike astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma and neurons (all neuroectodermal), are of mesodermal/bone-marrow (yolk-sac monocyte) origin, so option D is correct. In injury they proliferate, become elongated 'rod cells' and form microglial nodules with neuronophagia. Oligodendrocytes (not microglia) myelinate central axons, ependymal cells line the ventricles, and the choroid plexus epithelium produces CSF.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Cellular constituents: microglia)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis characteristically causes haemorrhagic necrosis of the medial temporal and orbitofrontal lobes. Reason (R): HSV-1 produces cytoplasmic Negri body inclusions in infected neurons. Select the single best option:
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: HSV-1 is the most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis and produces haemorrhagic, necrotising inflammation of the medial temporal lobes and orbitofrontal cortex, causing seizures and behavioural/memory changes. The reason is false: HSV-1 forms Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions, whereas Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions specific to rabies (affecting brainstem, cerebellum and hippocampus). Because A is true but R is false, option C is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed. — The Central Nervous System (Viral encephalitis: HSV-1)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the earliest lesion of atherosclerosis, composed mainly of lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) within the intima and known to appear even in childhood?
questions.concept: The fatty streak is the earliest recognizable lesion, seen even in infants/children, and consists of intimal foam cells (lipid-laden macrophages and smooth muscle cells) with T cells; it is not necessarily obstructive and not all progress. The fibrous plaque is the advanced intimal lesion with a fibrous cap over a lipid core. Complicated plaques (calcification, ulceration, hemorrhage, thrombosis) and aneurysms are late complications, not the earliest lesion.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Atherosclerosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The foam cells that characterize atherosclerotic plaques are derived predominantly from which of the following cell types after they accumulate intracellular lipid?
questions.concept: Foam cells arise mainly from macrophages that engulf oxidized LDL via scavenger receptors (not down-regulated by intracellular cholesterol, so uptake is unchecked) and from intimal smooth muscle cells that migrate from the media and also ingest lipid. Neutrophils, mast cells, endothelial cells, pericytes, plasma cells and fibroblasts are not the source of the classic lipid-laden foam cell, making the other options incorrect.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Pathogenesis of Atherosclerosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Endothelial injury/dysfunction is regarded as the cornerstone initiating event in the response-to-injury hypothesis of atherosclerosis. Reason (R): A dysfunctional endothelium shows increased permeability to lipoproteins and enhanced leukocyte (monocyte) adhesion.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The modern response-to-injury model holds that chronic endothelial injury/dysfunction is the initiating lesion. Dysfunctional endothelium becomes more permeable (allowing LDL entry and its oxidation) and up-regulates adhesion molecules (VCAM-1) that recruit monocytes, which become intimal macrophages/foam cells. Thus both statements are true and R correctly explains the mechanism by which endothelial dysfunction drives plaque formation, making option A correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Response-to-Injury Hypothesis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In systemic atherosclerosis, which vessel is characteristically the most severely and extensively involved?
options: Abdominal aorta, below the renal arteries
questions.concept: The usual order of severity is: abdominal aorta (especially the infrarenal segment) > coronary arteries > popliteal arteries > internal carotid > circle of Willis. The infrarenal abdominal aorta is the classic site of predilection and of atherosclerotic aneurysm. Pulmonary arteries are generally spared unless there is pulmonary hypertension, and upper-limb (radial) vessels are typically spared; renal ostia may be involved but are not the most severely affected.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Sites and Consequences of Atherosclerosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): A vulnerable (unstable) atherosclerotic plaque is more prone to rupture than a stable plaque. Reason (R): Vulnerable plaques characteristically have a thin fibrous cap, a large lipid-rich necrotic core, and increased inflammatory (macrophage) content.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.concept: Vulnerable plaques rupture more readily precisely because of their structure: a thin fibrous cap, a large soft lipid/necrotic core, and dense macrophage infiltration. Macrophages secrete matrix metalloproteinases that degrade collagen in the cap, while reduced smooth muscle collagen synthesis further weakens it. Stable plaques have thick fibrous caps and small lipid cores. Both statements are true and R is the correct mechanistic explanation of A.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Plaque Vulnerability and Rupture)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man develops crushing chest pain at rest with ST-segment elevation, and angiography shows acute total occlusion of a coronary artery. The immediate pathologic event most responsible for acute transmural myocardial infarction in this setting is:
options: Gradual concentric luminal narrowing by a stable fibrous plaque
Monckeberg medial calcification of the coronary artery
Disruption (rupture/erosion) of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombosis
Vasculitic aneurysm of the coronary artery
questions.concept: Most acute coronary syndromes/MIs result from acute plaque disruption (rupture or erosion) that exposes the thrombogenic lipid core and subendothelial collagen, triggering platelet aggregation and occlusive thrombosis. Stable fibrous plaques cause fixed narrowing and stable/exertional angina, not sudden total occlusion. Monckeberg calcifies the media without narrowing the lumen, and coronary vasculitic aneurysm is a rare cause, making C the best answer.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Ischemic Heart Disease / Acute Plaque Change)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Ring-like calcific deposits confined to the tunica media of medium-sized muscular arteries in a person over 50, producing no luminal narrowing and usually clinically insignificant, are characteristic of:
questions.concept: Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis is calcification limited to the media of muscular arteries in patients typically older than 50; because it does not encroach on the lumen it rarely causes ischemia, though it may be palpable or visible radiographically. Hyaline and hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis affect small arterioles (hypertension/diabetes and malignant hypertension respectively), and atherosclerosis is an intimal disease of large/medium elastic and muscular arteries.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Arteriosclerosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presents with BP 220/130 mmHg, severe headache, and papilledema. Renal biopsy shows arterioles with concentric, laminated ('onion-skin') thickening of the wall, some with fibrinoid necrosis. This vascular change is:
questions.concept: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis is the lesion of malignant/accelerated hypertension: concentric laminated 'onion-skin' thickening of arteriolar walls, often accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis (necrotizing arteriolitis). Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is the homogeneous, pink, hyaline wall thickening of benign hypertension and diabetes. Monckeberg is medial calcification of larger muscular arteries, and atheroembolism produces cholesterol clefts, not onion-skinning, so B is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Hypertensive Vascular Disease)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient dies 3 hours after the onset of an acute myocardial infarction. Which finding is most likely on routine light microscopy of the infarcted myocardium?
options: Essentially no change (at most early wavy fibers and hypereosinophilia)
questions.concept: In the first 4-6 hours there is essentially no change on routine light microscopy; the infarct is detectable only by special stains such as TTC (which shows loss of formazan). The earliest histologic clues are wavy fibers at the border and hypereosinophilia beginning around 4-12 hours. Coagulative necrosis with neutrophils appears at 1-3 days, granulation tissue at 7-10 days, and dense scar over weeks, so at 3 hours option A is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Morphologic Evolution of Myocardial Infarction)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: At autopsy of a patient who died 2 days after an acute myocardial infarction, the microscopic appearance of the infarct is most characteristically:
options: Contraction band necrosis as the only finding
Macrophage-rich phagocytosis of debris with early granulation tissue
Coagulative necrosis with a heavy neutrophilic infiltrate
questions.concept: At 1-3 days the infarct shows established coagulative necrosis (loss of nuclei and cross-striations) with a prominent interstitial neutrophilic infiltrate that peaks in this window. Macrophage-driven removal of dead myocytes and early granulation tissue characterize days 3-10, and dense fibrous scar forms over weeks. Contraction band necrosis is a marker of reperfusion, not a stand-alone 2-day finding, so coagulative necrosis with neutrophils (D) is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Microscopic Evolution of MI)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: During which post-infarction window is the ventricular wall most susceptible to free-wall rupture, corresponding to maximal macrophage-mediated removal of necrotic myocytes?
questions.concept: Free-wall rupture, septal rupture and papillary muscle rupture peak around 3-7 days, when macrophages have digested dead myocytes and the necrotic wall is maximally soft and weak but new collagen has not yet reinforced it. In the first hours the wall has not yet weakened, and by 6-8 weeks a dense collagenous scar has strengthened it, greatly reducing rupture risk, so 3-7 days (C) is the answer.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Complications of Myocardial Infarction)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Well-developed granulation tissue with prominent neovascularization, macrophages, and early collagen at the margins of a myocardial infarct is most characteristic of which interval after infarction?
options: 7-10 days, extending into the second week
questions.concept: Granulation tissue (new capillaries, macrophages, fibroblasts, and early collagen deposition) is best developed around 7-10 days and into the second week, marking the transition from debris removal to repair. At 4-12 and 24-48 hours the infarct still shows necrosis with a neutrophilic response, and by roughly 2 months a dense acellular collagenous scar has formed, so option C is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Healing of Myocardial Infarction)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The gross appearance of a myocardial infarct as a yellow-tan, softened center surrounded by a hyperemic (red) border is most typical of an infarct that is approximately:
questions.concept: Gross evolution: 0-12 hours shows no visible change (TTC needed); 12-24 hours dark mottling; 1-3 days a pale/yellow center; 3-7 days a soft yellow-tan center with a hyperemic (red-brown) rim of granulation tissue at the margin; 10 days-2 weeks a red-gray depressed border; and weeks to 2 months a firm gray-white scar. The yellow soft center with hyperemic border therefore corresponds to about 3-7 days (B).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Gross Features of Evolving MI)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Contraction band necrosis is a hallmark of reperfusion injury after blood flow is restored to ischemic myocardium. Reason (R): Reperfusion causes massive calcium influx into irreversibly injured myocytes, producing hypercontracted sarcomeres seen as intensely eosinophilic transverse bands.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: When ischemic (but not yet dead) myocardium is reperfused, restored oxygen and a surge of intracellular calcium cause exaggerated hypercontraction of myofibrils in irreversibly injured cells, producing contraction bands: intensely eosinophilic transverse bands. This is a classic sign of reperfusion injury, alongside oxygen free-radical damage and microvascular injury. Both statements are true and R correctly explains A, so option A is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Reperfusion Injury / Contraction Band Necrosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Three days after an inferior-wall myocardial infarction, a patient suddenly develops flash pulmonary edema, hypotension, and a new loud holosystolic apical murmur. The most likely mechanical complication is:
options: Ventricular septal rupture producing a left-to-right shunt
Rupture of a papillary muscle causing acute mitral regurgitation
questions.concept: Rupture of a necrotic papillary muscle (classically the posteromedial papillary muscle, supplied solely by the posterior descending artery and therefore vulnerable in inferior/RCA infarcts) occurs around days 2-7 and causes acute severe mitral regurgitation with flash pulmonary edema, a new holosystolic murmur, and cardiogenic shock. Septal rupture gives a shunt with a harsh left-sternal-border murmur, Dressler occurs weeks later, and a true aneurysm is a late complication, so D is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Mechanical Complications of MI)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Several weeks after a myocardial infarction, a patient develops fever, pleuritic chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and a raised ESR. This is most consistent with:
options: Dressler (post-cardiac injury) syndrome, an autoimmune pericarditis
questions.concept: Dressler syndrome is a delayed, immune-mediated (antibodies to released myocardial antigens) pericarditis appearing weeks to a few months after MI, presenting with fever, pleuropericarditic chest pain, a friction rub, and elevated ESR. Early fibrinous ('epistenocardiac') pericarditis instead overlies a transmural infarct within the first 1-3 days. The latency of weeks and autoimmune features distinguish Dressler, making option B correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Pericarditis / Dressler Syndrome)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient who had a myocardial infarction 4 days ago develops recurrent chest pain, raising concern for re-infarction. Which cardiac biomarker is MOST useful to confirm re-infarction at this time?
questions.concept: Cardiac troponin remains elevated for about 7-10 days after the initial infarct, so at day 4 it may still be high and cannot reliably signal a new event. CK-MB rises within hours and returns to normal by 48-72 hours, so a fresh re-rise of CK-MB is the preferred marker to detect re-infarction in this window. LDH and AST are nonspecific and now obsolete for this purpose, so CK-MB (C) is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — The Heart (Serum Cardiac Markers)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A tall young man with long limbs, arachnodactyly, and lens dislocation dies suddenly of a proximal aortic dissection. The underlying change in the aortic media most associated with this condition is:
options: Cystic medial degeneration (elastin fragmentation with myxoid/proteoglycan pooling)
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
Medial calcification of the Monckeberg type
questions.concept: Marfan syndrome (defective fibrillin-1) predisposes to cystic medial degeneration: fragmentation and loss of elastic fibers with pooling of amorphous proteoglycan ('cystic' spaces) in the media, weakening the wall and favoring dissection, typically in the ascending aorta/first few centimeters. Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum underlies syphilitic aneurysm, granulomatous inflammation is seen in GCA/Takayasu, and Monckeberg is unrelated, so A is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Aortic Dissection / Cystic Medial Degeneration)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Tertiary syphilis classically produces an aneurysm of the ascending aorta and arch with a wrinkled 'tree-bark' intima. The primary vascular lesion responsible for this is:
options: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with medial ischemia
questions.concept: Syphilitic (luetic) aortitis causes an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with perivascular plasma-cell cuffing; the resulting ischemia leads to scarring and loss of medial elastic tissue, weakening the wall and dilating the ascending aorta and arch, producing the wrinkled 'tree-bark' intima and potentially aortic regurgitation or coronary ostial stenosis. It is not caused by atheroma, cystic medial degeneration, or arteriolar fibrinoid necrosis, so D is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Syphilitic/Luetic Aneurysm)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old Asian woman has absent radial pulses, markedly unequal blood pressures between the arms, and visual disturbances; imaging shows narrowing of the aortic arch and its major branches. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aortic arch and its branches, classically in women younger than 50 (often Asian), producing weak/absent upper-limb pulses ('pulseless disease'), blood-pressure discrepancies, and ocular/neurologic symptoms from arch-vessel stenosis. PAN affects medium arteries, Buerger affects distal limb vessels in smokers, and Kawasaki affects young children with coronary involvement, so B is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Takayasu Arteritis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, transient monocular vision loss, and an ESR of 90 mm/hr; temporal artery biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleate giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina. Besides biopsy, the most important immediate step is:
options: Start high-dose corticosteroids immediately to prevent blindness
Observe and repeat the ESR in 6 weeks
questions.concept: This is giant cell (temporal) arteritis, a granulomatous vasculitis of medium/large arteries in the elderly, presenting with headache, jaw claudication, high ESR, and risk of irreversible blindness from ophthalmic/posterior ciliary artery involvement. High-dose corticosteroids must be started immediately (even before biopsy) to prevent visual loss; biopsy remains positive for a short window and shows skip lesions. Waiting, cyclophosphamide monotherapy, or anticoagulation are not the correct first step, so A is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Giant Cell/Temporal Arteritis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old hepatitis B surface antigen-positive man develops hypertension, abdominal pain, mononeuritis multiplex, and renal impairment; angiography shows microaneurysms of medium-sized arteries, and the lungs are spared. The most likely vasculitis is:
questions.concept: Classic polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, associated with hepatitis B in about a third of cases, showing transmural fibrinoid necrosis with lesions of different ages and 'rosary-bead' microaneurysms; it characteristically spares the pulmonary arteries and is ANCA-negative, presenting with renovascular hypertension, GI/abdominal pain, and mononeuritis multiplex. GPA, EGPA, and MPA are small-vessel ANCA-associated vasculitides that commonly involve the lung, so B is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Polyarteritis Nodosa)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 32-year-old heavy male smoker presents with painful ischemic ulcers of the toes and fingertips and episodes of migratory superficial thrombophlebitis; angiography shows segmental thrombosing inflammation of small and medium distal extremity arteries. The single most important management step is:
questions.concept: This is Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), a segmental thrombosing and inflammatory vasculitis of distal extremity arteries, veins, and adjacent nerves seen almost exclusively in young tobacco users, and strongly tied to smoking (possibly hypersensitivity to tobacco components). Complete, permanent smoking cessation is the only intervention that halts progression and prevents amputation. Corticosteroids, statins, and splenectomy are not indicated, so C is correct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (Thromboangiitis Obliterans / Buerger Disease)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following pairings of a vasculitis with its most characteristic ANCA is correct?
questions.concept: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) is most characteristically associated with c-ANCA directed against proteinase-3 (PR3). Microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) are more often p-ANCA/anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO). Classic polyarteritis nodosa is typically ANCA-negative. Options A and B swap the antibody, and option C mislabels GPA as p-ANCA, so the correct pairing is GPA with c-ANCA/anti-PR3 (D).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Blood Vessels (ANCA-Associated Vasculitides)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which statement about unconjugated (indirect-reacting) bilirubin is correct?
options: It is tightly bound to albumin in plasma, is water-insoluble, and does not appear in the urine
It is water-soluble and is readily filtered and excreted in the urine
It is conjugated with glucuronic acid within the spleen before reaching the liver
Its elevation characteristically produces dark, tea-coloured urine
questions.concept: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and circulates tightly bound to albumin, so it cannot be filtered by the glomerulus and never appears in urine (acholuric jaundice). Conjugation with glucuronic acid occurs in hepatocytes via UGT1A1, not the spleen.
