Only water-soluble conjugated bilirubin can be excreted in urine and produce dark urine, so options B, C and D describe the conjugated fraction or are simply false.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (bilirubin metabolism and jaundice)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 22-year-old with hereditary spherocytosis develops scleral icterus and pigment gallstones. Which bilirubin fraction predominantly rises, and what is the expected urinary finding?
options: Unconjugated bilirubin, with absent urinary bilirubin but increased urinary urobilinogen
Conjugated bilirubin, with absent urinary urobilinogen
An equal rise of both fractions, with pale clay-coloured stools
questions.concept: Chronic haemolysis overwhelms hepatic conjugating capacity, so unconjugated (albumin-bound, unfilterable) bilirubin predominates — there is NO bilirubinuria. Increased haem turnover raises gut and then urinary urobilinogen, and darkens the stool. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with bilirubinuria and pale stool typifies obstructive/hepatocellular jaundice, not prehepatic haemolysis. Calcium-bilirubinate pigment stones are a classic complication of chronic haemolysis.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed — The Liver, Biliary Tract and Exocrine Pancreas (classification of jaundice)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In the van den Bergh reaction, a positive DIRECT reaction (colour develops immediately with the diazo reagent, before any alcohol/accelerator is added) indicates a predominant increase of which bilirubin fraction?
options: Delta-bilirubin only — as seen in Gilbert syndrome
Conjugated bilirubin — as seen in obstructive or hepatocellular jaundice
Biliverdin — as seen in physiological neonatal jaundice
questions.concept: The direct van den Bergh reaction measures water-soluble conjugated (direct-reacting) bilirubin, which couples immediately with the diazo reagent; it is raised in hepatocellular and obstructive jaundice. The indirect reaction (requiring alcohol/methanol to solubilise) measures unconjugated bilirubin, elevated in haemolysis and Gilbert syndrome. Biliverdin is the upstream green pigment reduced to bilirubin and is not what the reaction measures, making A, B and D incorrect.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed — The Liver, Biliary Tract and Exocrine Pancreas (van den Bergh reaction)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A newborn develops severe non-haemolytic jaundice in the first days of life with serum bilirubin >25 mg/dL (almost entirely unconjugated). There is no response to phenobarbital and the infant develops opisthotonus. The underlying molecular defect is:
options: Impaired canalicular excretion of conjugated bilirubin (MRP2 defect)
Reduced hepatic uptake of bilirubin with only mildly reduced UGT1A1 activity
Deficiency of the biliary copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B)
Complete absence of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity
questions.concept: Crigler-Najjar type I is complete absence of UGT1A1, so bilirubin cannot be conjugated — producing extreme unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, kernicterus (opisthotonus), and death unless liver transplant/phototherapy is given. Because there is no residual enzyme, phenobarbital (an enzyme inducer) has NO effect. An MRP2 defect causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Dubin-Johnson); mild UGT reduction/uptake defect causes Gilbert; ATP7B defect causes Wilson disease.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (hereditary hyperbilirubinemias)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II shows a marked fall in serum bilirubin after phenobarbital therapy, whereas type I does not. Reason (R): Type II has a partial, inducible deficiency of UGT1A1, whereas type I has complete absence of the enzyme.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Crigler-Najjar type II (Arias syndrome) retains partial UGT1A1 activity, and the residual inducible enzyme responds to phenobarbital with a bilirubin fall (often >25%), whereas type I has complete enzyme absence so phenobarbital cannot induce anything and there is no response. The partial-versus-complete enzyme difference is precisely why type II is phenobarbital-responsive and type I is not, so R is the correct explanation of A.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (Crigler-Najjar syndromes)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has mild chronic jaundice with predominantly conjugated bilirubin, normal transaminases, and a normal life expectancy. Liver biopsy shows a grossly black liver with coarse dark pigment granules in hepatocytes. The responsible defect is in:
options: The sinusoidal OATP uptake transporter, with intact canalicular excretion
The canalicular MRP2 (cMOAT/ABCC2) transporter for conjugated bilirubin
The bile salt export pump (BSEP), causing progressive cholestasis
questions.concept: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is an autosomal-recessive defect in canalicular MRP2 (ABCC2/cMOAT) that impairs excretion of conjugated bilirubin, giving benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Accumulated dark, melanin-like pigment (epinephrine-metabolite polymers) turns the liver grossly black. A hepatic storage/uptake (OATP) defect with a normal-coloured liver is Rotor syndrome; UGT1A1 defects cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (Gilbert/Crigler-Najjar); BSEP defect causes PFIC.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (Dubin-Johnson and Rotor syndromes)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Rotor syndrome is best distinguished from Dubin-Johnson syndrome by which feature?
options: Rotor causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia whereas Dubin-Johnson causes conjugated
Rotor shows characteristic ground-glass hepatocytes on biopsy
Rotor invariably progresses to cirrhosis, unlike Dubin-Johnson
In Rotor the liver is grossly normal (no dark pigment) and total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly elevated
questions.concept: Both Rotor and Dubin-Johnson cause benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, so option A is wrong. Rotor is a defect in hepatic storage/handling (OATP1B1/1B3) so the liver is NOT pigmented (grossly normal), and total urinary coproporphyrin is markedly increased — unlike Dubin-Johnson, which has a black liver and near-normal total coproporphyrin (with a high proportion of isomer I). Ground-glass hepatocytes indicate hepatitis B; neither syndrome progresses to cirrhosis.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed — The Liver, Biliary Tract and Exocrine Pancreas (hereditary conjugated hyperbilirubinemias)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A liver panel shows ALT 60 U/L, AST 55 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 640 U/L (markedly raised) and GGT 480 U/L (markedly raised), with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. This enzyme pattern is most consistent with:
options: A predominantly hepatocellular (hepatitic) pattern of injury
An isolated skeletal (bone) source of alkaline phosphatase
A predominantly cholestatic/obstructive pattern of injury
questions.concept: A disproportionate rise in ALP and GGT with only mild transaminase elevation defines a cholestatic/obstructive pattern; the parallel GGT rise confirms a hepatobiliary (not bony) origin for the ALP. A hepatocellular pattern would show AST/ALT rising far out of proportion to ALP. Bone-source ALP would not raise GGT. Haemolysis produces unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with essentially normal liver enzymes, so A, B and C are excluded.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Evaluation of Liver Function (patterns of liver test abnormalities)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which statement about hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection is TRUE?
options: It is transmitted by the faecal-oral route and does not cause a chronic carrier state
It is a DNA virus that integrates into the host genome
Chronic infection with progression to cirrhosis develops in about 80% of cases
It is transmitted mainly by blood transfusion and sexual contact
questions.concept: HAV is a small non-enveloped RNA picornavirus spread by the faecal-oral route (contaminated food/water); it causes an acute, self-limited hepatitis with NO chronic or carrier state and no progression to cirrhosis. HBV is the DNA virus capable of genomic integration. Chronicity and cirrhosis characterise HBV/HCV, and parenteral/sexual transmission is typical of HBV/HCV — so B, C and D are false.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (viral hepatitis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops jaundice, encephalopathy and fulminant hepatic failure after drinking contaminated water during a monsoon outbreak. The most likely agent and reason for her high mortality is:
options: Hepatitis A virus, more severe here because it establishes chronic infection
Hepatitis E virus, which carries a markedly increased risk of fulminant hepatic failure (~20% mortality) in pregnancy
Hepatitis C virus acquired from the contaminated water
Hepatitis B with hepatitis D superinfection
questions.concept: Hepatitis E is an enterically transmitted (waterborne) RNA virus that causes epidemic hepatitis and is usually self-limited, but in pregnancy — especially the third trimester — it can cause fulminant hepatic failure with mortality approaching 20%. HAV and HEV do not cause chronicity (so A is wrong). HCV is bloodborne, not waterborne, and HBV/HDV is parenteral, making C and D inconsistent with a waterborne monsoon outbreak.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (hepatitis E in pregnancy)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient recovering from acute hepatitis B has this serology: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, IgM anti-HBc positive. This profile represents:
options: The window period of acute hepatitis B
Distant past infection with complete recovery
questions.concept: In the hepatitis B window period, HBsAg has already cleared but protective anti-HBs has not yet appeared, so the ONLY positive marker is IgM anti-HBc — making it the sole indicator of recent infection at this stage. Vaccination gives isolated anti-HBs with negative anti-HBc (A wrong). A chronic carrier has persistent HBsAg (B wrong). Resolved past infection shows anti-HBs plus IgG (not IgM) anti-HBc (D wrong).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (serologic diagnosis of hepatitis B)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The presence of HBeAg in a patient with hepatitis B infection primarily indicates:
options: Active viral replication and high infectivity
questions.concept: HBeAg is a secreted protein derived from the precore/core region and is a marker of active HBV replication and high infectivity (high viral load). Seroconversion from HBeAg to anti-HBe signals reduced replication and lower infectivity. Immunity is indicated by anti-HBs, vaccination gives anti-HBs alone, and hepatitis D requires separate anti-HDV/HDV-RNA testing — so A, B and C are incorrect.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed — The Liver, Biliary Tract and Exocrine Pancreas (hepatitis B markers)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A healthcare worker's hepatitis B panel shows: HBsAg negative, anti-HBc (total) negative, anti-HBs positive. The correct interpretation is:
options: Immunity due to prior hepatitis B vaccination
Immunity due to resolved natural infection
Acute hepatitis B in the window period
questions.concept: Isolated anti-HBs positivity with NEGATIVE anti-HBc indicates vaccine-induced immunity: the recombinant vaccine contains only HBsAg, so no anti-core antibody is ever generated. Resolved natural infection would show anti-HBs PLUS anti-HBc (IgG), so B is wrong. The window period is defined by IgM anti-HBc positivity, and a chronic carrier has persistent HBsAg — so C and D are excluded.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (interpretation of hepatitis B serology)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Compared with the other hepatitis viruses, hepatitis C virus (HCV) is MOST notable for:
options: Being a DNA virus preventable by an effective vaccine
The highest rate of progression to chronic infection, with substantial risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
Exclusive faecal-oral transmission with no chronicity
Causing infection only in the presence of hepatitis B
questions.concept: HCV is an RNA flavivirus, chiefly bloodborne, and has the highest chronicity rate of the hepatitis viruses (roughly 50-85% become chronic), driving progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. There is no HCV vaccine because of its high genomic variability/quasispecies, so A is wrong. Faecal-oral, non-chronic spread describes HAV/HEV (C), and dependence on HBV is the feature of the defective HDV (D).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (hepatitis C, chronicity and HCC)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Hepatitis D superinfection of a chronic hepatitis B carrier tends to be more severe — with higher risk of fulminant hepatitis or accelerated cirrhosis — than simultaneous HBV-HDV coinfection. Reason (R): Hepatitis D is a defective RNA virus that requires the HBsAg coat of hepatitis B to replicate.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are individually true: HDV is a defective virus needing HBsAg to assemble and replicate (R true), and superinfection of an established HBV carrier is indeed more severe than co-infection (A true). However, R only explains why HDV depends on HBV at all — it does not explain WHY superinfection is worse than coinfection (which relates to a large pre-existing pool of HBsAg permitting rapid HDV replication). Hence R is not the correct explanation of A.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (hepatitis D coinfection versus superinfection)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Councilman (acidophil) bodies seen on liver biopsy in acute viral hepatitis represent:
options: Intracellular accumulation of hepatitis B surface antigen (ground-glass change)
Aggregates of damaged keratin intermediate filaments (Mallory-Denk material)
Apoptotic hepatocytes that have shrunk into rounded, intensely eosinophilic bodies
questions.concept: Councilman/apoptotic (acidophil) bodies are individual hepatocytes dying by apoptosis — they shrink into rounded, deeply eosinophilic (acidophilic) globes and are a hallmark of viral hepatitis. Ground-glass hepatocytes reflect cytoplasmic HBsAg accumulation (chronic HBV); Mallory-Denk bodies are damaged keratin intermediate filaments seen in alcoholic/NASH hepatitis; iron-laden Kupffer cells indicate haemosiderosis. Thus A, B and D describe different entities.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (histology of viral hepatitis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In a patient with a long history of heavy alcohol use and deranged liver enzymes, which biochemical pattern is MOST characteristic of alcoholic liver disease?
options: AST elevated to about twice ALT (AST:ALT ratio >2:1), usually with values below 500 U/L
ALT elevated far more than AST (ratio well below 1)
Normal transaminases with an isolated very high alkaline phosphatase
questions.concept: Alcoholic liver disease classically shows an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2:1, with transaminases usually only modestly raised (below ~500 U/L). This is partly because alcohol depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate needed for ALT synthesis and causes release of mitochondrial AST. ALT-predominant elevation is typical of viral hepatitis and NAFLD; values above 2000 U/L suggest ischaemic, toxic (e.g., paracetamol) or acute viral injury; isolated high ALP suggests cholestasis.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed — Alcoholic Liver Disease (AST:ALT ratio)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 48-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia (denies significant alcohol use) has hepatic steatosis on ultrasound and mildly raised ALT. Biopsy shows steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies and scattered neutrophils. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: NAFLD/NASH is strongly linked to the metabolic syndrome (obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia). Its histology — steatosis, ballooning degeneration, Mallory-Denk bodies and neutrophils — is essentially indistinguishable from alcoholic steatohepatitis, but occurs in the ABSENCE of significant alcohol intake, and can progress to cirrhosis. PBC (AMA-positive middle-aged women), Wilson (young, KF rings, low ceruloplasmin) and autoimmune hepatitis (ANA/anti-SMA) differ clinically and serologically.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which pairing of cirrhosis morphology with its typical cause is CORRECT?
options: Macronodular cirrhosis — the classic pattern of early alcoholic cirrhosis
Micronodular cirrhosis — the usual end-stage of chronic viral hepatitis B
Micronodular cirrhosis (uniform nodules <3 mm) — classically alcoholic liver disease
questions.concept: Micronodular cirrhosis (uniform nodules under ~3 mm) is classically caused by alcohol (also haemochromatosis and biliary disease), where ongoing injury and metabolic suppression limit regeneration. Macronodular cirrhosis (variably sized nodules over 3 mm) typifies chronic viral hepatitis B/C and Wilson disease. Alcoholic cirrhosis can evolve into a mixed/macronodular pattern late, but its classic early form is micronodular — so A, B and D are mismatched.
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan Textbook of Pathology, 8th ed — The Liver, Biliary Tract and Exocrine Pancreas (morphological classification of cirrhosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 52-year-old man presents with skin hyperpigmentation ('bronze' colour), new-onset diabetes mellitus and hepatomegaly. Which laboratory profile and gene are MOST consistent with hereditary haemochromatosis?
options: Low ceruloplasmin with high urinary copper, and an ATP7B mutation
Low serum iron with high TIBC and no genetic association
Raised alpha-fetoprotein with entirely normal iron studies
High serum ferritin and high transferrin saturation, with an HFE (C282Y) mutation
questions.concept: Hereditary haemochromatosis, most often from HFE C282Y homozygosity, causes systemic iron overload — raised serum ferritin and high transferrin saturation. Iron deposition damages the liver (cirrhosis, HCC risk), pancreas ('bronze diabetes' from combined skin pigmentation and diabetes), skin, joints and heart. Low ceruloplasmin with an ATP7B mutation defines Wilson disease (A); low iron with high TIBC is iron deficiency (B); AFP with normal iron studies does not fit (C).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (hereditary haemochromatosis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 19-year-old with hepatitis and a new resting tremor is being evaluated for Wilson disease. Which combination of laboratory findings best supports the diagnosis?
options: Decreased serum ceruloplasmin and decreased TOTAL serum copper, but increased FREE (non-ceruloplasmin-bound) serum copper and increased 24-hour urinary copper
Increased serum ceruloplasmin with decreased urinary copper
Increased serum ceruloplasmin with increased total serum copper
Normal ceruloplasmin with a high transferrin saturation
questions.concept: In Wilson disease the defective ATP7B impairs both incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin and biliary copper excretion. This lowers serum ceruloplasmin and lowers TOTAL serum copper (most circulating copper is ceruloplasmin-bound), yet the FREE non-bound copper rises and spills into urine, so 24-hour urinary copper is increased; tissue deposition causes Kayser-Fleischer rings and hepatic/neuropsychiatric disease. High transferrin saturation with normal ceruloplasmin points to haemochromatosis, not Wilson.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (Wilson disease, copper studies)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A young non-smoking adult with early panacinar (basal) emphysema is found to have chronic liver disease. Liver biopsy shows cytoplasmic globules in periportal hepatocytes that are PAS-positive and diastase-resistant. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (classically the PiZZ genotype) causes accumulation of misfolded AAT within hepatocytes, forming cytoplasmic globules that are PAS-positive and diastase (PAS-D)-resistant, with associated liver disease/neonatal cholestasis. Reduced circulating AAT leaves neutrophil elastase unopposed, producing early panacinar emphysema, especially in non-smokers presenting young. Copper (Wilson) and iron (haemochromatosis) stains and large-duct cholangiographic disease (PSC) are distinct.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pruritus and xanthelasma. Alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated and anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA) is positive. Biopsy shows granulomatous destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts. The diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Primary biliary cholangitis typically affects middle-aged women with fatigue, pruritus and a cholestatic profile (high ALP), and is characterised by AMA positivity (anti-M2, highly specific) with granulomatous destruction of small/medium intrahepatic bile ducts (the florid duct lesion). PSC instead affects large ducts (beaded strictures on cholangiography), is AMA-negative, and is linked to ulcerative colitis and p-ANCA. Autoimmune hepatitis shows ANA/anti-SMA and interface hepatitis, not duct destruction.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (primary biliary cholangitis vs primary sclerosing cholangitis)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: The MOST common malignant tumour involving the liver overall is:
options: Metastatic carcinoma (e.g., from colon, breast or lung)
questions.concept: Metastatic tumours far outnumber primary liver malignancies; the liver is one of the commonest sites of metastasis, especially from colon, breast, lung and pancreas, classically producing multiple nodules with central umbilication. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the commonest PRIMARY liver malignancy (linked to cirrhosis, HBV/HCV; raised AFP), and cholangiocarcinoma arises from bile-duct epithelium. Haemangioma is the commonest BENIGN liver tumour, not a malignancy, so A, B and C are incorrect.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed — Liver and Gallbladder (tumours of the liver; metastases)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops an episode of visible (gross) hematuria within 1-2 days of an upper respiratory tract infection, and similar episodes recur with subsequent infections. Renal biopsy immunofluorescence shows mesangial deposits of which immunoglobulin?
questions.concept: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. Synpharyngitic gross hematuria (concurrent with, not 1-2 weeks after, a mucosal infection) with mesangial IgA and C3 deposits distinguishes it from poststreptococcal GN, where hematuria follows the infection by weeks.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has nephrotic-range proteinuria, and renal biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall with subepithelial deposits producing a 'spike and dome' pattern on silver stain. Circulating autoantibodies against which podocyte antigen are most characteristic?
questions.concept: Primary membranous nephropathy is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and older Caucasians; roughly 70% are driven by autoantibodies to the podocyte antigen PLA2R. Subepithelial immune-complex deposits with reactive GBM spikes give the silver-stain 'spike and dome' appearance.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 40-year-old African-American man with HIV infection develops heavy proteinuria and full nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows sclerosis involving portions (segments) of some (focal) glomeruli, with the rest appearing normal on light microscopy. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially in people of African descent and in HIV, heroin use, sickle cell and obesity. Light microscopy shows sclerosis of segments of some glomeruli; unlike minimal change disease it causes non-selective proteinuria and often responds poorly to steroids.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a malar rash, arthralgia and positive anti-dsDNA develops hematuria and proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with thickened, homogeneous eosinophilic capillary loops ('wire-loop' lesions) and a 'full-house' immunofluorescence pattern. This corresponds to which class of lupus nephritis?
questions.concept: Class IV diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is the most common and most severe form. Subendothelial immune-complex deposits produce 'wire-loop' capillary loops, and immunofluorescence shows 'full-house' staining (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q). It carries the worst renal prognosis and drives aggressive immunosuppression.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A young adult presents with a mixed nephrotic-nephritic picture and persistently low serum C3. Renal biopsy shows a thickened glomerular basement membrane with a 'tram-track' (double-contour) appearance caused by mesangial cell interposition. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Membranoproliferative GN presents with a combined nephrotic/nephritic picture and low complement. Duplication/splitting of the GBM from mesangial cell interposition and new basement-membrane synthesis gives the classic 'tram-track' double-contour appearance on silver/PAS stain.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent hematuria, progressive sensorineural hearing loss and anterior lenticonus. Electron microscopy of the glomerular basement membrane shows irregular thinning and thickening with 'basket-weave' splitting of the lamina densa. The defective protein is:
questions.concept: Alport syndrome is a hereditary nephritis, most often X-linked, caused by mutations in type IV collagen (alpha-3/4/5 chains). The clinical triad is hematuria progressing to renal failure, sensorineural deafness and ocular defects (anterior lenticonus), with a pathognomonic 'basket-weave' GBM on electron microscopy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has persistent asymptomatic microscopic hematuria with normal renal function, normal hearing and no significant proteinuria; several relatives have similar isolated hematuria. Electron microscopy shows diffuse uniform thinning of the glomerular basement membrane. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria)
questions.concept: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria) causes lifelong isolated microscopic hematuria with an excellent prognosis; EM shows diffusely thinned GBM (roughly 150-250 nm versus the normal ~350-400 nm). Unlike Alport syndrome it lacks deafness, ocular lesions and progression to renal failure.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with rapidly progressive renal failure and hemoptysis. Renal biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis, but immunofluorescence reveals NO immune deposits (pauci-immune). Which serologic test is most likely to be positive?
questions.concept: Pauci-immune crescentic (RPGN type III) glomerulonephritis lacks glomerular immune deposits and is associated with ANCA — c-ANCA/PR3 in granulomatosis with polyangiitis and p-ANCA/MPO in microscopic polyangiitis and EGPA. Anti-GBM disease (type I) instead shows linear IgG, and immune-complex RPGN (type II) shows granular deposits.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Glomerular Diseases

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient develops acute kidney injury after prolonged hypotension from septic shock. Urinalysis shows muddy-brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis is the commonest cause of intrinsic AKI. Sloughed necrotic tubular epithelium forms pathognomonic 'muddy-brown' granular casts; unlike prerenal azotemia the FENa is greater than 2% and urine osmolality is low because injured tubules cannot concentrate or reabsorb sodium.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old diabetic woman with a long history of analgesic (NSAID/phenacetin) abuse develops flank pain, gross hematuria and passes sloughed tissue fragments in her urine; imaging shows destruction of the renal papillae. This complication is:
questions.concept: Renal papillary necrosis is classically caused by Diabetes mellitus, Analgesic abuse (NSAIDs/phenacetin), Sickle cell disease, and severe pyelonephritis/obstruction. Ischemic coagulative necrosis of the papillae produces flank pain, hematuria and sloughed papillary tissue passed in the urine.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 62-year-old smoker presents with painless hematuria, dull flank pain and a palpable abdominal mass; CT shows a solid renal mass extending into the renal vein. Histology shows nests of cells with clear, lipid- and glycogen-laden cytoplasm. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, linked to VHL gene inactivation and smoking, is the commonest renal malignancy in adults. The classic triad is hematuria, flank pain and a palpable mass; it characteristically invades the renal vein and can cause paraneoplastic syndromes (polycythemia, hypercalcemia, Cushing).
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome suddenly develops acute flank pain and worsening proteinuria; imaging confirms renal vein thrombosis. Urinary loss of which protein best explains this thrombotic tendency?
questions.concept: Nephrotic syndrome produces a hypercoagulable state largely from urinary loss of antithrombin III and other anticoagulant regulators, predisposing to renal vein thrombosis and venous thromboembolism. Membranous nephropathy has the strongest association with renal vein thrombosis among the nephrotic pathologies.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Glomerular Diseases

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which combination of findings best characterizes the NEPHRITIC syndrome, as opposed to the nephrotic syndrome?
options: Hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and sub-nephrotic proteinuria
Proteinuria over 3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminemia and generalized edema
Massive selective proteinuria without any hematuria
Isolated lipiduria with oval fat bodies and no hematuria
questions.concept: Nephritic syndrome reflects glomerular inflammation: hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts, oliguria, hypertension and mild-to-moderate (sub-nephrotic) proteinuria. Nephrotic syndrome, by contrast, is defined by proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia/lipiduria.
questions.reference: Robbins Basic Pathology — The Kidney and Its Collecting System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child develops acute nephritic syndrome about two weeks after impetigo. Which finding best supports poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis and its typically favorable prognosis?
options: Raised anti-DNase B / ASO titer with a low C3 that normalizes in about 8 weeks
Linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane
Persistently low C3 lasting beyond 3 months
questions.concept: Poststreptococcal GN follows pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo) by 1-3 weeks. Evidence of recent streptococcal infection (raised ASO or anti-DNase B) with a transiently low C3 that recovers within about 8 weeks supports the diagnosis. Prognosis is excellent in children; EM shows subepithelial 'humps'.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child has persistent hypocomplementemia and nephritic features; renal biopsy shows ribbon-like, intensely electron-dense deposits within the glomerular basement membrane itself. This finding is most associated with which autoantibody?
questions.concept: Dense deposit disease (formerly MPGN type II, now a C3 glomerulopathy) shows dense intramembranous deposits transforming the lamina densa into a ribbon. It is driven by C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase, causing unregulated complement consumption and persistently very low C3.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 3-year-old child presents with a large, smooth, unilateral abdominal mass that does not cross the midline, along with hematuria and hypertension. Histology shows a triphasic pattern of blastemal, primitive epithelial (tubular) and stromal elements. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) is the commonest primary renal malignancy of childhood, peaking at 2-5 years, and is associated with WT1 mutations (WAGR, Denys-Drash) and WT2/Beckwith-Wiedemann. It forms a triphasic blastemal-epithelial-stromal mass. Neuroblastoma, its main mimic, characteristically crosses the midline and encases vessels.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy stained with Congo red shows mesangial and vascular deposits that display apple-green birefringence under polarized light. These deposits are:
questions.concept: Renal amyloidosis (AA type in chronic inflammation such as rheumatoid arthritis; AL type in plasma-cell dyscrasias) deposits beta-pleated-sheet protein in the mesangium and vessel walls, causing nephrotic syndrome. Congo red staining is pathognomonic, showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: What is the earliest clinical indicator of diabetic nephropathy?
questions.concept: The earliest clinically detectable sign of diabetic nephropathy is microalbuminuria (urinary albumin 30-300 mg/day), reflecting early glomerular injury before overt proteinuria or a rise in creatinine. Structurally, GBM thickening and mesangial expansion precede the nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions; ACE inhibitors/ARBs are renoprotective at this stage.
questions.reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Diabetic Nephropathy

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower legs, colicky abdominal pain, arthralgia and hematuria following a viral illness. Skin and renal mesangial biopsies show deposition of which immunoglobulin?
questions.concept: Henoch-Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) is the most common systemic vasculitis of childhood. IgA immune-complex deposition in small vessels and the glomerular mesangium produces the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal (GI) pain and glomerulonephritis; the renal lesion is histologically identical to IgA nephropathy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease — The Kidney

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which is the most common cause of the nephrotic syndrome in children?
questions.concept: Minimal change disease accounts for the majority of nephrotic syndrome in children. It produces highly selective proteinuria, responds dramatically to corticosteroids, shows normal light microscopy, and reveals only diffuse podocyte foot-process effacement on electron microscopy. Membranous nephropathy predominates in adults.
questions.reference: Robbins Basic Pathology — The Kidney and Its Collecting System

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has 'oval fat bodies' in the urine that display a 'Maltese cross' appearance under polarized light. This finding reflects urinary loss of which substance?
questions.concept: Heavy glomerular protein loss in nephrotic syndrome is accompanied by hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria. Filtered lipoproteins are taken up by tubular cells and shed as 'oval fat bodies' and fatty casts; under polarized light the cholesterol esters produce the characteristic 'Maltese cross' birefringence. This confirms the lipiduria of nephrotic syndrome rather than loss of red cells or immunoglobulins.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which glomerular disease is now the most common cause of primary (idiopathic) nephrotic syndrome in adults, especially among African-Americans?
questions.concept: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) has become the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults, particularly among African-Americans, and its incidence is rising. Membranous nephropathy is the classic cause in older Caucasian adults, whereas minimal change disease predominates in children. FSGS shows sclerosis of segments of some glomeruli with foot-process effacement and is frequently steroid-resistant.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is newly diagnosed with membranous nephropathy on renal biopsy. In an adult of this age, which underlying condition most importantly needs to be actively excluded as a secondary cause?
options: An occult solid-organ malignancy (e.g., lung or colon carcinoma)
questions.concept: Membranous nephropathy is primary (anti-PLA2R antibody mediated) in about three-quarters of cases, but in an older adult secondary causes must be sought — above all an occult solid-organ malignancy (lung, colon, breast, prostate), plus infections such as hepatitis B, autoimmune disease (SLE) and drugs (NSAIDs, penicillamine, gold). Age-appropriate cancer screening is therefore indicated in a newly diagnosed older patient.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, the crescents that fill Bowman's space are composed predominantly of which elements?
options: Proliferating parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages, with fibrin
questions.concept: In rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis, breaks in the glomerular capillary wall let fibrin and plasma proteins into Bowman's space, triggering proliferation of parietal epithelial cells together with infiltrating monocytes/macrophages to form cellular crescents that compress the tuft. If untreated they organise into fibrous crescents with irreversible loss of function. Crescents are the histological hallmark whatever the immunologic type (I anti-GBM, II immune-complex, III pauci-immune).
questions.reference: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology, 7th ed., Ch. 22 (The Kidney and Lower Urinary Tract)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient presents with a nephritic picture. Which of the following is characteristically associated with a NORMAL serum complement (C3) level, helping distinguish it from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
questions.concept: Serum complement helps classify glomerulonephritis. Normocomplementaemic (normal C3) nephritides include IgA nephropathy, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, ANCA-associated pauci-immune GN and Alport syndrome. Hypocomplementaemic (low C3) causes include post-streptococcal GN, membranoproliferative GN/dense deposit disease, lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinaemia and endocarditis-associated GN. A normal C3 in a nephritic patient therefore points away from PSGN toward IgA nephropathy.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: In diabetic nephropathy, what is the earliest detectable histological (structural) glomerular change, appearing before the pathognomonic Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules?
options: Diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with mesangial matrix expansion
Cellular crescent formation in Bowman's space
Wire-loop lesions of the capillary loops
questions.concept: The earliest structural glomerular lesion of diabetic nephropathy is diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, detectable within a couple of years of disease onset, accompanied by progressive mesangial matrix expansion. Only later do the pathognomonic nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions and hyaline arteriolosclerosis appear. Clinically the earliest marker is microalbuminuria, but histologically the earliest change is GBM thickening.
questions.reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th ed., Ch. 20 (The Kidney)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase enzyme. Once activated, its bactericidal effect is due to inhibition of the synthesis of which cell-wall component of Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.concept: Isoniazid is activated by catalase-peroxidase (KatG); the active species inhibits InhA (enoyl-ACP reductase) and KasA, blocking synthesis of mycolic acids — the long-chain fatty acids essential to the mycobacterial cell wall — which is why it is bactericidal against actively dividing bacilli. Arabinogalactan synthesis is blocked by ethambutol (arabinosyl transferase), peptidoglycan is the target of beta-lactams and cycloserine, and lipoarabinomannan is not the isoniazid target.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antitubercular Drugs (Isoniazid); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Antimycobacterial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 34-year-old man on maintenance phenytoin for epilepsy is started on standard antitubercular therapy. Two weeks later he develops nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, and a raised serum phenytoin level. Which antitubercular drug most likely precipitated this?
questions.concept: Isoniazid inhibits several cytochrome P450 isoenzymes (CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, CYP2E1) and thereby slows the metabolism of phenytoin and carbamazepine, raising their plasma levels and causing toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, sedation), an effect greatest in slow acetylators. Rifampicin does the opposite — it is a potent enzyme inducer that LOWERS phenytoin levels — while ethambutol and pyrazinamide are not clinically significant CYP inhibitors of phenytoin.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Isoniazid (drug interactions); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Chemotherapy of Tuberculosis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on antitubercular therapy develops arthralgia, malaise, and a rash; investigations show positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-histone antibodies, suggesting a drug-induced lupus-like syndrome. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.concept: Isoniazid is a classic cause of a drug-induced lupus (SLE-like) syndrome, characterized by arthralgia, positive ANA, and anti-histone antibodies, and is more frequent in slow acetylators; procainamide and hydralazine are the other textbook culprits. Ethambutol (optic neuritis), streptomycin (ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity), and pyrazinamide (hyperuricemia/hepatotoxicity) do not produce a lupus-like autoimmune syndrome, making isoniazid the answer.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Isoniazid (adverse effects); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Antimycobacterial Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The dose-independent hepatocellular injury caused by isoniazid is attributed chiefly to which mechanism?
options: Accumulation of pyrazinoic acid in hepatocytes
Formation of an insoluble iron-drug chelate
Generation of toxic acetylhydrazine and hydrazine metabolites
questions.concept: Isoniazid hepatotoxicity is attributed to reactive metabolites — acetylhydrazine and hydrazine — generated during acetylation and hydrolysis, which cause hepatocellular necrosis; risk rises with age, chronic alcohol use, pre-existing liver disease, and concurrent rifampicin (an inducer). Pyrazinoic acid is the active metabolite of pyrazinamide, iron chelation is not an isoniazid mechanism, and ATP synthase inhibition is the mechanism of bedaquiline, not a cause of hepatic injury.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Chemotherapy of Tuberculosis (isoniazid toxicity); KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Pyridoxine is co-administered with isoniazid to prevent an adverse effect. By which mechanism does isoniazid create the underlying vitamin deficiency?
options: It increases pyridoxine excretion and forms inactive hydrazones with pyridoxal phosphate
It chelates calcium in the gut lumen
It induces folate deficiency by blocking dihydrofolate reductase
questions.concept: Isoniazid increases urinary excretion of pyridoxine and forms hydrazone complexes with pyridoxal phosphate, producing a functional vitamin B6 deficiency that manifests as peripheral neuropathy; prophylactic pyridoxine (about 10 mg/day) prevents this, especially in diabetics, alcoholics, pregnant women, the malnourished, and slow acetylators. Isoniazid inhibits (does not induce) CYP enzymes, does not chelate calcium, and does not act on dihydrofolate reductase (that is trimethoprim/methotrexate).
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Isoniazid (pyridoxine prophylaxis); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Rifampicin exerts its bactericidal action against Mycobacterium tuberculosis by inhibiting which bacterial enzyme?
questions.concept: Rifampicin binds the beta-subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (encoded by rpoB), blocking initiation of RNA synthesis (transcription); it is bactericidal against both intracellular and extracellular organisms, and resistance results from rpoB point mutations. DNA gyrase is inhibited by fluoroquinolones, dihydrofolate reductase by trimethoprim/pyrimethamine, and arabinosyl transferase by ethambutol — none of which is rifampicin's target.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Rifampicin (mechanism); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill is started on rifampicin-containing therapy and becomes pregnant despite reporting good compliance. What is the mechanism of this contraceptive failure?
options: Rifampicin displaces estrogen from plasma-protein binding sites
Rifampicin inhibits intestinal absorption of the contraceptive
Rifampicin induces hepatic CYP3A4, increasing metabolism of estrogen and progestin
Rifampicin acts as a progesterone-receptor antagonist
questions.concept: Rifampicin is among the most potent inducers of hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 (and P-glycoprotein), accelerating metabolism of estrogens and progestins and reducing contraceptive efficacy, so additional or alternative contraception must be advised. The same induction lowers levels of warfarin, HIV protease inhibitors, sulfonylureas, ciclosporin, and many other drugs. It does not act by protein displacement, absorption blockade, or receptor antagonism.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Rifampicin (enzyme induction, interactions); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on antitubercular therapy is alarmed by orange-red discoloration of his urine, tears, and sweat. Which drug is responsible and what is the appropriate advice?
options: Rifampicin; it is harmless but may permanently stain soft contact lenses
questions.concept: Rifampicin and its metabolites impart a harmless orange-red colour to urine, sweat, tears, sputum, and saliva; patients should be reassured but warned that soft contact lenses can be permanently stained. It is not a marker of toxicity, so the drug is continued. Ethambutol, pyrazinamide, and isoniazid do not cause this discoloration, and none of the alarming interpretations in the other options is correct.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Rifampicin (adverse effects); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Rifampicin can cause a flu-like syndrome with fever, chills, and occasionally thrombocytopenia. Reason (R): These immunoallergic, antibody-mediated reactions occur more often with intermittent or high-dose rifampicin than with regular daily dosing. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Rifampicin's flu-like syndrome (fever, chills, myalgia) and the less common thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and acute interstitial nephritis are immunoallergic reactions mediated by anti-rifampicin antibodies; these develop far more readily with intermittent, irregular, or high-dose therapy than with steady daily dosing. Both statements are therefore true and causally linked, so R correctly explains A, giving option A.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Rifampicin (intermittent-dose reactions); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An HIV-positive patient on a ritonavir-boosted protease-inhibitor regimen requires treatment for tuberculosis. Which rifamycin is preferred to minimize drug interactions, and why?
options: Rifampicin, because it is the least inducing of the rifamycins
Rifabutin, because it is a weaker inducer of CYP3A4 than rifampicin
Rifapentine, because it has no effect on CYP450 enzymes
Rifampicin at double dose, to overcome its own induction
questions.concept: Rifabutin is a weaker inducer of CYP3A4 than rifampicin, so it causes less reduction in protease-inhibitor plasma levels and is preferred (often with dose adjustment) in patients on PI-based antiretroviral therapy. Rifampicin is the MOST potent inducer of the rifamycins, not the least; rifapentine is a long-acting rifamycin that still induces CYP3A4; and simply doubling rifampicin does not resolve the interaction and risks toxicity.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Rifamycins (rifabutin in HIV); KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug that is especially effective against semi-dormant intracellular bacilli. Its activation and antibacterial activity depend on which of the following?
options: Activation by KatG, with activity confined to alkaline pH
Direct inhibition of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
Conversion to pyrazinoic acid by pyrazinamidase, with activity at acidic pH
Irreversible binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit
questions.concept: Pyrazinamide is converted to its active form pyrazinoic acid by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase/nicotinamidase (encoded by pncA), and is most active in the acidic environment inside macrophages and inflamed tissue, where it kills semi-dormant intracellular bacilli; this sterilizing action allowed shortening of therapy to 6 months, and resistance arises from pncA mutations. KatG activates isoniazid, RNA polymerase is rifampicin's target, and the 30S subunit is the aminoglycoside target.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Pyrazinamide (mechanism, sterilizing action); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Pyrazinamide therapy increases the renal excretion of uric acid. Reason (R): The active metabolite pyrazinoic acid inhibits renal tubular secretion of urate. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Pyrazinamide characteristically causes hyperuricemia precisely because its active metabolite pyrazinoic acid INHIBITS renal tubular secretion of urate, thereby DECREASING (not increasing) uric acid excretion — so the Assertion is false while the Reason is true, giving option D. The retained urate may be asymptomatic or precipitate gout/arthralgia; humans lack functional uricase, and pyrazinamide neither induces xanthine oxidase nor increases purine synthesis.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Pyrazinamide (hyperuricemia); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ethambutol is a bacteriostatic antitubercular agent added mainly to prevent emergence of resistance. It acts by inhibiting which target?
questions.concept: Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferases (encoded by the embCAB operon; resistance via embB mutations), blocking polymerization of arabinose into the arabinogalactan of the mycobacterial cell wall; it is bacteriostatic and is combined with other drugs chiefly to retard resistance. Mycolic acid synthesis is isoniazid's target, ATP synthase is bedaquiline's, and folate synthesis is inhibited by dapsone/sulfonamides — not by ethambutol.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Ethambutol (mechanism); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which statement about ethambutol dosing and monitoring is correct?
options: It is chiefly hepatically metabolized, so no dose change is needed in renal impairment
It is largely excreted unchanged by the kidney, so the dose is reduced in renal impairment, and visual acuity and red-green colour vision must be monitored
It is absolutely contraindicated in all adults over 60 years of age
Its optic toxicity is dose-independent and always irreversible
questions.concept: Ethambutol is largely excreted unchanged by the kidney, so the dose must be reduced (or the interval extended) in renal impairment to avoid accumulation and optic neuritis. Its dose-related retrobulbar/optic neuritis is usually reversible if detected early, so baseline and periodic visual acuity and red-green colour discrimination testing are recommended, and it is avoided in young children who cannot report visual changes. It is not primarily hepatic, not contraindicated by age alone, and toxicity is dose-related, not dose-independent.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Ethambutol (excretion, ocular monitoring); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Streptomycin and amikacin act against mycobacteria by binding to which target, producing which effect?
options: The 50S ribosomal subunit, halting peptide-bond formation
DNA gyrase, causing DNA strand breaks
The 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA
questions.concept: Aminoglycosides (streptomycin, amikacin, kanamycin) bind irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of the genetic code and inhibition of protein synthesis; they are bactericidal and act mainly on extracellular organisms. Streptomycin resistance is due to rpsL (S12 protein) or rrs (16S rRNA) mutations. Linezolid and macrolides act on the 50S subunit, fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase, and rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Streptomycin/Aminoglycosides (mechanism); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Streptomycin is considered safe for use throughout pregnancy. Reason (R): Aminoglycosides cross the placenta and can damage the fetal eighth cranial nerve, causing congenital deafness. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Streptomycin is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy, so the Assertion is false; it is not safe. The Reason is true — aminoglycosides cross the placenta and are ototoxic to the fetus, damaging cranial nerve VIII and causing irreversible congenital deafness. Because A is false while R is true, the answer is D. In adults, streptomycin additionally causes vestibular greater than cochlear toxicity and dose-related nephrotoxicity.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Streptomycin (toxicity, pregnancy); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Bedaquiline, used in multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, has a novel mechanism of action and one notable cardiac adverse effect. Which pairing is correct?
options: Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase; QT-interval prolongation
questions.concept: Bedaquiline is a diarylquinoline that inhibits the mycobacterial ATP synthase (atpE), depleting cellular ATP; its principal safety concerns are QT-interval prolongation — so it is used cautiously with other QT-prolonging agents such as moxifloxacin and clofazimine, with ECG monitoring — and hepatotoxicity, and it has a very long terminal half-life. The other mechanism/adverse-effect pairings describe fluoroquinolones, rifampicin, and aminoglycosides respectively.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Antimycobacterial Drugs (bedaquiline); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on prolonged linezolid therapy for extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis develops progressive numbness of the feet and pancytopenia. Which additional caution is specifically relevant to linezolid?
options: It is a potent inducer of CYP3A4
It is a reversible non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor, risking serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis with serotonergic drugs or tyramine-rich foods
It chelates with dietary calcium, reducing absorption
It causes harmless orange discoloration of the urine
questions.concept: Linezolid (an oxazolidinone that binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and blocks formation of the initiation complex) causes dose- and duration-dependent myelosuppression (thrombocytopenia, anemia, pancytopenia) and peripheral and optic neuropathy with prolonged use; it is also a reversible non-selective MAO inhibitor, so combining it with SSRIs or tyramine-rich foods risks serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis. It is not a CYP inducer, does not chelate calcium (that is tetracyclines/fluoroquinolones), and does not colour urine (that is rifampicin).
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Oxazolidinones (linezolid); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A second-line antitubercular drug frequently causes neuropsychiatric toxicity (seizures, psychosis, depression) and is routinely given with pyridoxine. By which mechanism does it act?
options: It inhibits mycolic acid synthesis after KatG activation
It inhibits alanine racemase and D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase, blocking cell-wall synthesis
questions.concept: Cycloserine is a structural analogue of D-alanine that inhibits alanine racemase and D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase, blocking peptidoglycan (cell-wall) synthesis. Its dose-limiting toxicity is neuropsychiatric — headache, tremor, psychosis, depression, suicidal ideation, and seizures — so pyridoxine is co-administered and it is avoided in patients with epilepsy, psychiatric illness, or alcoholism. The other mechanisms describe isoniazid, macrolides/linezolid, and ethambutol respectively.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Cycloserine (mechanism, CNS toxicity); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: In multidrug-resistant tuberculosis regimens a later-generation fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin or levofloxacin is a core drug. Which mechanism-of-action and class adverse-effect pairing is correct?
options: Inhibits RNA polymerase; harmless red urine
Inhibits folic acid synthesis; oxidative hemolysis
Inhibits DNA gyrase/topoisomerase; tendinopathy and QT-interval prolongation
questions.concept: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV and are core second-line/MDR-TB agents; recognized class adverse effects include tendinitis and tendon rupture, QT-interval prolongation (moxifloxacin greater than levofloxacin), dysglycemia, and CNS effects. Moxifloxacin's QT effect is especially important when combined with bedaquiline or clofazimine. The distractor mechanisms describe rifampicin, bedaquiline, and dapsone/sulfonamides respectively.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Fluoroquinolones and Antimycobacterial Drugs; KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Dapsone, a mainstay of multidrug therapy for leprosy, is bacteriostatic against Mycobacterium leprae because it inhibits which target?
options: Dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis
questions.concept: Dapsone is a sulfone that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis in M. leprae — the same folate pathway targeted by sulfonamides — and is bacteriostatic; it is combined with rifampicin (bactericidal, via RNA polymerase) and clofazimine in WHO multidrug therapy. RNA polymerase inhibition is rifampicin's mechanism, arabinosyl transferase is ethambutol's, and mycolic acid synthesis is isoniazid's — none is dapsone's target.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antileprotic Drugs (Dapsone); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient started on dapsone for leprosy develops fatigue, dark urine, and a falling hemoglobin, and is subsequently found to be G6PD-deficient. Which pair of adverse effects best characterizes dapsone?
options: Megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency
Iron-deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss
questions.concept: Dapsone characteristically causes dose-related hemolytic anemia — severe in G6PD deficiency — and methemoglobinemia, both driven by its oxidant hydroxylamine metabolite, so screening for G6PD deficiency is advised before therapy. It can also cause the 'dapsone syndrome' (fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia). It does not cause megaloblastic or iron-deficiency anemia, and agranulocytosis, although reported, is uncommon and is not the oxidant mechanism producing this presentation.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Dapsone (adverse effects, G6PD); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on multidrug therapy for lepromatous leprosy notices progressive reddish-brown to black discoloration of the skin. Which drug is responsible?
questions.concept: Clofazimine, a riminophenazine dye that binds mycobacterial DNA and also has an anti-inflammatory action useful in erythema nodosum leprosum, causes dose-dependent reddish-brown to black discoloration of the skin, along with conjunctival, urinary, and secretion pigmentation, plus dryness/ichthyosis and gastrointestinal disturbance. Rifampicin colours secretions orange-red (not the skin black), dapsone causes hemolysis, and ethionamide causes gastrointestinal upset — none produces this characteristic pigmentation.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antileprotic Drugs (Clofazimine); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A second-line antitubercular drug that is structurally related to isoniazid causes marked gastrointestinal intolerance and, with prolonged use, hypothyroidism with goitre as well as hepatotoxicity. Which drug is this?
questions.concept: Ethionamide is a thioamide structurally related to isoniazid; like isoniazid it inhibits mycolic acid synthesis (InhA) after activation by EthA. Its major adverse effects are severe gastrointestinal intolerance (nausea, vomiting, metallic taste), hepatotoxicity, and, on prolonged use, hypothyroidism with goitre (it inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis) plus peripheral neuropathy (pyridoxine is given). PAS also causes GI upset and hypothyroidism but is not an isoniazid structural analogue; capreomycin is an ototoxic/nephrotoxic polypeptide; cycloserine causes neuropsychiatric toxicity.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Ethionamide (structure, adverse effects); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Phenytoin and carbamazepine control focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures largely through a common molecular action. Which mechanism do they principally share?
options: Enhancement of GABA-A receptor chloride currents
Use-dependent (frequency-dependent) blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels, prolonging their inactivated state
Blockade of T-type calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons
Competitive antagonism of the NMDA glutamate receptor
questions.concept: Phenytoin and carbamazepine stabilise the inactivated conformation of voltage-gated Na channels in a use-dependent manner, selectively suppressing high-frequency repetitive firing while sparing normal transmission, which controls focal and tonic-clonic seizures. Option A describes benzodiazepines/barbiturates, option C describes ethosuximide acting on thalamic T-type Ca channels underlying absence seizures, and option D describes drugs such as felbamate/perampanel-type glutamate modulation, none of which is the shared primary action here.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antiepileptic Drugs (mechanisms)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Levetiracetam is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic whose novel target is distinct from that of the older sodium- and calcium-channel drugs. Its principal molecular target is:
options: The synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A), modulating vesicular neurotransmitter release
The alpha2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels
Prolongation of GABA-A chloride channel opening duration
questions.concept: Levetiracetam binds the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, altering calcium-dependent vesicular neurotransmitter release and dampening abnormal synchronised discharge; this unique mechanism explains its broad spectrum and relative lack of enzyme interactions. Option B is vigabatrin, option C is gabapentin/pregabalin, and option D is the barbiturate action on the GABA-A chloride channel. None of these describes SV2A binding, which is the defining feature of levetiracetam and its analogue brivaracetam.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th ed — Pharmacotherapy of the Epilepsies

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Gabapentin and pregabalin are structural analogues of GABA, yet they do not act on GABA receptors. Their anticonvulsant and analgesic effect is mediated mainly by binding to:
options: The alpha2-delta subunit of voltage-gated (presynaptic) calcium channels, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release
T-type calcium channels of thalamic neurons
questions.concept: Despite being GABA analogues, gabapentin and pregabalin do not bind GABA receptors or affect GABA uptake; they bind the alpha2-delta auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated Ca channels, reducing presynaptic Ca influx and release of glutamate and other excitatory transmitters, which underlies their use in focal seizures and neuropathic pain. Option A is levetiracetam, option B is vigabatrin, and option D (T-type Ca) is ethosuximide, none of which is the alpha2-delta target of the gabapentinoids.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Antiseizure Drugs (gabapentin, pregabalin)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is newly diagnosed with focal (partial) seizures with impaired awareness and no comorbidities. Which of the following is a classical first-line monotherapy for this seizure type?
questions.concept: Carbamazepine is a long-standing first-line drug for focal (partial) seizures with or without secondary generalization (levetiracetam and lamotrigine are modern alternatives). Ethosuximide is effective only in absence seizures and does not control focal seizures. Vigabatrin is reserved for infantile spasms/refractory focal use because of irreversible visual-field toxicity. Gabapentin is a weak add-on agent, not a preferred first-line monotherapy, making carbamazepine the best answer here.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Choice of drugs for seizure types

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient started on an antiepileptic reports tingling of the fingers, difficulty finding words, unexpected weight loss, and later develops a renal calculus. This adverse-effect cluster is most characteristic of which drug?
questions.concept: Topiramate causes paraesthesias, cognitive slowing with word-finding difficulty, weight loss, and (via carbonic-anhydrase inhibition) renal calculi and metabolic acidosis, plus a risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma; this profile fits option A. Phenytoin classically gives gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism, valproate causes weight gain, tremor and alopecia, and vigabatrin causes irreversible visual-field constriction, so options B, C and D do not match the described cluster.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Topiramate adverse effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A stable patient's phenytoin dose is raised from 300 mg to 400 mg/day; the plasma level rises disproportionately from 12 to 28 mcg/mL and he develops nystagmus and ataxia. Which pharmacokinetic property best explains this?
options: First-order elimination with a very short half-life
Saturation (zero-order, Michaelis-Menten) kinetics once metabolizing enzymes are saturated at therapeutic doses
Autoinduction of its own hepatic metabolism lowering plasma levels
questions.concept: Phenytoin's metabolizing enzymes saturate within the therapeutic range, so elimination switches from first-order to zero-order (Michaelis-Menten) kinetics; small dose increases then cause disproportionate, non-linear rises in plasma level and dose-dependent toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia). Option A is wrong because saturation, not a short half-life, drives the jump; option C is not a phenytoin feature; option D (autoinduction) applies to carbamazepine and would lower, not raise, levels.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Phenytoin pharmacokinetics (dose-dependent elimination)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman on carbamazepine for focal seizures becomes confused; serum sodium is 121 mmol/L with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Renal tubular acidosis induced by the drug
Cerebral salt wasting caused by hepatic enzyme induction
Hyponatremia due to a SIADH-like antidiuretic effect of carbamazepine
questions.concept: Carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine, more so) potentiates ADH action on the collecting duct, producing an SIADH-like syndrome with hypo-osmolar hyponatremia and inappropriately concentrated urine, especially in the elderly; this matches option C. It does not cause renal tubular acidosis (A) or cerebral salt wasting (B), and the low osmolality excludes pseudohyponatremia from hyperlipidemia (D). Management is fluid restriction and dose reduction or switching agents.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Carbamazepine adverse effects (hyponatremia)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): During the first few weeks of carbamazepine therapy its plasma level rises progressively because the drug inhibits its own metabolism. Reason (R): Carbamazepine is an inducer of hepatic CYP3A4. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is false: carbamazepine induces (does not inhibit) its own metabolism, so plasma levels fall and half-life shortens over the first 2-4 weeks (autoinduction), often requiring an upward dose adjustment. The reason is true: carbamazepine is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 (and other enzymes), which is exactly why autoinduction occurs and why it lowers levels of co-administered drugs such as oral contraceptives. Hence A is false while R is true, giving option D.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Carbamazepine (autoinduction)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Valproate (sodium valproate) is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic effective against focal, tonic-clonic, absence and myoclonic seizures. This wide spectrum is best explained by which mechanistic feature?
options: It has multiple actions: blockade of voltage-gated Na channels, reduction of T-type Ca currents, and enhancement of GABAergic transmission
Selective binding to the SV2A vesicle protein only
Irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase as its sole action
Pure blockade of thalamic T-type calcium channels only
questions.concept: Valproate's broad spectrum arises from several combined actions: use-dependent Na channel blockade, attenuation of T-type Ca currents, and augmentation of GABA (partly by inhibiting its degradation and enhancing synthesis); this multiplicity lets it cover focal, generalized tonic-clonic, absence and myoclonic seizures. Option B is levetiracetam's single target, option C describes vigabatrin, and option D describes ethosuximide, each of which is narrower and does not capture valproate's multimodal profile.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Valproic acid (mechanisms and spectrum)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An 18-month-old child on valproate plus another antiepileptic develops vomiting, increasing lethargy and encephalopathy; ammonia is markedly elevated with only mildly raised transaminases. Which statement is correct?
options: A Reye-like hepatic reaction is essentially impossible with valproate
Valproate can cause dose-independent (idiosyncratic) hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemic encephalopathy, with greatest risk in children under 2 years on polytherapy
This picture is simply expected CYP enzyme induction and needs no action
Valproate produces this by folate antagonism causing megaloblastic anemia
questions.concept: Valproate can cause idiosyncratic, dose-independent hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemic encephalopathy; both risks are highest in children under two years on polytherapy or with underlying metabolic/mitochondrial disease, and the clinical picture demands stopping the drug and checking ammonia and liver function. Option A is false (fatal hepatotoxicity is a recognised hazard), option C wrongly dismisses a dangerous reaction, and option D describes phenytoin's folate-related megaloblastic anemia, not this presentation.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Valproate hepatotoxicity and hyperammonemia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Regarding vigabatrin, which statement correctly links its mechanism to its hallmark serious toxicity?
options: It binds SV2A and characteristically causes renal calculi
It is a reversible GABA reuptake inhibitor and is free of ocular toxicity
It irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase, raising CNS GABA, and can cause irreversible concentric visual-field constriction
It blocks T-type calcium channels and typically causes hyponatremia
questions.concept: Vigabatrin (gamma-vinyl-GABA) irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase, the enzyme that degrades GABA, thereby raising synaptic GABA; its defining serious toxicity is irreversible, often permanent, concentric peripheral visual-field constriction requiring periodic perimetry, which limits it to infantile spasms and refractory focal seizures. Option A confuses SV2A/topiramate features, option B wrongly calls it a reversible reuptake inhibitor without ocular risk (that is tiagabine), and option D describes ethosuximide/carbamazepine features.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Vigabatrin (mechanism, visual field defects)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
