questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant has clusters of sudden flexor (salaam) spasms and the EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Which is an appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy for this syndrome?
options: ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) or vigabatrin, the latter especially if tuberous sclerosis is present
questions.concept: This is West syndrome (infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia); first-line therapy is hormonal (ACTH or oral corticosteroids) or vigabatrin, with vigabatrin particularly favoured when tuberous sclerosis is the underlying cause, making option D correct. Ethosuximide (absence only), carbamazepine and phenytoin (focal/tonic-clonic Na-channel drugs) are ineffective for infantile spasms and carbamazepine may even aggravate certain generalized epilepsies, so options A, B and C are inappropriate.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Infantile spasms (ACTH, vigabatrin)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman on a combined oral contraceptive becomes pregnant while taking an antiepileptic drug for focal seizures. Which drug most likely caused contraceptive failure through hepatic enzyme induction?
questions.concept: Carbamazepine is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 and UGT enzymes, accelerating metabolism of the ethinylestradiol/progestin in oral contraceptives and lowering their plasma levels, a classic cause of contraceptive failure (other enzyme inducers are phenytoin, phenobarbitone and topiramate at higher doses). Valproate is an enzyme inhibitor, and levetiracetam and gabapentin are not clinically significant inducers, so options B, C and D would not typically compromise contraceptive efficacy.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs and oral contraceptive interactions

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: In a patient needing parenteral phenytoin loading, fosphenytoin is often chosen instead of intravenous phenytoin. What is the main advantage of fosphenytoin?
options: It is available only for oral use, improving adherence
It is a water-soluble prodrug that can also be given intramuscularly and produces less infusion-site injury (e.g. purple glove syndrome) than IV phenytoin
It has no active anticonvulsant metabolite
Intravenous phenytoin is preferred because it is water-soluble and pH-neutral
questions.concept: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble phosphate ester prodrug rapidly converted to phenytoin in vivo; because it avoids the strongly alkaline propylene-glycol vehicle of IV phenytoin, it can be given IM and causes far less venous irritation, hypotension and local tissue injury such as purple glove syndrome, making option B correct. Option A is false (it is parenteral), option C is false (phenytoin is its active metabolite), and option D is wrong because IV phenytoin is highly alkaline and poorly water-soluble.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Fosphenytoin (prodrug advantages)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Phenobarbitone potentiates GABAergic inhibition at the GABA-A receptor. Compared with benzodiazepines, its principal effect on the chloride channel is to:
options: Increase the frequency of chloride channel opening events
Prolong the duration of chloride channel opening, and at high concentrations directly open the channel
questions.concept: Barbiturates such as phenobarbitone increase the duration of GABA-A chloride channel opening (and at high concentrations can open the channel directly, independent of GABA), whereas benzodiazepines increase the frequency of opening; the direct action partly explains barbiturates' narrow safety margin and respiratory depression. Option A is the benzodiazepine effect, option B is levetiracetam's target, and option D is ethosuximide's action, none of which describes the barbiturate mechanism in option C.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Barbiturates and GABA-A receptor (duration vs frequency)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Lacosamide is a newer sodium-channel antiepileptic used as add-on therapy for focal seizures. Its mechanism differs from phenytoin/carbamazepine in that lacosamide:
options: Blocks the alpha2-delta calcium channel subunit
Enhances fast inactivation of sodium channels, identical to phenytoin
Binds the SV2A synaptic vesicle protein
Selectively enhances the slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels
questions.concept: Lacosamide selectively enhances the slow inactivation of voltage-gated Na channels, stabilising hyperexcitable neuronal membranes without markedly affecting fast inactivation, which distinguishes it from phenytoin and carbamazepine that act mainly on fast inactivation; a notable adverse effect is dose-dependent PR-interval prolongation. Option A is the gabapentinoid mechanism, option B misstates its action as fast inactivation, and option C is levetiracetam's SV2A target, so option D is correct.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Lacosamide (slow inactivation of sodium channels)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): After a single intravenous dose, diazepam has a rapid onset but a relatively short duration of anticonvulsant action in the brain. Reason (R): Diazepam is highly lipophilic, entering the CNS quickly and then rapidly redistributing from brain to peripheral tissues. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are true and R explains A: diazepam's high lipophilicity gives near-immediate CNS penetration and rapid seizure control, but the same lipophilicity causes swift redistribution out of the brain into fat and muscle, so the central anticonvulsant effect of a single IV dose wanes within minutes despite a long elimination half-life. This redistribution pharmacokinetics is why lorazepam (less lipophilic, longer CNS retention) is often preferred for sustained seizure control, making option A the correct choice.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Benzodiazepine pharmacokinetics (redistribution)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman with well-controlled epilepsy is planning pregnancy and needs to continue an antiepileptic. Considering comparative teratogenic risk, which monotherapy is generally regarded as among the safest choices?
questions.concept: Comparative registry data rank lamotrigine and levetiracetam among the lowest-risk antiepileptics in pregnancy, so they are preferred when monotherapy must continue, alongside folic acid supplementation. Valproate carries the highest risk (neural tube defects and impaired neurodevelopment) and is avoided; phenobarbitone is associated with cardiac and other malformations and neurodevelopmental effects; topiramate raises the risk of oral clefts and low birth weight. Hence option B is the safest listed choice.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Antiseizure drugs in pregnancy (teratogenicity ranking)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Chronic phenytoin therapy can produce megaloblastic anemia. Reason (R): Phenytoin causes vitamin B12 deficiency by blocking gastric intrinsic factor. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: long-term phenytoin can cause megaloblastic anemia. The reason is false: the mechanism is impaired folate absorption and altered folate metabolism leading to folate (not vitamin B12) deficiency, and phenytoin does not block intrinsic factor. Because a true assertion is paired with a false reason, the answer is option C; the correct teaching point is that folate, given judiciously, corrects the anemia (very high-dose folate may slightly reduce phenytoin levels).
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Phenytoin adverse effects (megaloblastic anemia, folate)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A hypoalbuminemic patient with chronic kidney disease on phenytoin has a total phenytoin level reported as 6 mcg/mL (reference 10-20) but shows clear signs of phenytoin toxicity. What is the best interpretation?
options: Total phenytoin reliably reflects free drug even in hypoalbuminemia, so toxicity is unrelated to phenytoin
The dose should be increased because the total level is subtherapeutic
Phenytoin is not protein-bound, so albumin is irrelevant to interpretation
In hypoalbuminemia/uraemia the unbound (free) fraction rises, so a low total level can correspond to a therapeutic or toxic free concentration; measure free phenytoin or apply a correction
questions.concept: Phenytoin is about 90% albumin-bound, and only the free fraction is pharmacologically active; in hypoalbuminemia and uraemia (which also displaces the drug), the free fraction rises so a low measured total level can hide a therapeutic or toxic free concentration. Therefore option D is correct: measure free phenytoin or use a correction (e.g. Sheiner-Tozer) rather than raising the dose. Options A and C are false about protein binding, and option B would dangerously worsen toxicity.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Phenytoin protein binding and therapeutic drug monitoring

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Tiagabine is an antiepileptic that augments GABAergic transmission. Its specific mechanism of action is:
options: Selective inhibition of the GAT-1 neuronal and glial GABA reuptake transporter, prolonging synaptic GABA action
Binding to the SV2A synaptic vesicle protein
Blockade of thalamic T-type calcium channels
questions.concept: Tiagabine selectively and reversibly inhibits the GAT-1 transporter that mediates neuronal and glial reuptake of GABA, thereby increasing and prolonging synaptic GABA concentration; it is used as adjunctive therapy for focal seizures. This differs from vigabatrin, which irreversibly inhibits the degrading enzyme GABA transaminase (option B); option C is levetiracetam's SV2A target, and option D is ethosuximide's T-type Ca channel action, so option A uniquely describes tiagabine's reuptake-inhibition mechanism.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Tiagabine (GAT-1 GABA reuptake inhibition)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Felbamate is an effective broad-spectrum antiepileptic but is used only in strictly selected patients. Which statement best explains its restricted role?
options: It is first-line for all focal seizures because of an outstanding safety profile
It is reserved for refractory epilepsy (such as Lennox-Gastaut syndrome) because of the risk of aplastic anemia and fulminant hepatic failure
It is contraindicated mainly because it causes gingival hyperplasia
It is a benzodiazepine used only for status epilepticus
questions.concept: Felbamate has broad efficacy (including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and refractory focal seizures) but carries a serious risk of aplastic anemia and fulminant hepatic failure, so it is reserved for refractory patients under close haematological and hepatic monitoring with informed consent, which makes option B correct. Option A ignores its toxicity, option C wrongly attributes phenytoin's gingival hyperplasia, and option D is false because felbamate is a dicarbamate, not a benzodiazepine.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's, 13th ed — Felbamate (aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, restricted use)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has lancinating unilateral facial pain triggered by chewing and touch, diagnosed as trigeminal neuralgia. Which drug-and-monitoring pairing is most appropriate?
options: Phenytoin; monitor primarily for megaloblastic anemia
Carbamazepine; monitor complete blood counts for aplastic anemia/agranulocytosis
questions.concept: Carbamazepine is the drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia, and because it can cause aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis (as well as hyponatremia and hepatotoxicity), baseline and periodic complete blood counts are advised, so option C pairs the correct drug with the correct monitoring. Option A pairs a non-first-line drug with the wrong emphasis, option B (gabapentin is second-line and does not typically cause stones) and option D (valproate is not first-line; visual-field monitoring belongs to vigabatrin) are incorrect.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Carbamazepine (trigeminal neuralgia, blood dyscrasias)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A teenager with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (myoclonic jerks plus generalized tonic-clonic seizures) is started on a sodium-channel blocker and paradoxically has more frequent myoclonus and new absence-like episodes. Which statement is correct?
options: Carbamazepine (and phenytoin/gabapentin) can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures and should be avoided in idiopathic generalized epilepsies such as JME
questions.concept: Narrow-spectrum Na-channel blockers such as carbamazepine, phenytoin and gabapentin can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures and are best avoided in idiopathic generalized epilepsies like juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, where valproate (or levetiracetam/lamotrigine) is preferred, making option D correct. Options A and B are false because valproate and levetiracetam control these seizure types, and option C is false because ethosuximide treats (does not worsen) absence seizures.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Seizure-type selection and aggravation by inappropriate antiseizure drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) is the alveolar concentration of an inhalational anaesthetic at 1 atmosphere that abolishes movement to a standard surgical (skin) incision in 50% of patients. Clinically, MAC is used as an index of the agent's:
questions.concept: MAC is inversely proportional to potency — a low MAC (halothane ~0.75%) marks a highly potent agent, whereas a high MAC (nitrous oxide >100%) marks a weak one. MAC correlates with the oil:gas partition coefficient (Meyer-Overton lipid-solubility rule), NOT with the blood:gas coefficient, which instead governs speed of induction and recovery. Metabolism of modern agents is minimal and does not define MAC. Hence potency (B) is the correct answer, and the other options describe unrelated properties.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — General Anaesthetics

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The MAC of an inhalational anaesthetic is lower in an elderly patient than in an infant. Reason (R): MAC rises progressively from infancy through to old age. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: MAC is highest in infancy (around 6 months) and declines steadily with advancing age, so the elderly need less anaesthetic — the Assertion is TRUE. The Reason is FALSE because it states the opposite trend; MAC does not increase toward old age, it decreases. MAC is also lowered by hypothermia, pregnancy, opioids, benzodiazepines, alpha-2 agonists and acute alcohol intake, and is raised by hyperthermia, chronic alcoholism and hypernatraemia. Since A is true but R is false, the answer is C.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — General Anaesthetics (MAC and factors affecting it)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: An inhalational anaesthetic with a LOW blood:gas partition coefficient (e.g. desflurane, nitrous oxide) is characterised by:
questions.concept: A low blood:gas coefficient means the agent is poorly soluble in blood, so blood is quickly 'saturated' and the alveolar (hence brain) partial pressure rises fast — giving rapid induction and, because wash-out is equally quick, rapid recovery. This coefficient controls SPEED, not potency (that is the oil:gas coefficient / MAC). Highly soluble agents like methoxyflurane and ether give slow induction. Metabolism and muscle relaxation are unrelated to blood solubility, so only B is correct.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — General Anesthetics (uptake and distribution)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: During induction, delivering a high concentration of nitrous oxide together with a volatile agent such as sevoflurane accelerates the rise of the volatile agent's alveolar concentration. This phenomenon is termed the:
questions.concept: The second gas effect: rapid, large-volume uptake of the high-concentration 'first gas' (nitrous oxide) into pulmonary blood shrinks alveolar gas volume, which concentrates the remaining 'second gas' (the volatile agent) and augments its inspiratory inflow — speeding its alveolar rise. It is a consequence of the concentration effect (which describes only the first gas itself). Diffusion hypoxia is the reverse process at emergence, and the Bohr effect concerns haemoglobin–oxygen affinity, so B is correct.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Inhalation Anesthetics (pharmacokinetics)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: At the end of a prolonged nitrous oxide anaesthetic, the patient is at risk of diffusion hypoxia. The most appropriate measure to prevent this is to:
options: Continue nitrous oxide at a low flow rate
Extubate immediately and leave the patient breathing room air
Administer 100% oxygen for the first few minutes after discontinuing nitrous oxide
Hyperventilate the patient with added carbon dioxide
questions.concept: When nitrous oxide is stopped, its large stored volume rapidly diffuses from blood back into the alveoli, diluting alveolar oxygen and CO2 and producing transient dilutional (diffusion) hypoxia. Delivering 100% oxygen for 3–5 minutes offsets this dilution and maintains arterial oxygenation. Continuing N2O or leaving the patient in room air worsens hypoxia, and adding CO2 is not indicated. Hence C is the correct preventive step; this risk is greatest after high-concentration, prolonged N2O use.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — General Anaesthetics (Nitrous oxide)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Prolonged or repeated exposure to nitrous oxide can cause megaloblastic anaemia and myeloneuropathy. This results from irreversible oxidation of the cobalt atom of vitamin B12, which inactivates:
questions.concept: Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt of cobalamin (Co+ to Co3+), inactivating methionine synthase, the B12-dependent enzyme that converts homocysteine to methionine and regenerates tetrahydrofolate from methyl-THF. The resulting 'folate trap' impairs DNA synthesis, causing megaloblastic bone-marrow changes, and chronic exposure produces subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is the other B12 enzyme but is not the mediator here; DHFR and thymidylate synthase are folate enzymes not directly oxidised by N2O — so A is correct.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th ed — General Anesthetics (Nitrous oxide toxicity)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The dose of adrenaline infiltrated into the surgical field should be strictly limited during halothane anaesthesia. Reason (R): Halothane sensitises the myocardium to the arrhythmogenic effects of catecholamines. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Halothane (more than other halogenated agents) sensitises the myocardium to catecholamines, so exogenous adrenaline can precipitate multifocal ventricular ectopics or ventricular tachycardia — this is exactly why the infiltrated adrenaline dose is capped during halothane. Both statements are true and the Reason directly and correctly explains the Assertion, so the answer is A. Halothane itself is a myocardial depressant, not a beta-agonist. Isoflurane and sevoflurane sensitise far less and are preferred when adrenaline is required.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — General Anaesthetics (Halothane, adverse effects)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Thiopentone (thiopental) is ABSOLUTELY contraindicated as an induction agent in a patient with which of the following conditions?
questions.concept: Barbiturates induce hepatic delta-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) synthase, boosting porphyrin-precursor synthesis and precipitating an acute, potentially fatal attack of acute intermittent porphyria (and variegate porphyria); thiopentone is therefore absolutely contraindicated, and propofol is the preferred alternative. This hazard is distinct from thiopentone's ultrashort action (due to redistribution) and its tendency to trigger laryngospasm/bronchospasm. Diabetes, anaemia and osteoarthritis are not contraindications, so A is correct.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — General Anaesthetics (Thiopentone sodium)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic property of propofol that distinguishes it from thiopentone?
options: It has a long elimination half-life with marked cumulation
questions.concept: Propofol has intrinsic anti-emetic action (useful against postoperative nausea and vomiting) and gives a smooth, rapid, clear-headed recovery, making it the induction agent of choice for day-care surgery and for maintenance by infusion (TIVA). It does NOT precipitate porphyria (indeed it is the safe substitute for thiopentone), is rapidly cleared without cumulation, and, like most IV anaesthetics, has essentially no analgesic effect. Its drawbacks are injection pain, dose-dependent hypotension/apnoea, egg-soy caution and propofol infusion syndrome — so D is correct.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — General Anesthetics (Propofol)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Propofol infusion syndrome, associated with prolonged high-dose propofol infusion (particularly in critically ill or paediatric patients), is characterised by:
options: Metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, hyperlipidaemia and cardiac failure
questions.concept: Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS) occurs with high-dose (>4 mg/kg/h), prolonged infusions and reflects impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, producing severe metabolic (lactic) acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia, hyperlipidaemia, hepatomegaly and refractory bradycardia/cardiac failure that can be fatal. Treatment is to stop propofol immediately and give supportive/haemodynamic care. The other options describe unrelated toxicities not caused by propofol, so A is the correct constellation.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Intravenous Anesthetics (Propofol)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ketamine is generally avoided in a patient with raised intracranial pressure or an open-globe (penetrating) eye injury because it:
options: Increases cerebral blood flow, intracranial pressure and intra-ocular pressure
Reduces cerebral metabolic rate and cerebral blood flow
questions.concept: Ketamine, a dissociative NMDA-receptor antagonist, is sympathomimetic — it raises blood pressure, heart rate, cerebral blood flow, ICP and intra-ocular pressure; hence caution in raised ICP and open-globe injuries. Because it supports blood pressure and relatively preserves airway reflexes and respiration, it is valuable in hypovolaemic shock and in asthmatics (bronchodilator). Its principal drawbacks are emergence delirium/hallucinations (reduced by benzodiazepines) and hypersalivation. Only B correctly states the ICP/IOP-raising effect.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — General Anaesthetics (Ketamine)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ketamine produces 'dissociative anaesthesia' primarily through antagonism at which receptor?
questions.concept: Ketamine is a non-competitive antagonist at the NMDA subtype of the glutamate receptor, producing a cataleptic 'dissociative' state — profound analgesia and amnesia with open eyes, nystagmus and preserved reflexes. GABA-A potentiation is the mechanism of thiopentone, propofol and benzodiazepines; mu-opioid agonism underlies morphine/fentanyl; alpha-2 agonism is the mechanism of dexmedetomidine and clonidine. Therefore NMDA-receptor blockade (C) is the correct answer for ketamine.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — General Anesthetics (Ketamine)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Etomidate is valued for its cardiovascular stability at induction, but even a single bolus can cause which of the following adverse effects?
questions.concept: Etomidate reversibly inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, suppressing cortisol and aldosterone synthesis; even a single induction dose blunts the adrenal stress response, and continuous infusion increased mortality in ICU patients — so it is used cautiously in sepsis. Its advantage is haemodynamic stability with minimal histamine release, making it useful in cardiac and shocked patients; other drawbacks are injection pain, myoclonus and postoperative nausea/vomiting. It is not a malignant-hyperthermia trigger and does not cause paralysis, so D is correct.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Intravenous Anesthetics (Etomidate)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A young, previously healthy patient given suxamethonium (succinylcholine) for a brief procedure fails to resume spontaneous breathing and remains paralysed for over an hour. The most likely cause is:
questions.concept: Suxamethonium is normally hydrolysed within minutes by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase). In patients with a genetically atypical or quantitatively deficient enzyme, hydrolysis is markedly slowed, producing prolonged apnoea ('scoline apnoea'), managed simply by continued mechanical ventilation until recovery. The dibucaine number identifies the atypical enzyme. Neostigmine would worsen (not cause) this by inhibiting cholinesterase. This scenario deliberately excludes the separate hyperkalaemia and malignant-hyperthermia hazards, so C is correct.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Skeletal Muscle Relaxants (Succinylcholine)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Atracurium is a suitable neuromuscular blocker in a patient with combined severe hepatic and renal failure. Reason (R): Atracurium is eliminated by Hofmann degradation, a process independent of hepatic and renal function. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Atracurium (and cisatracurium) undergo Hofmann elimination — spontaneous, non-enzymatic breakdown at physiological pH and temperature — plus ester hydrolysis, so clearance does not depend on the liver or kidney, making them ideal in organ failure. Both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, so the answer is A. A degradation product, laudanosine, can rarely cause CNS excitation. By contrast, vecuronium is largely biliary, pancuronium mainly renal and rocuronium chiefly hepatic, all accumulating in organ failure.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Skeletal Muscle Relaxants (non-depolarizing blockers)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: At the end of surgery, residual non-depolarizing neuromuscular block is reversed with neostigmine. Neostigmine is deliberately co-administered with glycopyrrolate (or atropine) in order to:
options: Prevent the muscarinic effects of neostigmine such as bradycardia and excess secretions
Prolong the action of the muscle relaxant
Reverse the central sedative effects of the general anaesthetic
questions.concept: Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, raising synaptic acetylcholine to out-compete the non-depolarizing (competitive) blocker at the nicotinic neuromuscular junction. However, the extra acetylcholine also floods muscarinic receptors, causing bradycardia, bronchospasm, salivation and gut hypermotility. An antimuscarinic — glycopyrrolate (preferred, as it does not cross the blood–brain barrier) or atropine — is given alongside to block these unwanted muscarinic effects while leaving the nicotinic reversal intact. It neither potentiates nor prolongs the block, so B is correct.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Skeletal Muscle Relaxants (reversal of blockade)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Sugammadex reverses neuromuscular blockade produced by rocuronium (and vecuronium) by which mechanism?
options: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
Encapsulating (chelating) the aminosteroid relaxant molecule in plasma
questions.concept: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that directly encapsulates aminosteroid neuromuscular blockers (rocuronium greater than vecuronium) in the plasma, forming an inactive complex; this creates a concentration gradient that draws the drug away from the neuromuscular junction, giving rapid, complete reversal even of profound block, without the muscarinic side-effects of neostigmine. It does NOT act on acetylcholinesterase and is ineffective against benzylisoquinolinium agents such as atracurium — so D is the correct mechanism.
questions.reference: Morgan & Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 6th ed — Neuromuscular Blocking Agents (Sugammadex)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The analgesic action and most of the clinically important effects of morphine are mediated predominantly through agonism at which opioid receptor?
questions.concept: Morphine is a relatively selective agonist at the mu (μ)-opioid receptor; μ activation mediates supraspinal and spinal analgesia, euphoria, respiratory depression, miosis, constipation and physical dependence. Kappa contributes spinal analgesia with dysphoria and less respiratory depression, delta modulates analgesia and mood, and the ORL-1/nociceptin receptor is a related but distinct system. All opioid receptors are Gi/Go-coupled, reducing cAMP, closing calcium and opening potassium channels to depress neuronal excitability — so A is correct.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Opioid Analgesics and Antagonists

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Morphine should be used cautiously in a patient with chronic kidney disease. Reason (R): Morphine-3-glucuronide is a potent mu-opioid agonist that accumulates in renal failure and causes prolonged respiratory depression. Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Morphine is indeed hazardous in renal failure — the Assertion is TRUE — but the Reason is FALSE because it names the wrong metabolite: morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) is analgesically inactive (and may be neuroexcitatory), whereas it is morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), a potent renally-excreted mu-agonist, that accumulates and causes prolonged sedation and respiratory depression. Since A is true but R is false, the answer is C; fentanyl is often preferred in significant renal impairment.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th ed — Opioids (morphine metabolism)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding pethidine (meperidine) is TRUE?
options: Its metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide is responsible for its analgesia
Its metabolite norpethidine can accumulate to cause CNS excitation and seizures, and it is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors
It characteristically produces marked miosis and bradycardia identical to morphine
It is a pure opioid antagonist used to treat opioid overdose
questions.concept: Pethidine is metabolised to norpethidine (normeperidine), a neurotoxic metabolite that accumulates — especially in renal impairment or with repeated dosing — causing tremor, myoclonus and seizures that are NOT reversed by naloxone. Combined with a monoamine-oxidase inhibitor it can trigger a life-threatening excitatory/serotonergic reaction (hyperthermia, rigidity, coma). Unlike morphine, pethidine has antimuscarinic action, so it causes less miosis (even mydriasis) and can produce tachycardia. It is an agonist, not an antagonist, making B the only true statement.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Opioid Analgesics (Pethidine)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Codeine is a relatively weak analgesic by itself; its analgesic effect depends largely on hepatic O-demethylation to morphine, catalysed by which enzyme?
questions.concept: Codeine is essentially a prodrug that is O-demethylated to morphine by CYP2D6. Poor metabolizers (deficient CYP2D6) obtain little analgesia, whereas ultra-rapid metabolizers generate excess morphine and risk toxicity and respiratory depression — a recognised danger in young children and in breast-fed infants of ultra-rapid-metabolizer mothers. CYP2D6 inhibitors such as fluoxetine and quinidine blunt codeine's effect. CYP3A4 forms inactive norcodeine, while pseudocholinesterase and CYP1A2 are not the key pathway, so D is correct.
questions.reference: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists (codeine, CYP2D6)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient maintained on high-dose full-agonist opioid therapy is given buprenorphine and unexpectedly develops acute withdrawal symptoms. This is best explained by the fact that buprenorphine is a:
options: Partial mu-opioid agonist with very high receptor affinity
questions.concept: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-receptor — very high binding affinity but low intrinsic activity — and a kappa antagonist. Given to a patient on a full agonist, its high affinity displaces that full agonist while delivering only submaximal mu activation, so the net opioid effect falls and withdrawal is precipitated. Its partial agonism also produces a ceiling on respiratory depression, and its tight binding makes overdose relatively resistant to naloxone. It is neither a pure antagonist nor an NMDA blocker, so D is correct.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Opioid Analgesics (Buprenorphine)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Tramadol produces analgesia by a dual mechanism. In addition to weak agonism at the mu-opioid receptor, it also:
options: Inhibits neuronal reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline
questions.concept: Tramadol is a weak mu-agonist (its M1 metabolite, formed by CYP2D6, is the more active opioid moiety) that additionally inhibits neuronal reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline, enhancing descending inhibitory pain pathways. This monoaminergic action explains why it lowers seizure threshold and, particularly when combined with SSRIs, SNRIs or MAOIs, can precipitate serotonin syndrome. It causes comparatively less respiratory depression and constipation than classical opioids. It does not act via COX, NMDA or GABA-A, so C is correct.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th ed — Opioids (Tramadol)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Regarding the mechanism of action of local anaesthetics, which statement is correct?
options: They open voltage-gated potassium channels to hyperpolarise the axon
They activate GABA-A receptors on the peripheral nerve
They block calcium channels at the motor end-plate
They block voltage-gated sodium channels, binding chiefly from the axoplasmic (inner) side of the membrane
questions.concept: Local anaesthetics are weak bases: the unionized lipid-soluble form penetrates the axonal membrane, then the ionized cationic form binds the inner (intracellular) gate of the voltage-gated sodium channel, preferentially in its open/inactivated state — giving use- (frequency-) dependent block that prevents the action-potential upstroke. This explains why inflamed acidic tissue (more ionized, less penetration) reduces efficacy, and why small, rapidly firing fibres are blocked first. They do not act on potassium channels, GABA-A or end-plate calcium channels, so D is correct.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Local Anaesthetics (mechanism of action)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with HFrEF started on enalapril develops a persistent dry, tickling cough that resolves within days of stopping the drug. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Accumulation of bradykinin and substance P in the airways
Direct chemical irritation of the bronchial epithelium
A rise in circulating angiotensin II acting on cough receptors
questions.concept: ACE (kininase II) normally degrades bradykinin, so ACE inhibition raises bradykinin and substance P, which sensitise airway sensory nerves and produce the classic non-productive cough (and, rarely, angioedema). It is a class effect of all ACE inhibitors and reverses on stopping. Angiotensin II actually falls, not rises, so C is wrong; the cough is not from direct irritation (B) or histamine/allergy (D). Switching to an ARB, which does not affect bradykinin, avoids the cough.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Drugs Affecting Renin-Angiotensin System / Drugs for CHF

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: In the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) sacubitril/valsartan, the sacubitril component acts by:
options: Blocking the angiotensin II AT1 receptor
Inhibiting neprilysin, thereby raising natriuretic peptide levels
questions.concept: Sacubitril is a prodrug whose active metabolite inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme that degrades natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP, CNP); higher natriuretic peptide levels promote natriuresis, vasodilation and reduced sympathetic/RAAS activity. The AT1 blockade is provided by valsartan, so A describes the partner drug, not sacubitril. It is not an ACE inhibitor (B), and it does not directly stimulate guanylate cyclase (D). PARADIGM-HF showed ARNI reduced cardiovascular death versus enalapril; ARNI must not be combined with an ACE inhibitor (angioedema risk).
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Drugs Used in Heart Failure

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ivabradine, used in chronic HFrEF with sinus rhythm and an elevated heart rate, reduces heart rate by:
options: Blocking L-type calcium channels in the AV node
Selectively inhibiting the funny (If) current in the SA node
questions.concept: Ivabradine selectively blocks the hyperpolarisation-activated funny (If) current carried by HCN channels in the sinoatrial node, slowing the slope of spontaneous diastolic depolarisation and hence the rate of pacemaker firing. It is a pure heart-rate-lowering drug with no effect on contractility, blood pressure or AV conduction, which distinguishes it from beta-blockers (C) and non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers (A). It requires sinus rhythm to work and is added when heart rate stays >=70/min despite maximal beta-blockade. It does not touch the Na+/K+ ATPase (D, the digoxin target).
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Drugs for CHF / Antianginal Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which class of oral antidiabetic drugs has been shown to reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation in HFrEF, even in patients without diabetes?
questions.concept: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and worsening heart failure in trials such as DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced, benefits seen regardless of diabetic status; proposed mechanisms include osmotic diuresis/natriuresis, reduced preload and afterload, and favourable cardiac metabolic/energetic effects. They are now a pillar of guideline-directed HFrEF therapy. DPP-4 inhibitors are neutral (saxagliptin even increased HF hospitalisation), and sulfonylureas and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors have no HF mortality benefit, so A, B and C are wrong.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Drugs Used in Heart Failure

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which beta-blocker has proven mortality benefit in HFrEF and is one of the agents recommended for chronic heart failure?
questions.concept: Only three beta-blockers have documented mortality benefit in HFrEF: carvedilol, bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate (extended release); this is a drug-specific, not a class-wide, effect and they must be started at low dose and up-titrated in stable patients. Carvedilol additionally blocks alpha-1 receptors, giving vasodilation. Atenolol and propranolol were not established in the landmark HF trials, and esmolol is an ultra-short-acting IV agent used for acute rate control, not chronic HF. Beta-blockers are avoided during acute decompensation.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Drugs for CHF

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A man with HFrEF on spironolactone develops painful gynecomastia. The best mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist to switch him to, with fewer antiandrogen effects, is:
questions.concept: Eplerenone is a selective aldosterone (mineralocorticoid) receptor antagonist that, unlike spironolactone, has minimal affinity for androgen and progesterone receptors, so it causes far less gynecomastia, breast tenderness and menstrual irregularity while retaining the mortality benefit of MRAs in HFrEF. Amiloride and triamterene are potassium-sparing diuretics that block the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), not aldosterone receptors, so they are not MRAs. Furosemide is a loop diuretic. All MRAs and K+-sparing agents require monitoring for hyperkalemia.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Diuretic Agents / Drugs Used in Heart Failure

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with HFrEF cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors or ARBs because of renal dysfunction with hyperkalemia. Which drug combination has additionally been shown to improve survival, particularly in self-identified Black patients?
questions.concept: The combination of hydralazine (an arteriolar vasodilator reducing afterload) with isosorbide dinitrate (a venodilator/nitric-oxide donor reducing preload) improved survival in HFrEF and showed particular benefit in self-identified Black patients (A-HeFT trial). It is the standard alternative when ACE inhibitors/ARBs/ARNI are contraindicated by renal impairment or hyperkalemia because it does not raise potassium. Digoxin plus furosemide (B) relieves symptoms but does not extend survival; amlodipine/atenolol (A) and verapamil (D, a negative inotrope contraindicated in HFrEF) do not.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Drugs Used in Heart Failure

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Milrinone, used as an inotrope in acute decompensated heart failure, increases myocardial contractility primarily by:
questions.concept: Milrinone is a selective phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor; by blocking the breakdown of cAMP in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle it increases intracellular cAMP and calcium in myocytes (positive inotropy) while causing vasodilation (inodilator effect, lowering preload and afterload). Because it acts downstream of the beta receptor, it works even when beta receptors are down-regulated or the patient is on a beta-blocker, unlike dobutamine (A). It does not inhibit Na+/K+ ATPase (B, the digoxin target) or PDE-5 (C, the sildenafil target). It can cause arrhythmias and hypotension.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Drugs for CHF

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Dobutamine used in cardiogenic shock acts predominantly as a(n):
questions.concept: Dobutamine is a synthetic catecholamine that predominantly stimulates beta-1 adrenergic receptors, producing a positive inotropic effect with relatively modest increases in heart rate, making it useful for short-term inotropic support in acute decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic shock. Its mild beta-2 and alpha-1 actions tend to balance, so peripheral resistance changes little. It is not primarily an alpha-1 agonist (B, that describes phenylephrine) or a D1 agonist (D, low-dose dopamine effect). Tolerance develops with prolonged infusion and it can provoke arrhythmias and increase myocardial oxygen demand.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Adrenergic Drugs / Drugs for CHF

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which statement about digoxin is CORRECT?
options: It has a wide therapeutic index, so plasma monitoring is unnecessary
Life-threatening toxicity is treated with digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin immune Fab)
Hyperkalemia strongly potentiates digoxin binding to its receptor
It characteristically shortens the PR interval on the ECG
questions.concept: Severe, life-threatening digoxin toxicity (refractory arrhythmias, marked hyperkalemia) is treated with digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin immune Fab, e.g. Digibind/DigiFab), which bind and neutralise the drug. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index (~0.5-2 ng/mL) so monitoring is essential, making A wrong. It is hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, that potentiates digoxin toxicity by reducing competition at the Na+/K+ ATPase, so C is wrong. By enhancing vagal tone digoxin slows AV conduction and prolongs (not shortens) the PR interval, so D is wrong.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Drugs for CHF (Cardiac Glycosides)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug used in HFrEF provides symptomatic relief but has NOT been shown to reduce mortality?
questions.concept: Loop diuretics such as furosemide relieve congestion (dyspnea, edema) rapidly and are essential for symptom control, but no trial has shown they reduce mortality in HFrEF; they treat symptoms, not disease progression. The drugs with proven mortality benefit are the neurohormonal blockers: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), evidence-based beta-blockers (bisoprolol), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone) and SGLT2 inhibitors. Hence A, B and D all improve survival, whereas furosemide is symptom-only, as is digoxin (which reduces hospitalisations but not mortality).
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Drugs Used in Heart Failure

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient develops sustained ventricular tachycardia soon after an acute myocardial infarction. Which intravenous class Ib antiarrhythmic preferentially blocks sodium channels in depolarised, ischaemic ventricular tissue?
questions.concept: Lidocaine is a class Ib agent that binds sodium channels with fast on-off kinetics and shows use-dependence, so it preferentially blocks channels in rapidly firing or depolarised/ischaemic tissue while sparing normal myocardium; this makes it effective for ventricular arrhythmias, especially post-MI, with little effect on atrial tissue. Quinidine (A) is class Ia; verapamil (B) is a class IV calcium blocker for supraventricular arrhythmias; adenosine (C) terminates AV-nodal reentrant SVT. Lidocaine is given IV because of extensive first-pass metabolism and can cause CNS toxicity (perioral numbness, seizures).
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Flecainide should not be used to suppress premature ventricular complexes in a patient with a previous myocardial infarction. Reason (R): In the CAST trial, class Ic sodium-channel blockers increased mortality by provoking lethal proarrhythmia in patients with structural heart disease.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: Flecainide is a class Ic agent with potent, slowly-reversible sodium-channel block and marked slowing of conduction. The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST) found that suppressing asymptomatic PVCs post-MI with flecainide/encainide paradoxically increased mortality due to proarrhythmia in scarred, structurally abnormal ventricles. Therefore the assertion is true and the reason correctly explains it. Class Ic drugs are reserved for patients WITHOUT structural heart disease (e.g. paroxysmal AF, the pill-in-the-pocket approach) — making A the right choice.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Agents Used in Cardiac Arrhythmias

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A young patient presents with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (AV nodal reentry) unresponsive to vagal manoeuvres. The drug of choice for acute termination is:
questions.concept: Adenosine is the drug of choice for acute termination of AV-nodal reentrant supraventricular tachycardia. Given as a rapid IV bolus, it activates A1 receptors, opening potassium channels and inhibiting calcium current in the AV node, transiently blocking AV conduction and interrupting the reentry circuit. Its half-life is only a few seconds, so effects (flushing, chest tightness, transient asystole) are brief. Lidocaine (A) is for ventricular arrhythmias, digoxin (C) is too slow for acute conversion, and quinidine (D) is not used here. Effects are potentiated by dipyridamole and blocked by methylxanthines.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient on a QT-prolonging drug develops polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades de pointes). The drug of choice, given even when serum magnesium is normal, is:
questions.concept: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for torsades de pointes and works to suppress the early afterdepolarisations that trigger it even when the serum magnesium level is normal. Additional measures include stopping the offending QT-prolonging drug, correcting hypokalemia, and overdrive pacing or isoprenaline to increase heart rate and shorten the QT. Class Ia (procainamide, D) and class III (amiodarone, A) agents prolong the QT and can worsen torsades, so they are avoided; lidocaine (B) is unreliable here. This is a high-yield emergency management fact.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antiarrhythmic possesses BOTH class III (potassium-channel-blocking) and class II (beta-blocking) actions and is notably associated with QT prolongation and torsades de pointes?
questions.concept: Sotalol is a non-selective beta-blocker (class II) that also blocks the rapid delayed-rectifier potassium current IKr (class III), prolonging repolarisation and the QT interval; this dual action underlies both its efficacy in atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and its dose-dependent risk of torsades de pointes, especially with hypokalemia or renal impairment (it is renally cleared). Diltiazem (A) is a class IV calcium blocker, mexiletine (B) is a class Ib agent, and flecainide (C) is class Ic — none combine class II and III actions. Its l-isomer provides the beta-blockade.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Agents Used in Cardiac Arrhythmias

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient taking quinidine for an arrhythmia develops tinnitus, headache, blurred vision, and diarrhoea. This constellation of adverse effects is known as:
questions.concept: Cinchonism is the characteristic toxidrome of quinidine (and quinine, both cinchona alkaloids): tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, blurred vision, and gastrointestinal upset such as diarrhoea and nausea. Quinidine is a class Ia agent that also has vagolytic and alpha-blocking effects, can prolong QT and cause torsades, and can raise serum digoxin levels. Serotonin syndrome (B) results from serotonergic drugs; disulfiram-like reactions (C) follow alcohol with certain drugs; gray baby syndrome (D) is chloramphenicol toxicity in neonates. Recognising cinchonism is a classic FMGE association.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Long-term therapy with procainamide is most characteristically associated with which adverse effect?
questions.concept: Chronic procainamide use is classically associated with a drug-induced lupus erythematosus-like syndrome (arthralgia, fever, serositis) with positive antinuclear and anti-histone antibodies; it is more common in slow acetylators and usually reverses on stopping the drug. Procainamide is a class Ia agent that can also cause QT prolongation/torsades and agranulocytosis. Pulmonary fibrosis and corneal microdeposits (A, C) are amiodarone effects, and gingival hyperplasia (D) is seen with phenytoin, calcium blockers and cyclosporine. Hydralazine and isoniazid are other common causes of drug-induced lupus.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Verapamil should not be combined with a beta-blocker in most patients. Reason (R): Verapamil characteristically produces marked reflex tachycardia that beta-blockers are unable to control.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: verapamil (a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker) depresses SA/AV nodal conduction and myocardial contractility, so combining it with a beta-blocker risks severe bradycardia, high-grade AV block, asystole and heart failure. The reason is false — verapamil does NOT cause reflex tachycardia; by slowing AV conduction it tends to lower or steady the heart rate, and reflex tachycardia is instead typical of dihydropyridines like nifedipine. Hence A is true but R is false (option C). Verapamil also commonly causes constipation and can precipitate digoxin toxicity by raising digoxin levels.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Calcium Channel Blockers / Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with recent-onset atrial flutter needs rapid pharmacological cardioversion. Which intravenous class III agent is used specifically for this, carrying a risk of torsades de pointes?
questions.concept: Ibutilide is a class III antiarrhythmic given intravenously for acute pharmacological conversion of recent-onset atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter; it prolongs repolarisation (partly by activating a slow inward sodium current and blocking IKr), lengthening the QT and carrying a notable risk of torsades de pointes, so patients require cardiac monitoring. Lidocaine (A) is for ventricular arrhythmias, verapamil (B) and digoxin (C) provide rate control but do not chemically cardiovert. Dofetilide is a related oral class III agent used to maintain sinus rhythm, also with torsades risk requiring in-hospital initiation.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Agents Used in Cardiac Arrhythmias

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Amiodarone is added to a patient who is stable on a maintenance dose of digoxin. What is the expected interaction and appropriate response?
options: Serum digoxin levels rise, so the digoxin dose should be reduced (usually halved)
Serum digoxin levels fall due to enzyme induction, so digoxin should be increased
There is no clinically significant interaction between the two drugs
Amiodarone directly antagonises digoxin at the Na+/K+ ATPase
questions.concept: Amiodarone raises serum digoxin concentrations, mainly by inhibiting P-glycoprotein-mediated renal/biliary elimination and reducing digoxin clearance, so the digoxin dose should be reduced (commonly by about half) and levels monitored to avoid toxicity. Amiodarone similarly potentiates warfarin (via CYP2C9 inhibition), requiring a lower warfarin dose. It is an enzyme inhibitor, not an inducer, so B is wrong; the interaction is clinically important, so C is wrong; and it does not act at the Na+/K+ ATPase (D). This pharmacokinetic interaction is a frequently tested amiodarone fact distinct from its organ toxicities.
questions.reference: Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th ed — Antiarrhythmic Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The principal anti-anginal action of organic nitrates at usual therapeutic doses is:
options: Increasing heart rate to augment coronary blood flow
Venodilation that reduces preload and myocardial oxygen demand
A direct positive inotropic effect on the ventricle
Blockade of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors
questions.concept: Organic nitrates are converted to nitric oxide, which activates guanylate cyclase and raises cGMP, relaxing vascular smooth muscle. At usual doses the predominant effect is venodilation, which pools blood peripherally, reduces venous return (preload) and lowers ventricular wall tension, thereby cutting myocardial oxygen demand — the main mechanism of angina relief. They also dilate epicardial coronary arteries and relieve spasm. They do not increase heart rate as a therapeutic action (reflex tachycardia is an unwanted effect, A), have no positive inotropic effect (C), and do not block beta receptors (D).
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antianginal Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Patients on long-acting nitrates should observe a daily nitrate-free interval of about 8-12 hours. Reason (R): Uninterrupted nitrate exposure characteristically produces reflex bradycardia.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: continuous nitrate exposure causes tolerance (tachyphylaxis) with loss of anti-anginal efficacy, so a daily nitrate-free interval of 8-12 hours is deliberately built into dosing to restore responsiveness. The reason is false: uninterrupted nitrates cause tolerance, not reflex bradycardia, and nitrates in fact tend to produce reflex TACHYCARDIA (from baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic activation), not bradycardia. Thus A is true but R is false (option C). Proposed tolerance mechanisms include depletion of tissue thiols and increased oxidative stress reducing NO generation.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antianginal Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Ranolazine relieves chronic stable angina mainly by:
options: Blocking L-type calcium channels and lowering blood pressure
Non-selective beta-blockade that slows the heart rate
Inhibiting the late inward sodium current, reducing calcium overload, with little effect on heart rate or blood pressure
questions.concept: Ranolazine is a novel anti-anginal that inhibits the late inward sodium current in cardiac myocytes; reducing the sodium influx lessens sodium-dependent calcium overload, improving diastolic relaxation and myocardial oxygen efficiency without meaningfully lowering heart rate or blood pressure. This makes it useful as add-on therapy when nitrates, beta-blockers or calcium blockers are insufficient or not tolerated, and its haemodynamic neutrality distinguishes it from options A and B. It does not open K-ATP channels (C, the nicorandil action). It can prolong the QT interval and is metabolised by CYP3A4, so drug interactions matter.
questions.reference: Katzung, Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, 15th ed — Vasodilators and the Treatment of Angina Pectoris

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Nicorandil, used in angina, produces coronary and systemic vasodilation through a dual mechanism of:
options: ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channel opening plus nitrate-like nitric oxide donation
Late sodium current inhibition plus beta-adrenergic blockade
L-type calcium channel blockade plus alpha-1 adrenergic agonism
Neprilysin inhibition plus angiotensin AT1 receptor blockade
questions.concept: Nicorandil has a dual action: it opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in vascular smooth muscle (hyperpolarising the membrane, closing calcium channels and causing arteriolar dilation that reduces afterload) and it also acts as a nitric oxide donor (nitrate-like), causing venodilation that reduces preload; together these dilate coronary vessels and relieve angina. It does not inhibit late sodium current (that is ranolazine, B), block calcium channels (C), or inhibit neprilysin (D, an ARNI action). The K-ATP opening also confers a degree of ischaemic preconditioning; headache is a common adverse effect.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antianginal Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following insulin preparations has the most rapid onset of action (approximately 5-15 minutes) after subcutaneous injection, making it suitable for dosing immediately before or after a meal?
questions.concept: Insulin lispro is a rapid-acting analogue (like aspart and glulisine) with onset in 5-15 minutes, peak at 30-90 minutes and duration of 3-5 hours, allowing mealtime dosing that closely mimics prandial insulin. Regular insulin is short-acting but slower (onset 30-60 minutes), needing dosing 30 minutes pre-meal. NPH is intermediate-acting and glargine is long-acting basal, both unsuitable for rapid postprandial cover.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Insulin & Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A long-acting insulin analogue that forms microprecipitates at physiological subcutaneous pH, giving a relatively peakless basal action lasting about 24 hours, is:
questions.concept: Insulin glargine is soluble at acidic pH (pH 4) but precipitates when injected into the neutral subcutaneous tissue; slow redissolution gives a flat, peakless profile over roughly 24 hours, ideal as once-daily basal insulin. Detemir prolongs action by albumin binding and degludec by multihexamer formation. NPH is only intermediate-acting with a distinct peak, and aspart/regular are prandial insulins, not basal.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Insulin & Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes on bedtime NPH insulin has persistent fasting morning hyperglycaemia. A 3 a.m. capillary blood glucose is 45 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.concept: The low 3 a.m. glucose indicates the Somogyi effect: nocturnal hypoglycaemia triggers counter-regulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, GH, catecholamines) causing rebound morning hyperglycaemia. The correct response is to reduce the evening insulin or add a bedtime snack. Increasing insulin would worsen the nocturnal hypoglycaemia. This contrasts with the dawn phenomenon (early-morning glucose rise without hypoglycaemia), where increasing basal insulin is appropriate.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Insulin; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The most common acute adverse effect encountered during insulin therapy is:
questions.concept: Hypoglycaemia is by far the commonest and most dangerous acute complication of insulin, arising from excess dose, missed meals or exertion, and presenting with sweating, tremor, palpitation, confusion or coma. Insulin actually causes weight gain, not loss. Lactic acidosis is linked to metformin, and pancreatitis to incretin-based drugs (GLP-1 agonists/DPP-4 inhibitors), not insulin. Lipodystrophy at injection sites is another local adverse effect.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Insulin; Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Endocrine Pancreas

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: In the management of diabetic ketoacidosis, which insulin preparation is administered as a continuous intravenous infusion?
questions.concept: Only regular (soluble) insulin can be given intravenously because it exists as free monomers/dimers that act immediately; a low-dose continuous IV infusion is the standard for DKA, alongside fluids and potassium correction. Rapid-acting analogues can also be given IV but regular insulin is the traditional and most widely used choice. NPH, glargine and degludec are suspensions or depot analogues meant only for subcutaneous use and must never be injected IV.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Insulin (DKA management); Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — Diabetic Ketoacidosis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Sulfonylureas such as glimepiride and glibenclamide lower blood glucose primarily by:
options: Closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on pancreatic beta cells to stimulate insulin secretion
questions.concept: Sulfonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit and close ATP-sensitive K+ channels on beta cells; the resulting membrane depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and Ca2+ influx triggers insulin exocytosis. They are therefore insulin secretagogues and require functioning beta cells. Inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis describes metformin, blocking renal glucose reabsorption describes SGLT2 inhibitors, and inhibiting alpha-glucosidase describes acarbose.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Empagliflozin, a newer oral antidiabetic drug, lowers plasma glucose by:
options: Enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion via incretins
Inhibiting sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 in the proximal renal tubule, producing glycosuria
questions.concept: Empagliflozin blocks SGLT2 in the S1 segment of the proximal convoluted tubule, reducing glucose reabsorption and causing glucosuria that lowers plasma glucose independent of insulin. This class also produces weight loss, mild blood-pressure reduction and proven cardiovascular and renal protection. Enhancing incretin action describes DPP-4 inhibitors, PPAR-gamma activation describes thiazolidinediones, and DPP-4 inhibition describes gliptins.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Oral Hypoglycaemic Drugs (SGLT2 inhibitors); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A type 2 diabetic taking dapagliflozin presents with vomiting, high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis and ketonaemia, but the blood glucose is only 190 mg/dL. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.concept: SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate euglycaemic DKA, where ketoacidosis develops with near-normal or only modestly raised glucose (often below 250 mg/dL), because urinary glucose loss lowers blood glucose while promoting lipolysis and ketogenesis; the near-normal glucose can delay diagnosis. HHS by definition has very high glucose without significant ketosis, lactic acidosis relates to metformin, and salicylate poisoning gives a mixed respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis, not diabetic ketonaemia. Genital mycotic infection is another SGLT2 adverse effect.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — SGLT2 inhibitors; Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Endocrine Pancreas

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following antidiabetic agents is a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that characteristically produces marked weight loss and demonstrated cardiovascular benefit?
questions.concept: Semaglutide (and liraglutide) are injectable GLP-1 receptor agonists that enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite, producing substantial weight loss and proven cardiovascular risk reduction; the main adverse effects are nausea and vomiting. Sitagliptin (a DPP-4 inhibitor) is weight-neutral, while glimepiride (sulfonylurea) and pioglitazone (thiazolidinedione) both cause weight gain.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Incretin-based therapies; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Sitagliptin improves glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes by:
options: Inhibiting dipeptidyl peptidase-4, thereby raising endogenous incretin (GLP-1 and GIP) levels
questions.concept: Sitagliptin and other gliptins inhibit dipeptidyl peptidase-4, the enzyme that degrades incretins, so endogenous GLP-1 and GIP levels rise and enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion while suppressing glucagon. They are oral, weight-neutral and carry low hypoglycaemia risk. Directly agonising the GLP-1 receptor describes semaglutide/liraglutide, closing K-ATP channels describes sulfonylureas, and inhibiting SGLT2 describes gliflozins.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Incretin-based therapies (DPP-4 inhibitors); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Pioglitazone should be avoided in patients with NYHA class III-IV heart failure. Reason (R): Pioglitazone, a PPAR-gamma agonist, promotes renal sodium and water retention, causing peripheral oedema and plasma volume expansion. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Pioglitazone activates PPAR-gamma, increasing distal tubular sodium and water reabsorption; the resulting fluid retention and plasma volume expansion cause oedema and can precipitate or worsen congestive heart failure, so it is contraindicated in NYHA class III-IV failure. The reason directly explains the assertion, making A the answer. Other thiazolidinedione adverse effects include weight gain, increased fracture risk and possible bladder cancer risk.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Thiazolidinediones; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Acarbose reduces postprandial hyperglycaemia by inhibiting intestinal alpha-glucosidase. Its most common adverse effect is:
questions.concept: Acarbose competitively inhibits intestinal brush-border alpha-glucosidase, delaying carbohydrate digestion and absorption; unabsorbed carbohydrate is fermented by colonic bacteria, so flatulence, bloating, cramps and diarrhoea are the dominant dose-limiting side effects. It does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone, but if hypoglycaemia occurs with a sulfonylurea/insulin it must be treated with glucose (not sucrose), since sucrose splitting is blocked. It is weight-neutral, and lactic acidosis is a metformin effect.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with irregular meal timing needs a rapid-onset, short-acting insulin secretagogue taken just before each meal to blunt postprandial glucose spikes while minimising the risk of hypoglycaemia between meals. The most appropriate drug is:
questions.concept: Repaglinide is a meglitinide (glinide) insulin secretagogue that, like sulfonylureas, closes beta-cell K-ATP channels but at a distinct binding site, giving a fast onset and short duration; it is taken before each meal and skipped if the meal is skipped, which suits erratic eating and limits inter-meal hypoglycaemia. Glimepiride is a long-acting sulfonylurea with higher sustained hypoglycaemia risk, while metformin and pioglitazone are not insulin secretagogues and do not target postprandial peaks in this manner.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Meglitinide analogues; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Pancreatic Hormones

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Long-term metformin therapy is associated with malabsorption of which vitamin, potentially leading to megaloblastic anaemia and worsening peripheral neuropathy?
questions.concept: Metformin interferes with calcium-dependent vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum, so prolonged use can cause B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and aggravation of diabetic peripheral neuropathy; periodic B12 monitoring is advised in long-term users. This is a distinct adverse effect from its well-known metabolic complication. Vitamin C, D and K malabsorption are not features of metformin therapy.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Biguanides (Metformin); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Endocrine Pancreas

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The drug of choice for long-term replacement therapy in hypothyroidism is:
questions.concept: Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) is the drug of choice for hypothyroidism because it has a long half-life (about 7 days) allowing stable once-daily dosing, and is peripherally converted to the active T3 at physiologically regulated rates, giving smooth, steady hormone levels. Liothyronine (T3) has a short half-life and causes fluctuating levels, reserved for special situations like myxoedema coma. Carbimazole and propylthiouracil are antithyroid drugs used in hyperthyroidism, not replacement.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Thyroid Hormones and Antithyroid Drugs; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A woman in the first trimester of pregnancy develops Graves' hyperthyroidism requiring drug therapy. The preferred antithyroid agent during this period is:
questions.concept: Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester because methimazole/carbimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia (methimazole embryopathy). Because PTU carries a higher risk of hepatotoxicity, guidelines switch back to methimazole/carbimazole in the second and third trimesters. Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy as it crosses the placenta and ablates the foetal thyroid.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antithyroid Drugs; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Carbimazole and methimazole inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis mainly by:
options: Inhibiting thyroid peroxidase, thereby blocking iodide organification and iodotyrosine coupling
Blocking peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
Emitting radiation that destroys thyroid follicular cells
questions.concept: The thionamides carbimazole (a prodrug converted to methimazole) and methimazole inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking oxidation and organification of iodide and the coupling of iodotyrosines (MIT and DIT) to form T3 and T4, thereby reducing new hormone synthesis without affecting release of stored hormone (hence a delayed clinical effect). Only propylthiouracil additionally blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. Radiation destruction describes 131-I, and symporter inhibition describes perchlorate/thiocyanate.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antithyroid Drugs; Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — Thyroid and Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient who started carbimazole two weeks ago presents with high fever and severe sore throat. The most important life-threatening adverse effect that must be urgently excluded is:
questions.concept: Agranulocytosis is the most serious, though rare, idiosyncratic adverse effect of thionamides; it usually appears within the first 2-3 months and presents with fever and sore throat. Any such patient must stop the drug immediately and have an urgent white cell count. Patients are counselled to report fever/sore throat promptly. Hepatotoxicity is more typical of propylthiouracil, and aplastic anaemia and cholestatic jaundice are far less characteristic than the abrupt neutropenia of agranulocytosis.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Antithyroid Drugs (adverse effects); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Propranolol is a useful adjunct in the management of thyroid storm. Reason (R): Propranolol acts by inhibiting thyroid peroxidase and thereby blocking new thyroid hormone synthesis. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The assertion is true: propranolol rapidly controls the adrenergic features of thyroid storm (tachycardia, tremor, anxiety) and, at high doses, also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to the more active T3. The reason is false because propranolol does not touch thyroid peroxidase; blocking peroxidase and hormone synthesis is the action of the thionamides (carbimazole, methimazole, propylthiouracil). Hence A is true but R is false, giving answer C.
