questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Thyroid storm management; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Lugol's iodine given for about 10 days before thyroidectomy in Graves' disease is beneficial chiefly because it:
options: Transiently inhibits hormone synthesis and release and reduces gland vascularity (Wolff-Chaikoff effect)
questions.concept: High-dose iodide (Lugol's solution) acutely inhibits its own organification and hormone release and reduces thyroid size and vascularity via the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, making the gland firm and less vascular for safer surgery. The effect is transient, with escape after 10-14 days, so preoperative use is short-term. Iodide does not increase hormone release long-term, does not promote T4-to-T3 conversion, and unlike radioactive iodine does not ablate the gland.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Iodine and Iodides (preoperative preparation); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Radioactive iodine (131-I) used to treat hyperthyroidism produces its therapeutic effect by:
options: Competitively inhibiting iodide uptake at the symporter
Emitting beta particles that destroy thyroid follicular cells
questions.concept: 131-I is concentrated in the thyroid via the sodium-iodide symporter and emits beta particles that penetrate only 0.5-2 mm, selectively destroying follicular cells over weeks with little damage to surrounding tissue; hypothyroidism is a common late outcome requiring levothyroxine. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation. Peroxidase inhibition describes thionamides, T4-to-T3 block describes propranolol/PTU, and symporter competition describes perchlorate.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Radioactive Iodine; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which corticosteroid possesses the highest anti-inflammatory (glucocorticoid) potency together with negligible mineralocorticoid (salt-retaining) activity?
questions.concept: Dexamethasone (and betamethasone) have the highest glucocorticoid/anti-inflammatory potency (about 25-30 times hydrocortisone) with essentially no mineralocorticoid activity, making them ideal when fluid retention must be avoided (e.g. cerebral oedema). Hydrocortisone has equal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, prednisolone is intermediate (about 4 times) with slight salt retention, and fludrocortisone is a potent mineralocorticoid used for its salt-retaining, not anti-inflammatory, action.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Corticosteroids (relative potencies); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Adrenocorticosteroids

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: The anti-inflammatory action of glucocorticoids is mediated chiefly by:
options: Inducing annexin-1 (lipocortin-1), which inhibits phospholipase A2 and reduces prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis
questions.concept: Glucocorticoids bind cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptors that translocate to the nucleus and alter gene transcription; a key effect is induction of annexin-1 (lipocortin-1), which inhibits phospholipase A2, cutting the release of arachidonic acid and hence both prostaglandins and leukotrienes. They also suppress COX-2 induction and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Irreversible COX inhibition describes aspirin, H1 blockade describes antihistamines, and leukotriene-receptor blockade describes montelukast.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Corticosteroids (mechanism); Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics — ACTH and Adrenal Steroids

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Assertion (A): Long-term high-dose glucocorticoid therapy must be tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly. Reason (R): Chronic glucocorticoid use causes osteoporosis. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are individually true, but osteoporosis is not the reason for tapering. Chronic glucocorticoids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and cause adrenal atrophy; abrupt withdrawal can therefore precipitate an acute adrenal (addisonian) crisis, which is why the dose is tapered to allow HPA recovery. Osteoporosis is a genuine adverse effect but unrelated to the withdrawal risk, so R does not explain A, giving answer B.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Corticosteroids (HPA suppression, withdrawal); Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Adrenocorticosteroids

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which agent used in Cushing syndrome acts as a competitive antagonist at the glucocorticoid receptor (and is also a progesterone-receptor antagonist)?
questions.concept: Mifepristone (RU-486) is a competitive antagonist at the glucocorticoid receptor (and the progesterone receptor), and is used to control hyperglycaemia in inoperable Cushing syndrome. It differs from steroidogenesis inhibitors: metyrapone blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase (the final step of cortisol synthesis) and ketoconazole inhibits several cytochrome-P450 steroidogenic enzymes to lower cortisol. Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid agonist, not a cortisol antagonist.
questions.reference: KD Tripathi Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th ed — Corticosteroid antagonists/inhibitors; Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology — Adrenocorticosteroids & Antagonists

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The classic epidemiological triad describing the interaction of factors necessary for disease causation comprises which of the following?
options: Host, reservoir and portal of exit
questions.concept: The epidemiological (agent-host-environment) triad is the classic model of disease causation: an infectious agent, a susceptible host, and a favourable environment interacting over time. Option B (time, place, person) lists the variables of DESCRIPTIVE epidemiology, not causation; option C lists elements of the chain of infection; option D lists cohort-study concepts. Understanding the triad underpins all communicable-disease control, because breaking any one arm — reducing the agent, raising host immunity, or modifying the environment — interrupts transmission.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Principles of Epidemiology and Epidemiologic Methods

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In infectious-disease control, 'sterilization' is BEST defined as:
options: The destruction of vegetative pathogens but not necessarily bacterial spores
The complete destruction or removal of all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores
The physical removal of visible dirt and organic material from a surface
The killing of microorganisms on living tissue such as skin
questions.concept: Sterilization is the complete destruction or removal of ALL microorganisms, including highly resistant bacterial spores (e.g., autoclaving, ethylene oxide). Option A describes disinfection (kills vegetative pathogens, may spare spores); option C is cleaning (physical removal of soil); option D is antisepsis, which by definition is applied to living tissue. This hierarchy — sterilization above high-level disinfection above antisepsis and simple cleaning — governs instrument reprocessing and hospital infection control.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Disinfection

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The BCG vaccine used in India's Universal Immunization Programme belongs to which category of vaccine?
questions.concept: BCG (Bacille Calmette-Guerin) is a LIVE attenuated vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis (the Danish 1331 strain is used in India). Being live, it is heat- and light-sensitive, must be reconstituted, and is contraindicated in overt immunodeficiency. Option A (killed), B (toxoid, e.g., tetanus/diphtheria), and D (polysaccharide conjugate, e.g., Hib/pneumococcal) are other vaccine classes. Under UIP, BCG is given at birth and protects mainly against severe childhood TB such as miliary TB and tuberculous meningitis, not adult pulmonary disease.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Immunization and Immunizing Agents

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: As per current WHO status, which human infectious disease is the ONLY one to have been certified globally eradicated?
questions.concept: Smallpox is the ONLY human disease certified globally eradicated (WHO, 1980); rinderpest, an animal disease, is the only other eradicated infection. Eradication means permanent worldwide reduction of incidence to zero so that intervention measures can cease — distinct from ELIMINATION (interruption of transmission in a defined area, e.g., polio-free India certified 2014, or neonatal tetanus elimination) where importation risk persists and interventions must continue. Poliomyelitis and measles are targeted for eradication/elimination but are not yet globally eradicated.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under India's National Immunization Schedule, the birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine should ideally be given within how long of birth?
options: Only at 6 weeks along with pentavalent vaccine
questions.concept: Under India's National Immunization Schedule the hepatitis B birth dose should be given as early as possible, ideally WITHIN 24 HOURS of birth, to prevent perinatal (vertical) transmission; the remaining hepatitis B doses are then given as part of the pentavalent vaccine at 6, 10 and 14 weeks. Timeliness of the birth dose is a key hepatitis B control indicator. Options B and C are too late to reliably block perinatal transmission, and option D omits the crucial birth dose. Verify the exact schedule against the current national immunization schedule, which is periodically revised.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Immunization / National Immunization Schedule

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The time interval between the onset of symptoms in a primary case and the onset of symptoms in a secondary case infected by that primary case is termed the:
questions.concept: The SERIAL INTERVAL is the time between symptom onset in a primary case and symptom onset in the secondary case(s) it infects; because it is directly observable, it is widely used to estimate transmission dynamics and to time quarantine. Contrast: the incubation period is infection-to-symptom-onset within one person; the latent (pre-infectious) period relates to when a person becomes infectious after infection; and the generation time is the interval from infection of the primary case to infection of the secondary case. These intervals are frequently confused in examinations.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Dynamics of Disease Transmission

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The secondary attack rate is BEST expressed as the number of exposed persons developing the disease within the range of the incubation period, as a proportion of:
options: The total population of the community
All primary cases in the outbreak
The total number of susceptible contacts exposed to the primary case
The total number of people ever infected during the outbreak
questions.concept: Secondary attack rate (SAR) = number of exposed contacts developing disease within one incubation period divided by the total number of SUSCEPTIBLE contacts exposed to the primary case, times 100. It measures infectiousness/communicability and the impact of interventions within closed groups such as households. Option A gives an overall community attack/incidence rate, not SAR; primary cases (B) and all cumulative infections (D) are not the correct denominator. Immune contacts are excluded from the denominator, since only susceptibles are at risk of becoming secondary cases.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Dynamics of Disease Transmission

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A cluster of dengue cases is reported from an urban colony in September, and the medical officer plans vector control. Which mosquito, breeding in clean stored/collected water in and around houses, is the principal transmitter of dengue in India?
questions.concept: Aedes aegypti is the principal urban vector of dengue (and of chikungunya and Zika) in India; it is a day-biting mosquito that breeds in clean, stored or collected water in and around houses (coolers, tyres, discarded containers), which is why source reduction and elimination of breeding sites are the mainstay of control. Anopheles culicifacies transmits rural malaria, Culex quinquefasciatus transmits bancroftian filariasis and Japanese encephalitis, and Phlebotomus (sandfly) transmits kala-azar. Vector-borne disease control now sits under NCVBDC (formerly NVBDCP).
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Dengue Syndrome)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The Mass Drug Administration (MDA) strategy under India's lymphatic filariasis elimination programme uses which drug combination for annual single-dose therapy?
questions.concept: DEC (diethylcarbamazine) plus albendazole, given annually as a single-dose Mass Drug Administration to the eligible population, is the core strategy of India's lymphatic filariasis elimination programme; triple-drug therapy (IDA = ivermectin + DEC + albendazole) is being rolled out in selected districts to accelerate elimination. Option C (rifampicin + dapsone) relates to leprosy multidrug therapy, and the other combinations treat malaria/schistosomiasis. MDA to suppress microfilaraemia plus morbidity management aims to interrupt transmission; verify the current IDA district list, which is change-prone.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Lymphatic Filariasis)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with sputum-positive pulmonary TB is started on treatment under NTEP. His household includes his wife, two children under 5 years, and his HIV-positive brother. After active TB is ruled out, TB preventive treatment (TPT) is MOST clearly indicated for which of the following?
options: The under-5 child contacts and the HIV-positive household contact
No one, since the index case is already on treatment
questions.concept: Under NTEP, after active disease is excluded, TB preventive treatment is strongly indicated for household contacts — especially children under 5 years — of a pulmonary TB case and for all people living with HIV, because their risk of progressing from latent infection to active disease is high. The programme has been progressively expanding TPT to ALL household contacts irrespective of age, a change-prone policy to verify against current NTEP/national TPT guidelines. That the index case is on treatment does not remove contacts' need for evaluation and prophylaxis.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana under NTEP provides notified tuberculosis patients with which of the following?
options: A one-time cash award given on completion of cure
A monthly Direct Benefit Transfer for nutritional support during anti-TB treatment
Free chest radiography and CBNAAT testing
questions.concept: Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana provides notified TB patients a monthly Direct Benefit Transfer for nutritional support throughout anti-TB treatment, addressing the strong TB-undernutrition link and improving adherence and outcomes; it is over and above free drugs and diagnostics (which are provided anyway, so options A and D are wrong). The monthly amount is change-prone — it was enhanced under the scheme's revision (reportedly to a higher figure with effect from late 2024) — so verify the current amount and eligibility against the latest NTEP circular. It is not a one-time award.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under India's malaria surveillance, the Annual Parasite Incidence (API) is calculated as:
options: Number of blood slides examined per 100 population per year
Percentage of blood slides found positive out of those examined
Proportion of Plasmodium falciparum cases among all positive cases
Number of confirmed malaria cases per 1000 population per year
questions.concept: Annual Parasite Incidence (API) = number of confirmed malaria cases per 1000 population per year; it is the principal indicator for stratifying areas and tracking progress toward elimination (an API below 1 is a key sub-district target). Option A defines the Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER), option B the Slide Positivity Rate (SPR), and option C the P. falciparum proportion. These NCVBDC/NVBDCP surveillance indicators are frequently tested together and are interpreted jointly, since a low ABER can artificially depress the API through under-detection.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Malaria)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: India's National Framework for Malaria Elimination targets elimination of malaria (zero indigenous cases) by which year?
questions.concept: India's National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030) and subsequent strategic plans target a malaria-free India (zero indigenous cases) by 2030, aligned with the WHO Global Technical Strategy and the Asia-Pacific elimination goal. Districts are stratified by API into categories, each with tailored interventions such as IRS, LLINs, surveillance and radical treatment. This target year is a change-prone national-programme fact — verify against the latest NCVBDC framework. Options 2025, 2027 and 2035 are distractors reflecting other milestone or interim years.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — National Vector Borne Disease Control (Malaria Elimination)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A hospital reviews four documented HIV exposures. Which single exposure carries the HIGHEST per-exposure probability of HIV transmission?
options: A percutaneous needle-stick injury from an HIV-positive source
Transfusion of one unit of HIV-infected whole blood
A single episode of receptive vaginal intercourse
A single episode of insertive vaginal intercourse
questions.concept: Per-exposure HIV transmission risk is HIGHEST for transfusion of infected blood (roughly 90-95% per unit), far exceeding perinatal transmission (about 15-45% without intervention), percutaneous needle-stick injury (about 0.3%), and sexual exposures (receptive vaginal roughly 0.1-0.2%, insertive lower still). This is why blood-bank screening and safe transfusion are among the most efficient single control interventions, and why occupational needle-stick, though greatly feared, carries a comparatively low per-event risk. Cumulative sexual exposure nonetheless drives most infections globally.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (AIDS/HIV)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The UNAIDS '95-95-95' targets are: 95% of people living with HIV knowing their status, 95% of those diagnosed on antiretroviral therapy, and 95% of those on therapy achieving which of the following?
questions.concept: The UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets aim for 95% of people living with HIV to know their status, 95% of those diagnosed to be on antiretroviral therapy, and 95% of those on ART to achieve VIRAL SUPPRESSION (an undetectable viral load), which both improves survival and, through 'undetectable equals untransmittable', reduces onward transmission. These superseded the earlier 90-90-90 targets (for 2020), so the exact figures are change-prone and should be verified against current NACP/UNAIDS goals. CD4 count, cotrimoxazole, and confirmatory testing are not the third '95'.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — National AIDS Control Programme (NACP)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A mother brings her healthy 9-month-old infant, immunised so far exactly per the National Immunization Schedule, to the clinic. Which vaccine dose is due at this visit?
options: Birth dose of OPV and BCG
questions.concept: At 9 completed months, a fully immunised infant is due the FIRST dose of measles-rubella (MR) vaccine under the National Immunization Schedule (given with Vitamin A, plus JE-1 in endemic districts and the PCV booster). BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B birth dose are given at birth; pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib) with OPV/fIPV is given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks; DPT/OPV boosters follow at 16-24 months and 5-6 years. India replaced standalone measles vaccine with MR. Verify the exact schedule against the current national immunization schedule, which is periodically revised.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Immunization / National Immunization Schedule

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: For a disease with a basic reproduction number (R0) of 5 in a homogeneously mixing population, the herd immunity threshold using Hc = 1 - 1/R0 is approximately:
questions.concept: For a homogeneously mixing population and an effective vaccine, the herd immunity threshold Hc = 1 - 1/R0. With R0 = 5, Hc = 1 - 1/5 = 0.8, i.e. about 80% of the population must be immune to interrupt sustained transmission. Option 20% equals 1/R0 (the susceptible fraction remaining at equilibrium), 50% corresponds to R0 = 2, and 95% corresponds to R0 = 20. The higher the R0, the higher the immunity coverage needed — the epidemiological basis for setting national immunization coverage goals for each disease.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Dynamics of Disease Transmission (Herd Immunity)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Annual Risk of Tuberculosis Infection (ARTI) is CORRECT?
options: It is measured directly from sputum smear microscopy of symptomatic patients
It is estimated from tuberculin (Mantoux) surveys and reflects the trend of TB transmission in a community
A rising ARTI indicates that the TB control programme is succeeding
It measures the proportion of drug-resistant tuberculosis cases
questions.concept: ARTI (Annual Risk of Tuberculosis Infection) is the probability of acquiring new TB infection in one year; it is estimated INDIRECTLY from tuberculin (Mantoux) surveys in children (the prevalence of infection is converted into an annual risk) and is a sensitive index of the trend of TB transmission in the community. It is not derived from sputum microscopy (option A) or drug-resistance data (option D), and a FALLING — not rising — ARTI indicates programme success (option C is wrong). Historically about a 1% ARTI corresponded to a substantial smear-positive case load.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Tuberculosis)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In malaria surveillance, the Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER) represents:
options: The percentage of blood slides found positive out of those examined
The number of confirmed malaria cases per 1000 population per year
The number of blood slides examined per 100 population per year
The proportion of Plasmodium falciparum among all positive cases
questions.concept: The Annual Blood Examination Rate (ABER) is the number of blood slides (or rapid tests) examined per 100 population per year — an operational indicator of the intensity of malaria surveillance, with an adequacy target generally around 10% or more. It is distinct from the Slide Positivity Rate (positives among those examined, option A), the API (confirmed cases per 1000 population, option B), and the P. falciparum proportion (option D). A low ABER can mask true burden through under-detection, so ABER is always interpreted alongside SPR and API under NCVBDC surveillance.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Malaria)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the public-health rationale for using primaquine in malaria is CORRECT?
options: Primaquine is the drug of choice for rapidly clearing asexual parasites during an acute severe attack
A single dose of primaquine gives durable causal chemoprophylaxis for travellers for several months
Primaquine reduces the emergence of chloroquine resistance in P. falciparum
Primaquine acts on P. vivax hypnozoites (preventing relapse) and on P. falciparum gametocytes (reducing transmission)
questions.concept: Primaquine, an 8-aminoquinoline, is given for its public-health / transmission-control value: it kills the dormant liver hypnozoites of P. vivax (and P. ovale), preventing relapses (radical cure), and it is gametocytocidal against P. falciparum, reducing onward transmission to mosquitoes. It is NOT the rapid blood schizonticide for the acute attack (that role belongs to chloroquine or ACT, so option A is wrong), it is not durable prophylaxis (option B), and it does not affect chloroquine resistance (option C). G6PD status must be checked, as primaquine can precipitate haemolysis.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Malaria)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Under the WHO/India multi-dose Open Vial Policy, an opened vial of which of the following must be discarded at the end of the immunization session (and cannot be kept for reuse)?
questions.concept: Under the WHO/India multi-dose Open Vial Policy, opened vials of OPV, DPT, TT, DT, hepatitis B and liquid pentavalent (preservative-containing) may be reused for up to 28 days if storage and labelling conditions are met. However, RECONSTITUTED vaccines — BCG and measles/MR (and live JE) — must be discarded at the end of the session or within about 4 hours, whichever is earlier, because they contain no preservative and readily support contamination once reconstituted. The policy reduces vaccine wastage while protecting safety; verify specifics against current national cold-chain guidelines.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Immunization / Cold Chain and Open Vial Policy

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) is CORRECT?
options: It arises from the injectable inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)
It results from prolonged circulation and genetic reversion of the attenuated virus in oral polio vaccine (OPV) among under-immunised populations
Being vaccine-derived, it cannot cause paralysis
Its occurrence is unrelated to population immunity levels
questions.concept: Circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus (cVDPV) results from prolonged person-to-person circulation of the live attenuated virus in ORAL polio vaccine (OPV) within under-immunised populations, allowing it to regain neurovirulence and transmissibility — hence it CAN cause paralysis (option C wrong) and IS driven by low population immunity (option D wrong). It does not arise from injectable IPV, which is killed (option A wrong). This risk is why the world is shifting from OPV toward IPV; India uses IPV in the schedule alongside pulse polio campaigns, and cVDPV surveillance is central to the polio endgame strategy.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (Poliomyelitis)

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: At the Primary Health Centre level, the Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) is used to store most vaccines at which temperature range?
questions.concept: The Ice-Lined Refrigerator (ILR) stores vaccines at +2 C to +8 C and is used for FREEZE-SENSITIVE vaccines (DPT, TT, hepatitis B, pentavalent, IPV and diluents) at the PHC level. The Deep Freezer (-25 C to -15 C, option A) stores OPV and measles/MR stock. Freezing damages adsorbed (alum-containing) vaccines, so these must never be placed in the deep freezer, while heat-labile live vaccines tolerate freezing. Correct cold-chain equipment and temperature ranges are core UIP knowledge; verify equipment norms against current national cold-chain guidelines.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Immunization / Cold Chain

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: India's HIV Sentinel Surveillance has traditionally used which group as a proxy to estimate HIV prevalence trends in the general (low-risk) population?
questions.concept: India's HIV Sentinel Surveillance (HSS), run by NACO since 1998, uses pregnant women attending ANTENATAL CLINICS as a proxy to estimate HIV prevalence trends in the general low-risk population, complemented by high-risk group sites (female sex workers, MSM, injecting drug users, migrants, truckers). Voluntary blood donors are a pre-screened, non-representative group and TB patients are a special population, so neither serves as the general-population proxy. HSS data, together with integrated behavioural and biological surveillance, feed the national HIV estimates under NACP.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases (AIDS/HIV) / HIV Sentinel Surveillance

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Assertion (A): India is currently placed in the "late expanding" stage of the demographic cycle. Reason (R): In the late expanding stage, both the birth rate and the death rate remain persistently high, producing a stable population.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Park describes five stages of the demographic cycle: high stationary (high birth + high death), early expanding (death falls, birth stays high), late expanding (birth begins to fall, death low — India is here), low stationary (both low), and declining (death exceeds birth). The Reason wrongly describes the FIRST (high stationary) stage; in late expanding the death rate is already low while the birth rate is declining, so A is true but R is false. India's stage placement is change-prone as fertility approaches replacement — verify current TFR against latest NFHS/SRS.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A population age-sex pyramid with a very broad base that tapers steeply towards the apex is MOST characteristic of which type of population?
options: A constrictive (contracting) population with a low birth rate
An expansive population with a high birth rate and a young age structure
A stationary population where births roughly equal deaths
An ageing population with a high proportion of the elderly
questions.concept: The shape of a population pyramid encodes fertility and mortality history. A broad-based, steeply tapering (triangular) pyramid signals an expansive population: a high birth rate feeds large young cohorts at the base while higher mortality trims the older bars — typical of developing/high-fertility settings. A constrictive pyramid narrows at the base (declining births), and a stationary pyramid has near-vertical sides with a rounded top. Recognising the young base is key to understanding the demographic dividend, in which a bulge of working-age adults can boost the economy if productively employed.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The population census in India, which enumerates the entire population, is conducted at what interval?
questions.concept: The census is a complete, direct, individual and periodic enumeration of the whole population; in India it has been carried out decennially (every 10 years) without interruption since 1881, most recently in 2011. It is distinct from the vital-statistics system: the Civil Registration System (CRS) records births and deaths continuously, while the Sample Registration System (SRS) estimates vital rates on a sample basis between censuses. The scheduled census has been change-prone recently (the 2021 round was delayed) — verify the latest completed census year before quoting figures.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: What is the PRIMARY function of the Sample Registration System (SRS) in India?
options: To provide reliable estimates of birth rate, death rate and infant mortality rate on a sample basis using a dual-record system
To legally register every birth and death occurring in the country as a compulsory civil requirement
To carry out the complete decennial enumeration of the entire population
To register and follow up all eligible couples for family planning services
questions.concept: The SRS is a large-scale, continuous demographic survey that yields dependable estimates of fertility and mortality indicators (CBR, CDR, IMR, MMR, TFR) at national and state level between censuses. It works on a DUAL-RECORD system: a resident part-time enumerator does continuous recording of vital events, and an independent half-yearly retrospective survey cross-checks these; discrepancies are field-verified. This differs from the Civil Registration System (compulsory legal registration of each event under the RBD Act) and from the census (complete enumeration). Reported SRS figures update annually — flag them as verify-latest.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is BEST defined as:
options: The number of live births per 1000 mid-year population in a given year
The number of live births per 1000 women aged 15–49 years in a given year
The average number of daughters a woman would bear during her reproductive life
The average number of children a woman would bear if she passed through her reproductive years (15–49) experiencing the current age-specific fertility rates
questions.concept: TFR is a synthetic cohort measure: it sums the age-specific fertility rates across the reproductive span and is read as the average number of children a woman would have if current fertility patterns persisted. It is superior to the crude birth rate (option A) because it removes the effect of population age-sex structure, and unlike the general fertility rate (option B, births per 1000 women 15–49) it captures completed fertility. Option C describes the gross reproduction rate (daughters only). A TFR of about 2.1 is the replacement level; India's current TFR is change-prone near replacement — verify against the latest NFHS/SRS.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR) from the Net Reproduction Rate (NRR)?
options: GRR counts total children (both sexes); NRR counts only sons surviving to adulthood
GRR accounts for female mortality before the end of the reproductive period, whereas NRR ignores it

GRR is the average number of daughters a woman would bear at current fertility, IGNORING mortality; NRR is the same but ADJUSTED for the mortality of females before they complete the reproductive period
GRR and NRR are identical measures and the terms are interchangeable
questions.concept: Both are female-replacement measures counting DAUGHTERS. GRR is the average number of daughters a woman would have if she survived through her whole reproductive period at current age-specific fertility — it assumes NO mortality. NRR corrects this by factoring in the probability that a female child survives to and through the childbearing ages, so NRR is always ≤ GRR. NRR is the more realistic index of generational replacement; NRR = 1 means each generation of mothers is exactly replaced by an equal generation of daughters. Option B reverses the relationship, and option A confuses the sex counted (daughters, not sons).
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The Crude Birth Rate (CBR) is calculated as:
options: Total live births in a year ÷ number of married women aged 15–45, × 1000
Number of live births during a year ÷ estimated mid-year population, × 1000
Number of live births ÷ number of women aged 15–49, × 1000
Number of live births ÷ total pregnancies in the year, × 100
questions.concept: CBR = (number of live births in a year / estimated mid-year population) × 1000. It is 'crude' because the denominator is the whole population, including men, children and the elderly who cannot give birth, so it is heavily influenced by age-sex composition and is a poor tool for comparing fertility across dissimilar populations. Option C describes the general fertility rate (denominator = women 15–49). For like-for-like comparison, age-specific fertility rates, GFR or TFR are preferred. India's CBR is a change-prone SRS figure — verify the latest release rather than quoting a fixed number.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The crude death rate is not a satisfactory measure for comparing mortality between two different countries. Reason (R): The crude death rate is strongly influenced by the age and sex composition of the population.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The crude death rate (deaths per 1000 mid-year population) mixes together populations with very different age structures: a country with many elderly people will show a high CDR even with excellent health services, while a youthful population may show a deceptively low CDR. Because age-sex composition drives the crude rate, direct comparison is misleading — hence standardization (direct or indirect) or age-specific/cause-specific rates are used for valid comparison. Here A is true and R is not only true but is the precise reason A holds, so both are true and R correctly explains A.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In the DIRECT method of age-standardization of death rates, what is done?
options: The age-specific death rates of each study population are applied to a chosen standard population's age structure to yield comparable standardized rates
The age-specific death rates of a standard population are applied to the age structure of each study population
The crude death rates of both populations are simply averaged together
Only the deaths in the 15–49 year age group are compared between the two populations
questions.concept: Standardization removes the confounding effect of differing age structures so two populations' mortality can be fairly compared. In the DIRECT method you need the age-specific death rates of each study population; these observed rates are applied to a single 'standard' population's age distribution, generating the number of deaths that WOULD occur if both populations had that same structure, and hence directly comparable standardized rates. The INDIRECT method (option B, giving the Standardized Mortality Ratio) is used instead when age-specific rates of the study population are unavailable but the age distribution is known. Option A is the correct description of the direct method.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The neonatal mortality rate is defined as the number of deaths of:
options: Live-born infants under 1 year of age per 1000 live births in a year
Stillbirths plus deaths in the first week per 1000 total births
Live-born infants under 28 days of age per 1000 live births in a year
Children between 1 and 4 years of age per 1000 children in that age group
questions.concept: Neonatal mortality rate = (deaths of live-born infants under 28 days of age in a year / total live births in that year) × 1000. It is subdivided into EARLY neonatal (first 7 days, dominated by endogenous/prenatal causes such as prematurity, birth asphyxia and congenital anomalies) and LATE neonatal (7–28 days, more exogenous causes like infection). In India neonatal deaths make up the largest share of infant mortality, so newborn survival is the key lever for lowering IMR. Option A is the infant mortality rate, option B is perinatal mortality, and option D relates to the child (1–4 yr) death rate. India's NMR is change-prone — verify latest SRS.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The perinatal mortality rate is conventionally expressed as:
options: Deaths under 28 days per 1000 live births
Late foetal deaths (stillbirths of ≥28 weeks/≥1000 g) plus early neonatal deaths (first 7 days) per 1000 total births
questions.concept: The perinatal period bridges late pregnancy and the first week of life. The perinatal mortality rate = [(late foetal deaths at ≥28 weeks gestation, i.e. stillbirths) + (early neonatal deaths in the first 7 days)] per 1000 TOTAL births (live births + stillbirths). Uniquely, its numerator and denominator both include stillbirths, unlike infant/neonatal rates that use only live births. It is a sensitive index of the quality of antenatal, intranatal and immediate newborn care and of maternal health, capturing losses often missed by other indices. Options A, B and C describe neonatal, maternal and infant mortality respectively.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) in India is conventionally expressed per how many live births, and its recent SRS value is approximately:
options: Per 100,000 live births; approximately 97 (SRS 2018–20 — verify latest)
questions.concept: The Maternal Mortality RATIO relates maternal deaths (death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy from causes related to or aggravated by the pregnancy/its management, excluding accidental/incidental causes) to the number of live births, conventionally per 100,000 live births. India's SRS estimate has fallen steadily and was around 97 for 2018–20 — this is a change-prone figure that must be verified against the latest SRS special bulletin. Note the distinction from the maternal mortality RATE (per 100,000 women of reproductive age) and the lifetime risk measure.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The under-five mortality rate is expressed as the number of such deaths per 1000 mid-year population. Reason (R): The under-five mortality rate reflects the probability of a child dying before reaching its fifth birthday.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The under-five mortality rate is the probability (expressed per 1000 LIVE BIRTHS, not per mid-year population) that a child born in a given year dies before completing 5 years, given current age-specific mortality. It is a key composite indicator of child health, nutrition and socioeconomic development and is a Sustainable Development Goal target. The Reason correctly states what the indicator measures, but the Assertion misstates the denominator (it is live births, not mid-year population), so A is false while R is true. India's U5MR is change-prone — verify the latest SRS estimate.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The dependency ratio is BEST expressed as:
options: Population aged 15–64 years ÷ population aged 0–14 years, × 100
(Population aged 0–14 years + population aged 65 years and above) ÷ population aged 15–64 years, × 100
Number of females ÷ number of males, × 1000
Population aged 65 years and above ÷ total population, × 100
questions.concept: The dependency ratio compares the economically 'dependent' population (children under 15 and older adults 65+) with the working-age population (15–64): ratio = [(0–14) + (65+)] / (15–64) × 100. It is split into a young (child) dependency ratio and an old (aged) dependency ratio. A high young-dependency burden is typical of high-fertility populations, while a falling total ratio creates the 'demographic dividend' window; a rising old-dependency ratio signals population ageing. Option C is the sex ratio and option D is the proportion elderly — related but distinct indicators of population structure.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In India, the sex ratio is conventionally defined as the number of females per 1000 males. According to the 2011 Census, the overall sex ratio was approximately:
questions.concept: In India the sex ratio is expressed as the number of females per 1000 males (the reciprocal of the convention used in some other countries). The 2011 Census recorded an overall sex ratio of about 943, while the child sex ratio (0–6 years) was lower at around 919, reflecting son-preference and sex-selective practices that the PC-PNDT Act seeks to curb. These are change-prone census-linked figures (the next full census will revise them) — always flag the census year and verify the latest available value before quoting.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Life expectancy at birth in India is currently approximately (flag as change-prone — verify latest SRS):
options: About 69–70 years, with females generally living a few years longer than males
questions.concept: Expectation of life at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if current age-specific mortality persisted; it is derived from a life table and is a sensitive summary index of a population's overall mortality and development. In India it has risen dramatically from around 32 years at independence to roughly 69–70 years in recent SRS estimates, with female life expectancy typically a few years higher than male. This is a change-prone figure updated with each SRS abridged life-table release — verify the exact latest value rather than relying on a fixed number.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A woman is counselled about the copper intrauterine device Cu-T 380A for spacing. What is its approved effective lifespan?
questions.concept: The Cu-T 380A is a long-acting reversible copper-bearing intrauterine device approved for use for up to 10 years, making it one of the most cost-effective spacing methods. Copper IUDs act mainly by preventing FERTILIZATION: released copper ions are toxic to sperm and impair sperm motility/viability, and the device induces a sterile inflammatory endometrial reaction hostile to sperm and ova — they are NOT primarily abortifacient. Contraindications include pregnancy, active pelvic infection/PID, unexplained vaginal bleeding and distorted uterine cavity. Copper IUDs can also serve as emergency contraception if inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman requests combined oral contraceptive pills. Which of the following is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to combined (oestrogen-containing) OCPs?
options: Past history of confirmed venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis / pulmonary embolism)
History of a single uncomplicated urinary tract infection last year
questions.concept: Combined OCPs work chiefly by suppressing the mid-cycle LH/FSH surge and thus inhibiting ovulation, plus thickening cervical mucus and altering the endometrium. Their oestrogen component is prothrombotic, so a past or current venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE), history of stroke or ischaemic heart disease, known thrombogenic mutations, active liver disease, current breast cancer, uncontrolled hypertension, migraine with aura, and smoking in a woman over 35 are recognised absolute contraindications (WHO MEC category 4). In such women progestogen-only methods or non-hormonal options such as the copper IUD are preferred. The other options are not contraindications.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A woman opts for the injectable contraceptive DMPA (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate). At what interval is it administered?
questions.concept: DMPA (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate) is a progestogen-only injectable given 150 mg intramuscularly once every 3 months (12 weeks); a subcutaneous 104 mg formulation exists. It acts mainly by inhibiting ovulation, thickening cervical mucus and thinning the endometrium. Being oestrogen-free it can be used in many women for whom combined pills are contraindicated and during lactation. Notable considerations include menstrual disturbance/amenorrhoea, a reversible but sometimes delayed return of fertility after stopping, and a reversible decrease in bone mineral density with long-term use. NET-EN is another injectable given every 2 months.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: For the Lactational Amenorrhoea Method (LAM) to be relied upon as an effective contraceptive, ALL of the following conditions must be met EXCEPT which combination is required?
options: The mother is menstruating regularly again
The infant is older than 12 months
The mother has resumed mixed/complementary feeding of the infant
The mother is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, is amenorrhoeic, AND the infant is under 6 months of age
questions.concept: LAM relies on lactation-induced suppression of ovulation and is up to about 98% effective only when THREE conditions hold simultaneously: (1) the mother is exclusively or nearly exclusively breastfeeding (frequent day and night feeds), (2) she remains amenorrhoeic (no return of menstruation), and (3) the infant is under 6 months old. If ANY one fails — menses return, breastfeeding is reduced/complemented, or the baby reaches 6 months — effectiveness falls and another method should be started. Options A, B and C each describe a situation in which LAM is NO LONGER reliable, so the required combination is that stated in D.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A woman presents after an episode of unprotected intercourse and requests emergency contraception with levonorgestrel pills. These are most effective when taken within what time window?
options: Within 72 hours (3 days) of unprotected intercourse, the sooner the better
Only after the next expected period
Any time up to 3 weeks later
questions.concept: Levonorgestrel-based emergency contraception (1.5 mg as a single dose or 0.75 mg × 2) is licensed for use within 72 hours (3 days) of unprotected intercourse, with efficacy being greatest the earlier it is taken. It works chiefly by delaying or inhibiting ovulation and is NOT effective once implantation has occurred (it does not disrupt an established pregnancy). The copper IUD is the most effective emergency method and can be inserted up to 5 days after intercourse. Emergency contraception is a back-up, not a routine method; counsel on ongoing regular contraception afterwards.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A man undergoes vasectomy for terminal contraception. What advice regarding contraception must be given immediately afterwards?
options: He is not immediately sterile; an alternative contraceptive must be used until azoospermia is confirmed (about 3 months or roughly 20–30 ejaculations)
He is completely sterile from the moment the procedure is finished
Sterility is guaranteed within 24 hours of the operation
He will never regain fertility and no follow-up semen check is ever needed
questions.concept: Vasectomy is a permanent (terminal) method achieved by ligating/occluding the vas deferens, but it is NOT effective immediately: viable sperm persist in the distal reproductive tract for some time. The couple must therefore use an additional contraceptive method until azoospermia is documented, usually after about 3 months or roughly 20–30 ejaculations, confirmed by semen examination. Vasectomy is simpler, safer and cheaper than female tubectomy. It does not affect libido, erection or ejaculate volume appreciably. Tubectomy (female sterilization) can be done as interval, post-partum or concurrent-with-caesarean procedures.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The Couple Protection Rate (CPR) is defined as:
options: The proportion of the total population using any health service in a year
The number of live births prevented per 1000 eligible couples
The percentage of eligible couples effectively protected against childbirth by one or another approved family-planning method at a given time
The percentage of pregnant women who complete at least four antenatal visits
questions.concept: The Couple Protection Rate is an outcome indicator of a family-planning programme: it is the percentage of eligible couples (typically the currently married couple with the wife of reproductive age, conventionally 15–45 years) who are effectively protected from childbirth by an approved contraceptive method — sterilization, IUD, condom, oral pills, injectables — at a given point in time. A CPR of around 60% is regarded as the level needed to bring the net reproduction rate to 1 (population stabilization). It measures programme reach, unlike unmet need which measures the gap between desired and actual contraceptive use.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes a key objective of India's National Population Policy (NPP) 2000?
options: To immediately reduce the population to zero growth within one year
To make sterilization compulsory for all couples with two children
To ban all forms of temporary contraception nationwide
To bring the Total Fertility Rate to the replacement level (about 2.1) and achieve a stable population by around 2045, consistent with sustainable development (verify targets)
questions.concept: The NPP 2000 set objectives on three horizons: the IMMEDIATE objective was to address unmet needs for contraception, health infrastructure and personnel; the MEDIUM-TERM objective was to bring the Total Fertility Rate down to replacement level (about 2.1) by 2010 through inter-sectoral operational strategies; and the LONG-TERM objective was to achieve a stable population by around 2045 at a level consistent with sustainable economic growth and social development. The policy is voluntary and target-free at the individual level, explicitly rejecting coercion (options B and C are wrong). Specific NPP targets/dates are change-prone policy facts — verify against the official document.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Demography and Family Planning

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Specificity of a screening test is best described as which ability, expressed by which formula?
options: Its ability to correctly identify people who truly HAVE the disease; TP / (TP + FN)
Its ability to correctly identify people who truly do NOT have the disease; TN / (TN + FP)
The probability of disease given a positive test; TP / (TP + FP)
The probability of being disease-free given a negative test; TN / (TN + FN)
questions.concept: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) is the true-negative rate, the proportion of genuinely non-diseased people the test correctly labels negative. Option A is sensitivity (TP/(TP+FN)), C is the positive predictive value, and D is the negative predictive value, so only B pairs the correct definition with the correct formula.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a screening programme, the positive predictive value (PPV) answers which question for an individual whose test is positive?
options: What proportion of all diseased persons will the test detect (its detection rate)?
What proportion of non-diseased persons will correctly test negative?
Given a positive test, what is the probability that the person actually has the disease, i.e. TP / (TP + FP)?
Given a negative test, what is the probability the person is truly free of disease?
questions.concept: Positive predictive value = TP / (TP + FP) is the post-test probability of disease given a positive result and it rises with prevalence. Option A describes sensitivity (the detection rate), B is specificity, and D is the negative predictive value; only C states the PPV correctly.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The negative predictive value (NPV) of a diagnostic test is calculated as which of the following?
questions.concept: NPV = TN / (TN + FN): among all who test negative, the fraction who are truly free of disease. Option B is specificity (TN/(TN+FP)), C is sensitivity (TP/(TP+FN)), and D is PPV (TP/(TP+FP)). Predictive values use the row totals of test result, whereas sensitivity and specificity use the column totals of true disease status.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The overall accuracy of a test, i.e. the proportion of ALL results that are correctly classified, is given by which formula?
questions.concept: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) is the fraction of all classifications that are correct. Option B is the complementary misclassification (error) rate, A wrongly adds false positives to true positives, and C is not a standard index; hence D is correct.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Reproducibility (reliability) of a screening test refers to which of the following?
options: The degree to which the test agrees with the gold standard and measures the true value
The consistency of the test in giving the same result on repeat testing under the same conditions
The proportion of diseased individuals that the test detects
The probability of disease among those who test positive
questions.concept: Reliability (reproducibility/precision) is consistency of results on repeat testing and is degraded by random error; for categorical results it is quantified by Cohen's kappa. Validity/accuracy (option A) is agreement with the gold standard and is degraded by systematic error. C is sensitivity and D is PPV, so B is correct.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The positive likelihood ratio (LR+) of a diagnostic test is defined as which expression?
questions.concept: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) is the true-positive rate divided by the false-positive rate; values above 10 strongly rule disease IN and, being derived from sensitivity and specificity, it is prevalence-independent. Option B is the negative likelihood ratio, and C and D are not valid likelihood-ratio formulae; hence A.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: The negative likelihood ratio (LR-), which strongly rules OUT disease when very low, equals which expression?
questions.concept: LR- = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity is the false-negative rate divided by the true-negative rate; values below 0.1 strongly rule disease OUT. Option A is the positive likelihood ratio, while B and D are not valid definitions; hence C is the negative likelihood ratio.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Assertion (A): The positive predictive value (PPV) is an intrinsic property of a test that does not change with disease prevalence. Reason (R): As prevalence rises, the ratio of true positives to false positives among those who test positive increases. Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: The Assertion is FALSE: predictive values are not intrinsic, unlike sensitivity and specificity; PPV rises as prevalence rises even when sensitivity and specificity are fixed. The Reason is TRUE, because higher prevalence increases the true-positive-to-false-positive ratio. A true Reason with a false Assertion corresponds to option D.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Assertion (A): As the prevalence of disease increases, the negative predictive value (NPV) of a fixed test decreases. Reason (R): At higher prevalence, a greater proportion of those who test negative are actually false negatives. Choose the correct option:
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.concept: Both statements are TRUE and the Reason explains the Assertion: at higher prevalence more diseased people exist, so among the test-negatives a larger share are false negatives, which drives NPV down. Because R is the correct mechanism, the answer is A. In summary, as prevalence rises PPV increases while NPV decreases.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In sequential (two-step / serial) testing a person is called positive only if BOTH tests are positive. Compared with either test used alone, this strategy:
options: Increases net sensitivity and NPV but decreases specificity
Increases net specificity and PPV but decreases sensitivity
questions.concept: Serial testing (both tests must be positive) removes false positives, raising net specificity and PPV, but it adds false negatives, lowering net sensitivity, so option B is correct. Parallel testing produces the opposite pattern described in A. Options C and D are impossible under a rule that requires agreement of both tests.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A clinician orders two tests simultaneously and treats the patient as positive if EITHER test is positive (parallel testing). This approach:
options: Increases specificity and PPV but lowers sensitivity
Leaves both sensitivity and specificity unchanged
Increases both sensitivity and specificity equally
Increases net sensitivity and NPV but lowers specificity
questions.concept: Parallel/simultaneous testing labels the patient positive if either test is positive, which minimises missed cases: net sensitivity and NPV rise while specificity falls because more false positives are accepted, so option D is correct. This is preferred in emergencies where missing disease is dangerous. Option A describes serial testing; B and C are wrong.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A new screening test is applied to 500 people, of whom 150 truly have the disease by gold standard. The test is positive in 135 of the diseased persons and in 70 of the non-diseased persons. What is the sensitivity of the test?
questions.concept: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). Of the 150 diseased people, 135 test positive so TP = 135 and FN = 150 - 135 = 15; sensitivity = 135 / 150 = 0.90 = 90%. The 70 false positives among non-diseased people do not enter the sensitivity calculation, so the answer is C (90%).
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Using the same data (500 people screened, 150 truly diseased, the test positive in 135 diseased persons and in 70 non-diseased persons), what is the specificity of the test?
questions.concept: Non-diseased persons = 500 - 150 = 350. False positives = 70, so true negatives TN = 350 - 70 = 280. Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) = 280 / 350 = 0.80 = 80%. Diseased counts do not affect specificity, so the answer is A (80%).
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A screening test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 80%. What is its positive likelihood ratio (LR+)?
questions.concept: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.90 / (1 - 0.80) = 0.90 / 0.20 = 4.5. Option A (0.125) is instead the negative likelihood ratio LR- = (1 - 0.90) / 0.80 = 0.10 / 0.80. Options B and D do not follow from the formula, so the answer is C (4.5).
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: In a community of 2000 people the prevalence of a disease is 10%. A screening test with sensitivity 90% and specificity 80% is applied to everyone. What is the positive predictive value (PPV)?
questions.concept: Prevalence 10% of 2000 = 200 diseased. Sensitivity 90% gives TP = 180 and FN = 20. Non-diseased = 1800; specificity 80% gives TN = 1440 and FP = 360. PPV = TP / (TP + FP) = 180 / (180 + 360) = 180 / 540 = 0.333 = 33.3%. Low prevalence keeps PPV low despite good sensitivity and specificity, so the answer is B.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: For the same 2000-person community (prevalence 10%, sensitivity 90%, specificity 80%), what is the approximate negative predictive value (NPV)?
questions.concept: Using the same table, true negatives TN = 1440 and false negatives FN = 20. NPV = TN / (TN + FN) = 1440 / (1440 + 20) = 1440 / 1460 = 0.986 = 98.6%. In low-prevalence settings the NPV stays high because very few diseased individuals exist to be missed, so the answer is D.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Youden's index (J), used to identify the best cutoff on an ROC curve, is calculated as which expression?
questions.concept: Youden's index J = Sensitivity + Specificity - 1, ranging from 0 to 1. The optimal cutoff maximises J, which geometrically is the ROC point lying farthest above the chance diagonal. J = 0 means a useless test and J = 1 a perfect one. Options A, C and D are not the standard formula, so the answer is B.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve is constructed by plotting which of the following?
options: Sensitivity (true-positive rate) on the y-axis against 1 - specificity (false-positive rate) on the x-axis, across all cutoffs
Positive predictive value against negative predictive value at different prevalences
Sensitivity against specificity at a single fixed threshold
questions.concept: An ROC curve plots sensitivity (true-positive rate) on the y-axis versus 1 - specificity (false-positive rate) on the x-axis over all possible cutoffs; the area under the curve (AUC) measures discrimination and the top-left corner represents the ideal test. Options B, C and D misstate the axes, so the answer is A.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: For a continuous screening marker (for example fasting blood glucose used to detect diabetes), LOWERING the diagnostic cutoff value will:
options: Change neither, affecting only the prevalence
questions.concept: Lowering the cutoff labels more people positive, capturing more true cases so sensitivity rises, but it also generates more false positives so specificity falls, which is option C. Raising the cutoff reverses this. This unavoidable sensitivity-specificity trade-off is exactly what the ROC curve depicts. Prevalence is a population property unaffected by the cutoff.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: According to Wilson and Jungner's criteria for a worthwhile screening programme, which of the following is NOT a required criterion?
options: The condition should be an important health problem
There should be a recognizable latent or early symptomatic stage
There should be an accepted, effective treatment for patients with recognized disease
The disease should be rare, rapidly fatal, and lack any detectable preclinical phase
questions.concept: Wilson and Jungner require an important, sufficiently common condition with a recognizable latent or early stage, a suitable acceptable and valid test, an accepted effective treatment, facilities for diagnosis and treatment, and a favourable cost balance. A rare, rapidly fatal disease with no detectable preclinical phase (very short sojourn time) is UNSUITABLE for screening, so D is NOT a criterion.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: A patient attends a clinic for an upper respiratory infection, and the physician takes the opportunity to also measure the patient's blood pressure. This form of screening is termed:
questions.concept: Opportunistic screening tests a person who has contacted the health system for an unrelated reason, such as checking blood pressure during a visit for a cold. Mass screening covers a whole population, targeted or selective screening focuses on defined high-risk groups, and multiphasic screening applies several tests at one sitting, so the answer is A.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Screening appears to improve survival simply because disease is diagnosed EARLIER, adding the interval between early detection and the usual clinical diagnosis to the measured survival time without postponing death. This spurious effect is called:
questions.concept: Lead-time bias occurs when earlier detection lengthens the measured time from diagnosis to death without actually changing the date of death, falsely inflating survival credited to screening. Length-time bias (A) is the over-representation of indolent cases, C is selection bias from healthy volunteers, and D is overdiagnosis, so the answer is B.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Screening programmes preferentially detect slowly progressive, less aggressive cases that spend longer in the detectable preclinical phase, making screen-detected disease appear to have a better prognosis. This is known as:
questions.concept: Length-time bias arises because slowly growing tumours have a longer sojourn (detectable preclinical) phase and are therefore over-sampled at any screening round, making screen-detected disease look more benign than it truly is. Lead-time bias (A) is about earlier diagnosis, and overdiagnosis is its extreme form, so the answer is C.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.stem: Screening detects a condition (for example some indolent prostate cancers) that would never have caused symptoms or death during the person's lifetime. This is best described as:
questions.concept: Overdiagnosis is the true-positive detection of disease that would never have become clinically significant during the person's life, as with some indolent prostate cancers. Because the disease is genuinely present it is NOT a false positive, yet it still leads to unnecessary treatment; it is the extreme of length-time bias, so the answer is D.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine — Screening for Disease

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: The SI unit of absorbed dose, defined as one joule of energy deposited per kilogram of tissue, is the:
questions.concept: The gray (Gy) is the SI unit of absorbed dose, defined as one joule of energy deposited per kilogram of tissue (1 Gy = 1 J/kg). It replaced the older rad (1 Gy = 100 rad). It quantifies energy deposition irrespective of radiation type; biological weighting is applied only when converting to equivalent dose in sieverts, and it must not be confused with the becquerel (activity).
questions.reference: Christensen's Physics of Diagnostic Radiology / ICRP recommendations — Dosimetric Quantities

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: Equivalent dose and effective dose, which weight absorbed dose for radiation type and tissue sensitivity, are expressed in:
questions.concept: Equivalent dose and effective dose are expressed in sieverts (Sv). Equivalent dose equals absorbed dose in gray multiplied by the radiation weighting factor (wR); effective dose additionally sums tissue weighting factors (wT). The sievert reflects biological harm and allows stochastic-risk comparison across radiation types and exposed organs; 1 Sv = 100 rem. The gray measures only physical energy deposition.
questions.reference: ICRP Publication 103 (2007) — System of Radiological Protection

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: The continuous spectrum of X-rays emitted from a diagnostic X-ray tube is produced by:
options: Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) as electrons decelerate near target nuclei
Characteristic radiation from inner-shell electron transitions
Compton scattering within the anode target
Pair production in the tungsten target
questions.concept: Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) forms the continuous X-ray spectrum: high-speed electrons decelerate in the electric field of target nuclei, losing kinetic energy as photons of a continuous range up to the peak kVp. Characteristic radiation, by contrast, gives discrete energy lines from inner-shell electron transitions and superimposes spikes on the continuous curve. Pair production requires photon energies far above the diagnostic range.
questions.reference: Bushberg — The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging: X-ray Production

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: At diagnostic X-ray energies, the photon interaction chiefly responsible for the scattered radiation that reaches personnel is:
questions.concept: At diagnostic energies (roughly 30-150 keV) Compton scattering predominates in soft tissue and is the principal source of scattered radiation reaching staff, which is why distance and shielding are emphasised. Photoelectric absorption dominates at lower energies and with high-Z materials such as bone, iodine and barium, providing image contrast, while pair production needs photons above 1.02 MeV and is irrelevant in diagnostic imaging.
questions.reference: Sutton's Textbook of Radiology and Imaging — Physics of Diagnostic Radiology

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.stem: In radiography, increasing the kVp (kilovoltage peak) while keeping other factors constant primarily:
options: Increases only the number (quantity) of photons
Has no effect on the X-ray beam
Increases the energy and penetrating power (quality) of the beam, whereas mAs governs quantity
Reduces the maximum photon energy produced
questions.concept: kVp (kilovoltage peak) sets the maximum photon energy and therefore the penetrating power or quality of the beam; raising kVp increases penetration and scatter and lowers subject contrast. mAs (milliampere-seconds) governs the quantity or number of photons and is the main determinant of patient dose for a given technique. Optimising both quantities is central to dose reduction under the ALARA principle.
